This is the only well-designed 3D Sonic game. The other games can be fun and have their setpieces, but this functions AS a GAME. It's not a series of poorly made levels to fascillitate a satisfying rush of speed. It's a series of levels that design FOR speed as a central interaction. Speed is its currency (boost meter), speed is its master (your Score Rankings aren't based on ring count or enemies killed or ANTYHING, just time cleared).
It can't be understated how important the camera being zoomed out is. It's SO important. Before, where only rote memorization and the inexplicable reflexes of an 8-year old would save you, you can now... REACT to THINGS on SCREEN. There are also many clever level design queues, like branches in paths being forewarned by dramatic lighting shifts in the background.
Half of the optional missions are garbage, sure. But this is the only -great- mainline Sonic game when it comes to gameplay (aside from perhaps Colors, quite similar in design, or Sonic 3/Sonic & Knuckles, which are unique in the series thanks to their slower, denser levels).

I got this game with completely 0% knowledge of what it was and...it was basically getting hit to the face with a log.
The easiest way to describe Freedom Planet is THE hidden gem. It should be illegal that a game this good doesnt have Undertale levels of popularity (then again considering what the undertale community is, I suppose its for the better).
The common statement about this game is that its a sonic fan game and while this is defninetly true to an extent, if youre experienced with retro games youll notice so much more than just sonic elements. this game has vibes from Mega man X, Yoshis island, Gunstar heroes and even a bit of Smash Bros.
The gameplay works extremely well even if it takes a lot of ideas from other series and its helped by the 3 playable main characters, Lilac the dragon is the speedster, Carol the wildcat is the more combat focused characters and can wall jump like X and use a logic noping motorcycle and then theres Milla who...I dunno whats she supposed to be apart from her fantastic flutter jump. what helps the gameplay further is the beautiful soundtrack and colorful levels. For a seemingly low budget Indie title FP also has a suprisingly solid story and acting, its nothing too special but its defnitely nowhere near bad, but I do really enjoy the various characters you meet along the way.
Just to throw this out there, the game is pretty challenging...especially with the bosses, but since this is supposed to be a living, breathing, retro experience...its excused.
So yeah...Freedom planet, this is one of those games you only really stumble upon by accident, its downright fantastic with no real low points, to top it all off: this game is getting a sequel SUPPOSEDLY in the summer of 2017 so theres that to look forward to. This game is easily worth its low price, lets just hope Galaxytrail keeps up the good work and look forward.

So, I beat Cloudbuilt. It only took about 4 hours, but I can tell I'll be back for more. However, I’ll probably only play the opening 3/4ths of the levels in this game, because the entire last 4th of the game is a goddamn mess.
Let's go over some of the pros and cons.
Pros:
-looks great and runs excellently
-great electronic soundtrack that really adds to the ambience, great sound design and Demi (the MC) has good voice acting
-gameplay is a hell of a lot of fun
-level designs for the most part are a blast
-concept is neat
-Demi controls great, the sense of speed is perfect
-satisfying gameplay that encourages replayability
Cons:
-the gun
-the enemies
-later levels
*Story:
The story, all in all, is actually pretty cool. You basically play as a military veteran of an unspecified country after a bomb has severely wounded her and her squad- you control her in her coma dreams as she grapples with her unfortunate situation. While the writing can be extremely ham-fisted at times, Demi has good enough voice acting that it's at least tolerable. That being said, what's most interesting are the multiple paths- as you progress through the game it splits off into different interpretations of Demi's injuries, resulting in 4 very distinct endings about how she has coped with the accident, which I found very cool. This story, while unnecessary, is a neat idea.
*Gameplay:
Here’s what you wanna buy this game for. Demi controls well, moves quick, and shoots guns fast. The moment to moment gameplay in Cloudbuilt is simply exhilarating, jumping and dashing through the variety of terrain. The jetpack, a refueling boost maneuver greatly increases tension in the game. It never quite feels like you have enough to make things safely, but you usually do, which provides excellent tension and incentivizes learning your momentum and your remaining gas. The level design incentivizes this blend of speed and percision, and it feels very rewarding to even *beat* a level. It feels really damn good to play Cloudbuilt, and I’ll definitely be coming back to mess around with Demi's kit.
* Design:
And here's where the game, frankly, ♥♥♥♥s it all up. Level designs from the initial 3/4ths of the game are great and challenging, encouraging fast, on the fly movement with split second reactions and timing due to a very prominent design choice of multiple branching paths through the level. Levels are designed well for these parts, filled with hazards and enemies to kill in large but fair numbers, allowing the player to skillfully dodge weapon fire. However, as the game progresses the open and branching levels become small and cramped, filled with annoying enemies with too much health and too much accuracy. The game goes from challenging but fair to infuriatingly and unnaturally hard, jamming the great pacing of the game to a halt as you have to learn patterns and memorize levels. However, to add to frustration, you have a life system, something of a cardinal sin in hard platformers, which, instead of adding tension instead adds further irritation. These last levels are boring and time consuming, and you'll soon be wishing for the open walls and platforms of the previous levels. Also, ♥♥♥♥ the enemies in this game man. They are incredibly irritating and add nothing to the challenge of the game properly, instead just introducing a terribly implemented shooting system with pathetically weak bullets and poor auto-aim, against powerful enemies with razor-sharp aim. At top speed you need the reaction time of freaking Neo from the Matrix to hit some of these things, and most take multiple hits, put up a shield, then heal to full health. Oh, did I mention your gun has limited ammo? Yeah, it has 5 shots then needs a reload. Moving, boosting and shooting at the same time is like trying to rub your head and pat your tummy at the same time. Its ridonkulous. It's hard to criticize a game for being difficult, as that was the intended nature of the game. But when something becomes difficult and changes what made earlier levels fun, then it becomes a big problem.
*Presentation:
Overall, the game looks and runs DAMN good. The crosshatch-shading art-style looks great and you can clearly define everything in the environment. The shading and lighting need special interest as they in particular look excellent. The games soundtrack is an energetic electronic piece, really keeping up the tempo during tough times. The game also runs great- I ran the game at max settings with a decent rig and it ran like butter, aside from some moments during the last level of one path (Redeployment) causing some slowdown from all the♥♥♥♥♥♥on screen.
Overall:
Despite the last levels sucking, Cloudbuilt is a hell of a lot of fun.  Despite the widest portion of this review complaining  about the toughness of the last few levels, they're not mandatory and are unconsequential. In the end, MOST of Cloudbuilt is great fun. I don't know if it's worth 20 big ones, but I can tell you that if you can get it on sale for lower than $15, grab it, because it's great fun. Just mind those last levels, eh?

This was the first Final Fantasy game I played, and it's my favorite.  There are too many positives to list here, but to name a few:

The music

As for any potential negatives to this game, I have trouble finding any that aren't total nit picks.  The UI in battle is sometimes a tiny by too big, so it blocks the action sometimes, and the camera angles sometimes make navigating difficult.

Despite being fourteen years old at the time of this review, this game is still entertaining. I think a huge part of it is how well it ages - it came out in 2003, but there are no musical or UI or humor clues that would tie it to the early 2000s. you won't experience any issues with the game crashing, plus you get to play it in HD. The modding community is still alive and well, somehow.
But most of all, SC4 just looks
. The art style is cohesive, the colors and day-night cycles are on point (mostly), and despite almost everything being 2D pixel graphics it looks beautiful, especially if you know how to arrange your city.
My one issue is that the game, like any single-player simulation, feels a little lonely sometimes. And if you get creative with Dropbox you can play a sort-of multiplayer, but there's no true MP built into the game. It's a good thing for the most part, because there's none of the always-online ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that comes with a lot of "single-player" games these days.
Basically, if you like any of the tycoon games, Civ, or model railroads, this game's for you. You can raise the difficulty if you want a more hardcore planning-focused experience, or mod in some demand multipliers if just want to build some nice interchanges.

Oh it's just so classic and so brilliant. Not only as a game, but as social commentary. Sure, you're a dictator in a single-party system, but you can't just do as you please. You can't rule without legitimacy, you must please various factions. You can't please a faction without annoying another one. You can't build everything in your term. There are no easy solutions. Mass housing? Eyesores. Mining and industry? Ruined environment. Sustainable tourism? More crime. More soldiers to protect yourself? Lower liberty. Kill or imprison someone? Their family and friends hate you forever. Higher wages for the precious educated? The communists hate you. Same wages for everyone? The ambitious leave. Closed borders? People just run to the woods. Ignore international politics? Get invaded. The most you can hope to achieve - an average satisfaction rating of 65. Life just isn't pretty.
Just not very enjoyable.

Tropico is fun.
What other series lets you act out your fantasies of total dictatorship of a Caribbean island, ruling with either a kind heart or an iron fist?
Seriously. I'm waiting.
I own all the Tropico games except Tropico 4, and this is the one I've played the most (I've put about ~20 hours in so far, but steam won't count them). Tropico lets you deal with your people's welfare, either by promoting it or ignoring it and facing their wrath. You can build farms, mines, factories, and other buildings on your island to further your goal of ruling as long as possible. The farms never turn a profit because they feed the people, and the mines, fisheries, factories, and other buildings I could never get to function. So I made all of my money off logging, which was OK. There's also the political element, in which you can do favors for particular factions (such as building factories for the capitalists, or public housing for the communists), that can help you earn their support, as well as either allying with the US or USSR or trying to please both. Tropico delivers a fun and lighthearted dictatorship simulator with its wide bevy of buildings, edicts, diplomatic options, and economic management. It's definitely worth whatever pittance you'll pay for it on sale, and the original Tropico the simplest and most fun.
That said, the game can be exceedingly frustrating at times. Like I said, I could not get any factories or mines or farms or cattle ranches or fisheries to turn a decent profit, only the logging camp and the lumber mill. It is also difficult trying to get provide housing, as that's one of the people's main complaints but is expensive, and some of the larger buildings (such as the airport) can be exceedingly difficult to build. I once ruled for 42 years and probably would've ruled longer but that my overwhelming concern for building an airport caused me to ignore the people's demands for the island.
When it's all said and done, Tropico delivers a simple, yet deep, contruction and political simulator that's really one of a kind. Tropico 5 may have the fancy graphics, but Tropico is where the charm is. Viva el Presidente!

Well for starters this review might have most if not all of its content mentioned by someone somewhere in past reviews but even so now that i finished first 3 chapters i feel the need to point few things out. Firstly i am huge fan of visual novels, i have played quite a few and Major/Minor despite it's flaws has great potential. So i'll start with the most important thing to a visual novel aside from visual aspect, the story. For starter there is this aura of mystery that from one point is very cool until the point it makes you feel like its overcompensating for lack of character development. Some things are just being thrown around to fill in the blanks. Here it seems like writter/s attempted to make story more interesting by adding plot twists on every turn, just when you think you figured it out it turns around 180* degrees and makes you reconsider everything so far. It just seems very forced to me and while no story ever is perfect i would love to see more tact and smoother transitions. Because after first or second, for some, plot twist you start to expect it and it boggles down your choices making it seem like no matter what you pick you won't be comfortable with the choice for the current playtrough. Which brings me down to second flaw, the save and skip system. It's crude and leaves lot to be desired. For a visual novel ability to skip parts over converstations that you've already read multiple times while trying different choices is one of important factors and the sluggishness showed here is one big minus from me. Also the saves seem more like pre-designated checkpoints at irregular intervals, and no menu during the storytelling is seriously limiting. Especially since the "feature" of the game, so called rollback essentially forces you to quit to main menu and load the previous checkpoint save. It needs a LOT of polish there and it seriously needs to implement ability to save game when you want  at least from my perspective. It would give a lot more fexiblity to the gameplay along with improved skip feature. I could drone on and but this review when i look at it seems to be turning into unsatisfied moaning at some point and i hate that so i will just narrow it to pros and cons.
Pros:
- Story has great potential
- The furry note is a refreshing one
- Art is cute
- Price is affordable in comparsion to some other titles
Cons:
- Story tends to be forced, at some points lacks fluidity
- Some game mechanics are completly lacking and one it does have can get frustrating at some point
- Needs more options
In short this could be refreshing visual novel with great potential if few things are tweaked and more focus was added. Quality over quantity :)
At the end this is just my own personal opinion, some will disagree, some will partially or completly agree, some will put it on a pyre but i felt i said what needed to be said. I hope to see more of this Novel. Peace out :>

The story is terrible, a ton of garbage, unecessary missions that have absolutely nothing to do with the story or adds any plot, it's basically there to artificially extend the playtime. There are 15 chapters and it's basically one mission per chapter. The side missions? What side missions? Steal cars for cash? What for? This game robs you of your money...constantly. There is never a need to buy guns even when the game robs you of those too because they're plentiful and nothing special is sold. So essentially, you never need any extra money than from the ones you make during your mission playthrough. The checkpoint system is also really stupid, who thought it was a good idea to make such ridiculous checkpoints? The world suffers greatly from "Lifeless Open World Syndrome" because there is absolutely nothing to do in it. Oh and if you're thinking at the end of this game, you'll be the head boss of the Mafia or some cool thing, DON'T, I'm not spoiing it for you, I'm saving you from a huge let down. It will definitely remind you of tower defence games BUT WITH A DIFFERENCE!
Instead of laying down traps to stop an enemy getting through, you're the enemy getting through and it's your task to get through alive by destroying the defence towers and picking up tools to aid you.
The story is kinda good and easy to follow, with voice acting that makes an Englishman like myself giggle everytime they attempt to do an English accent).
The story is that aliens have attacked earth and it's your job ("English" "accented" army dudes) to investigate and defeat the threat. You play as a character who can run anywhere you want, your job is to guide the vehicles along a path that will complete multiple objectives. You choose what path they take, choose wisely because you may find yourself sending those vehicles to their doom.
Each type of vehicle has a different ability, some shield other vehicles, others are for light attack towers and others are for heavy ones. There may be more but it's been a while since I played this.
It's a very nice game and it's a very welcome change to how tower defence games are made. I found myself enjoying this game more than most tower defence games I've played.
So if you want to give it a go, buy it. You won't be disappointed, unless you don't like tower defence games. But then again, you might like this because it's DIFFERENT!
I recommend this game, check it out on YouTube if you're still unsure, or check out other reviews that go into more detail.

A tower offence game where you lead a small group of tanks them around a tower filled map. Unlike the mobile campaign, you actually get to run around as the commander, the main interactions you have are:
1)	Buying and upgrading tanks. The main choices being heavy armour, high firepower or support (like a shield tank). Upgrading is very simple with no branching upgrade paths.
2)	Choosing which way your tanks navigate around the map, to either avoid clusters of towers or to go after the currency to buy more tanks.
3)	Deploying power ups. These are plentiful and the main way of keeping your tanks alive, by repairing them, deploying smoke or decoys to divert the attention of the towers.
Other than some poor voice acting, the game is well presented. It’s not the most in depth game, but it’s easy to get into repetitive (almost the opposite of Gratuitous Tank Battles, another take on tower offence). Overall the concept it interesting enough to just about last the length of the fairly short campaign.

I feel the need to preface this by saying that, while I do enjoy fast paced games, I’m really not a speedrunner. That being said, I’m completely in love with Cloudbuilt. This game is gorgeous, has fantastic level design and the soundtrack is one of my absolute favorites. On the surface, it may be a niche game for speedrunners, but there’s more to it – if you’re up for the challenge.
Cloudbuilt gives you all the tools you need from the start, and promptly kicks you out the door letting you figure out how you’re going to use them. It has a steep learning curve you will certainly smash into face first pretty early on – it can be frustrating, but is still manageable. There are countless paths to take, there’s no time limit, and you don’t need to do anything more than to complete a level to progress. After completing a level for the first time, various game modes are also unlocked that make some fun, or in some cases more challenging, alterations to the gameplay. I think they also encourage players to learn more of the mechanics, like conserving energy (rather than recording your time, it tracks your energy consumption – as someone who enjoys puzzles, this is probably my favorite mode), and finding other routes or ways to deal with enemies. Or, if you’d rather just zoom through the level with nearly unlimited energy, there’s a mode for that too. A story develops along each branch that seems to be pretty hit or miss with most people, but I thought it was a really great way to tie everything together.
Outside the game, there’s a level editor, and small, but absolutely fantastic community. A number of players (including many of the top players and some of the developers) still frequent the forums and subreddit who are more than happy to chat about the game and provide tips, tricks, or even just some encouragement.
This game is fast paced, but has elements that may appeal to those with an interest in puzzles and exploring as well. I’d recommend it to anyone looking for a 3D action platformer who’s ready to test their mettle.

Really was hoping this would be good. I had played a game similar to this called deadcore and enjoyed it. Unfortunately this game makes a lot of different control and design choices that just end up making it worse. First off, there's no story, just a few random cryptic lines betwen each level you don't care about. The levels all look pretty similar, just floating stone blocks covered in weeds. The level design is also poor, as half the time you have no idea where to go, because everything looks the same and the levels aren't layed out filtering you one way or another, theyre just a bunch of floating blocks and walls.
The biggest problem is the actual platforming. First off, this game isn't like deadcore in many ways. You don't learn new abilities or anything, as levels get harder. This game has added constraints that just make it more frustrating and repeititve, and add nothing to the experience. The rocket boost, which wears out way too quickly, as you jump or dash. This means if you make a single mistake or mis-press, you die. If you don't angle it perfectly to collect the refills on long runs, you die. Many times I would double jump to get somwhere, then not have enough left to dash. Taking away my ability to think on my feet because I didn't set up for the perfect amount of boost is dumb. It takes away any adaptability. Also you will constantly think boosting while wall-running sends you forward, but it just sends you up or down. And if you run out you cant move on the wall, which is dumb.
Then there's the controls. They are super finnicky. I would press jump and my guy would jsut sit there in the air and fall and die. Other times he woul;d jump off the wall instead of up it. Other times the jumps seemed to go barely anywhere at all. So many times I would do the same thing 5 times in a row, and it would work 2 times and not work 3. I usually didn't feel it was my fault. Then there's the checkpoints. There are barely any, and you can place some, but you barely get any to place and never know when you'll see one. And if you die, which is every time you make any mistake, you have to restart the level. Also there are limited lives, the dumbest thing I have ever seen in a game like this. This game you will die all the time, because you're floating in space, and any tiny mistake means your death. You will die dozens of times. But yet you only get like 8-10 lives per level before restarting the entire level.
It just all seems stupid to me. How inconsistent the controls are, the way boost doesn't recharge during jumps and you have to do everything or you run out too quickly and die. The poor checkpoint system, and the use of lives. All of it undermines how the game should be played. Go get deadcore instead of this dud.

I've played through this game probably around ten times, every couple of years since I first got it for Playstation, with each playthrough lasting upwards from 50 hours. Last time was somewhere during this past year if I'm not mistaken, and I could already play it again... though I think I'll wait for a while longer. Too many other games in my backlog anyway.
Now, that could be the review right there. Should be pretty obvious how much I love FF IX just from that. There's only one game that really contests it as my favorite game of all time. A different JRPG from the same era in fact, Tales of Eternia, but I digress.
Final Fantasy 9 is great. If you're a fan of this sort of a game (and I assume you do know what old Final Fantasies and JRPG's are like, unless you've lived on the surface of moon up to this point), then you're not going to be disappointed. The PC port also seems really solid from the little testing I've done so far. They seem to have added some new features and spiced up the graphics in places, but otherwise have kept it pretty clean, which is perfect. Have to play more to know for certain, but first impressions are definitely positive. It's a brilliant game all around. Buy it, play it, love it.
However, there are some things you should. First, the random encounters can get annoying, especially with this version of the game, that doesn't have the speed up function of emulators. Second, the plot has some holes and weak moments. Like all JRPG's, sure, but you'll have to look past them. Third, there are a ton of missables, secrets, collectibles and other hidden content in this game. You could look up a list, but that sort of ruins the fun of searching, so don't be afraid of missing out some of the hidden things. Look 'em up during your next playthrough. Fourth, the jump rope minigame is a bird that you need to let go. Do it for your own sanity. The 100th noble as well. Fifth, Tetra Master is fun, but do read the instructions before playing it. Sixth, Grand Dragons appear in a small island on the Western side of the map. They are at level 65, and you can get the Blue magic skill Lvl 5 death for Quina by eating a zombie dragon at Lifa Tree. Cuts out some of the mid-game grinding. Seventh, if you're not going to be using a walkthrough/missables guide, don't bother with Ozma. You won't be able to win, save that fight for another playthrough.

Tropico Review (Reloaded) - Raymond KT
Summary: You are the sole ruler of a remote banana republic. Fight against poverty, corruption and rebels, make your own people happy or enforce your rule through military strength. However, do not forget to set aside a few dollars for your own retirement on a swiss bank account!
Most games of Tropico start with a few people scratching out a living on a small Caribbean island. You step in as their new presidente, with the background of your choice to give you a set of game-twisting traits. For instance, if you come from a moneyed background, you'll have an advantage in industry. If you're a radical student, the communists will be predisposed to support you. If you're Lou Bega--this is actually one of your starting options--you'll wow them with your nightclub acts.
Armed with your distinctive set of traits and your new bank account, you drop buildings onto the island: housing, farms, cattle ranches, churches, medical clinics, pubs, police stations, bauxite mines, fishing wharves, and cigar factories. Later on, there are power plants, casinos, cathedrals, and TV stations. And there are always the little landscaping touches, such as flower beds, trees, fountains, and the occasional statue to remind everyone who's in charge. Tropico is dazzling and can also be a little confusing in the breadth of things you can build.
Similarly, you can choose from a wide array of edicts, which are like the ordinances in SimCity 3000 or like spells in a fantasy-themed strategy game. You can arrest someone and bribe him or her, burn books to appease the church and keep the intellectuals in line, or make overtures to the United States for foreign aid. It's entirely possible to play without using the edicts, but they offer a touch of direct interaction for hands-on players. Similarly, you can influence most individual buildings if you're so inclined--you can set salaries, raise rents, or decide what your state-run TV station will broadcast.
All the information available in Tropico about your economy, your citizens, and your society as a whole is a welcome change from games that insist on running things under the hood. The thorough documentation leaves very few questions unanswered. When you hold the mouse over a piece of information, an excellent in-game help system spells out how it relates to the game's mechanics. The numbers and graphs are all there at your fingertips, but they're not overbearing. Tropico is as complex as you want it to be.
After an experiment as bold as Lionhead Studios' recent Black & White, Tropico is exactly what strategy gaming needs: a reminder that a game doesn't necessarily have to be weird, inscrutable, or unconventional to be great--it can get by on charm, broad appeal, and sophistication. Most everyone will find that Tropico is a real pleasure to play because of these qualities. - GameSpot

Also, this is an old school open-ended affair -- if you crave games with sharply defined win conditions, you should skip this one.  But if you like building for building's sake and can dig the tongue-in-cheek dictatorial trappings, there are hours of fun to be had.

Lichdom Battlemage is a game advertised as a limitless opportunity mage RPG. The object of the game is portrayed as having limitless possibility in the spells you can create and use in an epic adventure, kind of similar in style to Skyrim.
This isn't the case at all. Really. The game's crafting system consists of 3 aspects, all of which are decently limited. The type of Sigil (Sigils are most like elements, like Ice or Fire or Necromancy), the type of spell (Beam, ray, ect.), and augmentations (bonus stats). This game is incredibly misleading in the whole 'limitless' aspect. In my time playing, most of the spells I've made pretty much seemed to do the same thing, if not slightly different. Throughout the game I really just didn't feel like I needed to use anything besides a fireball. The game really gave me no reason to use anything else, because all spells are crafted using the same basic typings and that greatly hinders the actual variability of the elements. And, even when the game did influence me to use other Sigils, it was in really bold, childish, and boring manners. Some enemies either had shields that blocked one instance of damage, forcing me to use a ray (And navigating the awful crafting menu to equip it. Mercy.), or an enemy might have been resistant to an element. Also, speaking on categories of enemies and the like, this game was very unclear about anything that was happening. Enemies give you no warning when they attack, big or small, which wouldn't be an issue if the game was intended to be that way. It just feels like big hulking monsters can walk up to my backside and slug me for half of my health without me even noticing. Overall the game was just a big disappointment. Don't pick it up.

Garbage. Why?
-Needlessly obtuse crafting system compounded by a badly designed UI. Seriously. Its almost as bad as Dwarf Fortress's.
-Aforementioned crafting system offers basically no instruction on how to use it, making matters worse.
-They tried to build the game around the spell crafting system, and it's rubbish--terrible level design (it felt like old school FPSes from the 90s) and the story is so droll and uninteresting that they shouldn't have tried to take it seriously.
-Horribly bad game balance. Remember how annoying Deus Ex: Human Revolution's boss battles were before the Director's Cut? Yeah, like that. Decently challenged (if repetitive) gameplay, then BAM! You get curb stomped. You want to know what sucks the fun out of a game? Hard checks on progress.
-Still full of bugs. Do you like your games that crash but won't fully close so you have to restart your PC to make it close? Or push an enemy through the terrain so you can't kill them, which keeps the force field from blocking your path from disappearing and now you have to restart the level? Then you should by this game!
tl;dr its an unpolished gimmick-game that badly needs a UI overhaul, gameplay balancing, and level redesign.
still a great game even though its old.

SimCity 4 is a classic city building simulator, representing the peak of the SimCity franchise and the foundation upon which Cities Skylines was crafted. SimCity 4 packages the series' trademark complex yet accessible simulation in a refreshed fully 3D world and expands upon its predecessors by offering multi-city region play and, through the Rush Hour expansion, a deeper, more realized traffic and mass transit management element. SimCity 4 is truly a gem in the crown of PC simulation games.

I should start by saying this game isn't terrible.  You can play it for a bit and have fun.  That said...
This game really suffers from squandered potential.  The tagline is that you are a wizard and you don't have to deal with mana bars or cooldowns, so now that you have unlimited magic power you can go on a crazy murder spree.
In actuality to get to fight the same 5 guys over and over again in a storyline that doesn't make much sense (spoilers below).
The story starts with a bad evil dude coming up and messing with your family.  He is a bad evil dude because he likes stabbing people and has a goatee.  You are then visited by a wizard named Roth who raises you from the dead and gives you "unlimited power" and the ability to not die ever again.  Having thus removed any dramatic tension from the story, you then go fight a cult and some undead guys who may or may not be fighting each other and it may or may not matter.  Also, all the human antagonists give you long, boring monologues while invincible and then teleport away unless the game arbitrarily decides they're going to stop and fight the guy who is, as a reminder, completely invincible and cannot be killed.
Now this would be forgivable if gameplay was actually good, but it gets boring fast.  The game makes a big deal out of its spellcrafting system - but for the most part spells are generally damage, status effect, or weird combo debuff.  Spells are created from randomly dropped items you can mess around with in interesting ways to upgrade them for upgrades that may or may not do anything.  There are some stats on the player screen - destruction, mastery, control - that get affected by these somehow and maybe sorta kinda determine spell effects?  I don't know, the game didn't explain and I couldn't tell you how the formula works.  Some of these drops are rarer but don't seem better.  You can pick 3 of 8 elements and of these three you get a nova (with weird trigger conditions), an aoe, and a single-target missile spell, all of which are upgradable to have different numbers that do...stuff.  It's not a terrible system, it's just repetitive and you never feel you are getting anywhere.  At the beginning of the game you can call down a firestorm.  At the end of the game you can call down a firestorm, but with bigger numbers.  Maybe if you futz around with the numbers you can use a completely separate subsystem and call down a meteor.  Now, many video games have this problem, but for a game about "Unshackling the mage", the fact that a wizard in Baldur's Gate can pull off more impressive and interesting feats of magic kinda sucks.
Of course, there's a reason you don't get interesting magic like long-range teleportation or invisibility - the game is a linear line where you run through and fight the same 5 guys.  I'm not even talking palette swaps here.  There is a model of a black-clad lady with some kind of acid vial she throws at you.  She has the same 3 lines.  You will hear these same lines at the beginning of the game, the end of the game, and the part of the game where I got bored and quit.  You will meet a teleporting undead guy.  Later in the desert, you will meet the same teleporting undead guy.  He is one of like 3 different skeletons in the game.  Maybe if you are lucky you will meet a wolf.  Maybe you'll even get to the demons in the desert before giving up in boredom.
At the end of the day the game had potential, but squandered it on recycling the same old crap with bigger numbers.

Game Summary: You get to choose 3 different classes from the start before you ultimately find another one later in the game. It has a fun but short dark souls like PvE with connected zones as open world. Players can seamlessly connect into your world kind of like dark souls invasions, but they can decide whether to fight you or to help you. The combat here is the best part of the game that provides extreme amounts of experimentation and fun. The devs also said they plan on adding more moves and fighting styles to the game for free.
Combat Overview:
A game where if you spend some time with it, you can develop some pretty intense combos. There's a learning curve to it, especially when trying to get all your moves to flow together with ease but with ability to customize 16 different attack slots, there's a lot of variety here and experimentation.
PvE Summary:
A Short PvE mode that will take you anywhere from 6 to 10 hours, it is designed to teach you the game and to learn some moves, It's actually kind of brilliant because not only do you learn the moves by blocking them, you actually get to learn the timing of how to block here. It's a connected world a la dark souls but is not as grand as dark souls. There's 3 main bosses to fight and 6 minibosses you must defeat before you are able to fight the bosses, with enemies in between. But once you beat it. The devs said they're going to add  PvE dungeons shortly after launch to add some more content.
PvP Summary: This is the main draw to this game, Currently the PvP consists of Open World "invasions" a la dark souls, or the dedicated PvP mode which only supports 1v1s as of now. The devs are working on bringing 3v3s, a ranked mode, and a spectator mode soon. This is the most fun part of the game, If you ever played dark souls PvP, you'll feel right at home. With the customizable movesets, you can have a lot of fun experimentation.
Positives:
+ FashionAbsolver ( Fashion Souls)
+ PVP is really fun
+ customizable movesets for fists, swords, wargloves, and soon to be staves
+ all content added to the game will be free
+ Unique artstyle
Neutrals:
= PvE, I'm enjoying it actually but since it's kind of short I wouldn't get this game if your only looking to play PvE as of now.
= P2P, but every fighting game uses it so it can be seen as a plus or minus
= It could run better
Negatives:
- Region locked, while it's good to prevent bad connection, people who are friends with someone who lives in a different region from them are screwed.
- Terrible, Terrible Map it's hard to know where you are on it, or where the areas are. It only shows bosses and marked ones.
- It's easy to get lost in PvE
Review Summary:
In short, this is an enjoyable experience for fans of dark souls pvp, there's a lot of experimentation here with the different moves you can learn and use for the different types of weapons (Fists, Wargloves, Swords). But If your coming only for the PvE you will be upset as it's only about 6-10 hours long. Come here for the PvP and enjoy the PvE as a added bonus/tutorial.

This is a "prequel demo" for Resident Evil 7 : Biohazard,
This is a very short demo, but holds a good amount of interesting tidbits for new players and veterens alike. It is similar in style to the popular P.T. demo from the now-cancelled Silent Hills, but has a Resident Evil flavor injected in. This demo, however, is different from the actual game, so be wary that this is not how the game plays out (a.k.a there ARE weapons, enemies, bigger environments in the full product)
Pros:
+ The 1st-person perspective is finally introduced into a RE title, and it is evident that it is a different change of pace for the series
+ Nothing to fight here, just a introduction into the game and some background of the main story
+ Lots of easter eggs for the diligent
+ Free :)
Cons;
- A little too barebones of a demo for my taste GAMEPLAY WISE, but atmosphere is definitely exceeding of a typical tech demo
- The different endings in the demo are too similar to each other, although I believe the demo has been updated once again with a new area to explore (haven't gotten the chance to look at)
Rating:

If you're at all interested in RE7, you have no reason not to try this out. This demo, while it has different design in some parts, conveys the base game's tone flawlessly and should let you decide if you want it or not.

Cloudbuilt has done for me what only few other games have managed to do. The graphics are good, they paint that dream-like world quite well with an anime-esque spin. The story was surprisingly in-depth despite not really being the focus of the game, I still found myself becoming fond of the well-voiced Demi and her thoughts on her situation. The gameplay itself is tight and responsive, as you'd expect/require it to be considering how punishing this game is to tiny mistakes.
When I first started playing I didn't think I'd be able to achieve what I intended, as in games similar to this I always set my goal for the best ranks on each level. Everytime I failed it was frustrating, and I only had myself to blame as the game requires pin-point precision and the ability to think incredibly quickly while under pressure. I kept trying though, and I got better. Before I knew it I was performing manoeuvres I didn't think were possible at first - getting crazy air and speed with different techniques that I picked up along the way - as the game doesn't explain how everything works.
Cloudbuilt will beat you down repeatedly until you adapt to it's steep learning curve, but once you do the reward is great in satisfaction and all that self-loathing you had for yourself during your failures will be rectified :P. I recommend this game to anyone with a taste for speed, punishment and the patience to become better at something. 10/10, would hate self again.

Call of Duty: World at War is a must have for Call of Duty players.
World at War is my favourite Call of Duty to this date (pre COD:WW2) and no other CoD comes close to beating this in my opinion, and I believe this is the only perfect Call of Duty.
But first of all, the campaign. Now for me and most CoD players, we'll buy a CoD game and go through the campaign once or twice, it's not the highlight of why we buy it, but it's fun to hop onto, get some insight into how the weapons and engine work, and for most Call of Duty games, the stories are usually good. For World at War, I've replayed certain missions countless amounts of times, and have gone through the campaign start to finish about four times, it's really that good. World at War has the most unique and best campaign out of any Call of Duty, as it doesn't glorify war in any way at all, for example, the Modern Warfare series, you play as SAS soldiers and marines, save the world from WW3, nuclear wars and cool stuff like that, but with World at War, there is no glory, no mercy, no "yeah, we're a bunch of badasses that save the world and kill the bad guys". In World at War, you feel like you're that soldier more so than Black Ops or Modern Warfare, for example, and that's great. World at War features some of the best CoD characters, that you actually care about, unlike games like Black Ops 3, in which I can't remember a single persons name, as I didn't care at all for the campaign.
You play as Pvt Miller, US Marine that fights against the Japanese on islands like Makin Atoll, Peleliu and Okiniwa, which is so cool. Not only that, you also get to play as Dimitri Petrenko, a Russian soldier fighting in Russia and Germany alongside Viktor Reznov, probably my favourite character in the Call of Duty franchise. Spoiler alert:
I could carry on talking about the Campaign, it's just so damn good, but I'll move onto Multiplayer.
The Multiplayer in World at War is my favourite Multiplayer out of any CoD game, and I really don't enjoy many CoD Multiplayers. Sure there are OP weapons, but loads of them, and loads are fun to use, compared to MW1 where the M16A4 was just so OP and hardly anything matched it, there's a range of godlike guns in WaW, like the PPSH, MP40, Type 100, etc. Despite being released almost a decade before this review, the Multiplayer is still alive. Sure there are hackers, but not to a point where every match is unplayable. The World at War Multiplayer has some really good maps, pretty good Weapon balancing, not many guns are unusable, and it's just an all round awesome experience.
Did I also mention the Multiplayer has tanks?
Zombies - oh do I love CoD zombies. The majority of what I play on Steam now is CoD zombies, whether it be World at War, Black Ops 1, 2 and 3, hell, even Advanced Warfare and Infinite Warfare. World at War is one of the few CoD games to feature Custom Zombies, something absolutely amazing. But I'll be honest here, the vanilla maps ain't that special, Nacht der Untoten, Verrückt and Shi no Numa aren't very innovative, epic maps with so much to do, but if you want to hop onto a quick game of zombies with your friends, these three maps are perfect, they're so fun to play, especially if you have played them before, the nostalgia is great. World at War also features Der Riese, a very innovative map, and a very fun one at that too. Der Riese is a very popular, fan favourite map that's all around awesome. It features Pack a Punch, allowing you to get to higher rounds with any gun, if looking for a long game, Der Riese is the map for you, easy to set up on, relaxing, not tedious and a fun experience. As previously mentioned, CoD: WaW on PC features Custom Zombies, which is awesome, I'd really recommend maps like Der Berg, Leviathan and Stairway to Hell, as they're absolutely amazing maps to play.
Also, you get all DLC for FREE, meaning you don't need to buy any of these maps!
CoD: WaW features one of the biggest PC CoD communities, meaning it's not dead at all, which is great. I may sound biased, but in my opinion, CoD: WaW features the best campaign, best multiplayer, and a damn good Zombies experience. For £20 I'd definitely recommend this for Call of Duty players.

A classic JRPG, with depth in story and gameplay, and a memorable track. If you've played any Final Fantasy game, then this game will follow the cookie cutter formula of story and gameplay that the others do. There is a seemingly generic plot to which the protagonist are thrown into. This game is honestly the most mature, complete and perfectly structured Final Fantasy story of them all. It could make a great film, or even a trilogy of films. It has 3 clearly defined parts that form a perfect narrative where I feel a lot of video games struggle to find an ending to fit.
Every single character barring Quina goes through an arc of personal growth that I haven't really felt in a video game before. They experience love, loss, loneliness and even terror. The destruction of Lindblum at the hands of Atmos was my first jaw dropping moment in a game, and seeing how helpless Zidane and Garnet are while witnessing it is a turning point for both their characters, and you see it in their Ps1 era faces perfectly.
There are a lot of lessons to be learned by playing this game too. Vivi and his experience with the Black Mage village taught a young me about the meaning of existence and the concept of death (or as the mages put it, "stopping"). Garnet's moment with her dying mother and Kuja's sacrifice taught me that an antagonist isn't always 100% evil. Even the Chocobo minigame has a meaningful conclusion.
The way this game deals with the party splitting up and going their separate ways is masterful. It makes something that would usually annoy me in a game bearable, and even important to my enjoyment. This is helped with the inclusion of "Active Time Events" which are mostly optional 'flash sideways' (like a present day version of a flash back). It gives the game a very cinematic experience. Instead of just seeing and knowing information that the main character is present for, you are getting the rest of the story filled in as you progress on the character you're playing at the time. A section of the game that uses this well is during Steiner and Garnet's trip to Treno to gather the Supersoft.

I honestly can't think of a single bad thing to say about this game. As part of the FF series, it was way ahead of it's time. FFVII was a huge success and hit at a time where it's cyber punkish athestic was cool and it's edgy and brooding characters resonated well with an audience of kids and teens growing up listening to Nine Inch Nails and Nirvana. VII was my favourite for a long time and it wasn't until I played VII and IX again when I became an adult I realised how much more I loved IX.
On it's surface it has the cartoon fantasy art style and cute character design with exaggerated features that may make you think it has no substance, but I assure you this is the deepest, darkest and most adult of the series. So glad it came to steam so I can replay it and enjoy it once more, and I'm already noticing things that I missed the last few times or didn't grasp when I was younger.
Highly recommended.

Imagine the Powerpuff Girls...Plus Sonic...Minus actual teamwork, then go back in time to slap it into a genesis, then BAM. That's Freedom planet.
It's like a long lost genesis game, filled with slightly anime-esque pixel art, speedy and challening gameplay, and a...story.
The main three girls are the highlight of this for me , their personatilies and drives are so interesting and work off each other well, Again, it's like the powerpuff girls.
Lilac, the headstrong, hero-bound leader, and really, the main character you've already seen in a smutty fan fiction somewhere because the internet loves her for some reason. Basically the Sonic/Blossom.
She's the most like an actual sonic character, with a sort of "Spindash" like dash either forward or diagonally in the air, and she certainly feels the fastest out of the group, though it's hard to tell.
Carol, the sporty, rough and tumble, fun-loving girl who really just wants to keep her girl friends close, she's my personal favorite in both gameplay and character.
Being the Knuckles/Buttercup of the group, she's the character with the most fighting capabilty, with simple combos, and even an air kick, enemies will crumble to the wildcat. She even has a motorcycle you can access at gas cans...that climbs ladders and walls...hey, not complaining, it's awesome.
Milla, The timid, but friendly and resourcful little orhpan child of the group who just wants to find her parents.
Being the cute Tails/Bubbles of the group, she can, of course, hover in the air, but she can also create blocks, and even a shield that she can use as a weapon, but she is a child (Well, even more so then Carol and Lilac)so, yea, she's a bit weaker then the other girls. She's certainly the hardest one to get used too, she has less health and an strange moveset. She makes you stop and think about your approach, making this fast paced game more of a puzzle platformer, which I kinda like.
A little gripe I have is that in order to play as these characters, you need to make a NEW file and play through the WHOLE ADVENTURE as that ONE character. It's interesting to see their different stories, I mean, there's obvious points where the characters go off from one another and you just know "Yea, that's their cue for their level." But when the characters work together to defeat a boss, not in a cutscene, but in the ACTUAL boss, they're coming out and helping you with health, and even dishing out hits as well. You just wanna SWITCH out with these characters, they're such a good TEAM. There is many times in the story, where you think there's going to be a hubworld of sorts where you can talk with people, change characters, maybe even find out what the hell those elemental shields and gems do, but NOPE...Oh yea...
Now, with my main problem of this game...The story.
Don't get me wrong, I LOVE the characters, like I said, it's like Sonic and the Powerpuff Girl had offspring, the girls are just so CUTE together and work off each other well...my problem is that...it gets...WAY too serious. I'm okay with the Girls having turmoil and issues, because I really care about them and want them to suceed, but when it goes of into the dark stuff, the girls are all sepurated and scared, things look bad...it...it just doesn't feel genuine. When I said it feels like a Sonic game, or a Powerpuff girls episode, I meant that, the writing for the characters are so quirky and outlandish, and FUNNY, so when it dives into the world-building and the politics in the three main kitchen and dragons and all that, I just...It just feels so out of place. I wanted more of the team being...A TEAM, seeing cute scenes of them working together, or them just being FRIENDS. I understand there's a villian and such, but when I start caring, is when the team's an actual team.
Galaxy Trail made a very fun and enjoyable game, with fun characters...but it really gets too serious for what it is. It's a fun ride...I'm not saying to take the story out all together, far from it, Brevon is an AMAZING villian...But Galaxy Trail...You made a team of three very cute and lovable girls...please...let them BE a team in other then a few boss fights or A few cutscenes. Let there be an opition to switch bewteen the girls during the level, and lighten up the story. I mean LOOK at your game, I litterally want to hug the TREES thier that adorable! Do I still recommend the game? HELL YEA! Just...don't ask me to tell you all about the lore, because everytime the girls weren't all together or being adorable I just sorta toned it out.

I'm a couple of years late to the party but I FINALLY finished this game.
Aaaaand I hated it.
I really wanted to love this game. As a Sonic autist I heard about this game during it's early development, and bought it sometime after it came out. I put it down halfway through, but the game's awesome style and presentation would ultimately convince me to give it a second chance years later. After finishing the game I have to say that I do not recommend this game to anybody who hasn't bought it already.
For starters, it's a 2D action platformer with speed and flow similar to... Sonic 4 at best (And we're talking Ep2). You've got 3 playstyles that are very similar to Sonic 06. The speed, combat, and psychic character. Levels are supposed to be fast and done under 7 minutes or so, but you'll find yourself getting lost and being stopped by stray projectiles or large AoE attacks. Later on, when the game becomes the most annoying, the floor is lava and no part of the screen is safe for you.
So, like your typical first Sonic playthrough. These levels do get better with every run through. However, unlike Sonic you have probably some of the most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t bosses that I have ever had the displeasure to encounter. Again, the floor is lava, and no part of the screen is safe. For some reason, Freedom Planet confuses itself for a bullet hell and you will find yourself dying TIME and TIME AGAIN. I found myself wondering if i'm ignoring an important game mechanic that's making these so hard, but no it's just that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Sonic bosses are easy, are fun to fight, but typically underwhelming. Freedom Planet's bosses are AWESOME to look at, but they're hard and annoying as hell. There are tons dividing the acts, so whatever fun you just had in a stage is cut short by the next boss encounter.
If you can push the bosses, you can enjoy the levels by themselves and break the bosses as you replay it. But, god, this game just sucks on your first playthough. Avoid this game if you don't enjoy the absolutely stellar style, visuals, and soundtrack.

Overview: Anomaly: Warzone Earth is a reverse tower defense game that pits you vs alien towers. You command a single infantry unit to lead a convoy of vehicles through the game's 14 missions. Sound: The voice activng is pretty bad and the music is repetetive, but it doesn't take away much from gameplay.
Gameplay: 3 modes (Casual, Advanced and Hardcore) makes Anomaly quite fun and challenging...if you want it to be. Very easy to grasp and smooth difficulty scaling. Very polished game.
Conclusion: If you are looking for a game with a good story, this isn't it. If you are looking for a fun tower defense type game worth your money, Anomaly: Warzone Earth is it.

I should start by saying this game isn't terrible.  You can play it for a bit and have fun.  That said...
This game really suffers from squandered potential.  The tagline is that you are a wizard and you don't have to deal with mana bars or cooldowns, so now that you have unlimited magic power you can go on a crazy murder spree.
In actuality to get to fight the same 5 guys over and over again in a storyline that doesn't make much sense (spoilers below).
The story starts with a bad evil dude coming up and messing with your family.  He is a bad evil dude because he likes stabbing people and has a goatee.  You are then visited by a wizard named Roth who raises you from the dead and gives you "unlimited power" and the ability to not die ever again.  Having thus removed any dramatic tension from the story, you then go fight a cult and some undead guys who may or may not be fighting each other and it may or may not matter.  Also, all the human antagonists give you long, boring monologues while invincible and then teleport away unless the game arbitrarily decides they're going to stop and fight the guy who is, as a reminder, completely invincible and cannot be killed.
Now this would be forgivable if gameplay was actually good, but it gets boring fast.  The game makes a big deal out of its spellcrafting system - but for the most part spells are generally damage, status effect, or weird combo debuff.  Spells are created from randomly dropped items you can mess around with in interesting ways to upgrade them for upgrades that may or may not do anything.  There are some stats on the player screen - destruction, mastery, control - that get affected by these somehow and maybe sorta kinda determine spell effects?  I don't know, the game didn't explain and I couldn't tell you how the formula works.  Some of these drops are rarer but don't seem better.  You can pick 3 of 8 elements and of these three you get a nova (with weird trigger conditions), an aoe, and a single-target missile spell, all of which are upgradable to have different numbers that do...stuff.  It's not a terrible system, it's just repetitive and you never feel you are getting anywhere.  At the beginning of the game you can call down a firestorm.  At the end of the game you can call down a firestorm, but with bigger numbers.  Maybe if you futz around with the numbers you can use a completely separate subsystem and call down a meteor.  Now, many video games have this problem, but for a game about "Unshackling the mage", the fact that a wizard in Baldur's Gate can pull off more impressive and interesting feats of magic kinda sucks.
Of course, there's a reason you don't get interesting magic like long-range teleportation or invisibility - the game is a linear line where you run through and fight the same 5 guys.  I'm not even talking palette swaps here.  There is a model of a black-clad lady with some kind of acid vial she throws at you.  She has the same 3 lines.  You will hear these same lines at the beginning of the game, the end of the game, and the part of the game where I got bored and quit.  You will meet a teleporting undead guy.  Later in the desert, you will meet the same teleporting undead guy.  He is one of like 3 different skeletons in the game.  Maybe if you are lucky you will meet a wolf.  Maybe you'll even get to the demons in the desert before giving up in boredom.
At the end of the day the game had potential, but squandered it on recycling the same old crap with bigger numbers.

This is a really cool game, but it's also disappointing. On one hand, the concept is awesome: be a mage that's actually a badass. But the execution is a bit lacking, because you don't exactly feel like a badass. This feels like a solid first game in a series, but therein lies the problem: you feel like you'd be best off waiting for a sequel that fixes the problems.
For starters, you can only cast one spell at a time, which effectively eliminates all real experimentation with combining spells. Sure, you can (for example) freeze an enemy with an ice AOE then switch to a fireball and blow them up with flames, but it feels slow and sorta clunky. That example process which would take a fraction of a second in a game like Skyrim instead takes a full 2-3 seconds or so to execute. This rather slow-feeling casting system, combined with the oftentimes exorbitant amounts of health of enemies, means that in my few hours of play so far, I've spent most of that time kiting enemies and repeatedly throwing a lightning ball in their faces. Yes, it's absolutely awesome at first, but then the repetitiveness starts to set in. I spent an hour and a half doing nothing but kiting enemies and throwing my fireball-equivalent spell at them and repeating. Offense is pretty much just a test of your ability to backpedal without running into things while spamming your basic direct attack.
Defense isn't a lot different. There are three primary types of shields in the game; I've thus far really used only one, the 'agile' shield. It has the fastest recharge speed and enables you to dodge infinitely. Dodging is done via teleporting a few feet instantaneously. But while I've only used one shield type for any real period of time, I don't think any of the others would be worth using in terms of in-game efficiency. Mashing the 'dodge' button and spamming attacks makes every fight a cakewalk, it's simply a matter of time before any group of enemies dies, oftentimes without even hitting you. The few basic enemy types have a nearly impossible time connecting with any attacks when you're dodging constantly. I've yet to die from a single standard non-boss encounter playing on the 3rd of 4 difficulty levels ('the intended difficulty for Lichdom: Battlemage').
This game is also extremely linear. Not every game needs to be an open-world sandbox like GTA or Assassin's Creed, but this feels almost like Medieval Fantasy Hallway Simulator 2014. You walk straight ahead, occasionally explore a short, basic side route, then continue trudging forward. It's sorta like Frodo and Sam in the Return of the King trudging towards Mordor and Mount Doom, except you don't have hairy feet and you can blow skeletons up with fireballs. There is nothing extra to do aside from kill whatever's in your path; there is one type of 'chest' per level that you can destroy for extra spell components, but that is it. The closest things to collectibles are journal entries you can pick up that you don't really care about. I'm all for games that are pretty linear (Call of Duty singleplayer, Max Payne, Shadow Warrior, stuff like that), but this is a little too much.
It might seem like I hate this game. I don't. I'm just disappointed in it. It had the potential to be one of the coolest, most different games of the year in my opinion, and it turned out...decent. The magic crafting system is really cool (if slightly confusing at first), the concept behind the combat is amazing, and it is fun to throw fireballs into a skeleton's face. I just wish it didn't feel so repetitive in so many ways. I hesitantly recommend buying this game, but not at full price. I don't feel like I'll get $40 of enjoyment out of it, but that's okay, because I WILL have enough fun to justify the $13.60 I paid for it. If you want to play something different with a great concept, go ahead and grab this for $20 or less. If you want flawless execution of a concept, pass. I'd give this a 6.5/10.

While the magic and spell-crafting components are absolutely amazing, the game is lacking everywhere else. Spell crafting includes a wide variety of sigils, or energy-types, like fire, ice, time (phase), and necromancy. These enrgy-types are crafted into "shapes" like a ray, homing-missle, area-affect, shield. The spell shape is then given an additional layer of effect by an "augment" focusing on destruction (damage), control (paralyzing emeies), and mastery (stacking damage with a sigil-specific special effect). Additional, you collect a wide array of these different components, each with their own bonuses, which can then be combined to increase their rarity and effect. The result is a very rewarding game of exploring spells and experimenting with the results of these combinations.
Unfortunately, that's where the fun of this game ends. With an uncompelling story, the painfully liniar route quickly has you begging for anything different, until the different appears. The linear routes are replete with magically poofing-in enemies in clearly delineated battle arenas connected by short narrow walking paths from one to the next. As predictable as it gets, until one member of the third identical wave of enemies spawns in right behind you. Five enemy types over and over again: archer, swordsman, mage (archer who teleports), wraith (flying enemy with an unblockable freeze attack), and "captain" (one of the previous types with tripple-health and boosted damage). After your fifth arena battle of cheapness on both sides, you're ready for a change... the bosses. Unfortunately, boss battles just turn into drawn-out pattern matching endurance games. 1: Spam damage. 2: Retreat and kill small mobs. 3: Dodge. 4: Rinse and repeat.
This whole leaves you nothing but frustation, unless you happened to already know the best spell combos, in which case you're just blowing through everything. Unfortunately, if you DIDN'T already know those combos, it will take a LONG time to re-collect enough components to craft a new set, now that you know what you SHOULD HAVE done with those spells. Realizing that your best option is to start the game over, you will most likely quickly decide against going through the same linear repetitive grind, just to try a new spell combo.
I really wish the story and journey had been better thought-out.

This is, by far, one of THE best Sonic games to date. And I am not kidding on this. After years of bad games, SEGA finally got some idea with Unleashed, messed around a little more in Colors, but then finally got the formula right in Generations, nailing down something fans like me have wanted for a long time. Also, don't worry, this is
.
The gameplay is split up into two halves among nine levels and three bosses between both the classic Sonic you knew and loved from the Genesis days, and the modern Sonic gameplay from Unleashed and Colors, giving you about 21 levels in total, along with a set of missions in that level. Plus, added with Red Rings returning from Colors (only this time they're actually worth getting), and you have a game that is fun AND extremely replayable after beating the main story. Take this into account with the fact that is it moddable with SonicGMI, and you'll have infinite reasons to come back to this game (I literally have over 50 hours on this game and 100% completed it, and I'm still playing it for mods like Unleashed Project).
Even if you think the missions are stupid and unecessary, you still have at least 6 hours worth of good fun that doesn't spread itself thin, even if you play all the missions.
Plus, one of the biggest things about this is that they finally perfected the boost gameplay. With Unleashed, it was certainly fast fun, but one of the criticisms about it is that it's too much like a racing game, and less like a platformer. Colors fixed that, but at the expense of slowing the game down immensely, making boost sparative, and having too many 2d sections with block platforming. Well, Generations' modern gameplay finds a middle ground between both and it is excellent! You have your moments of high speed boosting (which is now not only fueled by rings and drifting, but destroying enemies as well like in Color plus doing tricks from trick ramps, replacing the QTE ramps of Unleashed, and also adding tricks to rainbow rings, both of those which help to hyper-extend your boost meter), but also has moments where you need to slow down a little and tread carefully along platforms. Add it with the fact that you have ALL necessary skills right from the get-go, and you got an awesome experience.
Plus, as of late, the game here now includes the Casino Night DLC for free! It's just a pinball machine with a nice jazzy remix (hence why it became free because it isn't much), and it's a nice little distraction.
Easily this game has the best gameplay for the franchise thus far. Hopefully, the future games like Project 2017 take note.
Admittedly, while the gameplay is certainly great, the story however, takes a major hit. This could be either a bad thing or a good thing depending on the views of the person. Me, personally, I consider a bad thing. There's definitely a hint of a story they had going here, but it feels rushed and like something is missing, almost making the story and reasoning behind the eventse empty and dull, especially when compared to the superb writing of Unleashed, and the basic BUT entertaining nature of Colors.
And don't get me wrong, it has its moments where it gets great, but I feel like as if they could've tried better or, if given more time, finish it completely.
And this is an unfortunate trend among Sonic games sometimes. But don't worry, the story isn't something so bad it detracts from the experience. It definitely doesn't, but it's disappointing to say the least when compared with previous games.
The visuals of this game are absolutely stunning, thanks in part to the Hedgehog Engine, which was reused from Unleashed. All the classic worlds are remade beautifully in 3D, and much like Unleashed, the colors of the environments are vibrant and pretty, while at the same time, thanks in part to the shaders, Sonic still blends with the environment enough that he doesn't pop out unnaturally like previous games, but is still visible enough to track easily.
Plus, thanks in part to messing around and modding ReShade, you could make the game look even better with tiny adjustments (like adding Anti-Aliasing) or even bigger ones like SSAO or DOF. It's quite the beaut.

Even if you don't like the games, there is something you gotta admit when it comes to Sonic. The soundtrack is amazing. And Generations, even if it's just remixes, doesn't fall short on it. The remixes are wonderful and sometimes end up MUCH better than the original track, and the OST even has themes in the sound for each Sonic. A more electronic, Genesis-sounding remix for classic Sonic, while modern Sonic has more upbeat, blood-pumping rock-esque remixes that even sometimes speed up along with you whenever you boost or hit a dash panel or basically any moment you go faster.
It's definitely worth a listen, and you can even find it on Spotify, which I definitely suggest!
Plus, the sound effects and voice acting are great as always!
Sonic Generations is a Sonic game done right. It panders to the nostalgia of older fans who played the Genesis, and newer fans as well. Generations is a great entry point into the Sonic series for newcomers, even if you don't get the references or where the games come from. But however it invigorates curiosity that makes you want to discover these games.
Even if it doesn't interest you to check out the others, I guarantee this game will hook you in.
And if you're a Sonic fan who doesn't have it yet, well what are you waiting for? Buy it as soon as you can!

This was a good game honestly. After watching all reviews on it I still decided to purchase because it was on sale for 2 bucks. The gameplay was easily its weakest spot. The driving was tideous. The shooting mechanics were good but it is just a cover based shooter. The selection of weapons are good. If you want to sit back and pick people of with the m1 Garand you can (once it is available of course), if you want to dunk down and pop shots at the enemy with a shot gun like a violent game of pikaboo then you can, or if you want to just walk towards the enemy like an untouchable mafia god and just mow them down with your Tommy gun then you can do that as well.
The worst part of the game was easily how much you have to drive. The streets are narrow and crowded. A lot of the cars are stiff on the controls so you hit a lot of cars (This will have nearby cops trying to chase you) and things on the sidewak. This is my only big complain about this title. The driving was a drag but the story and shooting were what kept it interesting.
The story is good. It details a man named Vito Scalleta who after his service in the war, joins up with his best friend Vito Barbaro and eventually ends up being tied up with the mob. This is a great story and shows the culture and reality of that time period very well. As these were some of my favorite times in American history (other then the wars of course), this game kept me feeling like part of this time. Whether it is the music, the cars or the women, this was a great time culturally to me.
This game really shows you how Vito got invoolved with the mob expecting so much but after its highs he realize the cost of being involved in such a dangerous "profession".
Great story that kept me interested. I would easily recommend this game. Especially if you can get it at a reasonable price as I did.
