I've never written a review for any games on Steam. A mix of having little time and a feeling of not being sure of what to say of the game. But this game, this one, connected to me in a way that made me feel compelled to write one.
Like many other reviews, I'll give my personal experience with this game, but, hopefully, among the gameplay commentaries that follow it's tread, it can lead to conclusions that you, the doubtful buyer, might have. The
that this game provides is something very worth mentioning.
In this review, I could tell you a lot more about the campaign, about the single player modes, but you most likely have read it already, either in another review or in any website around. If you want to know more, I can tell you in the comments. I suppose that you want to know about the multiplayer aspect of it, particularly after it was brought back into the game. So here it is, one experience, among many, many others that I had in these first hours of PC multiplayer, amongst countless hours that were already played in singleplayer and splitscreen on the PS2, and in the modded PC version.
________________________________________
The map was Hoth, ground battle. In this one, much like in the new versions of EA, two AT-ATs move foward and the objective in the Conquest mode was to capture command posts, similarly to Battlefield. The difference is, players can spawn in the AT-AT's which also makes pushing them up an important factor. As the Empire, I was playing as the AT-AT, driving it and shooting from it - not on  rails, like the newest games -, for a couple minutes into the game. Both the AT-ATs, the other drove by the AI, which does the job with these kind of vehicles, made it to the range of the Shield Generator, and started shooting it to pieces. In a huge firefight, the AT-AT to my right falls to the ground, dropped down by heavy fire. I see the health of mine dropping fast as the rebels desperately try to shoot me down, even from across the map, but, in the last seconds, I take out the Shield Generator. It works as a fisical uncapturable spawn point, a safe spot per se, and the Rebels lost it. There are still many tickets left, the host - a player - set it to a reasonably medium-large amount, so the battle isn't over yet.
Dead, I realize that one crazy guy playing as Vader conquered the Rebel Hangar for the Empire, and there I spawn as a Dark Trooper. From there, we have the Rebels surrounded, there is just one more Command Post left for them, but that one is connected by a tunnel network to the Hangar. We must secure that tunnel or they'll retake the Hangar in a blink. So, with no one around me, but a couple bots, I order them to follow me - You can do that, and make a small assault squad with bots, when there are less players than the max - and move into the tunnels. An enemy player shows up, and in the claustrophobic cluster of tunnels we do our best to stand. Two of my mates die, one of them remains, a tough fellow Dark Trooper. That guy kills the enemy players - bots are a real threat - and we push on.
In that moment, the enemy respawns and brings other players, killing us both in the Tunnels. THAT is the moment that is the real gamechanger in this review: I go to the chat and tell the team that we "Need more people at the tunnels, lots of em are pushing through". And there, one guy respawns with me, at the Hangar Command Post. We hold like hell, dying and respawning, and then, I see even more of them coming. Once again, in the chat "Tunnels are getting real intense! Really needing more people!". And, behold, the team unites. While some hold them off in the other front, me and 6 guys move against their 6-7 guys and the battle is nearly even. Until this moment:
I was doing good in the match, so Darth Vader pops up as a choice - the first choices prioritize the top players, after that it randomizes a bit, and also, you can decline it. I just type to the guys, letting them know what will happen. "I'm bringing Vader to the party :3".
Spawned at the hangar, meeting the truthful formed-in-3-minutes squad and lead the assault as Vader. It's amazing how everyone follows and starts pushing like a bulldozer. We reach the Rebel Command post, and we finally make them lose the Command Post. As we thought it was over, there he is.
Luke. Pilot Luke, jumping into the CP and killing my squad, as I'm left alone facing him. A bloody frenetic fight, clashes all over the place, the expectation of winning this match after a beautiful teamplay... ends with Luke down. We got it. We took it. And right there, with my health extremely low, the timer starts couting - It ticks after all CPs are taken. Victory.
It is over. One of the most frenetic 10 minutes I've ever played in a Star Wars game, one of the biggest in a shooter, even one so simple as this one. Not only frenetic, but fun, compelling, engaging, immersive and, most of all, shared. Shared amongst, not only our teammates, but with our enemies, who were all commenting on that duel of Luke vs Vader, of how this game could still provide such an amount of fun after 12 years of it's release, and how amazing it was to see us all togheter, in both sides...
________________________________________
And there it is. Battlefront II is an experience in itself, even more so if you're a Star Wars fan and just want to enjoy the stories that you love with a gameplay that's, not only enjoyable, but one that
like Star Wars: In the movies, in the stories, we all know that it is all about joining together to face a common enemy, that unity, that friends, can, together, make a difference. Luke would've never brought down the Death Star if Han hadn't shown up to hit Vader in that trench. He would not be alive, had he not found him in Hoth walking alone. The Rebels woudln't have the courage to escape Hoth and keep up the hope, hadn't Luke got into that Speeder and took out one of the AT-ATs. Leia wouldn't be able to return to the Rebellion if Luke and the others hadn't joined to rescue her on the Death Star. And, what's also big amongst these stories... They were, at first, all strangers one to another. Luke knew nothing of Obi-Wan, neither knew nothing of Han, Han knew nothing of Leia and Leia knew nothing of Luke.
So, who is gonna be your Han Solo while you're in need as Luke? Who's gonna guide you at the start, like Leia did to bring the Rebels togheter? Who is going to destroy the shield generator as you fight your battles with Vader? This is the essence of the cooperative experience, and Star Wars is all about finding friends in unusal places, joining in a moment of need, against odds that pose a challenge. In this game, this is the
that you can get.
Of course, not every match is going to be this "substancial", or this "cheesy" as some will SURELY say, but what you'll see here is that this game has the possibility to offer you this experience, capturing the feeling of the Star Wars universe, exposing it into it's gameplay through a good portion of it's community.

I really wanted to love this, as it is my favourite Final Fantasy game - the one I can come back to time and time again, but instead it became the first Steam game I refunded. Unfortunately, the lack of true analogue control made the game feel unpolished, and the contrast of the higher detail character models against the low detail prerendered backdrops is hard to ignore. Final Fantasy IX has an incredible soundtrack and sound design, but it too has suffered with this updated version.
In the original, when using a Dual Shock controller, you had full control over the speed and direction your character faced. Having fluid movements and control really helped with immersion, however in this updated version, the analogue stick of your controller will only simulate the d-pad (allowing only 8 different directions to move in) and a button is used to allow you to walk or run, depending on how you set up the movement options. In the original, you could push the analogue stick with more or less force depending on the speed you wished to travel. This change feels very clunky.
The character models no longer look to be a part of the world they wander about in, and instead look superimposed and as if they are wandering about on top of a flat 2D image, due to the vast difference in detail between the two. Adding to this, the sound quality is not of the standard of the original PS1 version. There's certainly not as much depth to the sound (similar to the difference in sound found in the Final Fantasy Tactics: War of the Lions updated versions).
I would only recommend this version if it is the only one you have access to, or if the control issues don't sound like an issue to you (which for many, I'm sure it won't be). While not preferable, the difference in detail between characters and backgrounds and sound quality loss are bearable and I would not disregard this version on those problems alone.

You know that game? That one that has 9's and 10's for review scores? That one everyone seems to be talking about? That one game you actually give into the hype for? Then you play it, sink multiple hours into it, and walk away "depressed" and wondering where the magic was everyone was talking about?
Freedom Planet? Knew about it for quite a long time and finally caved. So I bought it...
Then beat it in the same day and promptly returned to this store page to purchase the soundtrack.
Oh my goodness, if you want old-school platforming with a modernized slant, believe the "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating for this one.
So what, truly, is Freedom Planet? Freedom Planet takes its inspiration from old-school Sonic while opting to intertwine and finely balance combat with speed. Its important to note that I was never a hardcore Sonic person growing up so I'm not particularly qualified to sing its inspirational roots, but not being in the fandom hasn't dimmed my enjoyment of this game in the slightest. Gameplay is stellar and on top of it is layered an amazing presentation at every turn.
The story of Freedom Planet is about soon-to-be heroes Lilac and Carol, along with their friends, stopping the alien warlord Brevon from stealing their world's most precious artifact. The plot here isn't anything mind-blowing; it has a few surprises in store but by and large keeps things pretty simple. And that's fine, because what the plot does do is give excellent justice to the cast of characters. Full voice acting with highly emotive animations make Lilac, Carol and company jump straight off the screen. It may be another "save the world" plot, but the characters make you believe in its urgency. From Lilac's unrelenting protectivness to Brevon's cruel sense of morality, this cast means business.
But even if you put the plot aside, the gameplay is top-notch. Still have to play through the entire game with Carol (who seems more combat-oriented so far,) but Lilac's toolset gives her a lot to work with. Cyclone jumps, speed bursts, drop-kicks... the game expands combat beyond the "tuck-and-roll" combat of good ol' Sonic. I will admit that the inter-level combat sometimes feels a little off, but where the new combat system really shines is in boss battles. Particularly near the end (be warned: the difficulty does spike a fair bit in true retro fashion,) I felt like I was really flexing my platforming muscles defeating the last several bosses. Full use of your toolset is expected and the game's willingness to commit to this aspect makes it feel that much more rewarding. There isn't much hand-holding either, though apparently there is the option to switch mid-game to a "casual" difficulty (or any of them) if you find the latter difficulty spike to be too offputting.
Then there is the rest of the package. Gorgeous graphics and animations? Check. Diverse stages and set pieces? You got it. Amazing soundtrack? *gushing intensifies* ...OK, seriously, I'm just not that easy to impress anymore. That's why I want to make it so clear that I came in knowing the bar was set high... and even that high bar was surpassed. The music isn't pure retro, but again the retro-modern blend is executed exceptionally well here. If you are a fan of ye olde VG music in any capacity, don't hesitate to snatch up the soundtrack. In fact, just do it now. Buy the game and the soundtrack right now. Seriously, why are you still reading this?
Hopefully I've given you the perspective you need to see if Freedom Planet is for you. Its different on purpose, balancing out the old and the new to deliver one fantastic ride that's all its own. And if you're a seasoned vet like myself looking for the modern progression of the old-school platformer, give Freedom Planet a fighting chance. I'd like to think you won't regret it.

Never being a fan of classic Sonic games despite having tried to play the early entries multiple times, I wondered for a long time why this game appealed to me so much. Here is what I came up with: First of all, the game features three characters that play completely differently from each other. If I would have to compare them, then Lilac feels like Sonic, but not like Sonic in Main Series Sonic Games, but rather like Sonic in Smash Bros. (since you actually have an "attack"-Button), Carol feels a lot like X from Megaman X since she has an infinite Walljump and a little Boost (which is a little different because X can only boost from the ground while Carol can only Boost while in the Air) and Mila feels like Yoshi from the games like SMW2: She has a Flutterjump (though not infinite like in most Yoshi Games) as well as a projectile attack that can also shoot diagonal. So to sum it up, you have three characters that feel kind of like characters from other really good games. What makes this even more impressive is the fact that the level design actually compensates all three of them. And to top it off, almost each character has one stage that only they get to play and really make use of that characters mechanics.
Overall while this game looks and feels a lot like Sonic, it always felt to me like it played even more fluently. One of the reasons for that is that each character has some form of move to gain some momentum instantly, while Sonic (at least in the classic games) had to accellerate anew whenever he got hit. And speaking of getting hit: You can actually run through most enemy sprites or even stand on them. They each have some kind of animation that can hurt you, but the enemy itself doesnt harm you. And the game is designed around this aspect which gives you a better sense of speed if you want to.
One more difference that I realized was that the bosses felt a lot more like Megaman bosses than like Sonic bosses. Also they get really challenging if you start your first playthrough on normal difficulty. But they never get unfair, since each patter can be learned and adapted to. TL;DR: If you like 2D-Sonic games, you are in for a real treat. If you do not like Sonic, I would still give this game a fair chance.

Never before has a game made the mage feel so powerful when compared to Lichdom: Battlemage. There are other good games out there like Magicka, but Lichdom feels different and better. Maybe it’s something about the first person perspective, I’m not entirely sure. I’ve gone back and forth on this game as to why it’s so good and where the difficulty actually lies in it. I’ll try to elaborate for you guys.
The difficulty in Lichdom is hard to pin down. It’s not that it’s terribly difficult, but it can be if you end up making the game harder on yourself. This all revolves around your spells of choice. You’ll have more choices then you’ll need when it comes to classes of magic here. By all means, pick anything you’d like. The early game is easy and lets you get a feel for how it all handles. Then, sometime later in the game there is a bit of a difficulty barrier.
That point in Lichdom is when you will you’ll need stronger or more well crafted spells. There’s a basic crafting tutorial in-game, but most information can be found outside of the game proper. While this works with most games, this time it doesn’t jive well with me. There are some really cool combinations you can create when crafting and there are some really crappy ones. You can be busy exploring your options and end up screwing yourself over by having spells that will only add up and/or store damage and not have one that deals the direct damage to unleash all that you’ve setup. (I know it takes a special kind of someone, but I am speaking from experience here.) There is a lot of combinations to work with. You seriously need to pay attention when the in-game tutorials pop-up or do some extracurricular reading to get those awesome spells to work out for you. Unfortunately, I haven’t found a guide on making specific spell combinations to be really freaking awesome… I’d like one… a lot. I’m not 100% on how it would work, but something like: find these components and put them together like thus to make X spell. That or a guide on how to get my freaking Undead Hulk from Necromancy and Delirium.
On the other hand, you could pick up Necromancy and call it good. It’s definitely not as shiny as well… any other spell class, but it does make things worlds easier. When you kill something with a Necromancy mark on it, that will summon an undead minion to your side and it will fight for you. This is too freaking useful to pass up for first-timers who may like a challenge, but don’t want to get too frustrated. It’s not a cake-walk, but it’s a lot nicer if you’ve got the patience to back it up. I’ve beaten a few of the challenge levels/instances (marked by these artifacts that look like ancient green laser pointers) on my first try with Necromancy where it would have taken me maybe four to five tries with other spell combinations up to not being able to finish them at all.
Since I’ve found my groove with Necromancy, the difficulty isn’t much of a gripe. My main gripe with Lichdom is in how the game “feels”. I really enjoy it in a general sense: the spells, the power and the story that makes you want to punch that weasel of a villain in his mustache. Also, I like the first person perspective too! It’s just that the game is so linear. I’m usually the guy that loves a good ‘ol linear game too. The story drives the game well and there’s enough to explore and find on your way so that’s not really the issue. I think it’s the fact that you’re playing a mage… and that’s usually in RPGs… and lately those have been more open. This doesn’t reduce the fun had at all, but there is a tiny lingering thought in the back of my head most of the time wanting to not be constrained to a path that only really arches if there is a side-challenge to be had. The guys at Xaviant are trying to establish an I.P. so they are just laying the groundwork here.
I really hope Lichdom has done well because I cannot wait to see what else they’ve got up their sleeves the next time they put out a game. This was a great concept for a game and with this much work done already on the systems and lore, can you imagine what the next game would be like? I hope they don’t make the main focus as a versus multiplayer experience, but I would love a two player (at least) coop experience. It’d be sweet to be setting up and making things explode with a friend! I’m reaching out to see if they have any plans for a sequel.
EDIT: Xaviant got back to me and Lichdom did well enough to warrant a sequel! There is no comment on how soon we’ll see it, but the fact that it is in the works is awesome. Great job guys!
Score: Gewd.
Lichdom has everything you would expect from a AAA game while not being made by a AAA company (kudos to Xaviant for that!) The graphics are amazing, the controls are good, they’ve got a well implemented crafting system all while the story keeps you playing because it’s actually interesting. (I love revenge in my games more than my movies.) It feels very linear because it is, but this is one of the best ways to tell a story and not have you get too lost. There is also no multiplayer, but they are laying the groundwork for an I.P. so it’s forgivable (read as: get over it). It’s easy for me to do because I’m still one of those guys that misses my longer that three hour campaigns in my shooters. Also, it’s better to have a solid single player campaign than an almost finished one with a tacked on multiplayer. It’s only natural to have a game make you feel completely B.A. and want to flaunt your powers in front of your buds while destroying them or helping them destroy another team. We’ll just have to be patient is all. Over all, Lichdom: Battlemage is completely worth the money if you want a game that treats the mage like you feel they should. (Next time let me jump though.)

Hi, I'm Crow-Father and I used to be a guy that wrote lengthy reviews on games that I had only played for a few hours and quite possibly have never finished. This is one of them. So I'm going in and editing my over hyped reviews for games that I liked and trying to make them more realistic for the amount of time I sunk into them. Before I get to my review I want to remind readers that a gamer can only judge a game by his/her own experiences with said game. Don't just go by what others say about it, but do take it into consideration for a lot of people may have insight that you don't.
Lichdom Battle mage is decent. It's not amazing, it's not aweful. That in itself makes it a little disappointing. Here's a game where your supposed to be a bad♥♥♥♥♥mage with almost no limitation on what you can do. Sad thing is your limited by sigils and swapping out crafted spells for stat differences. In my honest opinion I do believe the game suffers from trying to keep the RPG aspect a little too much. The crafting system wasn't really necessary and it gets tiresome to deal with. Swapping spells you can use like you would guns in FPS games makes sense so that was pretty solid. However I believe this game would have had a better time being like old Quake, Duke Nukem, Doom games where you picked up all the weapons in the game and scroll through them with the mouse wheel or switch using the num keys 1-7 (or 8 I can't remember how many sigils are in the game right now). I do like how you have different methods of firing off said spells, like using a fire ball single target attack or the area of effect attack. I also like that you can have a Ray of fire instead of a fire ball, or how the fire ball can explode on impact and do the maximum amount of damage or start burning a target over time based on what you crafted the spell to be like. That brings me to how spells could have been a little more interesting.
Now I'm all for challenges and intricate game mechanics but this game feels like it couldn't decide on being an FPS fantasy game or an RPG. Now with that being said I still don't understand why every one compares it to skyrims magic mechanics and yes I have played the game. Anyway, like I said earlier about being like the old FPS games they should also take mechanics from games like Crysis and others that allow you to switch the fire mode of a rifle capable of being automatic to semi-auto to burst, with just a key stroke. The switching between fireball impact, fireball burning, and heat ray should have been simplified. I'm using the one spell as an example because I haven't unlocked Necromancy yet and there is another spell type I have that I don't wanna use as an explanation besides you start with the Fire sigil. However instead you have to go through this crafting system inventory that seems pretty cool at first but then become pretty tedious later on. I feel the crafting system should be replaced with a skill tree or skill trees that give bonuses and buffs to the players abilities when leveled and yes I know the crafting system was made so that you can switch things out and not be stuck with your choice by deconstructing spells but you could easily do that with a tree system where you just switch out what skills you want. Kinda like you can have one perk or the other activated at a time.
The gameplay it self is pretty linear now where most may find that annoying I actually can see why it was necessary for this game. Besides it gives the chance to encounter really cool monsters and bosses... and stuff. Like I said trying to be realistic I think I've fought one boss and I can't remember who that was and the last time I played this game was a few months ago. The story isn't the most interesting but it's not dull either. Your characters motivation for wanting to kill the antagonist is simple. He killed your wife/sister (depending on gender choice) and a wizard type guy who has a history of showing up in times of stife (and also has a history with the dude to boot) revives you and turns you into a dragon. (Battlemage) Now I am actually intrigued with the story between the antagonist and the wizard guy, and there are these memory things that you find through out the game that give you some insight on the last dragon this wizard dude had. I have this weird feeling that your mentor isn't all what he's cracked up to be, but hey I need to beat the game to find that out.
Ultimately I still recommend this game because I do really like it but it gets kind of repetitive and the crafting system is really bloody tedious. It's nice that it's not too open but it does have secrets to find. It's a little too linear and it would be more understandable if there was variety in gameplay but this game is reminiscent of a game where you do nothing but be involved with combat and moving forward. No back tracking or anything and from what I have seen so far no real puzzles to solve. Maybe wait for a sale but definitely check it out.

This game is the bomb diggity, even after 13+ years.
PROS:
++Great, mostly balanced gameplay
++Good looking 2.5D graphics
++Endless amount of mods and assets
++Has full 1080p support, in a *13 year old game!*
++Runs pretty well on nearly anything
CONS:
--Hard to get working properly (I suggest looking for the SC4Launcher and 4GB patch if you want to really boost how the game works)
--Can crash a lot without the right settings
--Mods are difficult to install w/o Steam Workshop support
--The simulation is often finicky, but granted, there was only so much devs could do back then (pickup the Network Addon Mod for improved traffic simulation)
--The tutorial isn't super-helpful in helping you understand how the regional simulation works
Overall, if you're looking at this vs Cities: Skylines (and have a PC that can run C:S), go pick up Cities. It's a newer game with generally a more powerful and realistic simulation. However, I highly suggest dropping this into your wishlist and waiting for a sale, which is quite often on this title, because this game has a certain charm that I don't think any city builder has or ever will replicate.

tropico reloaded includes both tropico 1 and 2. this is mostly for 1 as i haven't played 2 much.
tropico 1 is  more of a economic simulator than a city builder since it has objectives you must meet in a certain time limit.
it has no campaign to speak of just a bunch of premade scenarios to choose from and a random map generator for when you tire of those. if you go into this game with the mindset of it being a city builder your going to be disappointed as the working space is rather small (being an island and all.) and the construction times can be atrocious if you build too far away from you starting city. rather your expected to slowly build outwards plus the ground has to be leveled before actual building commences and the workers go back to their houses to sleep and eat every so often. the islanders have needs that must be met and if you fail to meet them they eventually rebel and kick you off the island. so it's a lot like the sim series in that regard.  The time limit ranges from 10 to 70 years which sounds like a lot but it isn't since construction of bigger, more important buildings can be painfully slow at times or if you place your buildings far away. tropico reloaded will run on modern machines with windows 7 64 bit. it has a fun atmosphere but the graphics can be offputting to some as this is a game made in the late 90's(i personally don't care about graphics much). by itself it is a really fun game but compared to 3 it may seem a bit lacking. get this game if you can get it on sale for 5$ or less otherwise you might want to buy tropico 3 instead unless your looking for a challenge in which case this game is for you. word of warning the game can still ctd every couple hours in windows 7. (for me it's about every 3-6 hours.) so SAVE OFTEN if you value your progress. still a better effort than most older games ported to steam. unlike 3 there is no option to select a avatar with specific traits your just a generic dictator of some nameless island. it DOES have a sandbox (god) mode and tutorial but the tutorial is really bare bones. this game really expects you to learn most of the ins and outs yourself the tutorial even says as much. lastly there doesn't seem to even be any tooltips as to what the buildings actually do which is kind of harsh on the player.
as for tropico 2 i haven't played it much but it seems to be a pirate themed rts style economic simulator with far less customization and much shorter time limits than tropico 1. it has less maps and seems to be a step backwards in most respects to 1. you need resources to build buildings along with being required to have a construction camp to build most buildings. 2 does have a campaign though and seems to have tooltips to better aid the player in sorting out what buildings do.
bottom line: it's more of a economic simulator than a city builder. it's harder than 3 and has less buildings and no radio dj but i find it's music more interesting than 3's. if you go into this looking for a city builder....look elsewhere. but if your looking for a fun island economic sim with city building on the side this is the game for you.

Tropico 1 (and its expansion, Paradise Island) holds a special place in my heart as one of the games in my childhood that drew me into city builders and management sims. If you've never played it, this game has lots of charm; buyer beware for those of you who are frustrated by retro graphics, or have played Tropico 3, 4, or 5 - you may find that the gameplay is a little dated.
Tropico 2, on the other hand, has amazing replay value because nothing like it has tread on the same ground. A pirate themed city builder in which you have a "negative" economy based exclusively on kidnapping captives to produce supplies and send pirates out raiding trade convoys for plunder. While there are some frustrating ticks in this game (e.g. grumpy pirates who refuse to go spend their gold satisfying their needs), this is still a fun and unique experience. This title alone is nearly worth the price of the bundle!

It is very easy to learn the basic mechanics of running your own banana republic, but it is incredibly hard to master. After years of playing I still haven't managed to complete some of the harder difficulty scenarios.
The extra missions provided by the DLC pack provide a significant increase in scenarios available, and with the random map generator you can generate any scenario you might like.
Be warned, its incredibly addictive.
Also, the soundtrack is top notch. I believe it won several awards, and if it fails to get your feet tapping along to the latin rhythms then you have my sympathy.
10/10 would El Presidente again.

This is a game that... I wouldn't say I'm used to. In fact, it's hard to call it a "game," per say. It has the feeling of a visual novel, created in what seems like an RPG maker software, but has the whole, "your actions will decide your fate." And by that I mean the game changes based on your choices. And to say the least, all these factors put into one "game" is different to me. But that's not to say that it's bad, the exact opposite really.
I love games that allow you the choice for you to "forge your own path," if you get what I'm saying. And altough I'm not a huge fan of visual novels, I was strangley entranced by this. Not only that, but the use of anthropomorphic animals (or, Furries, if you will) was a nice take on things. Most visual novels I've come across are mainly based on anime/ manga characters.
And not only that, the art is amazing! The characters look great and the use of backgrounds fits beautifully. The only real problem I have is the sound effects, which don't always fit too well with the scenario. With that aside, the story is rather nice, and the novel is portrayed greatly.
If you're like me and are looking for a visual novel that alters based on your desicions, has great art and story and fun characters, I'd definetly reccomend this.

After some deliberation, I am giving this a reluctant thumbs up, with the caveat that this game isn't going to do so much for a person who's not already head-deep in the furry fandom. There are a few issues, but I see potential here.
The first thing to note is that the game is updating on a chapter-by-chapter basis, and was originally released only as Chapter I. As of this writing, Chapters I, II, and III are now in the game, and the developer plans to add more and has been improving content based on feedback. Don't come in expecting a complete narrative arc, but if nothing else consider it the equivalent of a seasonal pass to game content.
I feel that the setting and overarching narrative pose a great deal of interest, and could be better realized by sharpening weaknesses in prose and dialogue. The actual setting concept, the situation the main character finds themselves in, the twists - I enjoyed those aspects very much. I also appreciate the developer's use of gender-neutral dialogue in the early game, and was a bit surprised that the gender question came up as late as chapter 2.
The prose and dialogue, as mentioned, need work. This includes some segments where the game feels the need to spell out lines of reasoning redundantly (An example from early in the game: "Before? I thought he said this was his first time on a train. That statement just now seems to imply otherwise."), and occasionally the use of "it's" in situation that calls for "its." There are also times where I feel the game is pushing a little too hard to decide players' reactions for them – after meeting the first two characters in Chapter I and garnering first impressions of them, I was rather taken by one, and found the other a too naïve. My character’s internal monologue seemed rather biased against the character I was interested in pursuing as a romantic / friend interest – and after replaying the game, it seems like a lot of the internal reactions play into the assumption that the player planned to visit the maid café with the first character. The result I’ll internally go ‘Thank god, Rook actually said what I was thinking, and I like that he’s honest and straightforward’ and my character will internally go ‘Wow, Rook is blunt and rude! That must just be his nature I guess…’
The game gets better about this in later chapters, but doesn’t ever quite shake the tendency.
The game has excellent art assets. Currently characters are static, but the developer has commissioned an expanded set of expressions, which will do a lot to enhance the quality of the game. The aesthetics and character designs are decidedly very 'furry' in ways that most games with anthropomorphic characters usually aren't (think bizarre fur colors, large expressive eyes, heterochromatic eyes, atypical species), but I'm a sucker for that stuff, and I imagine that the target audience will be people who embrace that characteristic of the game as well. Whoever they're hiring for this, they're good, and I look forward to seeing what the expanded poses / reaction images will do to bring these characters to life!
A few gameplay / input suggestions for improvement: If a simple menu could be added to the corner of the screen to give access to save and quit functions, it would enhance the gameplay experience significantly. Currently, the game allows a soft reset with F5, but it's very hit or miss whether mashing / holding escape will bring up a menu that allows me to quit or create a new save, or whether it will instead power through dialogue at lightning speed. Because the game explicitly encourages savescumming, it would also be useful to make it easier to scroll through dialogue-heavy segments without accidentally registering a hit when a player decision comes up; on replays, I've had to reload multiple times because holding 'A' on my controller or 'ESC' on the keyboard would immediately power through a player decision box (frequently the choice I had decided to revisit in the first place). It represents a similar problem for save slots – when the save screen pops up as it occasionally does between legs of the plot, if you’re still holding A it will automatically override the most recent save, similar to the dialogue option problem above.
What I found strong about the game as it currently exists (2/16/16): it has good art assets, a good setting, the characters have distinct personalities, and despite all of the misgivings above I found myself playing it from start to finish in a single session. The developer has done a great job of drumming together great artistic and musical talent, they've created an engaging setting, and although the prose and dialogue can be weak at times, the plot is solid. Despite everything said above I will be waiting with bated breath to see how the plot continues to develop, and hope that the promising beginning develops into an involved plot that explores the characters we've met and helps us to understand their motivations, how they tick, and the world they live in better. And I'll be waiting to see if future updates will give me the opportunity to date my sweetheart Rook, who despite things I've learned in a different timeline is still my endearingly straightforward crush.
Good luck, Minor/Major team! I'm legitimately looking forward to the continuing installments of the game.

So, I've played this for a bit more an hour and probably will never play it again. Here's the reason why:
First the positive points that goes for this game:
- Nice drawings of the characters, all look good
- Musik does fit the context of the text
- ... nothing else that I can say.
Now, it would be better to not to call this a game, it is a visual novel. It does claim it and does fulfill that.
But it also claims to be inspired by greats like Steins;Gate, Tales of Symphonia and Persona 4. Biggest and most devestating problem with all that is while Steins;Gate is a visual novel, Tales of Symphonia and Persona 4 are games. While the stories of the later two are good, they are reinforced and made great through play, interaction. Major/Minor tries to use those stories as a kind of template as a visual novel.
From what I could bear of the whole story it felt like, those stories mashed together and then put into the mechanics of Steins;Gate. It felt like a parody of the very enjoyable stories of those two games. Much of the narrative is bland. It mostly works as a info dump. The thoughts of the character you play as is undistinguishable from the narrative. No person that has a personality thinks like that. The reader/player is a puppet master that directs the puppets down the path he/she wants. Those puppets are characters, fully developed characters. Here it felt like I'm looking at cardboard cutouts of stock characters.
It may all just be a failing of writing there though as to me, the writing compares to lower-grade mediocore fanfictions. The whole story even starts out making the main character like a Mary Sue. To use fanfiction tags: godlike, AU, OC.
It all doesn't blend well together. It might have been that I, myself, had some higher expectations of Major/Minor and it failed to even come close to the expectations but even with the expectations of it not being engaging, this product would have failed to meet that expectation. It felt insulting to the place this whole plot plays in, Tokyo, Japan.
So I would not recommend this game. My reasons are stated above.

Castle Story is a fun little game, send out your troops to gather resources from the mine or chop down some trees snd use it all to build you very own fort or go all out and aim for a full feldged castle!
Survival mode is lots of fun, gather and build during the day, defend your base and workers at night from an ever increasing number of enemies.
Sounds perfect right? Well this is an Early Access title still under development and it is not without its fair share of bugs, some of them game breaking.
Sometimes your workers will get stuck, path finding can be tricky for the little guys at times, although it was much improved upon in a recent patch. Also pre plan your build because trying to dismantle your structures can be a tricky business, there has been many times I've allocated a block to be destroyed only for it to be ignored, they game can't make up its mind if it exists or not, I can't build on top of it or through it but I can't delete it either, it stays forever as a red "delete me" hologram.
Over all Castle Story is fun, animations are nice and the general look fo the game can be considered "cute", i'd recommend this game for Tower Defence fans, the pros outweigh the cons.

PS: If you want to play this game on a keyboard and a mouse? than I think there is no trouble for you.
- Another thing what I've noticed was you don't have Achievements on the PC version, It's not really a big deal but when I played it on my Playstation 3 you had the Achievements what made the game also enjoyable.

For me  ''this is the best Call Of Duty of all time''  if you love playing Zombies and Story mode and want to Experience the WW2? Than i recommend this game for you.

WWII oversaturation. Call of Duty, Medal of Honor, Battlefield, Wolfenstein...franchises have milked that war hard. By this point in the franchise, I was pretty darn tired of it. I completed the game, didn't care about competitive multiplayer, and thought the zombie mode was kinda okay, but a bit rough around the edges. I don't ask for every game to innovate, but World War II has been done to death. If a dev is going to make another WWII game, there needs to be something clever and interesting to get me excited. CoD WWII has been announced, and my apathy is tangible.
World at War isn't an awful game, but if you showed me several screenshots from it, mixed with screenshots of other WWII shooters than came out in the 2000s, I could not tell you which screenshots came from this game. Aside from originating zombie mode (I think?), CoD: World at War was yet another forgettable entry into the piles and piles of WWII games that I never thought I would get sick of, but here i am. =/

Ahh gaming.
Such a wonderful hobby, and one that I have dedicated many, many years to. So many that now a-days many gaming activities, whilst still fun, seem a bit bland.
I remember the days when I would retire to bed, some three hours after I should have done, because I needed just one more turn to complete the Great Pyramids, and then in bed I would dream about defeating Sarevok, or have nightmares about my tank being killed by a spearman.
Gaming has been a wonderful mistress, but I feared that the days of being so immersed that I dreamt of games were long since passed.
But last night I had a dream.
I dreamed I was playing what seemed to be a simple platform game. Levels suspended in the ether with the simple task of making it to the exit. There were patrolling robots, force shields and laser turrets, standard gaming fare, which you could disable with a quick blast of your hand gun. The controls, initially a bit twitchy, but with a bit of practice would see you wall sliding and leaping bottomless chasms with ease, gliding around the level like a gazelle on speed.
However the levels themselves were only the introduction, the real fun began once you had completed the level, once you knew how to "do it" as it were, for at this point the clock is unlocked and the world opens up.
What was once a simple platform game, becomes the ultimate parkour simulator, with times being stored on a central server for the world to observe.
The level of satisfaction as your level time drops from ten minutes to five, to three as you fine tune your sprints, dodge the lasers, discover the superleap that will shave a fraction of a second off your level time is something that I havn't experienced in a long time. The frustration at when you miss a jump to plumet to your death, coupled with the elation at executing the perfect wall slide is only matched by the amazement you will feel that your two minute level time is still a minute and a half slower than the top of the leaderboard.
I have no freaking idea how they are doing it! But I was damn well determined to find out.
Its cell shaded art style seemed the perfect choice for the atmosphere the game was going for, and whislt it seemed to have some bobbins story involving you in a coma whilst your astral projection took part in the game proper.
Of course I immediately thought that I was reminiscing of Mirrors Edge, but this would have been like comparing Wipe-out to Gran Turismo.
But Discalceaterabbit, you all cry out in unison, surely you are describing indie game "Cloudbuilt" by Coilworks,  You must have played that and not had a dream at all!
Pfft, don't be ridiculous.

I gave this game another try one year after I last played it, and I really enjoy it now. The concept is simple: You gotta go fast from A to B (Parkour, essentially). Obstacles will be your least concern, however; you'll face various enemies which will quite often make you fall off the platform you're standing on - if they don't outright shoot you. Each map features various alternative paths that you can take; for instance, you can try to avoid your enemies, or you can choose the direct approach and shoot them before they shoot you. Quite often you can also choose between a risky, but fast path or a safer, slower one; whatever suits you more.
You also have a jet pack to aid you, but use it with caution - Running out of fuel when there's no ground below you is not fun. Speaking of which: Since the game is set in a surrealistic dream-world, there are no laws of physics to confine what a map can look like, which allows for a big variety of map layouts.
But back to my first point: Why did I quit this game for a year after a mere 3 hours of playing? The answer is: It's hard. If you're new to the game (and even if you're not), you're going to die a lot. This causes a lot of frustration, but in turn makes it jsut as rewarding if you actually succeed.
Therefore: Play this game if you like extremely fast-paced gameplay and are not afraid of failure. Other pros include a great soundtrack and having multiple alternative endings.

Well, this was a snake in the grass.
Sonic the Hedgehog was always kind of a sloppy platformer. It sold itself on speed, but often delivered right angles, hazards, and enemies that slowed you down... when it wasn't throwing you underwater or forcing you to hang on bars, anyway. It's memorable for its colorful graphics and sense of wonder, but the design was always pretty loose. For the record, I've only played through as Lilac (the Dragon) on normal difficulty to story completion, but I think that's enough to pass judgement, and seems intended as the core game.
And so Freedom Planet sells itself as a Sonic-styled retro platformer with colorful furry characters and, to some extent, that holds true. They definitely know how to do a game that feels like Sonic, coming from Sonic modding, and so Freedom Planet at least feels like a Sonic game for the first half or so. There's also some influence from the Japanese studio Treasure in some of the boss design (there's one that may as well have been lifted right from Gunstar Heroes), and just the lack of modern upgrades - what you start with is what you get.
Unlike Sonic, thought, it requires more thought, for better or worse, thanks to a power bar that's used up by special moves. And honestly, that's a bit unsatisfying, but at least lets you do power charges with proper forethought. But it works against the notion of implusive, speedy play, and instead sometimes forced me to literally stop and wait for my power bar to fill before launching myself through a platforming challenge, and that's a problem. Recharges for that bar are few and far between, so expect to occassionally just have Lilac park herself while waiting for that bar to charge.
The bosses are more elaborate than the original Sonic games (once again, the Treasure influence), and that's where the trouble starts. In the latter half of the game, the bosses become tremendous difficulty spikes that require study and rote memorization- unless you know what they're going to unleash, they'll throw full-screen attacks that will slice off half your health bar without you noticing. And no, there's no dashing to snag that one ring like Sonic does and retain your life. You beat that boss with the health bar you've got. And to be clear, I died 70 times in Freedom Planet, and about 90% of that was in the latter half of the game. Bosses frequently deal out a lot of damage or do screen-clearing attacks, and unless you've managed that power bar for a moment of dash invincibility, you'll often be at their mercy. And this is on "normal" difficulty. I hesitate to see what controller-breaking misery awaits on "hard". It's indicative that some of the final boss fights don't start with the boss themselves, but instead throw you through a quick gauntlet of enemies that can weaken you before what are already punishing foes to face. It certainly doesn't encourage me to play with the other characters, or, indeed, play this game again.
The misery doesn't begin and end with the frustrating boss fights. In the game latter half of the game, it takes a darker turn thematically, with explicit torture, death, and body horror, and Lilac howling in constant pain or rage in each cutscene, or moaning in despair. It's a bizarre turn that's remarkably unpleasant, and though it doesn't go into the depths of many grim modern platformers, it comes without warning. It doesn't help that Brevon, the villain, is just a charmless dealer of misery, and I sighed every time he came on screen to gloat. Yes, I get it, devs, he's a bad bad guy. He also looks goofy and is written hammily in the worst way. Having a Saturday morning cartoon villain burn a character's skin off is... I don't know what they were thinking. It doesn't work.
Also, why the hell does it only save at the start of a level and not within its individual stages? Why does it bother having a life system? I didn't realize a level wasn't complete at one point and quit out, only to find out I had to complete all the stages and a very hard boss on top of that. It's particularly bizarre because it lets you continue infinitely, but still doesn't save at that point. I'm not sure what the point of all that is, other than to waste my time in redoing sections the game should know perfectly well that I've done.
All that in mind, I can't recommend Freedom Planet. It will appeal to some, and for those hungering for another Sonic game deeply, you'll probably find it worth your while. It's frustrating to me, because the designers obviously know what they were doing, but just took it in ther wrong direction. But it doesn't quite have the wonder or charm those games did, instead trying to drag Sonic- er, Lilac kicking and screaming into an adult's world of hardcore challenges and grim themes. And in that, that shine wears off and the sloppiness that Sonic has always had is the only thing left showing through.

Disclosure: I was gifted this game in return for an honest review. Check the "Final Verdict" section for the review summary.
Freedom Planet was created by GalaxyTrail and is the only released game by the developer as of the writing of this review. This game was apparently started as a Sonic fan-game, but the developer wanted to create something new and Sonic inspired, as opposed to a direct fan-game.
I'll go over a few aspects of the game below and rate them on a scale of 1 to 10.
Story/Writing: 4/10
-----------------------
There may be spoilers here, but I'll try to keep it spoiler free.
The story is a pretty basic. Ancient creatures used their power to create a crystal. Bad guy wants crystal. Good guys want crystal more. Nothing wrong with the story, it's just a by-the-numbers storyline. The writing for the dialogue is pretty lackluster. All of the characters kind of sound like each other in the way they are written. The voice actors do a good job of changing this up some with their inflections, but if you were to just be reading the dialogue you could change around all of the names with what's being said and not really see any difference.
All in all, though, you can play through the "Classic" mode which is basically just the levels without the story. I'd recommend playing through it once, at least, in "Adventure" mode so you can know the character motivations and what-not.
Design: 6/10
----------------------------
The sprite work on this game is very nice with a lot of detail in the backgrounds. There are many different enemy types and all have decent designs and their attacks and movements tie into the designs very nicely. The main characters look decent but do feel kind of ameteurish in their design. Sometimes they look great and other times they seem rather wonky. It kind of goes back and forth.  I'll get back into some of the design of the characters a little later.
Gameplay: 6/10
-------------------------
I really wanted to give this a higher rating, like an 8, but there are a couple of definite problems. The controls are really tight and there is a lot of variation in the gameplay style of each of the playable characters. They all have their own unique abilities and ways to traverse the levels and that is a lot of fun, and really ups the replay value. The thing that brings this score down is that the last few levels and a couple of the bosses are extremely cheap. Playing through the game I loved the level design and how expansive the levels are, given the 2D platformer style, but the last few levels (namely the 4 "acts" of the final level) get rid of the good level design in favor of throwing as many enemmies onto the screen as possible to create "difficulty." It got to a point where it was no longer fun and just a frustrating mess. Outside of those final "acts" the gameplay is varied and feels very balanced most of the time.
Sound Design: 6/10
--------------------------
Music: 8/10 - The music in this game is very nice. It hearkens back to the music of Sonic 3 & Knuckles with tracks matching the level designs nicely, multiple tracks per level that accompany area transitions and the sound effects are enjoyable and fitting.
Voice Acting: 5/10 - The voice acting is alright. Not particularly great, but definitely not terrible. It's a small cast of (at the time) ameteur voice actors. Some have gone on to do work with Funimation on anime dubs. Overall, I thought everyone did a fine job and I didn't really feel like the voices were annoying or unfitting.
Sound Quality: 3/10 - The biggest issue with the voice acting is the variance in recording quality and volume. It might be, given that this is a small, independent developer, that each voice actor was recording their lines on their own computer/recording system, thus giving it the variance. It was a little annoying to have two or three characters talking to each other in a scene with the volume and sound quality rising and dipping as they each talked.
Final Verdict: 7/10 [Final score edited. Less weight given to "Story/Writing" rating.]
----------------------
This is a solid game with a few issues. Some can be overlooked and others are a little more frustrating. The music is fun and poppy and fits all of the areas and the gameplay is enough like Sonic that you'll feel very comfortable, but has lots of variations and fun ways for the characters to fight the enemies. The writing is "meh," and there are some very cheap levels in regards to difficulty, but otherwise this game is a great addition to anyone's collection if they love 90's platformers.
Bits & Bobs
-----------------
This is just a section for various thoughts that don't really reflect any of the ratings.
~ I wish the game had gone into the backstory of dragons. Lilac is a dragon (or a half dragon?) but she's obviously an anthropomorphic character that doesn't look like a "standard" dragon. This is fine, but they show in-game that there used to be dragons that look like "standard" dragons. Would have been nice to get more story about what happened to them and why Lilac looks so different.
~ On the subject of character designs, I thought Milla was a rabbit, but according to Wikipedia she's a dog? I don't know. *shrug*
~ I also wish there was more information on way the governments/countries/whatever work in the game. They list three places of note which I thought at first were cities, but maybe they're countries? There is a Magister over one of them and a Mayor over another and I don't think they talked about the third one other than that it exists. There is also obviously some power struggles between them, but it was barely mentioned outside of characters bad-mouthing the other cities/countries/provinces/whatevers.
~I found out that if you hold the "down" button and press the "special attack" button when in cutscenes that it replaces the cutscene with bloopers, which is great. This has given me a reason to go back through Adventure mode. I watched a couple on Youtube and they were pretty funny. The characters are animated to follow the bloopers as well. Awesome!
~ According to the internet there is a sequel in the works, but the last info given appears to be from late 2015 to early 2016 without any new info. Based on the initial trailer it looks like it would be be great and that the writing might be improved. There was new art and sprite work that looked really nice! Hopefully they finish it. I would definitely buy it.

I admit I wanted this game when it first came out. It went on my wishlist, which I use as a "buy later" list and I forgot all about it until my cousin bought it for me as a gift.
The only thing I regret about this game is not getting it sooner.
This game has an excellent running gameplay style that will remind you of certain games with a certain blue guy with red sneakers who, let's face it, hasn't been doing games in this style as of late. If you've played any of the older Sonic Games, the playstyle will be right at home.
This game doesn't mimic the old SEGA style of play however, merely the asthetics. Instead of running and jumping, the game adds an attack button and life counter, and THAT changes everything. The combat mechanic changes the game from stale but still fun to innovative and exciting in half a heartbeat. The mechanics of the attack button are intuitive and fun and the fact that each player has a different style of play makes the game very fun.
Graphics are cartoony and remeniscient of the oldschool while keeping its own new style. The story and graphics match the gameplay seamlessly and the music binds it together into a whole that I honestly enjoy more than I probably should.
The only bad thing I have to say about this game, like I mentioned earlier, is that I should've gotten earlier. This game is a definite must buy for fans of Sonic who are looking for the old school gameplay and a little something new.

I picked this game up during the Black Friday Sale in 2014 for $10. I have to say I was pleasantly surprised. The game is well polished and looked very clean. I found the enviornments and ambience to be fairly well done and enjoyable. The voice acting, characters, and scrolling combat text all reminded me heavily of Bioshock Infinite (might even be the same actors).
The loot progression system steals from Wow/Diablo, right now to the color rarety. It can be a little overwhelming, but they have a smart system which will do auto upgrades for you, however, it isn't perfect. For the number cruncher and experimenter, I think you will really enjoy the spell crafting system. There are small guantlet type encounters where they will reward you with 10-20 spell crafting items all at once. This was something to look forward too every level, and I found it kept me engaged.
The gameplay itself is fun, and you feel like a badass mage, however the crafting system encourages one spell progression, so it can get a little repetitive constantly spamming the same three or four spells. The boss encounters were somewhat lame and fairly easy with the same dodge and shoot mechanics over and over, but I still liked the game.
Overall I would give the game a 7/10 and I think there is a solid foundation here for some really good sequels if they do them right. Definitely worth buying if it is on sale.

This game is the bomb diggity, even after 13+ years.
PROS:
++Great, mostly balanced gameplay
++Good looking 2.5D graphics
++Endless amount of mods and assets

++Runs pretty well on nearly anything
CONS:
--Hard to get working properly (I suggest looking for the SC4Launcher and 4GB patch if you want to really boost how the game works)
--Can crash a lot without the right settings
--Mods are difficult to install w/o Steam Workshop support
--The simulation is often finicky, but granted, there was only so much devs could do back then (pickup the Network Addon Mod for improved traffic simulation)
--The tutorial isn't super-helpful in helping you understand how the regional simulation works
Overall, if you're looking at this vs Cities: Skylines (and have a PC that can run C:S), go pick up Cities. It's a newer game with generally a more powerful and realistic simulation. However, I highly suggest dropping this into your wishlist and waiting for a sale, which is quite often on this title, because this game has a certain charm that I don't think any city builder has or ever will replicate.

I love the graphics and the concept, but the user interface is too complicated.  Too many m enus and too many buttons to push.  A few suggestions that might make the game easier to play...maybe some of them are already into the game, but I couldnt get far enough to find them.  I only played for about 5 hours but couldnt seem to make much progress.
1) Pressing space bar everytime you want to move the camera is a pain.  Scrolling could be accomplished more easily by moving the mouse cursor to the edges of the screen.  Camera rotation should be as simple as pressing the right mouse button and moving the mouse.
2) Too many menu options make it difficult to wrap ones head around the game.  For example, there are two build options. Each build option has its own menus.  Why not put them all under the same menu, and order them from simple to more complex.  Its the same with mining.    There is mining for the ground, and then a mining menu for mining cliffs.  It would be easier to put them all under the same menu.
3) Creating tasks can be really fun, but not for simple things like harvesting wood.  In order to harvest wood, you have to create a wood harvesting zone and then send workers to harvest the wood.  The zone is currently too small and harvests only a few trees.  What would be really neat would be to left click on a worker, hold down the left mouse button to bring up the worker menu, then mouse button up to select the "harvest wood" option.  The menu dissappears and the cursor changes to an axe.  Left mouse button down where you want the center of the zone and then mouse button up when the zone is large enough (basically create a custom size circle by dragging the mouse).  You can do something similar with mining, although you could have a couple of different shapes (circle, square, straight line, etc)
4)  The AI is messed up.  I dont have any suggestions there because I cant see the code, however, the little buggers keep pausing while doing tasks, If I had to guess I would say that they are stuck in a code loop.
These are just a few suggestions.  I wrote code to pay for my college degree, and have been designing software for over 25 years.  One thing i learned is that the interface is everything.   This is a REALLY COOL game but its just too difficult to play.

I paid close to full price on this when it was first released on Steam. From the trailers, it's obviouly a great looking game, amazing concept - who doesn't want to build castles and an army?
Pros:
-build a base, be creative, build a castle with your minions (not a lot of games allow you to do this)
-endless survival, resource gathering, day and night cycles
-minions with different roles -> archers, warriors, peons:unarmed
Cons:
-AI, although "improved", still have collision and task issues. Will get "stuck" or "confused" as to which task to continue with there is a number of tasks scattered throughout the map. It's not very "intelligent"
-game still "lags" many waves in on survival - lags as in, your minions get "stuck"/confused but game timer keeps going.
-AI AI AI. If they just fix the AI, this game would be bearable. All they would need to do is add more building blocks and unit types.
As an early access game, when it was first released, I was forgiving in that it was an early access game. The concept was there, the delivery, not so much. Fast forward a year and a 6 months, and a tutorial (very basic) was added. AI was improved - yes, improved, but still has issues, albiet less than before. Menu and resources have been "tweaked".
They make a lot of updates, but like other reviewers have said, it feels like the sum of all the updates have been very meager. They are not wrong - the sum of all the updates, even though the developers consistently work on the game, hasn't amounted to anything impactful/meaningful. Their design mentality is a little OCD, release a small update to gameplay, spend the next 2-3 months patching it; repeat.
But that's okay - the devs have a commitment to "finishing" this game, even if it takes an additional 2-3 years. I can see that they want to release a great game when it's finally finished. The current state of the game doesn't help their cause 1.5 years later. Then again, the risk these developers take by not finishing this game and or releasing a subpar one as a "finished" product is something that they'll live with forever, and their names and reputations will be tarnished as well.
Based on the current state of the game, I would value the game at $2 or $3, with goodwill factored in the price due to the future promise of the game. You can buy a lot of amazing/fun games for $2-3. Your mileage may vary

Castle Story has been in development for well over a year and in that time not a large amount of progress has been made. However with that being said I believe there is real promise with this game, all be it if it gets finished! There are some things which make it very unique and some which make it mainstream.

Cons:

- Limited Gamemodes
- Very basic Tutorial (Controls are very simple but was lack of proper tutorial, can be frustrating)
- Limited building options (2x2 Block | 1X1 Block | Arch Block | Wooden Pillar | Wooden Plank)
- Time period of development is worrying (Over a year and not a large amount of progress)
- Pricing (£15/$20) Is very constly for an almost Alpha/Beta
Overall the game is fun to play for a Short/Medium amount of time however given the number of issue's addressed above  I would hold off buying it untill there is improvement or unless it is discounted down to around £4-8/$12. However because of these issues I would have to rate it probably a 4/5 out of 10!

So as McJapan goes on, we find out a lot of conflict is actually waiting in Japan, but thankfully not too much. An odd murder, an odd otter, and an odd cafe. Cool, I can deal with that. My gripe is that the conflict between the characters and not the action in the world seems to be driving at different speeds, leading us to a sobbing character we know nothing about and then are forced to make a decision. It's like a ball and chain, of the two are mismatched, then your effect won't follow through quite was well.
Chapter one ended and I felt happy that it was over. Riddled with, yes fixed, but still glaring issues of run on sentences and an overwhelming amount of detail and repeating sentences that was wholly unnecessary. This was my first impression, and the first part of your game is the most important. Again, i'm not here to just bash and I don't want it to seem that way, but on the subject of bashing...I know every visual novel is different, both in art style and amount of character reaction, each one costing more money and more time to program. I understand a lack of expression changes, but your maid cafe girl had her thumbs switched to the wrong side of her hands when you flipped the image to move her around. After that I started to notice more and more how the images never changed, but were flipped, and even could see when a image was first show to me and I could tell that it was a reverse. A small detail, but one that me a my friends laughed at for a while seeing as so many had their thumbs broken by the reverse fairy. The artwork itself is pleasing to the eye, soft brush use makes the characters appear simple in texture so you can focus more on the important parts of the game and avoid being distracted, but color use is key when designing a character. The assassin's apprentice has a color palette made my head strain trying to understand where it started and where it began.
this artist has the best and simplest ways to design a charater and just by color alone you can see what this person is about, what their personality is and still find it pleasing to the eye. Also if your servant fox character is as poor and in dire straights, maybe avoid hot pink hair on clashing orange and a gold piercing with brown rags for clothes. I can't tell if he's about to get whipped or go to a really weird rave.
Enough about the art. Lastly is the writing itself. It isn't bad. Really, it isn't the worst thing ive ever seen; you convey your intent well and have a few interesting characters running that do keep me in the story. Avoid pitfalls that take a lot of writers down; an easy one to fall into that I myself have trouble with, is trying to build your characters faster than your world, or vice versa. Call it the Lucas effect, and say you have this vast world like Avatar or Star Wars, then decide to never focus on the characters. Or take great heros and villans, then put them in boring worlds. Pacing is the most important part of writing, and I've sorta fallen in love with this game and just want to see it reach it's full potential; the ideas presented are new and refreshing, so don't let hype or just a desire to finish detract from the quality being pushed out.
Overall, I want to see this become better; it has a good foundation and the strength is there, it just needs more polish and time. I can't say I recommend it right now, but if I'm proven wrong in the end, I will gladly take this down and put up a positive review.
As an added note, Klace, if you read this, I have been a write for seven years, if you ever have the want or time, I'd gladly help in shaping the writing out more where I can.

Freedom Planet is a game developed by GalaxyTrail in the style of Classic Sonic the Hedgehog games. However, if you're expecting some really bad Sonic clone with silly OCs and a plot that feels too similar to the game - fear not! Freedom Planet stays consistent with the Sonic style while feeling fresh and new, and is damn fun to play. It really brings some unique things to the table I've never seen a Sonic-style game accomplish before. The game itself is really well made. A ton of love and care went into the creation of.. well, everything. From what started as a Sonic fangame, it sure came far.
The game starts off with two characters, known as Sash Lilac the Water Dragon and Carol Tea - her best friend and a wildcat. The two hear of the Kingdom Stone being stolen and rush off to save it from the clutches of alien invaders and their leader, the power-crazed Lord Brevon. Along the way, you'll meet some cool characters too, but I won't say anything  else due to spoilers!
You'll be able to play as a total of (currently, since I think there's one more in the works) four characters, each with their own unique style of gameplay. Lilac plays similarly enough to Sonic, but with a stamina meter that controls how much of your dragon powers you can use at once. Thankfully this isn't a hinderance unless you're fighting a boss, but even then it's not bad. Carol functions a bit more like Knuckles, being able to wall-jump. When you find an oil can in her stages, she can ride her motorcycle, giving her a nice speed boost and some big time destructive power. Each character has their own bit of a story arc, so you'll want to give them all a try and see what each has to offer.
The game is beautiful in terms of both sound and music. Nothing feels like it's rehashed, and the levels are very diverse. To be honest, the only thing I'd say is similar to Sonic is the gameplay itself, with the exclusion of some story similarities. The stages are all very nicely designed - my favorite is probably Fortune Night. They all come and go pretty easily to Sonic veterans, but each is memorable for their different styles of gameplay. Some stages have memorable mini bosses, others have memorable puzzles, and most combine the two, but keep it fresh and unique every time, so they're not a bore. The music is very nicely composed and is pleasing to the ear, and the graphics themselves are very colorful and well-done. The Genesis aesthetic is definitely present. Oh and as a nice treat, the game is fully voiced and subtitled.
However, if story mode isn't your thing, there's a standard gameplay mode without the cutscenes, which plays more like a traditional Sonic game. To be honest, though, I definitely prefer the story mode - it's fun to learn about the characters and see why and what they're fighting for.
Tl;dr, if you like platformers in the Sonic style and want something familiar but fresh and fun, pick this game up! It's worth the money.

After playing this game several hours, I can say for a discounted price it's quite worth it. Don't expect too much from it though.
The centre of the gameplay is crafting. You find tons of parts to craft your spells. You first start off with just 1 spell-"element" and gain another with each level you finish. By using them you can level them up and choose between 3 things to upgrade which are damage, critical chance and critical effect.
The whole crafting thing is pretty much too complex to explain in detail here. With wrong crafted spells, bosses can become hard in a dark souls kind of way. With well crafted spells you might be able to kill them in under 2 minutes.
The fun really lies in discovering what spells you can create for your special needs.
Basically there are 3 type of spells you can cast. One of which is a offensive ball or ray. there are different types of those too. The other one is an AOE which can have many different effects and a shield (which I barely use ever so it's pretty useless to me).
The story doesn't really get rolling and isn't that exciting. The levels - although not open world but very linear - are beautifully crafted thanks to the Cryengine 3. Enemies spawn every few meters and you gotta defeat them. New enemies are introduced only about every level and there is much re-use in enemies.
For less than 10€ I'd still recommend it.

As one that has always loved playing mage in RPGs and other games, this is like a gift from the heavens, or at least in theory.
Don't get me wrong, I have loved every second of this game so far, from the slaughtering of helpless undead to defeating powerful bosses and learning the rich crafting system.
However, the game does indeed have some flaws.
The combats is, although fast paced and good looking, kinda repetitive. You don't get bored, but it's not varying battles or something like more open world games. Here you got 3 spells and then 2-3 variations of them, depending on your spell-setup.
Also,the variety of enemies isn't that great. You usually (as far as I've come in the game) just face off against some skeletons, zombies or the cultists that control them. The only exception is bosses and mini-bosses.
But enough about the bad, focus on what's great!
The graphics and setting of the world is stunningly beautiful, with varied environments and views.
It's actually fun to craft once you start getting the hang of the system in use, and there are great posibilities here. Sure, I don't know it all yet, but I'm getting there!
And of course it's always a pleasure to burn your enemies to death in a great blast, only to raise them as your loyal servants the next moment!
All in all I highly reccomend it for most people. It is story-driven and kinda narrowed down, so if an open world is your highest wish, this might not be for you though.
This is how mages should be, always badass!

Добро пожаловать в Empire Bay. Солнечное место, полное возможностей для тех, кто может их взять. Да, я говорю с тобой Вито и Джо. Да, ты тоже мистер Винчи. Я вижу тебя там Альберто Клементе. Да, это верно Карло Фальконе. Я могу продолжать называть этих парней снова и снова, потому что эта игра была заполнена этими джентльменами.
Vito Scalleta устал от бюрократического бульвара, поэтому подделали документы о ранении, чтобы он мог покинуть Европу и вернуться прямо к Джо, так что эти двое могут вступить в работу, встать в иерархии мафии, взлететь в небо по семейной лестнице, чтобы он мог получить то, что все хотят.
Эта игра может предложить вам 15 невероятных удивительных глав, полных отличных действий, роликов, скруток, сюжетных элементов и саги об одном мальчике из Сицилии, который хотел быть лучше своего пьяного трудолюбивого отца. Когда он выходил из лодки в детстве и впервые видел члена мафии, он знал, что однажды он будет таким. Мне нравится история тем, что она не сразу прыгает в семью, и он действительно должен проявить себя, прежде чем попасть в неё.
Некоторые из вас могут сказать, что, поскольку игра была такой короткой, это было не очень хорошо. Но лично я чувствую, что разработчики хотели показать, что жизнь мафиози очень короткая.Тогда мы еще не знали о том что Вито будет в mafia 3 .  поэтому вышеприведенное утверждение все же верное.
Empire Bay поистине прекрасна, большая и полная приятных мест. Различная одежда, оружие, мышины, варианты настроек или просто круиз по городу - это опыт. Должен признаться, однажды вечером я обнаружил, что блуждаю по городу пол часа прежде чем поехать на основное задание.
С другой стороны, правда, что из опционного спектра Empire Bay не так много предложить. Места, куда идти и что делать, очень ограничены, и для некоторых людей «бесплатная поездка» очень скоро повторится.
Саундтрек и музыка на протяжении всей игры очень хорошо подобраны, начиная с основной темы и заканчивая каждой из 130 песен, доступных в игре.
DLC. Я не собираюсь входить в это так много. Играл в длс ещё на пиратке, но мне действительно понравилось только одно DLC, и я думаю, вы уже знаете, что это такое - Joe's Adventure. Это добавит дополнительные 5-7 часов, зависит от того, как вы его играете, и покажет вам годы, когда Вито был в отъезде.
