While often compared to Sonic the Hedgehog, as someone's who's played a majority of those games, I can safely assure you that Freedom Planet manages to blow the entire library of it's inspiration out of the water in terms of raw gameplay, polish, and content.  Though I've yet to invest enough time into the game to experience all it has to offer, I can safely assure you that if you want fast-paced side scrolling action, you're going to regret not having this game in library.
While the art-style and use of anthropomorphic characters might put off some (and arouse several others) the questionable storytelling is easy enough to ignore  and, though the copious amount of cutscenes can indeed bog down the gameplay if you plan on forcing yourself to watch it all, can be skipped at your leisure.  Though presented well enough to keep my interest, it is a VERY simple story, and far from anything to write home about.
Gameplay wise the only issue I had with Freedom Planet stemmed from it's intense stage 8 difficulty curve. I say curve, I mean more like a mountain, one that gets bigger and steeper the higher you climb.  While I'm not adverse to hard-as-nails gameplay by any means, the sudden upswing of difficulty, combined with some frankly absurd damage sponginess, can turn them into pacing annihlators.
Nowhere near bad enough to invalidate my hearty recommendation, but it's definitely something to note.  Players inexperienced with 2D sidescrollers and high speed action should definitely consider scaling down the difficulty.

Like Shovel Knight did for Mega Man and Axiom Verge did for Metroid, sometimes a fake retro game goes beyond a mere homage. Freedom Planet not only captures the complete heart and soul of classic Sonic the Hedgehog, but contributes its own ideas that both improve upon the classic Sonic formula and are different enough to justify it being an original work.
The game looks, sounds, and plays like a top-tier Game Boy Advance title. The sprite work and animation are heartfelt and too good for their own good. The music is phenomenal; every single track is an earworm while still setting a strong mood for the stage. There are huge cutscenes with professional-level voice-acting (and numerous ways to skip/disable them if you just want to play the game). Stage design and gameplay are spot-on Sonic, with multiple paths and hidden secrets that reward exploration and experimentation. The engine is fairly bug-free as well; aside from a couple insignificant clipping glitches, I found no real problems during casual play.
There’s just not much I can think of to say about this game aside from gushing. It exceeded all of my expectations.
One thing I might criticize is the difficulty level; on Normal difficulty, the game gets very unforgiving near the end. One late-game level has some instant death traps that
kill you if you don’t already know they’re coming. The final normal level is just outright long (speedrun par is 12 minutes), and will force you to re-run long stretches of land you die in the wrong places. Many of the late bosses are unforgiving and will force you to take note of their patterns if you want to survive for more than thirty seconds.
However, this is all mitigated by the fact that difficulty levels exist; if Normal is too frustrating, you can turn the difficulty down to Easy or even Casual, and all your rage will go away. Even then, death is a slap on the wrist and using a continue won’t even make you lose your level checkpoint! I’m also willing to forgive the instant death traps because, compared to Sonic games, Freedom Planet has
in the entire game. But that’s not all; there are also no dreaded underwater segments! Unlike Sonic, the Freedom Planet characters can
and don’t just jump around with slow gravity while underwater. With this in mind, I think one level with one set of instant death traps is not only acceptable, but adds a nice sense of tension that is very fitting to the level in question.
If I’m going to honestly criticize one thing about this game, it’s that it’s technically unfinished. One playable character who was promised as a Kickstarter stretch goal is still not implemented, and another character hasn’t made it out of beta. The missing characters leave some odd holes in game design; for instance, you can collect elemental orbs scattered around the levels during gameplay that don’t seem to do anything – they were meant to be ammo for one of the missing characters. Another of the missing characters was patched in very, very late after the game’s release, and sports some strange bugs – attempting to skip one of her cutscenes will skip the entire stage.
But I’m just nitpicking at this point. This game is a polished, beautiful, adorable, and satisfying adventure. Achievement hunters can expect about 25 hours of gameplay and an achievement list that is fair, nicely-paced, and emphasizes the game’s strengths. Overall, this game belongs in the library of any fan of indie gaming, retro gaming, or Sonic the Hedgehog. 9.5 / 10!

Don't trust the trailer. It does zero justice to how wickedly awesome this game is. If you feel the need to get a better taste of the game before you buy, download the demo instead. Is free. :)
The game's soundtrack is awesome, the environments are beautiful, the gameplay is fluid. Coming from many a Sonic game, Freedom Planet's rethinking of what was once the Sonic formula is refreshing and enjoyable - most notably, the fact that Rings have changed to conventional health and the fact that attacks now have to be deliberate on both sides makes gameplay flow wonderfully.
I actually really like the story as well. Brevon is obviously, almost painfully, Saturday-Morning Cartoon evil, but many of the other characters are deep, compelling, and nuanced. Lilac has to balance her heroic valor and mythic identity with a desire to just be a normal teenage girl; Carol has to wade through her friend's determination and her own less-than-honorable past simply to find acceptance; Milla (who actually *acts* like a dog) is trying to cope with the loss of her parents; Torque has to carry a charge that only he knows about, because those with power don't trust him; Spade and Dail have to cope with the untimely murder of their father; Serpentine wants to overcome his physical limitations; Mayor Zao of Shang Mu wants people to recognize him despite his height. And Brevon, shallow as he is, plays to these - making false promises that he can get them what they want, and when they reject him, telling them that because of their guilt and shame, they have no room to retaliate against him. That's a deep, beautiful story that I can get behind any day - I willingly watch the cutscenes, even when they run long, because the story is so good. I can't say I like the ending fully, but it doesn't drop too far from what happens prior.
If there is anything that I don't like much about Freedom Planet, it's that it's quite *buggy* in some places. Lilac and Carol tend to play pretty well without incident, but especially with Milla (and even in a few sections as Lilac), I encounter platforming zips that send me shooting upward through solid platforms whenever I do seemingly normal actions, such as picking up a powerup when I have slightly not enough room above me. There are also some problems with cutscene skips and sequence breaks, and the cards screen also has some issues with navigation.
But overall, I would heartily recommend this game. You won't regret it in the slightest.

I finally got around to playing and beating Freedom Planet recently, and felt my opinion of the game was thoroughly formed enough to review it. Bear in mind I have ONLY beaten Lilac's version of story mode ( or Adventure, since its called that in-game ).
I remember when this was coming together, there was a lot of buzz behind it. Most of what I saw being "Finally a good Sonic game maybe?", which while being kinda funny, wasn't totally innacurate a description and honestly still isn't to a degree.
But now let's get down to the nitty-gritty of the pros and cons of this whatchamacallit. Bear in mind these are based on my -personal- experiences and is completely subjective.
NOTE: This game has been out a while now, and some things I talk about might include SPOILERS. So if you don't want to get spoiled in any which way, I don't suggest reading this review.
Pros:
-Arcade Aesthetic:
This game oozes it. It feels like it could have been ripped from an arcade cabinet, and I easily could see it being displayed and played in one. The sound effects to the animations of things really give off that flashy "Come look at this exciting thing" vibe.
-Good physics:
Again, I have only played as Lilac, so the other characters might be atrocious, who knows! Lilac handled very well though. INot too floaty, but not broken. It felt like I was playing, well, an older Sonic game for the most part.
-Decent Controls:
Lilac also responded very well to nearly every controller input. Never felt once like she was zipping wherever or doing whatever she wanted If I wanted her to do a move, she would do it.
-Story:
The story had a cheesy, B-movie charm to it....mostly. It could range from that to being rather... well, lets just say the thing that killed it though unfortunately will be addressed in the cons section later. If it was purely done in text, it would have been better.
-Music/sound effects:
Music was pretty good! What can I say, it was very much like the Genesis and the arcade. The sound effects were also satisfying and popped really well.
-Artwork:
Honestly its very well done. Its gorgeous and eye-catching. Wonderful work on that!
And now of course, here are the cons. I got a lot of gripes with these.
Cons:
-Volume:
This game is LOUD. Holy cow. I have the music volume in-game down to 50%, and my computer volume to 8% ( using headphones ) for this to be tolerable. The thing is too, this did -not- lower the volume of the sound effects, where were some of the biggest offenders, since stuff is constantly going on sound effects are playing -all the time-. If you're trying to talk to someone or stream this game, good luck hearing them as it makes hearing anything else a real issue.
-Voice acting:
It feels like they really tried, honest and truly. A lot of the voice acting though feels very phoned-in, or like it was performed in a very large room. Lilac, coincidentally, had probably the best acting out fo all of them.... voice quality and clarity-wise. The rest got rather annoying, or in the case of Torque, sounded like it was recorded over the phone or in a big empty room.
-Story:
Yes its a pro and a con. Now what made the story nearly cringe-worthy was it was really over or under-acted. It lead to a greta many situations coming off very awkwardly to just plain schmaltzy. Milla almost dying when you beat her due to her becoming a plot advancement boss. This was grossly over-acted. Who the heck is Milla? Why should we even care? We know nothing about this puppy girl practically. So it leaves Lilac's incredible response to it just, rather jarring. This goes for every moment in the story they try to evoke drama. It feels incredibly shoehorned in and it derails it. Going back to before that, yeah, the acting quality is rather questionable. Then some characters just didn't seem like they cared. There was a lot of misplaced emotion. There just isn't enough signifigant development of these characters for me to care. Also magic plot bath that fixes everything.
-Stages:
Good aesthetically, atrocious in their length. These stages went on for way too long. I think I never really clocked in below 12 minutes for a stage. Now, these are divided into sections mind you, butdue to the way it was done it just would start to feel like a slog.
Then there's the difficulty of these stages. Bear in mind again I played through the game on Normal.
The Dreadnaught stages in particular... good grief the Dreadnaught stages.... These were a test, and absolute test. I can safely say I never died much on any of the stages until these, -especially- the last two. It went from being rather cool and interesting designs to HOW MANY ENEMIES CAN WE THROW AT THE PLAYER AT ONCE. Considering the invincibility frames in this game, these were pure deathtraps. Lilac could no do enough damage to take these out and then you get hit by like 20 shots. Literally 20. You basically had to cheese through it, and at one point in particular there was no indication of how to move on. You were lead to go through these teleporters, and then it immmediately stops wanting you to do that. You have to actually rocket up andjust triasl and error where you can land while, again,m being shot at by these 20+ enemies. It wasn't frustration, but these stages would get annoying and tedious. Trying to beat them simply so it would be over.
The airship stage though I will say was an absolute blast and easily the best contructed and varied stage in the game. They're not ALL bad. But a lot of them are.
-Bosses:
This is more straightforward. They didn't really scale well. Some later bosses I could take down without getting hit, and some earlier ones I had died on. Brevon's first form probably being the worst, its an absolute onslaught of just stuff trying to hit you. Second form, much better but still was hard to determine a pattern. Final form, was incredibly exploitable.
The bosses did look cool though. Very much a Ristar theme to them.
I think that's really it. Now I know I went way more in-depth for the cons, this is only because these things are rather fundemental if you're going to include them. Doing them the way this game did, that they have officially released, is a very big pet peeve of mine and it stands out more blatantly than the good things. Had they forgone voice acting, maybe tried to keep the story more simple, and maybe balanced gameplay out a bit more, the game would have been super good! Honestly though I don't see myself playing through it again in the near future.
Would I recommend this game? I can and can't. To me the issues addressed are very glaring. But I opted to go for the experience I assume the developers wanted, a'la Adventure Mode. If you're craving a side-scrolling platformer with great visuals and music, yeah go grab it. Maybe wait for it to go on sale though.
Also, just play Classic Mode.

This is the game that brought me into the world of video games. It has been my favourite game since I was 8 years old.
The music, characters, artwork and storyline of Final Fantasy IX come together to create a compelling and immersive experience. For those of you who don't know much about Final Fantasy IX, the game was envisioned by its creators as the "true" or "perfect" Final Fantasy and was made to reflect the previous games. Easter Eggs of each previous Final Fantasy instalments can be found throughout the game, as a way to invoke nostalgia for fans of the series. As someone who first discovered Final Fantasy through this game, those details didn't initially matter. For me, this is the game I look back on and think of nostalgically. Every time I play it I can go back and discover something new as well, which really shows me how much work and detail was put into this game.
For me, what really brings this game together is its characters and how their own stories and journies come together. Each main character is trying to find their purpose in life throughout the story, and there are points in the story where you can play as some of these characters (besides Zidane, the protagonist) and really get to see things from their point of view. The player also does not have access to each party member all at once. They are slowly introduced into the story as the game goes on, and unfortunately the later members don't get fleshed out as much as the earlier ones, but they are still faced with the journey of finding themselves.  FFIX also has one of the most diverse worlds and cast of characters that I've ever encountered in a game. There are so many different races and creatures that are unique, that the world feels very whimsical and dream-like.
FFIX is also very inspired by Shakespearean theater and medieval music, which gives it an old European fantasy feel that is more tactfully mastered than most other fantasy games try to achieve. Nobuo Uematsu's soundtrack for this game is incredible and magical, and one of his best achievements as a composer for this series. The environments are also beautifully illustrated and it's unfortunate that they could not be remastered to a better quality for this  pc port because they clash with the updated character models.
If you are looking for an rpg with a lovely story and lovely music and environment, please give this game a chance. It deserves much more love than Square Enix's marketing team thinks it deserves compared to other Final Fantasy games.

Lichdom: Battlemage is not a perfect game, but it is a fun romp that I'd recommend.  First off, I'd classify it more as an FPS than an RPG; it's more crysis than DA:O.  Secondly, the claim that there are millions of spells is a bit misleading.  Really there are 3 spell varants: Targetted (ones you shoot), AOE (ones that affect an area), and Nova (ones that go off on your locatoin if you parry block or charged blink in) that you mix with 3 types of augments that will either 1) make the spell do damage 2) make the spell control (like freezing them in place) or 3) mark enemies to multiply damage taken.  There are no mana bars so you can cast spells in any way you see fit, though they take time to cast and charge up (though crafting mods can change the times as well).
On the good side, there are some really original ideas here, and the campaign is not skimpy in the least -- it took me about 30 hours being thourough and doing all of the side challenges.  There is some really beautiful enviroment art, with a few standout set pieces that are top notch.  The story is fairly straightforward but works.  The crafting and loot finding can be fun with some issues.  But mostly I liked how they made some great decisions to really let you go wild.  Want to blink around without cooldowns or counters?  With one of the shield types you can!   Want to maximize a spell to just crit like a mofo -- you can!  The combat is fluid and fast paced and exciting by and large.
The crafting system is neat and I had fun crafting spells along the way, but it does become clunky and hard to navigate so it is a mixed bag.  It is hard to compare spells you may want to build with spells you are using because of some bad design (like you have to unequip spells in order to look at their parts).  Also, the upgrade system requires you to keep upgrading the low rarity spells into higher ones so your higher ones that you might care about have food to upgrade on - this becomes a chore that takes too much time.  All this can be interesting to some, but could have been much more streamlined.
My main complaint is that the enemies always spawn in at intervals.  This to me completely takes you out of feeling like these beautiful, lush environments (very pretty Cryengine3) are really a place that is lived in or has purpose.  Instead it makes it feel like wallpaper that you run though, fight, move forward, fight etc.  Another issue is that I feel like the inclusion of "Mastery" spell type (that marks enemies to take multiplier damage) was original, but ultimately a poor design choice.  There seemed to be a best solution that I came upon early:  control enemy, add mastery, then hit with crit or super crit damage.  Once I had a few spells with high Crit chance or Apocolyptical chance (when a crit crits), this by far was the best combat tactic that rendered most of the other sigil powers useless in comparison.  Why infect with Corruption? Why confuse with Delirium?  Why move enemies around with Phase?  Why do any of that when the add mastery + crit damage is 10x more efficient?
To not end on the negative, this game was pretty, fast paced, fun, original in a lot of ways and definitely deserves to be played.  I look forward to what else this developer can come up with!

This game is absolutely stellar. I doubt I will play anything better this year, or perhaps even in years to come.
First and foremost, this game grants the player absolute control over the character. The movement is fast and responsive, and the more you learn about the game, the better you can maneuver, to the point where you can do things you never would have thought possible at first. This sense of control is absolutely wonderful because I can apply both my reflexes and timing as well as my puzzle-solving skills to the level in front of me. The level design features branching paths that allow you to tackle the level many different ways, and give the player a sense of exploration. Will you go the easier and slower path, take more difficult shortcut, or will you look for the perfect jump to create your OWN shortcut? The game also allows you to place your own checkpoints, and unlike They Bleed Pixels, they actually mean it, meaning that you get to tackle the level before you on your own terms without compromising the difficulty.
The gameplay features some of the best movement mechanics I've ever employed in a videogame. Walljumping, boosting, sliding, shooting, and occasionally soaring my way to the finish feels exciting and fast. Finishing a complicated set of walljumps, or streaking past a group of enemies and eliminating them all without taking damage or even stopping is just so deliciously satisfying. This is a game that manages to feel cinematic not through cutscenes, quick-time events, or other gameplay interrupters, but through gameplay itself. Moving around makes you feel so stylish and powerful, and it's a genuine feeling because you must EARN it by being skilled.
The aesthetics are tremendously enjoyable. The music combines orchestra, electronic, and 16-bit styles to produce a sort of Megaman vibe which injects a superb sense of energy into the gameplay. The art style uses cross-hatching to create a very unique look, and it’s bursting with color and pleasing to the eye. The levels are suspended above gorgeous sunsets, starry nights, and stormclouds. The main character is reflective without taking it too far and becoming wishy-washy or weak, and while I was initially unsure exactly how to rate the voice acting, I came to really enjoy the small exclamations that the character would make during gameplay. That frustrated "Come on!" when she runs out of gas and starts to fall will always be memorable to me because it reflects exactly how I feel when this happens. This means that the designers successfully created empathy for the character through *gameplay*, which is a little piece of genius in and of itself.
This game is difficult, so much so that I fear a lot of reviewers actually disliked the game. But the difficulty is, in my opinion perfect, because of the gameplay's very real depth. This game slowly teaches you how to play it: a classic mark of masterful game design. It has a skill curve that arcs gracefully and makes you feel elated and rewarded for finally achieving the improvement that the later levels require of you. I would add that this game assumes that you are relatively good at videogames, so you may find it frustrating if you aren't up to the task. I've read complaints about controls and difficulty spikes, to which I would answer that if you feel the controls are imprecise, you probably haven't spent enough time with the game. It operates consistently, but certain mechanics need to be figured out through experimentation and are not revealed to you by the tutorial, such as understanding  when your character will attempt to run up a wall upon making contact with it and when she won't. With regards to difficulty spikes, everyone has their own meter, but at the end of the day, Cloubuilt gives you a system with which to earn more lives and give yourself more tries before the game over, meaning you can work your way up to the harder levels both mechanically and by naturally becoming more proficient at the game for your time spent playing it. It even gives you alternate gamemodes to go explore when you're tired of getting your butt kicked by the endgame levels.
The first path I went down turned out to be the most difficult, but I was able to throw myself at it tirelessly until I finally prevailed because I was emotionally invested in the scenario. The game provides you with a simple but well-written story in the form of the comatose reflections of the main character, which vary in their emotional trajectory, be they triumphant or traumatized, depending on which path you progress down. The levels are presented as figments created by the main character’s brain, and so conquering them became parallel to conquering the turmoil within. I was able to persevere and conquer Redeployment (the final level of one of the paths) because the game provided me with this goal of eliminating the doubt within the character's mind, which worked doubly well with the inherent rewarding nature of the gameplay itself. The best part is that I was able to later come back and S-rank the level due to how much I had learned. Though it was incredibly difficult, I have nothing but happy memories of my struggle and eventual success.
In a perfect world, every game would be designed according this philosophy. Cloudbuilt compliments the intelligence of the player by granting full control over where you go, how you get there, and exactly how many boosts and wallruns you want to use on the way; and also by rewarding you handsomely for your hard work. This control is different in context to, say, RPGs that let you make moral choices. This is a type of control where I feel that the range and depth of my gameplay options is both extensive and satisfying. The only issue I have is that I want more! I want to explore an entire world using these movement mechanics. I want to see what the world looks like beneath the clouds. I want to see the great war that the main character alludes to. I want a fifty-hour campaign with crazy boss fights and weapon upgrades! And most of all I want everyone in the world to play this videogame and enjoy it the way I have, understanding that *this* is what videogames are supposed to be like. 10 out of 10. Doesn’t get much better than this.

Fast paced movement, involving wall-running, and jetpacks, and stuff is probably what drew you to check this game out.

In terms of gameplay, I've played a lot of time-trial games, and time-trial minigames that have had a slow input, or have been really limiting in tracks, but this game is probably among the most responsive out there alongside things like Trackmania Nations. And the courses don't just look cool, being overgrown, spikey, floating geometry, but they're beautifully designed so that you really get to create your own way around the course, and really have your own adventure in each level.
TL;DR If you like time-trial games, or are just looking for a cool parkour game or something, this is a must-play.

Mediocre game at best in my opinion, I played for as long as I could, I quit when I found out that you are guaranteed to lose the Silver fight if you don't have enough boost.
Here are my main issues with Modern Sonic and his levels
-For some reason there are two sets of controlls for moving side to side, there's the analog controls which steers you in that direction, and then there's the left and right bumpers that move you over to that direction.
But you are still required to use the analog controlls in order to move forward, while still having the wonky steering controls attached to it, making it easy to go off course and die.
-If you are going faster than walking speed, you have no time to react to anything in front of you unless you know what's going to happen beforehand, this wouldn't be so bad if it didn't lead to losing lives very frequently.
-Bashing into a flying enemy can often lead to you just fall to your death if it was so much as an inch away from it's top height.
-There are a lot of sections where you're expected to either to slow down extremely or stop entirely in order to do some platforming, neither of course becomes apprent until you smack into it and lose your rings/die.
-You're never fully explained what anything does or what button you're suppose to press.
-Sometimes mechanics are introduced with no explanation at all.
As the game goes on it becomes clear less and less thought was put into levels as development increased, parts where a jump stops right in front of an enemy for you to slide into become more and more frequent, long stretches of road that lead straight directly into spikes are more common, level desgin as a whole gets worse as you progress.
I havn't tried to play this with a keyboard because the game comes with no key binds for keyboards, it asks you to select keys binds for each button on a controller, which sounds awful.
I'm sure if you're willing to put up with floaty controls, imprecise movement, and horrible level desgin, you'll enjoy this game better than I did.

Holy crap.  I was about to give this a thumbs down, but after the ending and the story, I can't possibly do that.
This game gets an A++ in environment graphic design, atmosphere, and story.  However, it gets a major D- (not quite failing but pretty close) in gameplay, puzzle design, and gameplay mechanics.
My favorite thing about this game is the incredibly trippy atmosphere and animations.  Seriously: Think of the Doctor Strange movie, except instead of Benedict Cumberbatch you play as a 10 year old boy, and instead of finding medical help for your hand, in this game you find medical help for your pet monster.
The story is simple. You are a boy (quico) who loves two things with all his heart: His pet monster "yo," and his friend robot "lula."  The problem is, Yo is addicted to poisonous frogs, which turn him into a raging fiery demon when he gets them.  The entire story is really cute and happy-go-lucky.  For a while I thought the writers lived in a bubble of happiness and innocence.  But then in the last 10% of the game, it gets dark.  REALLY dark.  I'm talking "Bridge to Terabithia," childhood innocence-turned trauma status.  And not just because of violence or mature themes.  No, I mean this tackles a very real and serious social issue that ruins the lives of millions throughout the world.  You can't see it coming for a while, but when you realize the true "innocence lost" at the ending, it's incredibly harrowing.  I started tearing up.  For anyone who wants to spoil it, the social truth behind the game is:

The graphics, by the way, are top-notch, for 2013 and even for 2017.  It takes place in a south american favela-style environment.  The sunshine, shadow, and texturing effects look stunning.
There's one major flaw with the game, and that's the actual gameplay.  This game really doesn't have any puzzles whatsoever.  It's mainly just "see something that looks weird, go up to it, notice it moves a platform, jump on that platform and repeat."  I think there might have only been one or two times where I actually had to think about what to do and comprehend the situation, which should be a given for every single puzzle in any adequate puzzle game.  They're bland and straightforward.  There even came a point near the end of the game where the solutions *LITERALLY* showed up directly in front of your character as they arose.  That's ridiculous.  The game and its controls run very fluidly, but your movement sometimes feel stiff due to its seeming exception from the laws of physics.  Parkour-esque movement would have been KEY to this game, but it felt more like a literal platform-hopping game.
In conclusion, lemme repeat my original grading:
Story: A+
Environment: A+
Atmosphere: A
Puzzles: F
Gameplay: D
Graphics: B++

Gonna get several things out of the way before i say anything.
First, I'm not a furry nor do i hate or dislike furries to any extent, this game was gifted as a joke apology from a friend. Second, I'm going to ignore a bit of the stuff that is currently happening in the community portion of this game that i read from other reviews (i.e. Pop star based of Dev, reviews getting flagged, players banned from forums, ect.). Finally, there will be a TL;DR at the bottom.
With that being said i'm going to say that this game isn't all that bad, it has potential to be good. but it isn't quite there yet. The writing itself is decent, a few spelling errors here and there, but it's nothing to write home about. The monologue at the begining almost drove me away and feels rather unecessary, i felt as though my character could of easily been introduced to the higher plane of existence in a better way, but thats just me. Theres a huge focus on the theme of not making snap judgements and the whole "Don't judge a book by its cover", and it does a decent job of this depending on the choices you make regarding characters. And even though some of the characters have "cookie cutter" personalities from other stories, they're tolerable and one or two of them (so far) are a bit unique. What leaves me wanting more from this game is the visual aspect of this game. Now, as i said i'm not really into furries or anything of the sort, but the characters are well-drawn for the most part disregarding some of their weird designs of colorful explosions. However, throughout the entire game, they all have one expression/stance and never change in the slightest. It would be nice to see characters look like the expression instead of being told "They look defeated", show me don't tell me. Theres also a lot left desired for the backgrounds, but nothing to bad. Another big thing that this game advertises is that the choices you make matter. I played it twice just to see how different certain things are. For the most part there are noteable differences, for example on one playthrough a character known as "Rook" i earned a bad first impression with him and he would stare at me angerily when mentioning a contract i didn't uphold and we had a bad start, however on the second playthrough the character was more fond of me, and eventually near the end he had a confession scene that i previously didnt hear before. With that being said though, alot of the dialogue between choices doesn't change to much, but there are clear differences especially how one choice led me to a whole new location with new diaologue exchanges and choices and i didnt even meet a character i had met previously. But at this moment it isn't really clear of how these choices will affect the future or if i will ever meet or miss certain characters. All in all, it was interesting, but there are definitly things that need to be fixed and reworked.
So far i've kinda enjoyed it when i came in with low expectations, but with the current state that this Visual Novel is in, i can't recommend it, especially since its early access and the story is unfinished and wont be finished for another year, which makes reviewing it hard since i can't really say if a story is truly good enough based on one single chapter alone, no matter how interesting i found it.
TL;DR: The game isn't nearly as bad as people are making it out to be, but its not by any means a great/good game either . I cannot recommend the game in its current condition; so-so writing, a few cookie cutter and a few interesting characters, has potential but needs alot of work. Upon full release i'll change my review as necessary if it warrents it.

+++++++++++++++ Review +++++++++++++++
This is THE greatest city builder of all time. Today's reiterations like Cities: Skylines can't touch the beauty and intricacy of this game. Its "2.5 Dimension" style graphics style will probably never be seen again, and it's something you'll have to experience to appreciate.
Note that there's a huge difference between 'SC4' and a 'heavily modded SC4' - the community is still very much so alive on Simtropolis and SC4 Devotion, making great free addons to this game with real world buildings, restaurants, road addons, landmarks, trees and everything else you can imagine. Hardcore players of SC4 are typically sandbox builders and don't care for the actual game aspect - you can create some pretty mind blowing scenery with this game and the right mods. With that being said, it's a game with an insane amount of replay value...not just beacuse it has no "end," but it's a relaxing scenery builder that will give you a great deal of therapy through the years.
+++++++++++++++ About the Steam Version of Sim City 4 +++++++++++++++
If you're like me and have been playing SC4 from the original disc, it's worth re-purchasing it through a Steam sale to get this patched version, because SC4 does not work well from the get-go. You will need to do a little work to get the game to run on Windows 10, but this will simply take a couple minutes...here's what you need to know:
+++++++++++++++ Getting Sim City 4 To Run On Modern Day PCs +++++++++++++++
The version of Sim City 4 DX that you get from Steam is "1.1.641.0", which means that the old "EP1 Update" (UPDATE_SKU1_TO_P1.EXE) and "SC4Update4BAT" (SC4Update4BAT.EXE) are already included, and you won't have to hunt them down on the internet. These patches were necessary if you had the old CD version of the game; otherwise, buildings would not light up during the night time cycle.
Once you install the game, you'll have to edit its Steam launch options, which is pretty quick and easy:
- In Steam, click "LIBRARY" in the main menu.
- Next, right click "SimCity 4 Deluxe" in the right-side menu, and choose "Properties"
- Right within the GENERAL tab is a button called "SET LAUNCH OPTIONS..." - click it.
- In the field provided on this final pop-up, paste in the following variable string:
-w -intro:off -CustomResolution:enabled -r1920x1200x32 -CPUCount:1 -CPUPriority:high
(These variables are: -w (wide screen), -intro:off (skips past the annoying intro that runs every time the game opens, -CustomResolution:enabled -r1920x1200x32 (this tells the game to run at your monitor's resolution, change it if you have to), -CPUCount:1 -CPUPriority:high (this is the most important part...Sim City 4 cannot run on more than 1 core, so you have to force the program to run on only one. Otherwise, the game won't run).
+++++++++++++++ Getting Mods for Sim City 4 +++++++++++++++
Mods make this game what it is - you won't believe how different it will look once you've added some custom content. The two best sites on the internet for mods are Simtropolis and SC4Devotion. Even after all these years, the communities for SC4 are thriving on these sites. They'll also have plenty of resources that tell you exactly how to unpack and install mods - it's pretty easy.
The essential mods you'll really want (or have?) to get are:
- "NAM (Network Addon Mod)": adds a ton of new realistic roads, interchanges, ramps, etc.
- "SC4 DAT Packer": makes the game more stable by centralizing your mods into one big file
- "Cheats By Buggi": allows you to input a bunch of different cheats that will make your life easier if you're looking to play this game in sandbox mode
+++++++++++++++ Standalone Mods for Sim City 4 +++++++++++++++
There are two notable standalone mods for Sim City 4. They install as separate programs:
- "SC4 Terraformer": this program is really old and a little clunky, but it will all you to hand sculpt a Sim City 4 map by drawing mountains, valleys, hills, etc with your mouse across any or all regions - even over borders, which is impossible to do in-game. The regions can then be imported into your game.
- "SC4 Mapper": This program lets you modify the size of the regions in a current Sim City 4 map. If you wanted regions to be bigger or smaller, or if you wished that the borders of a certain region were located somewhere else (like, one region on your map that is not 90% water and 10% land), you can edit them with this program.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a brilliant Real-Time Strategy that puts you in control of a ship in space. Your objective is to save the Federation by delivering vital intel about the rebels. You must make your way across the galaxy sector by sector, deciding to help others along the way, or serve yourself in completing the mission. Every move you make the rebels advance upon your position. Do you travel through an uncharted nebula to lose your pursuit in exchange for unknown danger? Or make a jump through a hostile sector, potentially finding equipment to strengthen your ship. Each decision makes a difference in your survival, there are no freebies in this game. FTL is a great game to learn and explore.

Reviewing FTL: Faster Than Light.
Note: This is just my own opinion on the game, and I am but a regular gamer and not a professional games designer or critic of any sort. It is up to the reader to decide whether the statements found in this review is favorable or otherwise.
Introduction:
FTL: Faster Than Light is a rogue-like sci-fi game that keeps you on your toes and encourages you to plan your every move. It does not tolerate weakness in the game, making the player struggle to survive and rebuild his/her spacecraft or go down in flames.
The player plays as the Federation and commands a ship that is set sailed to stop the Rebel Army that is taking over the universe. Explore each galaxy with interesting events, fight enemy ships in various environments, strengthen your defences with upgrades and finally foil the plans of the Rebel Army to ensure peace and victory.
Pros:
1. The game brings up a unique set of mechanics, comboed with a some of the old RPG style and feels. With each event brings up a tragic or fruitful outcome to you and your crew. It provides the user with various, unique ships that are to be unlocked by the player, each having a different difficulty with a different style of play. There are also plenty of weapons, defense systems and utilities in the game that can assist the ships and form multiple builds.
Furthermore, the enemies in the game will have their own special ship arrangements who are located in different parts of the universe. The player will be given a choice to enter a friendly, hostile or neutral galaxy. Despite the nature of these galaxies, the enemies are not to be underestimated in the galaxies with peaceful races.
These mechanics made me continuously play the game time after time, as rogue-like games would suggest.
2. This game has a really brilliant soundtrack. It is very soothing at times and slightly more chaotic in others, but it fits the game atmosphere and environment very well.
The thing that got me hooked in the music, however, is the fact that there are actually 2 different sounds for a single track (except the title track): Battle and Explore. The songs will switch between each other, depending if the player is met with hostiles or in a situation out of combat. This was something that I've never seen before, and it has made the game truely unique in its own place.
3. Let us not miss out the beautiful backgrounds that appear throughout the game. They are but simple images that are not really HD, but they gave the feeling of being in space and sets the atmosphere where it should be. With the help of mods, downloading other better and spellbinding images is not an issue.
And well, the graphics are neat too.
Cons:
1. The difficulty of this game can be difficult to new players, even on easy mode. The early stages of the game are not too bad, but the difficulty quickly scales up if you do not have a good enough setup or had a setback earlier (also applies for the general skill range). The cost of unpreparedness can be an insidious killer to your ship and crew.
2. I've found that weapons like Flak Cannons are slightly game-breaking. They do not cost much power, which not only allow the player to use multilples of it but also can still be threathening despite the weapons systems being damaged. On top of that, they break multiple shields at a time and can deal quite a lot of damage. Flaks are strong throughout the game, making it the strongest weapon in the game with minor drawbacks.
On the other hand, weapon such as the Glaive Beam are weak alone in the later stages of the game. They will require some support from other weapons, but it would be difficult to do as the Glaive itself takes up 4 wapping supply of power. The destruction of the weapon systems will disrupt its super long charge time as well. Basically, this is a powerful but useless weapon.
Some missile-based weapons also prove to be pretty useless at the end of the game. The single-shot missiles are the worst onces as they cannot deal damage fast enough to penetrate all of the enemies' shields and other systems, which make missiles useful only in the form of high damage and temporary disruption. Late-game enemies will have high dodge, and missiles get more expensive throughout the game, too. However, missile launchers that clone missiles are still acceptable to use in the late game.
3. Unlocking the ships can take up a lot of time and is pretty frustrating if the player is not very skilled in the game. How it works is that all but one (the regular Federation ship) is locked and that the player must get certain achievements, do certain events or reach the 8th sector (the 9th is the last) to unlock the ships. Up to one point, I found it a waste of time unlocking the ships and just found a save file that has almost all of the ships unlocked (sorry, I don't have it now).
Conclusion:
Overall, the pros overweigh the cons by a great deal, and I would recommend anyone who loves a good challenge to play this game. The game has got me played for many hours, and the price is highly affordable for a game like this. The rogue-like genre has been one of my all-time favorites, and FTL brought in a new and impressive look. I'm truely looking forward to see more of these traditional games with a remarkable twist such as FTL out there in the future.
With that all being said, I shall give this game a 8.5/10.

FTL is amazing. It's a difficult game that's difficult to learn and master, but boy does it feel good to win.
It's kind of the Dark Souls of strategy / micromanagement games: You're going to die. A lot. But then you learn. Or there were just too many enemy ships that happened to have randomly-selected uber-weapons, so it was just chance and you were gonna die not matter what you did. That's a big difference with Dark Souls: there are plenty of random chance situations where you're just going to die no matter what.
If you can't take that level of frustration, find a different game.
There are times I tear my hair out. There are times I yell at the random number gods for having no mercy. But like Dark Souls, you keep playing it because you love it. The torture of gaining the second layer of shields only to find a ship that can shoot five laser pulses at once. The victory from taking down the final boss with only a handful of hull points left on your ship.
This game is damn cheap, and you're going to get a ton of time and entertainment out of it. I've played this game about as much as I've played Skyrim.
You've read this far, so I'll reward you with some tips:
- Be ruthless. When the world's about to end, it isn't exactly the time to be nice. Steal those civilian supplies. Don't take surrend for an answer. I never let anyone surrender unless it's by accident or I'm running out of fuel and they offer it (you might not get it if you destroy them).
- On the other hand, help everyone you can when they aren't initially hostile or sketchy. You might get damaged or lose a crew member, but the rewards are quite good.
- Focus on getting your second layer of shields in the first level. At stores, if it's not the Burst Laser Mark II, you don't need it. Repairs are difficult to get, so avoid it by protecting your ship. Once you're past the second level, focus on getting the third layer. If you don't have the power, take it away from something non-essential (that is, NOT O2, maybe an extra weapon). The fourth layer isn't going to help as much as you would think. Focus on getting cloaking, weapons, and upgrading engines after that.
- Run. If you're running out of hit points or the enemy has 2 missiles, 2 lasers, and 1 beam, for a total firepower of Infinity + 1, just give up and run. It's not worth the 3.5 scrap* you'll get. (*Adjusted for your inevitable death if you try.) The only time I'd engage in such a desperate attack is if I can destroy their weapons faster than they can mine, or if I'm out of fuel. If you have fewer than 3 shields and they have the Burst Laser Mark II along with other weapons, run. Take power away from weapons and put them into engines. Sometimes there are systems full of ships like this, and it's then we curse the gods of random numbers.
- Move your power around a lot, especially at the beginning. If you don't need 02 for a few seconds, put it on your engines when that missile is coming in. Then put it back after the missile hits / misses. See the point about shields. Take away power from your engines to power defense drones when missiles are used against you. This seems counterintuitive, but it's better to blow up the bomb instead of *maybe* evading it. If something is damaged, move the power somewhere else where it can be used until the broken system is fixed.
- Must buys: Scrap Recovery Arm, Burst Laser Mark II, Heavy Laser Mark I, Small Bomb / Breach Bomb I, Chain Burst Laser. Sell everything you own to get Burst Laser Mark II. Get cheap, low-powered stuff. If your weapons require 4 power and you have exactly 4 and you get damaged, you have nothing to shoot with. If you have 4 weapons with 1 power each, you still have 3 weapons when you take 1 damage.
- Screw missiles. Go for the teleporting bomb. I've won with this sucker more often than with missiles. The bombs won't get shot down by enemy drones, and they seem to miss less often. Bonus if you have the Zoltan Shield Bypass enhancement. I usually ditch my missiles for something better fairly quick, but if I find a 1-2 power missile or bomb after that, I'll hold on to it and build up missiles for when there's trouble (e.g., enemy with 4 shields).
- Before the final boss, make sure you have Cloaking AND drones with the basic defense drone. You don't need more power in cloaking, but an extra empty bar helps avoid damage that makes it unusable. I recommend every system have 2 slots, if possible, focusing on the non-powered systems last (e.g., piloting). If you can, get the teleporter and a few "rough" crew members. Use two members to take out the enemy missile system. Otherwise, you'll get ripped apart by never-ending missiles. On stage 3 of the boss, use your cloaks when the big attack goes off. Disrupt your own cloak by shooting something once the danger is passed so that you get it back faster to hide from the next volley.
Good luck. You'll need it.

(I have taken the time to prepare both a short spoiler free review video, and a long in depth review video discussing all key plot points, easter eggs and questions left unanswered! The links can be found below for anyone who is interested. I put quite a bit of effort into them.)
As a fan who has been there since 1996, i was one of the few people who saw in the teaser, what this game had the potential to be when it finally came out! I spent a lot of time covering the game and defending it from those who were so quick to dismiss it as a P.T. clone. In short, i have a long history with RE and RE7 so when i finally got my hands on it, and it was everything i hoped it would be, you can imagine my excitement!
The game isn't without its issues however, as a second playthrough has really opened up my eyes to the fact that, some more enemy variety would have been great. Hope to see some classic BOW's in the sequel! (Copy that Capcom?!)
-The graphics are very good, but some spots look "off" the outside areas can feel flat, and some textures just don't feel like they belong in an otherwise fantastic looking game.
-Sound is fantastic, especially with headphones (no brainer) <--- see what i did there? ;) Everything sounds great, creepy sounds, bumps and creeks will keep you on edge, enemies have distinct sounds to let you know they are just around a corner, or the other room, waiting to dismember you with glee. The music is very tonal, and dynamic, it typically goes with the pace of the game, but not many of those "iconic" Resident Evil tracks, like for example, the RPD main hall, or Spencer Mansion basement (kek). Which is unforunate, and i can't help but feel little else but the Aunt Rhody theme and Save theme will remain in 10 years time to those nostalgic listeners. But i understand why they made that decision.
-Controls are your standard first person fare, though a bit slowed down by default to match the more methodic pace they set for the game. I honestly didn't even check to see if you can adjust sensativity as it just felt right. Controller guys will be happy to know everything functions just fine in that department also.
-Performance is great for most people, but some of us have had issues with stuttering on AMD processors and other hardware incompatatibilities. I had to turn things down to about medium settings, which honestly still looks fantastic, and had no issues aside from a crash here and there. Hopefully Capcom patches these things for those of us with problems.
All in all i feel RE is back to what made it great! Isolation, backtracking, key items to progress, resource gathering, conservation, inventory management and a great mystery to unravel all topped with classic horror movie homages! The game will take on average, 10 or so hours to complete with plenty of reasons for a replay or two! Definitely recommend!

CloudBuilt is an intense, reflex taxing platformer that pushes the player to think and react with lightning speed. Pushing your reflexes to the limit this game requires skill, logic and a handful of bravery.
First experienced by myself at EGX Rezzed, Cloudbuilt instantly stood out amongst it's peers. It is fresh and clean with a unique look, hardly something you would expect from an Indie Dev Team. At first glance you may make the mistake of thinking it is all flash with no substance, however as you delve deeper you soon find the real appeal of the title.
The aim of the game is simple: reach the end by overcoming the obstacles that lie in your path. Sounds easy enough right? Wrong. There is no one clear path to take to complete a level, players must rely on their keen observations to carve a path out of the wasteland in the sky and put their bravery to the test. You have a variety of techniques at your disposal to help you reach your goal, such as wall running and double jumping, each of which depletes your energy bar at the bottom of the screen. The energy bar itself fills up steadily over time or as an alternative you can collect the yellow orbs that are dotted around the level which give you instant replenishment giving you immediate access to your abilities.
The fact that you get penalised for death with a time penalty is also an excellent addition. Rather than the level ending you return to the previous checkpoint with the timer back to what it was when you hit it. A three second penalty per death is added to your final time when you have completed the run, so it's worth bearing in mind that fast is good, but clean is equally as important.
It can at times be overwhelming with the constant feeling of being on the edge, having to strategically place every jump, every boost, every wall run, but then again, that's also a major part of the appeal. Playing through those levels over and over again mastering the tricky sections trying to shave those narrow seconds off your time can become incredibly addictive. Before you know it one quick game can turn into many in the hunt to improve your standing.
Although it is a difficult game to achieve perfection, the casual gamer in you can just take pride and a sense of achievement from merely completing the levels, some of which are not as easy as they first appear!  The game handles well and responds to every whim which is integral to a title such as this. A death by game mechanics is a rarity, usually blame falls at the feet of the player.
None of the sound effects and soundtracks were out of place in this extreme environment, really giving the player that feeling of being involved in something out of this world. The pace of the music was very fitting building a lot of momentum that really spurs the player on in the hostile habitat.
I did unfortunately experience a few issues whilst playing the game, one of which being the music at some stages did seem to completely lose control of itself and become white noise of nonsense pulsing away in the background. I experienced very few issues mechanically as most of my issues were caused by player inaptitude which I soon overcome with a little practice and dedication.
Overall Cloudbuilt is a very exciting and nerve racking game all rolled into one. It offers excellent replayability with the speed running aspect to its levels, however it does not alienate casual gamers. Retailing currently at £14.00 on steam the price can appear to be rather steep, however playtime alone that can be gained from the title more than warrants the price tag.

Okay, I originally rated this a bit lower but have changed my opinion since then so am doing a re-write.
Cloudbuilt weaves an incredibly dull narrative into a game about speedrunning through literally fanciful obstacle courses in the sky. I don't think I'm in danger of spoilers here by saying that the main character is recovering from some battlefield trauma, and all the events/levels of the game take place in her mind. (That is the entirety of the story, right there. Whoopee.)
Breakdown:
Story - 1/10 - The storytellers have apparently not heard the writers' maxim of 'show, don't tell' and decided upon dolling out the narrative to you in between each level. That is, none of the story progresses or is shown to you via events in the actual game. In between each level, the disembodied, ghost-like narrator stares at her own body recovering in a hospital bed as she tells you, at length, about how she feels concerning her being turned into a cyborg or whatever. This eminently skip-worthy narrative is about as disappointing as biting into an ice cream cone to only then discover that someone has managed to create cardboard-flavor ice cream, and you're eating it. I honestly might have preferred there to be no story in the game at all, as reflective silence would have been an improvement to the lackluster voice acting that was the narrative. Let's be honest, though - you're not buying this game for the story anyway.
Graphics - 8/10 - I'm always a fan of cel-shaded graphics and this game delivers well on those. I rate it a bit lower because some levels actually suffer from framerate loss because of an overabundance of rain or fog or whatever, but this is very minor. There were some minor graphical glitches here and there as well (e.g. in one of the ending cutscenes, it was raining so hard outside the building that it was also raining INSIDE the building.)
Gameplay - 7/10 - Although I found some of the explanations on controls to be a bit confusing in the tutorial, once you learn the ropes of all the cyborg-parkour schenanagans that your character can get up to, bouncing off the walls becomes a joyous little affair as you dance through the levels as fast as you can. I rate this lower because of the various obstacles that you come to face in the levels, though. A turret here or there, okay... some mines I need to shoot down, no problem... laser sniper turrets that never miss? Homing drones that hunt you down from across the map, no matter how far you run? Turrets that shoot more of said drones? Now we're getting a bit ridiculous.
Level design - 6/10 - Quite a few of the maps are really fun to play, and are just challenging enough to get through that you think to yourself, "yeah, I want to go back to that level and see if I can get that A-rank!" However, on a lot of the later levels the developers kind of go off the deep end and lose all control of the fun/difficulty balance. I had one situation where I jumped into a small corridor that had 4 turrets, two spider-drones, a homing drone and a bunch of mines littered everywhere, and then once I manage to (somehow) get through all that crap and catapult myself up a wall, there's a never-miss sniper turret hiding in one of my blind spots. Urgh. Now mind you, these kinds of levels are all beatable, of course, but while I was playing them I wasn't thinking 'yay, this level is fun!' but more along the lines of 'I really want this awful level to be over so I can go to the next and never play this one again. I hate you, game. I hate you so much.' Such levels are about as enjoyable as walking on asphalt with your bare feet on a hot summer day. In light of this, achievements such as 'Get an S-Rank on every level, in every mode' (upwards of 5 modes per level) require a severe degree of masochism (and unrealistic amounts of free time).
Music - 8/10 - The downtempo songs are kind of bland, but I love the music that plays during the levels, and was delighted to find out that they are contained in the installation as Ogg Vorbis files, so now I've happily added them to my phone's playlist.
Sound 5/10 - Game sounds are just fine, I'm rating lower for the lackluster voice acting of the boring narrative.
Sadly, the game lacks a level editor; Cloudbuilt is the sort of game that would shine with user-generated content, especially with how frustrating the late-game campaign content can get. But that apparently isn't a thing. Would be nice if they included it later on.
Overall 7/10 - Visual/Aural presentation is good; game is fun to pick up and play but some of the levels suck the fun out of it. Still, many of the levels are fun enough that you'll want to try to set decent records and do your best.
Fast, vertical and a lot of fun. Feels like a modern take on Sonic The Hedgehog. Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys platformers and good challenge

Free running at its finest. To get an idea of what this game is like, look up any runthroughs on youtube and they'll show you how fast-paced this game is. Music is great, graphics are sharp, controls are tight once you get the hang of them, and the sheer adrenaline rush you get from speeding through a floating castle of debris with your jetpack is incredible.
One of the best parts of this game is that nearly every level is open-ended, meaning that there's hundreds of ways to go through it. Branching paths and shortcuts abound make it really feel like you're blazing a trail your own way instead of completing challenges on rails.
The only downside is that some of the enemies are a real pain and cause what I felt to be some cheap deaths. They're the only thing that took some levels from challenging to frustrating, but thanks to the free DLC that's included, there's now an entire set of levels that don't have them. Those levels, the ruins, are the most free-spirited free-running of them all.
Overall, highly recommended, just be prepared for a challenge!

This game is a real adrenaline rush.  Expect to get a lot of C or D ranks when you start playing and don't worry about the A (or S) ranks.  After a while, though, you'll be the one who's flying across the maps at breakneck speeds - and you'll have a big grin when that happens.
If you're into platformers, Mirror's Edge or fast paced games then you should try this game.  There is some shooting too but it's just a way to help get through the levels and isn't a main focus.

8/10 - Highly recommended if you like fast-paced 3D platformers.
This game is a solid mix of gameplay elements from classic series like Sonic The Hedghog and Mega Man X in a 3D Platformer.
It's a speedy platforming game with light shooter elements. Your character has rocket boosters that let you dash fast, jump far, wall run vertically and horizontally to reach the goal point. Occasionally, you'll have small enemies and obstacles that you can blast with your laser gun. For tougher foes and barriers, the gun has a charged shot to destroy them.
The game does employ the use of a lives system. Run out of lives and you have to start a stage over again. You'll earn extra lives when completing a stage, or find them in the stages. Also, you are given a custom checkpoint that can be placed anywhere in a stage (you can pick up extras while in a stage). When you place one, your lives are replenished up to 6. And the checkpoint will last until you clear the stage or lose are your lives.
Your character is a woman in the army of the world who was wounded in a failed mission. Inside her own head as her body recovers, she recalls the events that brought her to this point, and comptemplates the meanings of the dreams she has of running through the obstacle courses in the sky.
The music in the game is nice mix of atmospheric melodies and upbeat electronic tracks to get you into the rhythm of the stages.
I recommend a controller if you have one. Default control scheme isn't very inuitive, but you can customize the button layout in the options menu.

When I bought this game, I had a feeling that it was more than the eye could see. And I was just right.
It's a short puzzle / platform game. While the gameplay is not particularly good or interesting, the game itself, as a tale, wins you over with its very touching (concealed) message.
Good

Papo & Yo is pretty decent puzzle platformer. It is also a very touching tale about a child dealing with an abusive father.
The story is clearly the highlight here. The game deals with a difficult subject matter in an excellent way. Most of the storytelling is done through actual gameplay too instead of long dialogues or endless cutscenes. This is certainly one of the stronger game narratives I have ever experienced.
The South American setting, the art style inspired by magical realism and the great soundtrack are all superb fits for the game too.
The game does have a number of issues, however. The puzzles and the platforming both tend to be on the easy side and the puzzles in particular feel like an extended tutorial for the actual game that never materializes. The game also suffers from a number of minor glitches and bugs.
Despite the somewhat weak gameplay I found Papo & Yo a great and touching experience. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys good stories.
The good:
- Superb story
- Great storytelling
- Fitting art style
- Nice soundtrack
The bad:
- Rather easy
- Little short (I finished the game in little over 3 hours)
The ugly:
- Quite a few bugs and minor glitches

In what might be a controversial opinion, I didn't love Papo & Yo, but could appreciate its message. Although many of the areas in the environment felt closed off and not conducive to exploration, the puzzle mechanics rose to the surface and succeeded in captivating my attention. Particularly the dream like sequences, and dream-infused interpretations of the character's father, his rebirth in an imaginary monster, were standouts. Papo & Yo approaches narrative excellence with its devastating final message, which will no doubt resonate with anyone who has had similar expereinces. An extremely moving, thought provoking game that masks an inordinate amount of pain. Well done.

Papo & Yo is a puzzle adventure game where you play as a Brazilian boy named Quico, who is hiding from his alcoholic father in the beginning of the game. While hiding in his closet during one of his father's drunken rages, clutching his favorite toy, a robot doll named Lula, Quico discovers a strange chalk mark on the wall, and touching it, finds himself taken to a dream-like world.
The dream world is incredibly whimsical and fascinating, and it turns its Brazilian environments into a dream where Quico can manipulate objects, enter portals, and use special panels. With special panels on objects, he can push, pull, and move objects with ease, moving houses in place and pulling staircases out of houses. Lula also becomes animated and helps guide Quico through the world.
Quico eventually meets a young girl named Alejandra, who doesn't understand him or his intentions, and attempts to slow him with puzzles.
Quico eventually comes across a creature known as Monster, a massively strong beast with razor-sharp teeth. Quico sees it as his friend, although the creature is powerful and has strength unknown to him.
Throughout the game, Quico sometimes has flashbacks of things that have happened, and bad memories of his father. These can be very haunting and sad, but are quite the wake-up call to what addictions can do, and the damage that an addicted parent can do to one's child.
Papo & Yo is an incredible game so far. The game is very whimsical and detailed, and the gameplay so far is quite fun, although certain puzzles can be a bit difficult. Its visuals and graphics are very nice as well, and breathtaking to see. Its exciting and beautiful soundtrack suit the game very well, and I really like how they often kept the theme true to traditional Brazilian music. I would definitely recommend this to anyone who enjoys puzzle games and anyone who enjoys whimsical game worlds. ^.^

I had little in the way of expectations, when I recieved Major/Minor. I do not identify as a "furry", or even a fan of virtual novels.
However, I find myself strangely looking forward to the next chapter of this game. I'll be waiting out the month until I can see how my choices effect the next part of the story.
Major/Minor has a lot of prominent flaws. The presentation and interface is not quite a polished as it would appear in the promotional video. Some of the dialogue is a bit cheesy, and the subject material is a little far fetched, in a sense. At first I was going to complain about the sound effects of the game, but the options menu gives you the choice to quiet or mute the sound of the dialogue text.
The thing I found most "offensive" about my first playthrough, was that when everything was said and done, and I finished the chapter, I received a message telling me what I had done right and wrong, and whether I was elligible for a perfect ending or not. While there is a great deal of fun to be had in going back and seeing what alternate paths have in store, this seems like something you'd want to do at the end of the game. Not every chapter.
What stands out most prevalently about this game so far, is that I feel that you are presented with choices that actually have an amount of weight to them, and that you are presented with them often enough that you really will make a lasting impact on the story. The characters have a little more depth than you would expect, and even in the brevity of the first chapter, you're presented with a couple surprises and interesting relationships between characters.
The music that is used in the actual game does not reflect the music that was used on the promotional video. Though, this isn't a bad thing. Once you get past the generic "ominous choire" music at the beginning, the rest of the background music is really pleasant and oddly uplifting. I'd imagine that because a certain percentage of the characters involved in the main storyline are all music-related, that music used in later parts of the game will sound a bit heavier.
It must also be acknowledged that it seems that the author of this game has inserted himself as one of the main characters. When I found this out, I immediately drew the worst conclusions (as It is a common sin to write one's self as an overly-important facet to the worlds we make). But after my first playthrough of the first chapter, I found this character's influence on this version of Japan to be kind of charming. He really is presented like a person that we've heard of.
If you like virtual novels, or you're a fan of furry art, or anthro characters interacting with one another, then you'll probably enjoy this game. I'd even go far as to saying this would be a good introductory game for anyone who is curious as to whether or not they'd like the virtual novel genre. When the next chapter comes out in January, I'll be interested to continue my interactions in Anthro-Tokyo.

: I enjoyed the game and would
recommend it. If the wind snatching a $10 bill out of your hand would ruin your day, give this game a few months, but if you're vaguely interested and the price tag isn't high for your budget, give it a whirl. It's definitely rough around the edges, but still a promising effort, with plenty of time to grow and improve.
First, a quick thing that seems to be causing some problems for other reviewers, where it's understandable why they'd be upset while not being the fault of the game: This is a visual novel, not an adventure game.  It's more akin to a 'choose your own adventure' book, where the reader makes infrequent decisions, but mostly is just reading a story, except with some character and setting art to augment the experience. If you're looking for more interactivity or player-character agency, this isn't your thing. If you're just in it for a laid-back story with a few different branching possibilities, read on.
Pros:
- There are a few different subplots that are interesting. This is, at the end of the day,
make-or-break factor for the genre, and so far, I'm feeling good about it.
- Characters feel like they have distinct and consistent voices.
- Character art looks good.
- Music is pretty nice.
- Furries. If you're into them, obviously, this is a win.
Neutral:
- Controls and options are minimal, but good enough for the genre and for Indie.
- Finite number of save slots - Not huge, but doesn't seem to make sense, either.
- Trading cards - may be a 'Pro' to some; I don't really care either way.
- Furries. So far at least, it's not at all yiffy-murry-purry. If you're on the fence about furries and the character art doesn't bother you, don't let it turn you off of this game.
Cons:
- Writing could use some tuning. Dialogue feels stiff in some places, which is a greater-than-normal detriment for this kind of game.
- Only one image per character. It can seem awkward or dampen emotional impact of some scenes or dialogue when the speaker is portrayed behind the text with a friendly smile, when the appropriate expression would be shock, anger, sadness, etc.
- Felt short. If each chapter is this long, the full game will be a
; a wonderful length for the price. However, a single chapter on its own feels like a too-short tease.
- Furries. Obviously, if you hate furries, this game is not for you.

I am going to be as spoiler-less as I can be.
The first chapter is short, I got through it in one playthrough in roughly 40 minutes. This game is not very well written. The two characters you interact with the most are insufferable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s (whether knowingly or not), and the way the protagonist responds to them are entirely unbelievable. The amount of chill the protagonist has is ridiculous. Not only does Kila sell you out as soon as he can, but you're also blamed for an event that is 100% out of your control (a train being delayed); when the train was delayed you could respond to a text sent to you from a person you're supposed to meet at the station, asking when you will arrive. Since the train was delayed, I decided to be honest. The protagonist figuratively nods and says he will explain what happened face-to-face and sends back "I don't know". He never does, and instead just lets him-/her-self get walked all over by these two "potential friends". The amount of♥♥♥♥♥♥the protagonist is willing to take from people whom he doesn't even know is staggering, especially when the game keeps hammering in that you're supposed to befriend these people.
Kila portrayed as a dopey idiot who can't keep things to himself, getting you in trouble on more than one occasion. Rook is just a jerk. All he does is complain and treat both you and Kila like♥♥♥♥♥♥ Jade seems to be a somewhat reasonable person, although she has trouble acting like a person (you'll see what I mean by that if you do buy this game). Inumi has one line of dialogue. Eclaire, so far, is the only person who seems like an actual person. A person hopped up on coke, or has bipolar disorder, but a person nonetheless.
If I had to describe the writing style of this game, then it would be.. Fanfiction as written by a person whose idea of a personality is taking articles from TVTropes and plastering them all over a character. I sort of doubt we will be seeing any development in terms of character in these upcoming chapters.
It gets worse as you progress through the "story". I suppose I should be thankful that chapter 1 is so short. But speaking of the story, there is none. You arrive in Tokyo, you speak to a grand total of 5 people and then the game is over. 42 minutes. The game wants you to keep loading up saves and trying out different choices, but I honestly wasn't too interested in that. If I wanted to hang out with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and probe them in various ways to see how they will demean my pushover of a character next, I'd hang out with my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ friends in real life thankyouverymuch.
Another complaint I have is the fact that there is just one static sprite for each character. You meet 5 characters during your playthrough (Kila, Rook, Jade, Inumi, and Eclaire) and each of them has one, and only one, portrait. Unchanging, each forever staring off to one side. That said, the portraits are very nicely drawn. There are some very minor issues, like the level of detail kind of fades along the edges of the characters, but other than that I have no actual complaints about the quality.
I feel sorry for the author and developer of this game. I think that the idea is solid, but the writing is not there yet and the game itself is entirely unfinished. $9 for 42 minutes of gameplay where most of it is spent being talked down to and backstabbed? Eh. I'm not going to presume to tell these people what to do, but this game is clearly not finished. The least they could have done is put it on Early Access or something.
EDIT: If you do decide to check the game out anyway, I think you should. $9 is not that steep of a price, and since the game is ridiculously short (averaging between 30 and 80 minutes for one playthrough from what I can see from other reviews) you can easily ask for a refund after.
