I've already reviewed this game once, but after playing Sonic 3 and Knuckles (For the most part. I'm far into Sonic 3 at the time of writing this review) I can see that Freedom Planet drew a lot of its inspiration from that game more than the other classic Sonic games. You play as 3 characters to go through (mostly) the same levels with the game focused on speed, and there are various shields in the game. Seeing these comparisons, I decided to come back and rewrite my review. Despite its attempts, many of the things that Sonic 3 does right, Freedom Planet does wrong.
First of all, the consistency. Freedom Planet has extremely easy stages. However, one you get to the boss fights, the difficulty increases by a lot. That's not to say the bosses are hard. They should only take a few tries. The problem is that the boss difficulty is not consistent with the level difficulty. The levels are too easy compared to the bosses. Turning down the difficulty makes the bosses easier, but it also makes the levels easier. This is because Freedom Planet focuses a lot on combat, and less on platforming. I think the game would be a lot more enjoyable if it had less combat and had a more consistent difficulty.
The second problem I had with the game was the dull levels. I'm going to compare it to Sonic 3 since that's the game they took inspiration from. Sonic 3 has detailed landscapes with many different paths, and memorable sections. However, Freedom Planet's levels feel uninspired and bland, making going through them dull. The long length of these levels doesn't help. This is especially a problem with my 3rd point.
The different characters. Similar to Sonic 3, you can play as 3 different characters to traverse the levels, each character having their own way of doing it. However, while Lilac felt great, the 2nd character (I can't remember her name, but she's the green one) had little mobility and was no fun to play, while the third one felt awkward to use since she relied on slowly making boxes to throw at enemies. In a game that should be focused on speed, this really drags down the pace.
All of this being said, while I am giving the game a negative review, I still think some people would want it. If you prefer the more combat focused gameplay of Freedom Planet, then you might want to consider picking it up. Unfortunately, I got bored during my playthrough of the 3rd character, and I stopped playing. In my previous review, I mentioned how I didn't like the classic Sonic games (1 and 2 at the time), and I was hoping an indie take on the Sonic franchise would feel fresh. While Freedom Planet lost me in my second playthrough, I am still interested in the sequel, and I might pick it up if it fixes at least 1 of the problems I have with this game.

Based on the marketing I will say: no NOT buy this game if you are swayed by the ads. It is a strange take on a bullet hell game, and most certainly NOT free-running/platforming or anything of that sort. This game is about dodging obstacles and freerunning and parkour and stuff are not just secondary or even tertiary, they are simply used to diversify the position of the obstacles you need to dodge. As oppose to other obstacle dodging games like Audiosurf, where you are dodging on one level all the time, you will be dodging in mid air, on the walls while wallrunning, edges, ground.
That's all there's to it. If you like Bullethell games and if you wanted an audiosurf that was not based on rythm and where you had more interesting things that colourd blocks to dodge, Cloudbuilt is up your alley. I never liked bullet hell games. I prefer to either run or fight. Doing both at the same time is annoying and results in either part being individually worse. Granted, Cloudbuilt at the core design makes no compromises on the dodging side of things, having a ton of various obstacles from robots to hominh missiles to different types of mines and lazers. But that's just yet another reason why it is not a free running game.
If you are like me, who like platforming and parkour games like Mirror's Edge, like Alice: Madness Returns or even enjoy parkour in♥♥♥♥♥Creed or the likes, this game is NOT for you and the part on it's Store page that says "free running" is blatantly false. There's NO *free* running in this game at all. Just none (aside from the first 3-4 intro levels). Your eyes will be on the next set of mines and lazers, not your path/angle of jump to save your momentum and speed.
Not a bad game, but based on the false impressions that it gives you on the store page, I will rate it down. If you are gonna make a obstacle course/bullet hell game, do not market it as a friggin free running game and get people confused. I thoroughly regret my purchase, I thought I was buying a free running game.
[Note: I have beaten the first ~10 levels before I uninstalled the game. The last 3-4 ones took about 20-50 tries each depending on whether I used custom checkpoints or not, but ultimately could be beaten very quickly. It will take you about 15 minutes per level the first time around. Once you remember the level and it's obstacles by heart, it takes about a minute beat it from start to finish. There are a lot of them in the game however.]

Going to start off by saying that aggressively difficult speedrunning precision platformers aren't usually my thing, mainly because I suck at them, and this is no exception. I will say though, that the game is mostly fair. If I fail, I know it's because I suck, not because it throws something at me that I couldn't possibly have seen coming.
I have to say though, the satisfaction of finally completing a level is pretty damn good (although for me, just getting to the end is an achievement on most levels). So while it's difficult and frustrating for me, I still keep coming back, because apart from the difficulty, the game feels fantastic. Stylishly zooming my way through a ton of obstacles that destroyed me before, gives a huge feeling of satisfaction, and it's one I want to experience over and over again.
To sum it up, it feels great, looks great, has an amazing soundtrack (even if you don't want that game, you HAVE to check out the soundtrack) and controls fairly well (when you're not spamming the buttons in panic like I normally do).
Overall, I don't regret getting it, and would recommend giving it a go if this seems like your thing.

Tropico the first's a classic. Having been a huge fan of Sim City and Tropico games (SC4/2000 and original Tropico) for years, I keep coming back to those games at least once in a couple of years just for nostalgia's sake.
Tropico 1 possesses that unique charm that nearly all the other installations, sadly, lack, alongside with some great tongue-in-cheek humor. I can say with certainty however that Tropico 4 more than made up for it and it's probably the only game out of the entire franchise worth purchasing (besides the very first one of course), seeing as T3 is just a watered down version of T4. Trust me, if you just skip on T3 you won't be missing ANYTHING. Kalypso really dropped the ball on that one.
So if you're looking to jump into the franchise, I recommend starting with either the 1st or the 4th installation, or better yet both. If you just want a fancy looking and relatively new city-building game in the spirit of SimCity, Anno and Cities XL, just skip this bundle entirely and buy T4.
Long story short: T1 started it all, T2 has pirates, T3 is an attempted but shallow reboot and T4 is an upgraded version of the previous game and what T3 should have been in the first place. Take your pick.

This game is an first-person Action Roleplaying Spellcasting Crafting Game.
And its great.
You've got to think about how your spells interact with each other, and how to best take advantage of each sigil.
Here's something that should be noted, cuz I've seen a lot of people annoyed about it.
You can only have 3 sigils equipped at a time, and you can  only level 3 spells. But the spells equipped don't have to be the ones you are leveled in. This lets you test out sigils without losing the levels you've put into other sigils. Its a tenuous balace between encourageing experimentation, and rewarding consinstent use of a sigil.
The crafting is very very deep, and they could have done a better job explaining some of the aspects of it.
Mastery, especially is an extremely important part of spells that the game does very little to explain.
As far as i can figure, Masterty, is a debuff that casts to other enemys in a radius of the opponent hit with a mastery spell. Mastery also stores and stacks damage to the target.
It definitly has the feel of a wiki game at times, but the game is very fun.
If you're the kind of person that complained that Shadow Warrior was only about killing enemys, then you probably won't like this game either.
Lichdom's focus is on the combat and crafting. But it does it very very well.

I've spent probably thousands of hours on this game before I even had a Steam account (big Sims fan in general). It wasn't until I got it a few months ago that I actually even had a clue on how to even properly play the game. But moving along from memory lane, this game is still amazing for being as old as it is.
Having been released in 2003 and made available on Steam in 2010, this game and even the game series itself can honestly be seen as revolutionary for the city-building and simulation games that have followed since the original simcity was released. This game was almost in a way ahead of its time and in my opinion STILL outshines many other city-building games (maybe I haven't played enough but who knows) that try to recreate in their own sense the management strategy that SimCity brought upon the world of gaming. The replay value of this game is beyond compare, for something different is always awaiting you, and the mods are endless to build off what the game originally provided.
The beauty about this particular game is that it can be both a "place anything anywhere and watch what happens" sort of game but it also can be a complex square by square city builder where you perfect every detail and the style of your houses to the taxes each individual industry and residential type pays. Many modern city builders try to play off this but say unlike City Skylines where you have to work your way up to get more land to begin with, there are countless areas and regions of all sizes for you to use and connect and even create to eventually have the ultimate city or state or nation or whatever you wish. Plus the music is pretty damn great as well. The game just allows you to almost settle down and lose yourself. SimCity 4 has to honestly be my FAVORITE city-builder out there, as it still is for many. But that's just a personal opinion. For it's current price of $19.99 and replay value that is seemingly endless, i'd say it's worth it.

Introduction:
Ten years on from Worms Armageddon and the turn-based comic mayhem continues in Worms Reloaded, an all-new edition available for PC through Steam. Worms Reloaded features up to four player online and offline multi-player, voice support, a raft of crazy new weapons and the return of some iconic weapons from the brand’s celebrated past.
We all know and love Worms, Worms Reloaded brings all we love and gives it a new lick of paint. Its all here from holy hand grenades to exploding sheep and even the odd poke for good measure.
Story:
There is no story per-say to worms, but it does feature a campaign mode that’s pretty comprehensive. Worms is simply about worms at war, there’s no rhyme or reason to it. But you will come to love your own group of worms. Worms has always oozed character and Reloaded is no different.
Gameplay:
If you have ever played Worms then nothing has changed, but if its not broken why fix it. Worms plays beautifully, even someone who hasn’t played before will soon be comfortable with the controls. In fact I put this to the test when reviewing it, we had a gaming night and after a few minutes my 8 year old had mastered the controls. For me that’s where Worms really shines, Its good to play on your own but even better with friends. There are very few games that span generations, but Worms achieves this as its loved by young and old alike.
Presentation:
The graphics looked great ten years ago and nothing has really changed, its still those loveable little guys brandishing heavy artillery. It wont push your system even without a discreet graphics card, but its all well drawn and looks great.
Worms isn’t about amazing graphics, its about fun. The presentation is great and you really will love these little guys but Crysis its not, nor does it want to be. The animation is smooth and its visually appealing.

Some people may argue that Worms Armageddon is superior in some ways. And, after actually learning Armageddon's controls and spending a lot of time with it, I have to agree.
I used to think this one was a lot more solid, too, and was the definitive Worms game in my eyes. But after playing a lot of Armageddon, once again, that has changed.
However, no one can argue that this one is a LOT more intuitive. You can use a gamepad if you want, and the keys are remappable for whatever method you're using. You aren't stuck having to look up the complicated and confusing controls of Armageddon on the internet (Though, they work pretty well once you know them. And they were actually quite easy to learn).
The fact is that if you want to get into Worms, or get your friends into worms, this is the best way to do it, bar none.
Also, Worms Reloaded is the best version of Worms 2: Armageddon. Don't settle for the less refined console releases. This game will run on whatever computer you have; you have no excuse.
(Another thing to note, is that this game does have some features that Armageddon doesn't, though that works both ways; Armageddon has a lot of things Reloaded doesn't have either. If you enjoy this one, try Armageddon. And, you know.....vice-versa)

One of my favorite games of all time is Sonic 3 & Knuckles. This game was built up to be a spiritual successor to it. It's not.
Although each character has different abilities in how they can traverse the level, this never really comes into play as the levels hardly deviate. Sure, you can get to tiny different sections of the level but all this amounts to is picking up a few gems before the path reconnects. On the topic of gems, collecting 200 gives you a 1-up, much like the typical 100 for a 1-up in classic platformers of yesteryear. The problem is that not only are there too many too close together (there's typically groups on the screen of 15 every few seconds) but getting hit doesn't cause you to drop them so you rack up extra lives very quickly. Playing casually on the default difficulty, I had 25 lives at the end of level 4.
Unlike Sonic, the game puts a heavy emphasis on combat. This works on the weak enemies that scatter the levels but when it comes to boss fights, the game falls flat. Bosses are damage sponges and seem to have random levels of health. The first boss takes 3 hits, the second seems to take anywhere between 3 and 5 "damage phases", the third takes so many hits that it's hard to tell exactly how much damage it takes in total (likely 80+ hits, lowballing)  before dying. There's seemingly no pattern and boss fights devolve into mashing attack close to the boss and then running away. It feels really slow and clunky and is honestly dissatisfying. Going back to the topic of regular enemies, fighting them is literally a waste of time. For the most part, they don't deal contact damage so you can run right past them, and they either drop nothing (in the case of small enemies), a few gems (which, as stated before, are so common it's unfunny), or a "core" which is used to roll a die in a end-of-level bonus game in which you can earn a shield or 1-ups (which you'll have plenty of through casual play anyways) so for the most part, they might as well not even exist. They also inhabit seemingly random sections of the level, with level 3 being a particularly egregious example with streetlight-looking enemies being found in literal dead ends or high up in the sky where you'll rarely be.
While I'm on the topic of levels, it seems like when they were being designed, the scenery was drawn first and then the level was made around that as opposed to the other way around. As beautiful as the levels look, I can't help but be confused by the world's design, with buildings that are cut off halfway by a large pillar and odd, curving geometry on the bottom of platforms. Additionally, since one of the characters' ability is to go up walls, there will often be upside-down "staircases" on the undersides of a lot of platforms that prevents you from climbing up them, which gets frustrating when you're exploring the level and looking for hidden cards. I love scouring games for hidden secrets, but it feels like Freedom Planet incorporated the 10 cards per level fairly poorly and as a last-minute thing. They're often in random spots that require you to backtrack a bit, in a random spot that you have to detour for, or hidden up high in a tiny nook. Not only this, but when you pick them up, they're often labeled in the wrong order, so you'll pick up card No. 2 early in the level and think you missed the first card and backtrack and search high up in the level, and go all around the different elevations of the level to try and find it, only to give up and move on, find another card, and be told that this card is No. 1. Searching for these cards easily quintuples the amount of time you can spend on a stage and making the game feel more like Metroid or Symphony of the Night, which is fine and all but not exactly fitting for a Sonic-inspired game.
There's a few flaws in how the game handles physics. For one, the concept of momentum is obnoxious in this game. Going down slopes builds speed fairly quickly as expected, but as soon as you start to head upwards at any angle, your speed drops like a stone from a dash to a jog. Like in Sonic, there's springs in this game, but the wall-mounted ones are far too "weak". Since you'll naturally be holding the control stick in their direction to be launched by them, there'll end up being a few frames where you're holding the control stick in the direction opposite of where you're being launched from. During those few frames, you'll "skid" and lose roughly 40% or so of the momentum you would've had. Not touching the control stick has the same effect and no momentum is maintained. Furthermore, for whatever reason you can literally walk up inclines and walls with no repercussions (unless it's a very high vertical structure in which case you'll slow down very slowly and promptly fall back down) and can often continue to move to slopes on the ceiling and walk upside down. And when I say walk, I mean literally walking. Things also seemingly cease to exist once they're off the screen, causing things like a string of bombs to stop detonating halfway through and gems dropped by enemies that fall offscreen to technically be "floating" in that if you jump past them, head down, then under them, they'll then continue to fall.
My biggest complaint was the poor voice acting and abundance of story in the adventure mode. Some of the lines are cringey and a lot of the time they're unnecessary exposition. The voice acting ranges from average to high school project-levels of bad. I actually got so fed up with it, I had to download a mod that essentially muted the voice lines in the cutscenes. Speaking of cutscenes, there are a lot of them. I like to think myself a quick reader, and even then I found cutscenes surpassing the 5 and 6 minute mark between levels with unnecessary elements (watching the main characters watch TV, watching them eating dinner with a provincial mayor, brooding). The amount of plot and backstory makes it seem like the game wants to be an RPG and not a platformer. Going back to Sonic 3 & Knuckles again, off the top of my head the longest "cutscene" with plot in it is around 45 seconds, during which you have full control of your character. Personally, I don't need or really want a rich full backstory of the game's world's lore when the focus of the game is going fast. The game does offer a "classic mode" that removes most cutscenes from the game, but then I'm left wondering why I'm doing what I'm doing and how I got from the previous level to the current one. In S3&K, there was a brief cutscene at the end of each level that showed how it connected to the next level. I shouldn't be punished by not knowing the story by simply wanting to not wade through unnecessary pages of dialogue.
What I will give this game, though, are its visuals. The game is visually reminiscent of Ristar for Genesis or Knuckles Chaotix on the 32x and it's simply gorgeous. Even some of the character designs are reminiscent of characters from Ristar. Most of the character designs are decent and original (even if Lilac is obviously hedgehog-esque) and there's a lot of extra frames making animations smooth and pretty. Backgrounds and levels have a heavy Chinese/Mongolian theme to them and while it's not exactly my taste, it's aesthetically sound. Musically, it's fairly good too, even if the Oriental-themed tracks don't do much for me and I find them a bit forgettable but they do their job of being decent background music that fits the mood.
Frankly, the game is spectacular...if you can seperate it from its inspiration and spiritual forerunner. If you can overlook the miles of dialogue with poor voice acting, strange level design, odd combat, and weird physics, it might be worth picking it up when it's on sale. Otherwise, I'd give it a pass.

The first few hours of Castle Story seemed to scratch a castle-building itch I had been having. Seeing as this is an Early Access title, I was more than willing to endure the countless AI bugs that left my Bricktrons doing absolutely nothing and repeatedly ignoring my commands. I was determined to build and epic, sprawling citadel to defend against the oncoming waves of enemies. Sadly, it wasn't long before defending against the repetetive waves of identical, easily dispatched foes lost its charm. I could not fault Castle Story for its lack of content, it IS and Early Access game. So, I waited. A check of their website said they were "re-factoring" their code. This was indeed a lengthy process and five or so months later, they announced its completion and that regular updates would soon resume. I held out faith that after the "re-factoring" of their code, updates would come much more quickly. After all, this was what the developers told us. However, here we are now, several months later and they've wasted time and money to create a "Pause" feature and some Halloween content. The addition of Halloween content to this game was just adding insult to injury. I find it incredibly difficult to believe that after months and months of waiting, Suaropod has failed to create anything of substance which could be implemented, even it were in a buggy state.
Abandon hope all ye who enter. Castle Story, is an empty, lifeless shell of what your hard earned money actually paid to see.

I don't recommend this game, but only because there isn't a "maybe" button.
First of all you can play virtually any country in existence at the time - but if you don't play one of the major powers you will probably end up getting side-swiped as you will have little ability to influence events (nor do events unfold in the slightest resemblance to history if you are playing a minor nation).
The economic model is well done and interesting.  It ties in well with the research model which is also well done and interesting.  It takes a bit of thought to both grow your economy while still carrying out research (and eventually build up your armed forces).
The military model is very basic and not reflective of the combined arms tactics of the era.  It is particularly weak with respect to the blitzkrieg of the early war.
The Foreign Affairs model is also particularly weak and it is impossible to recreate the diplomatic events of the 1930s.  Scenarios start at various times and those starting after Austria and the Munich "peace" agreement reflect those events, but don't expect to see those events generated in the scenario starting in 1933 either by the computer or yourself.
If you love the period and play every strategic level game out there, you will probably find some enjoyment in this game, particularly growing you country in the 1930s.  If you are expecting sweeping panzer dashes, you probably won't enjoy it, hence the "maybe."

Making History II is a cool concept for a game, but happens to be poorly exicuted. The primary problems lie in bad game mechanics and cheating AI. IE: when you play as any nation in the game, you will find the AI just spams you with rediculous numbers of level V infantry. Making History II also does not take into account the differences between colonies and direct terrirory (Even though it does label them). This basicly causes the British Empire to be transformed from one of the weaker allied powers of WW2 into an unstoppable collosus. While using only a handful of WWI era tanks and these masses of infantry, it still steamrolled by military of late WW2 era technology and plentiful artillery; which realisticly would have stomped it flat.
Now while I get that this game isn't meant to parrallel history, you (as the player) are normally not the one changing the outcome. I've seen the USSR break down into civil war while I was playing as the USA on the far side of the globe. I cannot recommend this game for either history fans or turn-based strategy fans. In fact, if you like the Idea that Making History II is built on, I would rather reccomend you purchase Hearts of Iron IV, which I have found is more realistic and more fun.

OK so rather than to make a review I will summarize it a bit:
Game plays as a combination of production management, and combat management.
Production management has three components(and corresponding use):
Industry Production - needed to expand IP further, to earn money, or to build units
Manpower - to expand IP, expand resources, build units
Resources - to expand IP, expand resources, build units
For the resources, there are four:
iron(steel) - you can expand that in provinces with iron
coal - you can expand that in provinces with coal
oil - you can expand that in provinces with oil once you have the (relatively late) tech
food - you can only build pre-defined number of expansions in each province(no food in some small provinces). As a side effect, it also earns considerable amount of cash.
Now what about money? Basically, you need to keep in positive numbers to prevent negative factors(unrest). The more multiplies of annual spending you have in reserve, the bigger the "happiness" bonus. Ideally you want to be earning enough not to have worry about it. Resources can be used as multipliers for factories from basic goods(doubles, triples, quadruples amount of income per industry production depending on resources used), but resources tend to be more of a bottleneck then industry power. As for spending, every building and unit has some upkeep.
Your bottleneck will likely be manpower - so you should be bit careful about spending it.
If you are starting the game long before likely war, you are probably best off expanding your industry and resources - that will consume your manpower as well as resources early on (and money will limit how much you can be spending on industry expansion mostly, i.e., how many factories you can be upgrading instead of generating cash). However if you are in bad starting position, you may need to expand your resource/manpower base as soon as possible(read: conquer your unfortunate neighbours).
Now I have avoided debts quite a bit (playing as UK so far only), but I have seen "revolutions" or "uprisings going off all over the place in conquered territories - I guess if you are in negative, or maybe just not enough in positive to counter negative population maluses, your territories with other nationalities will tend to uprise, which will mean you lose control and income, and have to distract yourself from real frontline issues.
Last but not least - research: It costs a lot(especially at the start), and takes time to build: later on it may become too easy, actually, either through industrial expansion(money cease to matter) or through conquest.
The negative part is, that the UI is not so nice, and the mass of the world you may conquer takes helluvalot of clickfest to control(there is some chance devs may still do something about it, even as they are working on new game).
Now comparison to HOI4:
HOI4 is realtime, and made(for multiplayer's sake) some problematic choices restricting control in order to avoid pausing the game (such as global combat awareness - unless you keep looking around, game will not tell you what is happening like it did in older HOI titles). On the other hand it simulates lot of things that are just completely uncovered in Making History (the convoys exist only for purposes of international trade, which you may want to try to avoid as much as possible, no equipment varians, relatively large scale conflict due to province sizes, etc.). So in the end each game is somewhat different and you may have some fun with each.
Very laggy map, even on up-to-date computers. Making History I 's map can scroll smoothly, but this is not the case for II.
If you can't be bothered to put even a basic tutorial in your game, I can't be bothered to play it. Life's too short. Refunded.

Papo & Yo is not the first game developed in the story direction of childhood abuse or parental issues, though it is understandable that people with such experiences want to make stories with that focus.
And that in a sense leaves me feeling uneasy about what I want to say for this game. It is the awkward borderline of judging a game for it being a game, and judging it for the overall intentions.
Now, I know the review began with giving away the premise of the game, but the reason I was fine with doing so is because of an immediate flaw in the game. Within the actual first minute of Papo & Yo, right after starting a New Game, there is a dedication and following scene which give away the game's purpose. That destroys any surprise completely. I definitely think that the game should have been set up differently for an even stronger impact of the parallels/metaphorical world.
Despite that, the game moved along properly story-wise with what the characters represent. And the general events that occur as well as the world's environment are very strong and unique because of how surreal things get. The graphics of the game are mostly well-done, with interesting setup of the favela you traverse, nice color for the world as it morphs around you. Towards the end of the game, some of the physical effects that happened to the map genuinely made me dizzy, which, while not exactly enjoyable, gave me the idea of how strongly I was grounded in the distorted world.
As I said towards the beginning of the review, though, how I want to judge this game is not exactly balanced. Though I became quite invested in Quico (the main character) throughout a short game that took me less than 4 hours, that does not mean that the game was perfect by any means.
In fact, the majority of the flaws were from its technicality as a game. The game is platforming and puzzle-solving. The puzzles as a whole were all extremely easy to find the solution to; but many were made simply annoying due to how you get around as well as the Monster's interactions. For instance, there are some places where the Monster is literally in rage, trying to hurt you, which is understandable for the story. However, due to your limitations, some of the puzzles with that end up taking a long time because the Monster easily catches you, can block your path and throw you around over and over, and so on. It's meant to be a challenge for some of the puzzles, but the ones where Monster is permanently angry tended to waste a lot of my time, instead of making me more sad for the child.
Most of the puzzles for a good chunk of the game require the same repeated actions. Flip a switch here; run somewhere else and flip a few more; return to your original spot and flip the switch back. Grab this item; run away from the monster; throw it somewhere. The game didn't get that unique until some of the extremely surreal areas of the game, or the puzzles that allow you to move or attach favela houses to one another to create bridges and platforms.
The platforming aspects of the game are also rather disappointing and need lots of cleanup. There are a lot of invisible boxes blocking you all over the place. Whenever I was climbing around or jumping across rooftops, for instance, I would very often find Quico hitting some invisible edge of the roof. Despite seeing his whole body being above it all, I would fall down and have to go back around. Or there were certain puzzles where I saw a way to physically reach an object or switch, but there was an invisible box floating in the air, intentionally preventing me from getting there. There's also graphical issues such as clipping, where Quico's body would be inside of a wall or through some object on the ground.
There was also horrendous lag during certain puzzles, and also any time I would enter a new area or a checkpoint occurred. Literally, everything would just freeze up and move choppily for several seconds, until the game got itself together again. The frequency of this was quite bothersome, usually being every handful of minutes.

The game looks great, and is incredibly fun for a great number of levels, then it became incredibly hard and some levels are downright frustrating. Mirror's Edge on crack.
My biggest complaint with this game is that it gives you lives, so if you screw up a spot too many times, you will be forced to restart the whole level. I've had cases where it takes me 15+ lives to clear a spot, get to a checkpoint, only to die in the next part and have to restart the whole level again. The lives system is a mistake for this game - the speedrunners don't need them, and the players that are trying to get through for the first time want to persevere the same section again and again, but are forced to redo everything after a number of tries.

A warning: Your first playthrough WILL be frustrating. The controls are just a bit different than in any other game and they don't spoil you, either. You move exactly where you input, for better or for worse. The developers are perhaps a bit (or very) mean to you as well, and chances are good you won't feel like you're being treated fairly as you learn to ropes.
Persevere.
The game's pros more than make up for the steep learning curve.
The feeling of freedom is immense. Even during your first playthrough, you will find that the levels are designed to give you many branching paths to get to your goal. It's up to the player to decide which is faster or opt for a safer route just to finish a level. If you are having trouble, explore the level! Many tough areas can be approached from a better angle or bypassed entirely. As you master how acceleration and inertia work within the game, you will find yourself skipping huge swathes of levels and performing stunts you (or sometimes it seems like even the developers!) couldn't forsee being possible.
Learning is ultimately where the joy of the game lies. As you learn new tricks, you will see your times improving and you will find yourself looking at levels differently. If self-improvment isn't enough motivation for you to grind through some tough times, I can't recommend this game to you. If, on the other hand, you want to put in some hard work and get the highest pay-off of fun possible, this might just be the game you want.

Cloudbuilt is fun.  It's also infuriating.
Think Mirror's Edge freerunning with light combat elements, an amazing art style, lots of speed, hundreds of deaths and thousands of four letter words being shouted in rage as you try to figure out what the hell you're doing, and how you can do it better.
Every level has an end, you just have to get there.  Mainly by freerunning, dodging lasers, bombs, different bombs, turrets, different turrets, missiles, mines and purple electricity.  The parkour works well enough, though the game does have a specific feel that you'll need to get acquainted with before you can start playing with anything resembling proficiency.  Sometimes moves do fail to register as you want them to, but it's not overly frustrating.
What is, is some of the levels.  Running along a wall, dodging moving lasers that will knock you off (killing you), followed by bombs that will blow up (killing you), only to get to the end of an area and be greeted by a barrage of lasers or missiles, which...well, you get the idea.  That's before we even get to $&%# like the solar panels that you have to precisely rocket slide on, lest you get hit with any 2 of the things listed above.
But when it works and you get a flow going, the game is incredibly fun.  Trying to master each route is rewarding when you pull it off, and the game isn't overly punishing when you fail (aside from slapping you with a mediocre C rating).  The art is fantastic, the music is fantastic, and the game just feels unique and different from anything I've played in some time.

If you've never played a Worms game before, WHAT THE CRAP, MAN?!  STOP READING THIS AND BUY IT NOW!!
If you have played a Worms game before, this is one is still a blast.  I played Worms Armegeddon when it came out, installed it on my high school's network harddrive so that every student who logged on could access it and play wonderfully silly local games.  And, boy, did we.  All the time.  And you could hear cursing and laughter throughout the computer lab (followed by everyone alt-tabbing or turning off the computer monitor when a teacher came over to question what we were doing).
Almost fifteen years later, Reloaded has been brought back all that hilarious joy that's definitely on par with Armageddon.  Local and online multiplayer is wonderful.  Lots of cursing and laughter with friends (we don't have to hide it from any teachers this time).  And really this is why you buy this game.  Hilarious, goofy weapons to blow up your friends and curse/laugh when you fail miserably and accidentally blast yourself to smithereens.
What?  You're still reading?  All right, I can say more.
Good things:
-Steam Achievements: a ton of achievements that make you work (some are ridiculously hard).
-Multiple platforms:  I play on Mac and Windows both.  It's nice to have an option.
IMPORTANT NOTE: You cannot play across platforms online (I have to play on my Windows laptop when playing with friends since most of them don't have a Mac).
-Map Editor is fun.
Some Blah things:
-The single player campaign is nice but it felt a bit short.  For a really great extended Solo experience, you'll want to buy the DLC or the Game of the Year Edition.  (GOTY includes all DLC and provides some excellent challenges.)
-A LOT of Steam Achievements are linked to the DLC, so you'll have to purchase them separately or the GOTY Edition to get all of them.  BUT DLC only works for Windows.  So even when buying GOTY Edition, you can only play the base game on Mac and Linux.
The game is worth the money at full price, but it goes on sale pretty often, so I recommend keeping an eye open to snag the game for $5 or better.  (~$6.50 for GOTY)

I'll try to avoid spoilers. As the description says, this game takes place on Mars and involves work to get it terraformed. Terraforming isn't the same as colonization, and if you aren't sure of the difference, what it means is that the planet has to be made habitable before people can survive there. Terraforming is what's happening here.
PROS: Your character is easy to move around. From reading around the game's Steam page, the character went through some work to get it to where it behaved as fluidly as it does now and isn't buggy as it used to be. You will find using your character to be very intuititve. The HUD: Blessedly there's no HUD. Hooray! More time to study the environment and get engaged with the story, less time reading a list of action items and setting up hot bars and checking mini-maps. Your NPCs provide incremental storyline and tell you what's up and what you're expected to do, and the environment provides visual cues to get you there. Audio: The NPCs beep a lot and it was annoying to me. Thankfully the dev has a slider that lets you quieten them down without quietening the rest of the game. Minor quibble, I wish there was a way to run-back to see what they said last because sometimes I missed because I was too busy running around, exploring. Exploring: Wow! The surface is beautiful and curious, but the underneath is pure imagination-fuel. Lastly, something surprised me and has left me veeeerrrrrry curious of what the full story will reveal when the full game comes out this Fall.
CONS: So far I have no cons. Just typical EA stuff. It's short, has a few annoying bugs, can be a bit clunky, and unfortunately the visuals options are few. However the game dev seems diligent and responsive to the community. And they made a post recently that explained the reasons for the changes to the sliders on the graphics. Game still looks great, though. None of this is a deal-breaker to me.
For such a small work, the game is a clever concept that has some really complex storytelling elements at work.

I bought this on a whim, because it looked cool. I had seen that it got mixed reviews, but it was on sale, and I guess I was sold by the video. I also knew that it was a short story, but I didn't realize how short, or that it's unfinished. It probably should be labeled as an early release. If I had known how short it is, and that it's unfinished, I'm not sure I would have bought it. I like supporting early releases when it looks like a cool game, but the story is so short that I'm likely not going to play it again for months, when I finally notice it's been updated.
That extreme shortness, and the abrupt switch to a cat suddenly at the end makes me want to give it a negative review, BUT it really is cool. Is it worth a few bucks? Probably. Barely. But if you go in expecting a full game, even a short one, you'll probably be disapointed.
The menu system is the first thing you'll see. They try to use this projected 3D menu that acts like an object. It's really gimmicky and hard to use. You play as a little floating robot, nicknamed Dog, or DAWG, or something like that. There are a few small glitches with objects that happen occasionally, like seeing through them by accident, but overall, it's pretty well done. The physics of objects you move isn't really though. They fall like styrofoam.
You basically have to pilot this little robot around this building to find your way to the mines. I found this way harder than I should have. I kept going in circles, and not being sure which way to go. There are two missions before the mines of just moving things, and another one that was getting around scary heights to access some panels. Once you're in the mines, you're basically just trying to navigate a maze, with no idea what rocks you're supposed to pulverize. Overall, the game is really nice looking, but way too short, and really should be flushed out more. The robots don't look great, and there are some lighting issues, but the caves and the rolling hills look awesome. The lighting issues make parts of the game really hard. I ended up eventually turning up the brightness, which kinda felt like cheating. The stupid humanoid robot that follows you at one point will totally block you into a corner as well, and you'll have to try to jump over him. My guess is that the final version won't be as short, but I have my doubts that it will feel complete to the massive setup they did.
They have this at such a low price point, I can't see them making it into more of a full game, but I think it's a waste to just throw away the world building they did. I think they should work on hashing it out to recover it's rating, and make it more fun, especially for repeatability, and then do either some DLC, or a sequal. As it is now, it's not even really fully playable once. Feels like playing an alpha, but with release level graphics.

Combat is diverse, but keeps from being excessive; it's just enough make fighting through enemies and bosses feel fluid. The story may be hit and miss for some (I personally didn't mind it), but I don't think that is enough to detract anyone from enjoying this game. On top of cutscenes being skippable, there's also a "classic" mode that allows you to play through the game without any interruptions. Overall, Freedom Planet is an incredibly balanced game that accomodates for a wide array of tastes, and is absolutely worth checking out.

Greetings!  The next step on my quest to review every game in my library (after replaying them of course) happens to be one of my favorite guilty pleasures.  I really enjoy playing FTL, the graphics aren’t amazing, the gameplay really isn’t something to write home about in the core but when the game starts and you realize there is a good chance this crew won’t make it.  I still feel a bit on edge playing it after these years.
Simple in Concept:  The game itself is pretty simple; you are leading a ship though a set of systems in an attempt to warn a fleet, you’ve seen this before.  What you haven’t seen is how difficult the game can be, I’ve lost many of times to the first ship I’ve encountered.  The game is easy to pick up, you simply click on your crew and tell them where to go, click on a weapon system and pick a target.  The challenge is in threat mitigation while trying to build up resources and equipment for the final battles.
Pick Up and Play:  One of the beautiful things about this game is the overall design of how you play a session.  It is designed to be short (relative to other games) so that the investment lost when you inevitably lose isn’t great but it has these amazing components of management, RPG and grueling difficulty that come together in a game that can be heartbreaking but addicting.
Instant Classic:  Really, I’m not sure why you are reading this, you really need to get this game.  It is amazing, deceptively so.  This is a game who help define a genre and even today I consider it I a league all its own.
You’re still here?  Oh…yeah, I’m kind of just filling text here, why are you reading this?  The game is $10, you spend more money than that on some dumb DLC for another game that gave you texture packs that probably should have been included and you’ve since stopped using them because you like the originals better.  What?  No, I’m not projecting…buy the bloody game.

There are some games that I consider both entertainment and art. Papo and Yo is one of those games. I was researching short games that I could complete in a relatively short amount of time. This game came up during my search, and I happened to own it from a previous Humble Bundle purchase. I decided to install without having any idea what the game was really about  aside from it being a metaphor for the creator's troubled childhood. I found that as I began playing I couldn't put it down, and I didn't exactly know why. This review is a summary of why I believe I kept playing and why you may find yourself wanting to give this game a try:
Graphics:
Created with the Unreal engine, the game looks good. The graphics aren't amazing in comparison to some other games created with the same engine, but they serve the purpose well and draw you into the South American inspired world.
Sound:
This is a soundtrack that I would purchase and listen to over and over. You will get lost in the atmospheric tracks as you guide Quico on his journey. Even if you decide not to play the game at least go listen to the music! You won't regret it.
Controls:
I used an XBOX 360 controller to play. Not much to say here. Controls are simple and the world easy to navigate. There's a basic jump and float mechanic that you will find yourself using throughout most of the game making the game feel somewhat like a 3-D platformer at times.
Story:
*Minor spoilers ahead*
This is where the game's primary focus lies. The game tells a dark tale of a boy and his relationship with his alcoholic father. The story evoked a wide range of emotions from me as I played. I felt myself smiling at times, but there was one moment in particular I remember. It was when the monster ate a frog for the first time, and it evoked some genuine fear and panic in me. I won't say much more than that in order to avoid any major spoilers, but the game does a great job of telling the emotional story that the game's creator set out to tell and bringing you (the player) along for the ride.
Puzzles:
I made this a category, because this game is technically a puzzle game. I found the puzzles to be fairly simple with only one or two that made me have to give any thought aso to how I would solve them. I was ok with the simplicity, because the game really is more about the story than it is about solving puzzles. However, if you are a player looking for deep puzzles and gameplay, then Papo and Yo may not meet your expectations in these areas.
Overall experience:
I genuinely enjoyed playing Papo and Yo. While it may not be the type of game that I'd typically find myself playing, I was pleasantly surprised how it drew me in and kept me engaged until the very end. While the story may not be the happiest story, I felt the ending fit the tale well and didn't leave me unsatisfied. The game's soundtrack also delivered, and will be one I listen to periodically when I'm in the mood for a great game soundtrack. The graphics and puzzles aren't the strongest, but they didn't detract from my experience at all. I recommend you give this game a shot! You might end up being just as surprised as I was!
TLDR;
I recommend you play Papo and Yo for the story and soundtrack, but don't come for the puzzles or any deep gameplay.

This game is excellent but it requires a keyboard, don't let the 'partial controller' support fool you. It is REALLY partial, such as there is no interact button on the controller so you can interact with any of the spells beacons to upgrade or change your powers. You HAVE to use a keyboard for that. It's got good graphics but it's pretty hardware demanding, I've run this on three different computers I own, all for gaming but only ones a serious gaming machine. On almost any graphics setting it lags pretty bad and is pretty choppy on the two weaker systems, on my main gaming PC however it runs beautifully at full settings. In the end my biggest issue is the 'partial controller support'. It's junk, literally the game cannot be fully played with just the controller and what makes that upsetting is that a handful of controller buttons simply aren't used in the game, it's like they started to develop support and then just dropped it. Overall if you're a PC gamer, loving your keyboard and mouse, it's great fun, but you'll need a pretty beefy system to play it smoothly. If you're a part of the controller trend like myself, then don't buy this, simply put you can't play Lichdom with a controller alone. To be honest, this game was amazing.
From reading the other reviews, what I can figure out is that how you play the game and what magic you use in the game really changes the experience you will have. I have heard someone complaining about kiting the first boss and taking 15 minutes to kill it in one go, yet when I encountered that same boss it took me two minutes (using lightning missiles with an agility shield). This game has a great many playstyle options to choose from, and it may take a little bit trying to figure out which style matches you. But once you find that style... my god. This game will make you feel like a god.
For me, my chosen theme was high-damage lightning bolts with an agility shield, allowing me to quickly dodge about the battlefield. A particularly awesome moment for me was during the third boss fight (no spoilers), where the deafening cracking sounds and the blinding flashes of white light literally disintergrated groups of enemies into satisfying puffs of black smote were so awe-inspiring, because I knew that it was me that was causing such chaotic destruction.
The story too was awesome. The developers put quite a lot of personality into the two main characters and, indeed, many of the villians you will encounter. I also appreciate the uniqueness of the whole situation. Instead of the usual cliché that a medieval fantasy would spin, this game seems to add a whole dose of reality to the world that your characters live in. The world seems very tactile, very real, despite being a set of linear pathways. Plus, the environments are absolutely stunning to look at.
As to the things I didn't like about this game? Well...
- Sometimes the dialog would bug out and mute, and characters would bug out, if I reached a destination too fast.
- I had an awesome legendary spell component, and I decided to upgrade it once more to make it even more powerful, and the random number generator spat out an item that I couldn't actually use, thus destroying the awesomeness that was. (This only happened once, but it was still annoying)
- While fighting 20 enemies at once can get pretty hectic, especially if you have archers, wizards and giant demon monsters who can all kill you rather fast... Fighting even more enemies would be even more awesome :D
9.5/10 - Will play through again. Willing to pay for a sequel.
(-0.5 for my negatives at the end there)

Only half of the in game text is proper, only half of the buildings/characters have color, and even the tutorials are just incredibly lacking.
Tutorial: Has no quest tracker/progress, and doesnt explain anything really. The only reason i knew how to actually get by was because i've played games like it before. The only thing it explains are what certain buildings do; not how to upgrade your citizens or how to make Denari, or how to improve the internal infrastructure.
Art Scheme: The pixelized art scheme makes the game fun, and is a personal plus. However, as i said before, they left the color out of many different things. Text: I noticed many typos throughout only the first two missions (meaning there must be much more later on), and in some places there is no text whatsoever. Mission details are incredibly lacking, and general information on how to play the game is non-existent.
Controls: Well, first off, the zooming in and out is inverted. Then there is the insanely high map dragging speed. I went into settings, and it was on the absolute lowest speed too. You can't place a building down anywhere were an animal is. For example, there was a... well i dont know honestly since it didnt have a texture... but there was an animal, and i tried placing down a senate building (which is massive) and it took about 30-45 seconds for the animal to move out of the space before i could place the building. Then directly afterwards, it walked back to the spot, and literally walked right through the building. On top of all that, the sound track is lacklastur, and will make random noises at unneccessary times. Finally, the options menu. Key bindings? Non Existent. Settings in general? Absolute crap.
Now, i know that this game is in the early stages, and they warn of a lot of bugs. But SERIOUSLY?!? When i think early access, i think playable. When i see this game, it screams "NOT EVEN STARTED". Definitely not worth the 15 seconds to download until they get their act together.

This game is an economic, political, diplomatic, and military simulator for World War 2, with scenarios for the different phases of the war, allowing you to play as any country, for any objective (country points, empire points, ideology points).  In doing this, it is very effective.
The time campaigns allow you to take on scenarios that were significant world-changing events, although they may not be too popular with WW2 historians.  For example: the Spanish Civil War between Falangist (Spanish Fascists) and a coalition of Anarchists and Communists (the militia unit models bear the iconic red-and-black, CNT-FAI cap); the Chinese Civil War between Mao TseTung (the Communists) and the Kuomintang (and their Authoritarian, psuedo-imperial branding); the diplomatic and strategic Cold War that developed between "Communist" and "Democratic" nations leading to a land-grab as the war increasingly drew to a close.
Everything is so well-detailed, and it unfolds using the game's own engine, without prefabricated events (so it's not like it's just an "interactive movie").  And when you participate in the events, whether it's Italian Partisans coordinating their attacks with Allied landings against Balkan fortresses, or Russian troops crossing the Ural mountains to claim Romania, Bulgaria, and Germany, you get to see it all, and you get to be playing as anyone.  You can be the nation doing the attacking, or be a larger ally of that nation and declare a War of Liberation, or you can be the nation doing the defending, or you can just assume the role of Brazil, and conquer all of South America while the world is too busy with what's happening in Europe.
If you're looking for a military/political/economic simulator of World War 2, this is it.

Sonic Generations is the last good Sonic game as of this review. If you are to get any Sonic game on Steam, please make it this one, or Sonic 3 & Knuckles. Trust me. This game gives you an awesome sense of speed that makes you strive to get the best time in each level, each mission.
That's not to say that there aren't any complaints though.
1. The game is VERY short, you can easily beat this game in less than 4 hours, which is a let down for a game released in 2011.
2. Despite trying to capture the best of Sonic's best adventures in the last 20 years, the game features only 9 stages, which, I mean, there are a good 60 Sonic games out there they could've taken stages from.
3. The bosses are embarrassingly easy.
But here are the good things about the game!
1. Each level is built with much love put into them, you will easily remember back to the days of the Genesis and Dreamcast with each and every reference and easter egg.
2. The gameplay is very fun, and it's always a blast to go at the speed of sound. Modern Sonic's gameplay is a vast improvement over that of Sonic Unleashed and Sonic Colors, providing more emphasis on 3D gameplay, rather than 2D gameplay. Classic Sonic's gameplay is a remix of the original Sonic game's playstyle, although not a perfect emulation of the classic physics. This however, doesn't affect how much fun it is to still play as Classic Sonic.
3. Fantastic graphics, and the modding community is still alive for this game, expect mods just about every month, adding new stages, new characters, and new features. It's always fun to play ported Sonic Unleashed stages on here!
I highly recommend this game to any 3D platforming lover, and Sonic fan!

is one of the best Sonic Games to come out in a while.  It has a minimal story, and focuses where it really counts, on the gameplay.  It's hybrid combination of 2D and 3D Platforming does a great job of both refrencing it's past, while being an interesting take on a modern platformer.
With it's plyethera of well-designed, satsifying levels, all of which are inspired by some of the best levels of the series, there is a lot to do.  Especially seeing as how not only does each level have two verison of it, one in which a modern verison of the titular character
goes through in a hybrid 3D-2D approach, and the other where a retro version of him goes through in a pure 2D stage.  And then there is numerous challenges for each stage, and on every verison of the stage five red coins to collect which unlock behind-the-scenes content for the game.  And finally, on every stage you get a grade, so you can always keep playing to get the best grade, and the best time.
Other things to be mentioned are that the soundtrack is a supberb reimagining of music from previous titles, and that the art style is clean and high fidelity, yet still retains that Sonic vibe.
Even though this is a clear gift to long-time Sonic series fans, this is game I'd recommend to both long-term Sonic fans, and those not familar with the series up to this point.  It's a great game, and has the ability to keep you beating levels at the speed of sound for a long time.

I purchased CAT Interstellar way back around when it was first released on Steam, and according to my time log I played for around 0.2 hours (which I have no memory of) and never touched it since. Today, though, after scrolling through my games and seeing CAT in my list for the millionth time, I decided to give it a go.
The game lasted just under an hour, which included exploring most every nook and cranny before I proceed on the main path. The story itself is very short and light, but is interesting
and left me wanting to know the fate of 42 and DOG. The short cat level at the end was a bit unusual, and the cat definitely needs some work (as the dev is aware of -- the shaders are a bit off on the fur, and the movement needs to be improved.) Though unusual, the closing cat level still left me wondering how things are going on earth, and how it ties into DOG and 42.
As far as controls, optimization, or bugs/glitches go, I didnt really run into any problems other than the cat controls (which are being worked on.) The audio is decent, though some voiceovers could use a little work. The UE4 rendered graphics are solid, not good nor bad. They get the job done.
Would I recommend it? Yes, if you got it for free or maybe on sale. Would I pay $4 for it? Probably not, but it's up to you if up to one hour of decent gameplay and a short but interesting story is worth your money. Gameplay realistically is around 20-30 mins for an A to B person or about 40-50 mins for someone who likes to explore.

Tropico is an oldie but a goodie if you're interested in strategy, citybuilding and/or politics. You're the dictator of a Latin American banana republic during the Cold War, one that's small enough that you order the placement of every individual building. You must balance the needs and wants of your citizenry with your own goals, whatever they may be, and other political factors if they appear. Depending on the conditions you set, your tenure can be anywhere from a sleepily relaxing downtime - the sort you play between other games - to an extremely violent white-knuckle challenge.
No matter your preference, the game is tinged with black comedy, as befitting a game where you basically play as Tiny Cuba and lose whenever ousted from power. The Tropico Reloaded pack you buy this in also contains Tropico's only expansion, Paradise Island, as well as Tropico 2, a less-than-stellar pirate-based sequel. I would at least recommend the first Tropico for strategy buffs interested in a novel offshoot of the genre, and retro fans who liked Tropico 3/4 (which were essentially progressively additive remakes of this game anyway).
Tropico was released in 2001 by my favorite defunct strategy developer, PopTop Studios. You might know that the series was picked up later by Haemimont Games and turned into a veritable franchise. Don't let the charming Y2K-era graphics fool you here: Tropico may be the most laid-back game in the series, but it's also the hardest in the series. You don't get quick construction, or a raft of DLC buildings to supercharge your economy, or
for that matter.
In fact, the most difficult aspect is arguably construction workers needing to manually clear and level the terrain for everything you build. This means you'll need to do some logistical planning before you want that airport built, and the sooner the better. The increased difficulty is mitigated by the fact that you can still choose what traits your Presidente has, the political and physical climate of the island, and how often random events happen.
The 60-odd included scenarios, like the game itself, range from pretty easy to almost stupidly hard. If the base game starts to wear thin for you, you'll probably like the challenges they have to offer. You don't get to choose your Presidente's stats or island conditions for a scenario, though, and they will often force your ruling hand whether you like it or not.
If there's anything to criticize, it's that the UI is somewhat dated, at least by the standards of Haemimont's sequels. It's more or less lifted from PopTop's earlier title Railroad Tycoon II, where it shared the same characteristic of being a somewhat archaic interface in a classic genre game. Tropico also has a slower pace than its modern sequels, but that's not a big deal if you're patient.
The biggest flaw in the whole series (and something I'm told Tropico 5 remedies, although I still need to play it) is that if you just focus on profitable industry early on, providing everything else you need and that your citizens want becomes much, much easier once the money starts rolling in. The solution here is to increase the challenge for yourself, whether by playing a scenario or generating a barren rock of an island.
In theory, the feeling you get from balancing all the national concerns would make up for that problem, but that's still kind of predicated on making mistakes every so often and dealing with the consequences. Every choice here has a consequence, big or small, whether you know it or not - and on a related tangent I would say Tropico is perhaps the most sim-like of the series. My advice is to try roleplaying if you need an extra challenge and haven't been doing so already; one of the other strengths of the series in my opinion is the dynamic between a player's ideals (or designs) and the gameplay reality they have to deal with.
At least Tropico's Latin soundtrack is just really, really nice. It's certainly the most bucolic and varied in the series. Best part is, it's still

. It even makes military coups seem...well, okay, not
stressful.
A bit of advice for new Presidentes. Citizens put satisfaction of needs above work in terms of importance in every Tropico game, but here it's especially important to make sure you build with that in mind. Also, don't be afraid to play nasty if you're about to be kicked out while still learning the ropes.

You want to captain your own spaceship in a tense chase across the galaxy. If also helps if you have delusions of being Patrick Stewart as Jean Luc Picard.
Do not judge this game on its graphics; that was my first mistake. My second was thinking I could take on giant, alien spiders... but that's another story.
Behind the simple graphics lies an indie-gaming goldmine: Straightforward concept, quick to dip into... yet packs immense strategic depth and subtlety the more you play it. The game is a mix of tight resource control, ship management and good old combat (in RTS style). You get to oscillate between the gallant feeling of "divert power from the engines to the shields and give them a full volley!" to musing over whether to make repairs, hire the funny-looking robot or install that big, shiny-looking weapon... and to helplessly watching your ship crumble as a fire rages in your engine room and your crew are being devoured by insectoid pirates. It's a tough nut to crack though, so not one for the casual market or easily frustrated. By the time you're done, aliens will ultimately be able to craft a new asteroid belt out of the debris of your dead ships, jus' saying.
Graciously though, you can complete a playthrough in around 2 hours (give or take) - so it doesn't demand an obscene investment of time or scupper several evening's-worth of hard work if you lose. But in terms of longevity, you have 29 playable ships to unlock and win with; each packing their own load-outs, crew and unique challenges... so you're not going to run out of content anytime soon either. In effect, it lets you invest as little or as much time as you like.
Additionally, the game is
paced. You're being chased by a deadly rebel fleet, so always have to be moving forward, regardless of how well or ill equipped you are (no grinding for resources)... But it's not in real time, so you're not forced to finish every encounter with urgency. Equally, the game lets you issue commands whilst paused (which is a highly recommended habit to get into) - so it doesn't require quick reactions either. Ultimately: It creates a fun, tense pressure without forcing you to rush.
It's very challenging but feels incredible when you win. I think it's safe to say that most players still fondly remember the feeling of winning their first, nail-biting finale... an effect that few games can boast about. If you have the perseverance for a challenge - then I think you'd love this one.
Fun idea: If you start running out of ship names... base them on the way your crew died in the previous game. Keeps things morbidly hilarious, especially when you name the crew after your friends.

So the reason i am writing both a short and a long review is because I wanted to go more in depth about the points made above and add some more that aren't in the short review. So let's begin!
+This one is pretty obvious.It's a rogue-like game (or rogue-lite as some people like to call it) so the developers made sure that there was a lot of replay value and goddamm does this game have a lot of replay value! From the many ships you can use to specific challenges you can undertake (they are fan-made however so you don't get something for completing it). It's a lot fun using OP ships and even if the ship isn't the best you can still have fun but it does limit the fun you can have somewhat.
+ The combat system in this game is fantastic!!! So you aim your weapons and you hit the ship in whatever system you want( you can hit their weapon system so their weapons can't fire, hit their crew teleporter system so they cannot send enemies to your ship) so there is great variety in combat and is very in-depth.
+This one is mostly tied with the replay-value of this game. There are tons of ships you can use and unlock during a run and there are tons of weapons you can buy from a shop ranging from ok to amazing.
+ This is pretty self-explanatory. The game is very difficult (almost unfair at times) but stays fun 99% of the time.If you don't like difficult games I woudln't recommend this game to you but if you do like hard games then get it!
+The variety of the weapons in this game is very big ranging from lasers to missile weapons that have limited ammunition. As I said the combat is the best part of the game so it's great that there are a lot of weapons to choose from.
So this game doesn't have big problems but rather it has some small annoyances so they don't really hinder my experience (they may hinder yours) but are worth mentioning.
- The final boss is VERY ANNOYING!!!! The game doesn't have more than one bossfight but GODDAMM AM I GLAD THAT THERE AREN'T MORE.This boss consists of three phases WHICH ALL OF THEM SUCK for different reasons.
After all that the game ends and it's admittedly satysfying to beat the final boss for the first time.
- So this honestly is my biggest problem with the game. Unlocking new ships is definently not bad but it is A PAIN IN THE A$$!!!! So there are ten ships (plus two secret designs) in total, the first ship is the default one and the second is very easy to get. As for the rest they can be unlocked by two ways: You either have to beat the game with a specific ship or you can do the quest which will unlock the ship that is for that quest so essentially it's a choice between difficult and random. I choose the quest because it isn't as hard as beating the boss with a specific ship but it is randomised as all hell!
However i have to admit that it is very rewarding to finally get a ship that you want for a while.
I think that this game is AMAZING and that you should all get it immedeately unless you don't like hard games. While at first you may be sceptical about this game because it's short, the game has so much replay-value that it justifies the price tag even if it's not on sale.It has some flaws but every single game on the market has flaws.

THIS IS AN EDITED REVIEW 2 YEARS AFTER I PLAYED THE GAME ORIGINALLY.
I was very excited when I heard people say "It's like if sonic, mirror's edge, and megaman had a love child."
Sadly, the enemies ruin the game. Instead of being a fun platformer that flows well, it is instead a frustating mess that doesn't know whether it wants to be Mirror's Edge or Dark Souls. Stationary enemies force you to avoid them, and the level design forces you to memorize where all the enemies are. You are memorizing levels instead of adapting to new situations.
If the enemies were removed, this would be an addictive, difficult third person parkour game.
The story sucks. Apparently it's about a girl who almost died during a war? I guess it's supposed to be emotional, but I didn't care. A game like this doesn't need a story, especially a story that's this sad.
Buy this game.

okay, so here's the deal. This game is really ♥♥♥♥in fun, really ♥♥♥♥in addictive, and really ♥♥♥♥ing hard. This game will kick pretty much everybodies♥♥♥♥♥when you first start, which is probably why they give you so many god damned lives for each level. It's a speedrunning precision platformer. It takes a while to get used to but when you do, expect to keep throwing yourself at levels until you finally beat them, and then play them again until you can start speedrunning them. It takes incredible reflexes and a quick mind to figure out the best possible path through the insane and interesting levels.
First, use a keyboard and mouse. I tried using a gamepad, expecting it to be better suited, but this game requires the accuracy of a mouse.
Second, you're expected to die over and over as you force your way through a level. Don't get frustrated when you die and be happy when you pass a level with a C ranking. B rankings on your first completion are rare but amazing. The A and the S ranks will require you to work for them.
Third, take your time with each level. Don't try and speedrun it on your first playthrough of each level. Take your time and explore and as you get better you will begin picking up time on your plays.
Good luck and have fun.
I will add this. The last few levels on each path do everything I absolutely hate in game design. I find them flawed and artificialy difficult in a way that requires throwing yourself at a brick wall until you figure out the exact way that works down to a science. The common idea for well designed difficult games is tough but fair, where is this is simply a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to do. It requires muscle memory and route memorization and explotation rather than ease with mechanics, exceptional reflexes and skill. This is where it becomes clear that this game's audience is very specific. I find the level design of the last few levels almost game breakingly bad. I beat them but with a bitter taste in my mouth from the experience. Of course after beating them finally, the levels are rather♥♥♥♥♥♥easy, because you already went through hell to play them over and over. I do still recommend this game, however I find the ending levels to be regretful and beyond disappointing. Ultimately, I disagree with the ending design philosophy and ended up hating the experience, which is a shame because I love the majority of the game.

I wanted to love this game. I really, really did. The concept was great, the art was fantastic, the music brilliant, and hey, I'm a math major/philosophy minor, so I'm totally down with all the introspection between levels. But the gameplay itself was a big, hairy scary ugly wad of fail.
+Forget turrets, mines, and pit falls, your biggest enemy, and one that will haunt you from minute one until you rage quit, is the camera. If you ever played Ninja Gaiden on Xbox  (or NG Sigma on the PS3), it's that level of terrible. Always where you don't want it, and it follows you way, way too closely for a third person runner. It would have been better to take the full on first person approach than this "three steps behind" business. It doesn't really change contextually either, so if you have to bounce from one wall to another vertically, and the one wall is behind you... yeah, uh... good luck with that because once you're on the first wall you can't even *see* the second, even once you turn.
+The controls are a nightmare: Way too touchy, overly complex, and not intuitive enough. Wall running is a sketchy business because your direction of run depends entirely on your angle of approach, and being off one way or the other, even by just a few degrees can bone you. Also, the boost mechanic just feels totally off to me. (Tap boost to keep running straight on a wall? Are you kidding me?!) Even basic jumping feels wongy, it's really difficult to guage distance and landings, and while I get the physics of skidding to a stop, landing on a concrete surface should not feel like landing on *ice.* Especially if I'm *not* coming in hot with my jet pack burning.
+The *flow* is awful, which is a sin for a runner like this. I'm forever finding myself standing still, just trying to understand the layout well enough to pick a route, and *if* my attempt is successful, I have to stop again, catch my breath, and reevaluate the landscape... lather rinse repeat. I suppose, if you had a map memorized, this would be a non-issue. But for a new player, it completely destroys the immersion a game like this is supposed to provide.
+Speaking of new players or players with less skill.... Look elsewhere, guys, because this is nothing but a frustration fest. This game has a completely and utterly POINTLESS "lives" mechanic. You screw up, you loose a life. You screw up too many times on a level, sucks to be you. You now lose all your progress on said level, and have to restart it from scratch. This is NOT a good way to teach people how to play. Constant do-overs are stressful and breed resentment. A lot could be forgiven if this one thing died in a fire. Even a "free play"  or "practice" mode for each level would be a huge help, but getting rid of it entirely would be best.
In closing, I'm glad I got this during the Steam Summer Sale, because I would have been heartsick if I'd paid full price for it. I was hoping for a really amazing free running experience, but this just isn't it. What a pity. Oh well... Guess it's back to running like a madman around Italy and Revolutionary era Boston.

Do you like Super Meat Boy? Are you okay with blistering difficulty, paired with instant respawn times and the smoothest control scheme possible? Are you a neurotic perfectionist? Do you LOVE JETPACKS?
Good! This game is the one for you. On the outset, the controls seem twitchy, and the levels are confusing, but trust me, when you figure it out, it all works perfectly. The moves that didn't make sense soon start to feel natural, and while the levels don't have a set path, you realize that ANY road can lead to where you want to go, since most lead in the same direction anyway. Don't like consecutive wall runs at 90 degree angles? That's fine, just make a left, and try the vertical wall run instead. Levels can usually be beaten in under a minute, and each level has 5 different modes, such as Infinite Boost, Pacifism Runs, Waypoints, and 1-Hit Kill. The plot is mediocre so far, but the voice acting isn't bad even to my standards, and it has a decent script.
