This is one of those times I wish there was a neutral option on Steam.
Then there is the obvious fact that these characters were all started as Sonic Fan Characters. Heck, I remember this character back in the Sonic Community. It kind of ruins this game into feeling stand-alone. When I see it, I just go 'Oh that sonic fan-character game'. Like, that is what this really is. I think this game would have been a lot better if the style and characters were designed a bit more to be more.. unique. Obviously they  tried a bit to tip-toe away from the sonic art... that is in the GashiGashi cover image. But the in game sprites still show that reminiscence of the original characters, as well as the other official art which is clearly from someone's Sonic fan-character work.
These characters actually kind of FEEL like Sonic OCs, as in they don't feel very... fleshed out? The actual game plot and dialogue feels eye-rolling at times, not to mention the bad voice acting. Actually, some of it isn't that bad, and you can get used to it at times, but that's probably because in game play you mainly hear grunting, and not the actual written dialog. Another problem with this is there isn't really a stabilized volume in the voices sometimes. Especially in the beginning, I noticed the two female protag voices were way off, then stabilized after the first level, but then OTHER characters were having the same issue right afterwards. I found myself kind of skipping through the dialog because of this. As I have been playing, I found myself actually wanting to skip scenes, because the lack of interest in this plot, and the painful sounding voices. Add that with long speeches and long boring scenes.... ick.
The game play isn't bad, and actually is quite fun.. although a bit cheese at times. It plays as a normal side-scroller, think Sonic 3 mixed with Rockman X or Zero, with a dash of Ristar (When playing as Lilac). I can't really tell though what the point of some of the items are. Red drops are obviously health, while the Blue drops... are kind of weird to me, I see times where I pick them up and my count actually WENT down, not up? There never really was an in-game explanation... at least from what I saw just playing Story Mode. The shields are a bit of a mystery to me as well. I assume they have the same rules as the Sonic 3 bubbles: Gold gathers currency?, Red stops fire damage, Green is just a Shield, and Grey...? I am not even sure with grey.
The music is really cute, and the colors and pixel work is very pretty. Though, I cant lie and say the music even sounds original, as I am hearing certain similar music that I would hear in other games as well (especially in some boss music.). A few songs here and there were pretty, and I did like the tracks from them, especially "Invisibility" track.
Heck, even some of the levels seem to be very... generic? You have your Forest Zone, Your Mine Zone, Casino (Er Shops?) Zone, Battalion Zone. Hell that's all Sonic right there...Which is a shame, because as I said, the pixel work is really cute and colorful, and a lot of the levels Do look nice. I especially liked the second part of the Casino/Store stage, with the slot machines and escalators. I thought that was actually pretty neat, and one of the more original levels of this game. But after a while, a lot of the uniqueness kind of ... phased out? The levels are pretty huge in this game, and there is a lot to explore, but after a while, it didn't feel like there was much uniqueness to it.
If you like class Sonic style games or side-scrollers, and are not scared away at the obvious Sonic Themed characters. You MIGHT like this game? But then at the same time, that might be the thing that makes you despise this game too. It disguises itself as being this new original game, but in fact just feels like someone picked out bits of games they liked, recolored and shopped some sprites, and called it their own. There are some neat things here and there, and as stated, if this game went a bit more away from the Sonic Style characters, and got better voice actors (or sound control) and fixed the plot a bit to be more interesting, this would be a game I would recommend to people for sure. For now.... eh... find something that feels like more though was put into it.

I bought this game to try out during a Steam sale a while back. I loved it so much that I purchased it for full price on my Wii U, recently purchased it again on Steam for a friend, and went ahead and bought the soundtrack for myself.  The game is filled with so much charm from its gameplay, level design, soundtrack, and characters that it quickly became my favorite Indie game of all time.
The gameplay can become more and more fast paced as you get to know the characters and how to utilize them, but the level design is also open ended enough for you to slowly platform and explore at your own pace if that's more your style. The controls are extremely tight and responsive, and each stage is very unique with a new gimmick or two thrown in to keep the game feeling fresh as you make your way through it as well as plenty of collectibles and powerups scattered around to discover. Every stage also has a different artstyle and theme that are all very pleasant to look at. Sometimes I'll end up finding myself admiring the back and foregrounds as I'm playing through a level. A cool feature is that the second half of each level doesn't usually look the same as the first half, and the music also changes to correlate with that effect. It offers a nice change of pace, especially if you're trying to check every nook and cranny for secrets as the levels can take a bit of time to get through on your first run. Every once and a while a stage will throw in a Metroidvania style segment in there, but nothing too confusing. If you just follow the flow of the level you should be able to make it through just fine.
The level design keeps you on your toes by offering some good platforming challenges while usually being broken up with a miniboss or two for you to defeat before progressing, but none of the bosses feel intrusive. In terms of instant death there are very few bottomless pits or crusher segments throughout the game, and whenever there are it's usually made obvious so that you can easily avoid them and not feel cheated. Underwater segments allow you to swim and are pretty short, and with air bubbles and bubble shields around you shouldn't have to worry about drowning. The main challenge will come from dealing with obstacles, enemies, and bosses as you make your way through various platforming sections. Luckily there's no touch damage to deal with, but that doesn't mean you won't feel overwhelmed at some points if you don't properly take care of certain enemies or screw up a platforming challenge. Things can get intense pretty fast. Oddly, lives in this game don't seem to mean anything even when you get a game over, so don't worry about them when you're trying to defeat a boss.
All the boss battles are very distinctive. They can range from taking down various machines big or small, to dealing with rival characters who get in your way. You'll have to discover and use a different tactic for taking down each boss, and some of them can get pretty difficult. Utilize all your character's moves to see what works best against each particular boss, and with a little patience you'll manage to get through them. It feels very satisfying once you figure out how to defeat a boss, especially the more difficult ones that can offer up quite a challenge. I love most of the bosses in this game, but I'll admit that there are a couple I don't really care to fight against. It's not really an issue though since the music for each boss makes up for the ones that I don't find too exciting to fight.
The soundtrack is top notch with each stage and many of the bosses having unique music to go along with them. Woofle and Strife did a very good job with the soundtrack and making sure each piece of music matches the stage they're attached to, and having the boss themes sound epic and thrilling with a hint of intimidation in some of the more intense boss battles to match the tone. The theme song is also fantastic, and I'll usually hum it whenever it plays. The soundtrack is definitely worth purchasing if you enjoy listening to gaming soundtracks in general. The music is definitely filled with a whole bunch of character. (Shameless segway)
The characters in this game are all very likable from the way they play to each of their individual personalities. Each character has a distinctive playstyle with Lilac being the all around fast paced character with pretty good offensive and defensive options, Carol being more oriented towards offensive play with quick and effective attacks, and Milla having a more defensive playstyle that can be effective with just the right amount of patience. Each character also has various abilities that help them to stand out such as Carol being able to ride on her motorcycle whenever she finds a gas canister. All of this makes repeated playthroughs a joy to experience as you'll need to switch up your previous tactics to see what works best with the particular character you're playing as.
Switching characters also allows you to experience the story from slightly different perspectives. One side of the story might reveal more about planet Avalice's history, and another side might reveal a little more backstory about the heroines of the game. The pacing of the story isn't the best as some of the cutscene breaks will alter between being pretty lengthy to pretty short, but if you're enjoying the story in Adventure Mode then you probably won't mind too much. The voice acting can be hit or miss, but I personally think the voice actors did a pretty decent job most of the time. If the game's story just doesn't appeal to you, then you have the option to switch to Classic Mode with very minimal to no cutscene breaks and very little dialogue. The story won't appeal to everyone, but I enjoy it. It's basically what I expect the story to be in a game like this. In fact it was even a bit more than what I expected, so I appreciate the effort. The world building in particular is fantastic. If that's something you look for in a story then you should be pleasantly surprised.
To any fans of the platformer genre of gaming, I wholeheartedly recommend giving this one a try. It's a fun platforming challenge with intense boss battles, a great soundtrack, and very likable protagonists. With plenty of reasons to replay the game such as trying different characters, finding hidden collectibles and easter eggs, going for achievements to unlock, and it being a delight to speedrun as you get better, I'd say it's definitely worth the asking price. GalaxyTrail did a great job with this one. It definitely left me wanting to see and experience more of what they create in the future.
It brings back memories of playing sonic on my genesis. I love this game. Definately reccomend it. Love the voice acting and music!

Brad really is a broken man because of his actions, and he becomes more and more ♥♥♥♥♥♥ as the game goes on.
The game can also get pretty creepy and unsettling due to some of the grotesque enemies and events in it.
The music really sets the tone for what happens in game. It could get really pumped up, silly, or serious. Sometimes the lack of music sets the tone nicely as well.

LISA; The Painful is a brilliantly told exploration of a broken mans imperfections and misconstrued desires to improve himself in a hopeless world, through the means of a compelling story and solid gameplay. These two elements are flawlessly intertwined to create an environment where your choices have a lasting impact on character relations and management of in-game resources. A somewhat jarring and potent soundtrack fortifies the games desolate, yet rich atmosphere, and amplifies feelings of constant uncertainty as you go about exploring it. The wonderfully (dis)tasteful humour of LISA is also a nice breath of fresh air from the usual macabre tone.
The only issue I have with LISA; The Painful is that I wish the usually taboo (at least in video games) themes of
were tackled with a bit more depth. When they are explored, it is done very maturely and provides a lot of introspection on the main characters personality and previous actions. You may also get depressed playing this game, I guess.
All in all, a very well-done RPG and I'd recommend it to those looking to play games of the RPG genre, albeit ones a little more left-field than its contemporaries.

This demo would be an 11/10 if it had a save state for a certain extremely frustrating part.
It starts out great, and has also been continously updated with new content (for a demo, no less!), letting you slowly discover more of the house and its secrets. The sweet killer is that when you 100% it, you get an item that carries over into the main game. THAT's the way to make a demo, people. Other developers should learn from this, as the hype train for the game in question becomes so much bigger and impactful.
Unfortunately, in my version of this, it's impossible to escape a certain encounter without getting infected, which made me super-salty. It reminds me when I could only afford the original Resident Evil game with no memory card, having to restart the game whenever I died.
A quick Google-search shows this instance put other players to the brink of insanity as well. The irony is, this could have been cured by simply having a...wait for it...progression save state. An ink ribbon or otherwise, I couldn't care less. Just don't force me to play through the same areas for hours and hours, because it turns the great horror into great boredom really £ucking fast. For now, I have to play over and over to get to that point and I always get infected, which is super tedious, and keeps me from getting the best ending.
I would recommend this, if and when they give you the ability to save your progression. As for now, having spent hours never making it out of that certain situation, this demo can eat a d|ck.
EDIT:
Okay, it's now obviously not even my apparently lacking skills that are to blame. I just kicked the item in the middle of the room into whats-its-face, and it didn't even register, the damn item went THROUGH him, and happy as a fat kid with cake in front of him, he just continues to attack me. Whereas in all my playthroughs before, he went unconcious when I kicked the object into him, so I could at least run for the door. Queue "You died". Again. Through absolutely no fault of your own. Yeah, we're done here. Game might be good, demo can not be recommended.

I downloaded it just to be able to submit this warning.
This game WAS fun...five years ago.
It was marketed successfully with advertisements that drew gamers at the time, especially those oriented to the TCG genre, to join. At its peak, players competed globally against thousands of other players.
After a while, however, the developers stopped their online advertising campain, seemingly confident that they had a stable and reliable customer base.
Players, over time, outgrew the game and many left for one reason or another. Since then, the company has very nearly failed.
The majotity of what remains of its players are a number of seasoned veterans who go about hoarding cards that are no longer obtainable through booster packs, players who then go on to use their massive collections to manipulate the game's virtual market in their favor, effectively alienating new players and further destroying the very game they support.
Graphics: 7/10 (Card art is all original illustrations by various artists, but game animations are generic.)
Sound: 4/10
Gameplay: 4/10
Overall: 5/10

I've been playing this game on and off since 2012, on the online browser which was far superior to this. It ran on flash and was smooth, reliable and easy to use. With this big influx of "flash is dead" mentality, the Urban Rivals staff/dev team which consists of about 10 people, as confirmed by a member of the team. This was a colossal mistake because they transferred to WebGL which is horrendous to use and the result is a load of bugs and terrible HUD/GUI on the online version from the card images not loading, to being impossible to make a new deck let alone update one. It took me about a week just to find out how to get out of deck builder (press the grey bar at the top).
It was clear cut. The broswer version was close to unusable and the android app is.
With the release of the steam version it gave them a chance to move away from,  sorry to say, but ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥WebGL. Instead of implementing an option to use flash which they did online up until about 2016, after which they removed it and I had extended arguments with the staff on why they decided to change it, surprise surprise, their numbers are plumetting since 2012, which is actually when I started playing.
The steam version offers little improvement over the web version, atleast you can see which card lost/won the previous round in game and all the images. Unfortunately this comes at some more bugs/mistakes which were overlooked such as not showing which player's turn it is with a white border around the profile icon. Another problem is the fact that there aren't many settings to change.
All in all the best part of the game isn't even the game itself, it's the community, which is a rare thing to say these days and the market. There is very little value or importance of playing in this game and you can just use basic economics to make a profit and collect the cards.
Finally I would like to say that I, and many others will not play this game until it is in a state that is reliable like the old flash version, dead or not, the version should still be available.
Thank you and kind regards, EpilepticRabbit.

In FTL: Faster Than Light, the player has control over a spaceship that carries extremely important documents regarding the Federation which cannot fall in the hands of the Rebels. In the midst of a large-scale conflict, the player needs to keep their vessel away from the Rebel fleet as long as possible while fighting their way through various dangers of space.
FTL is a Rogue-like mostly about strategy, but more precisely about risk-taking and micro-management. The player has an overview of their ship, its internals and crew, enemy ships during battles, and sector maps. They can choose to upgrade various characteristics of their ship, assign specific tasks to individual crewmembers, choose what deal to take and what deal not to take when encountering other spaceships whether they are hostile or friendly, and manage battles when they can't or shouldn't be avoided.
Several spaceships, with unique specifications and perks, are to be unlocked which play differently and add variety. Making significant progress requires dedication: FTL is not an easy game, but it is very rewarding.
Although a fair amount of random hazards and dangers are present, experience is key to go far in each space adventure. The ability to manage every aspect of small spacecrafts that you can then use into battles, coupled with the risk associated to the exploration of every sector, make this game extremely addictive.

This game is essentialy very good, if there wasn't the connection of minimal chances with maximum chance of occurance. To win is easy in theory: destroy the enemy before he can destroy you. tl;dr: Monotonous, slightly modified version of Skyrim's magic system, sans mana bar. Everything else is the same. Game's not bad, looks good, fun for a few hours. Doesn't feel too much like early access (not many bugs to speak of), but there are some obviously in-progress set pieces.
Personally, i didn't find the game all that compelling. The magic quickly becomes an exercise in "blink everywhere you go", each enemy takes exactly the same amount of damage to kill, the spells take just long enough to charge up that you never feel like you're playing something "quick", and overall it's just monotonous. Different spell effects claim to do different things, but ultimately you wind up with one damage-dealer, and a couple of "i wish these were cooler" spells. The crafting is good, and it's required to get through the game - but it doesn't change how you play. You're just min/maxing your spells when you craft, they all act the same otherwise.
I usually don't mind these sorts of things. Especially not when the game is trying to do something unusual. But in this case, it just doesn't feel like it's worth buying. Maybe they'll put more effort into it, maybe they'll fix the monotony. But as it stands, I can't honestly recommend it.

Freedom Planet is a rare homage to the 16 bit era of gaming. In a sea of "8-bit" games, Freedom Planet dares to throw in all that was great about owning a SEGA Genesis into the new millenium. The game invokes not just Sonic the Hedgehog, like people would expect, but also titles like "Rocket Knight Adventures." Each of the currently three playable characters play unique to each other and are fun in their own rights. My only complaint right now is that the adventure mode is rather samey for each of the characters. My favorite story is Lilacs, but I feel after you beat hers, you hardly have to play either of the others. Carol, maybe. Milla's came out recently, and while I loved playing her character, the way they handled her story was disappointing. I was expecting to get a new perspective on the game's story, but instead I got some possibilities squandered and others outright ignored. Don't be fooled, her story does not follow the other two. While it does tread its own path, it does so while sticking too close to the originals.
Regardless of storyline hiccups, I found the game itself to be wonderful, and the characters endearing. The game gets infuriatingly hard, but in a good way. If you want to play a 16-bit styled platform, this is the game for you.

Straight off the bat, I have to say that I've *always* wanted to play a game where you're dumped on a planet and told "terraform this". I don't think there are enough games that really scratch that particular sci-fi itch, so CAT Interstellar earns itself a gold star right there.
Then I have to take away the gold star because both times I've tried to start the game up, I had to try maybe four times before it actually worked. I don't know if that's the game's fault, or my computer's, but I'm not having that problem with other games. Similarly I don't see any reviews here saying it's difficult to start up. So that's neither a positive or a negative comment, it's just something that happened to me.
My first and immediate thought is that I don't understand the title. The game is called CAT Interstellar, but you play a DOG module. That was a constant thought in my mind while playing the game. Is it a pun? What's happening? What does CAT Interstellar mean? "Construction And Terraforming?" That'd be pretty cool - CAT Interstellar is like, an offworld construction corporation, similar to Weyland Yutani or something. But then what does DOG mean?
Movement through the areas is entirely functional, if completely standard. WASD to move, mouse to look, shift to sprint, and space to jump. My only complaint is that that default non-thrustered move speed is so slow that you pretty much just have to keep one finger on the thrusters constantly. The double jump is a pretty nice feature though, makes bouncing through the admittedly gorgeous terrain very fun.
I love the androids too. The plasticy looking bodies with their glowing faces when they talk is really cool. They look like they've been committee designed to be "non-threatening", and "approachable". However I can definitely imagine them having some sort of hidden programming and when they want to be, totally terrifying.
Now, on to the niggles. This is stuff that I think could definitely be looked at and improved upon, but is by no way a deal-breaker from a gameplay perspective:
1) The DOG drone that you play. The texturing is... non-existant. As far as I can tell, it's just an ambient occlusion shader on the model, with some blue and some particles at the bottom of the thrusters. I don't know if this is because it's a placeholder for a final model/texture, or if it's by design, but I'm not too fond of it. And since we're going to be playing a game where this is constantly going to be on our screen, I kind of want a little more from it.
2) The sound mix of of the androids is very very quiet. I'm glad they've got subtitles at the moment, because while it's not too difficult to hear what they say, the quiet tones make it hard to really take it in. This sort of links in with my next point too.
3) Lots of telling, not much showing. So the DOG is equipped with a spectrometer that can detect stuff. But information about it is given to us via the quiet tones of the androids. I'd have liked it if one of the androids had gone "This is graphite, scan it, so your spectrometer can detect its chemical signature" Or *something*. Then it would have clued us in to what the blue splodges were on the ground that we're supposed to follow. You could have different samples of chemicals, and scan them all, so you can detect them while you're going around the planet, thereby finding more resources as you learn what the signatures of other deposits are.
4) The android by the skylift tells you to go find three boxes, and put them in the skylift. I did that. He then says "You lost all three?" No man, I put all three in the lift like you said. I don't know if I'm just not getting what he says, or if the wrong speech file is playing, but it doesn't make sense to me why he would say that.
Overall, this early access bit is really very short - almost too short to really get a good picture of what to expect from the full release. I really do hope that this turns into a fantastic game, because it certainly has the potential, and as such, I recommend it.

I have been playing this game for over nine years and hope that this honest review can help interested new players, despite my low in game hour amount posted on Steam.
Objectively, what is Urban Rivals?
Urban Rivals is a trading card game. This means that you buy packs, buy sell and trade cards within the community, and play in various game formats.
Theme wise, this game is based off a science fiction city controlled by various gangs or clans. You as the player unite these clans together to fight in gang wars against other players to win glory and prestige for yourself.
Gameplaywise, this game most closely resembles Poker with a Magic the Gathering/Yu-Gi-Oh! life system incorporated into it. To win, you must reduce your opponent’s life total to zero or below yours within four rounds by utilizing your deck and resources given to at the start of every game.
Pros of Urban Rivals:
Short Gameplay Time – In a hurry? Each match of this game can be completed in under five minutes. You can get multiple matches in one gamming session and it is easy to put down or pick up whenever you have a few minutes to spare.
Single Player Mode – Don’t want to play against people online? You don’t have to. There are a currently four excellently designed single player campaigns that are available.
Great Strategy - There is a plethora of differing options at your disposal to pursue victory. While some strategies are more successful than others, there is no one deck that is unbeatable. Each deck type has its own strengths and weaknesses.
Great Tutorial –There are a wide variety of card abilities that you will encounter thanks to the decade that this game has been in existence. The tutorial does an excellent job of showcasing everything you need to know and rewards you with a decent amount of in game money for completing all the tutorial missions.
Respectable Number of Updates – This game does not stay stale for long. There are new cards put out monthly and a new clan rolls into town roughly once a year. Additionally, there are unique events that happen on a nearly weekly basis.
Cons of Urban Rivals:
Community Interaction – The major problem this game has is that it cannot connect to the online message boards. These message boards let you connect with a community that has been around for over ten years. Additionally, playing with friends online I feel will become more divided. There will be your Steam friends and your Message Board friends. Also, by not including the message boards, you miss out on joining an online clan/community of your choice. These groups allow you to help advance your financial gains and provide you a place to develop and hone your skills as a player.
Free to Play, Not Free to Win – This game acts like a traditional trading card game. The best way to build up a card collection is to buy packs. These packs costs credits that can be earned by some in game missions or be bought from Urban Rival’s online store. These packs vary in variety, but have a randomized allotment of value within each of them. There is a silver lining to this though, and that is in the marketplace.
The Marketplace – Nearly every card in the game can bought, sold or traded to other people within the community. While not necessary a con, this can get in the way of you wanting to collect certain cards. Cards have a fluctuating in game value according to basic principles of supply and demand. The success that a certain card brings to a deck heavily influences market prices. Additionally, there are people that like to manipulate market prices on certain cards, making them hard to buy or find at a reasonable price. However, overall the marketplace is a necessary part of the game and allows you to perform the trading part of this trading card game.
Card Balance – In recent years, card design in my opinion has been all over the place. Cards that are released either change the gameplay landscape or are unplayable trash. While every card can be played, the issue of power creep over the years has taken its toll.
User Interface – Poorly done when it comes to graphics. The online and phone OS versions of the game have much crisper images. Additionally, there is no exit game function that I can find. You have to push the X in the top right corner like it’s a 90s game. Finially, there is a tab in the menu bar that is not being used for anything. The user interface feels rushed to me.
Overall, I would recommend that you try this game, but would not suggest it to you.
You should try it preliminary and see if you enjoy the gameplay mechanics and ponder thought process that went into making this game the success that it has been for over a decade.
I will state that if you want to experience the real strategy that this game provides, you will be forced to put some money into the game. It is the way that this trading card games functions. If that is a turnoff for you, I completely understand.
I would rate this game a 7/10 despite my negative review. Its ten-year life proves that the developers know what they are doing, but that they don’t necessarily have something that will take the world of trading card games by storm. The major thing the developers need to do is to move away from a company that feels like it is stuck in the early 2000s and change it into a more modern looking game of the future.

The retro graphic style is brightly colored and crisp. It doesn't feel outdated as the game mixes new mechanics with an old school style. You can feel the inspiration of old school Sonic the Hedgehog, Megaman, and other sidescrollers.
That doesn't mean this game is perfect. Some of the voice acting isn't the best, but it isn't terrible. The sound mixing of each character seems to vary wildly with some being much louder than others. This isn't a deal breaker, but it's a bit of an annoyance. The story is a bit cliche but it does a good job telling it. Sometimes the boss rooms and stages are WAY too large. At one point you fight a large Mantis and the room is WAY too large. You can really easily loose the boss in the room If you are playing as Lilac. Again not game breaking but it gets really annoying.
But back to the good, the game in no way holds your hand but it also isn't super hard. You're introduced to concepts as you come to them by learning rather than being told what to do. This makes learning quick and seamless. The game doesn't suddenly ramp up in difficulty making it impossibly hard. It gradually increases but you never feel like it's too hard. It doesn't feel cheap and you don't feel cheated.
Overall I HIGHLY recommend this game.

Final Fantasy IX is awesome , and I can't give a non-biased review free of nostalgia no matter how hard I tried, so instead I'll focus on the port rather than the game itself. Overall, I believe this to be the definitive version despite a few nitpicks.
While not a HD remaster, the graphics have been greatly improved. The main character models have been redone and look fantastic, the UI is sharp and the prerendered backgrounds have received a bit of TLC too, though they haven't been redrawn. Some look a little dated -  a notable example is the main square of Alexandria. All in all, the improved graphics allowed me to enjoy the game on my HD monitor without reminding me that I'm playing a 16 year old game.
Unfortunatley, the command menu during battles is carried over from the mobile version rather than the PSX version and thereby takes up more screen space and feels cumbersome to navigate. While the option to use the PSX command menu would have been nice, I did get used to this version quickly and found it had no functional impact on battles as it can be hidden at any time.
There have been more beneficial changes to battles as well. The original’s battles took their time to load, much longer than the previous FFs on PSX. After loading, the camera panned around the battlefield for a while before you could take control of your characters. The steam version’s load times are thankfully much shorter and the option of skipping the camera panning is there, saving you a great deal of time over the course of the game.
Other features included with the intention of saving time are the speed up and no encounters boosters, which I abused frequently. The former helps you navigate the large locations of the game quickly or cheat at the Chocobo Hot and Cold mini-game, which I heartily suggest you do. I found skipping random encounters most useful when exploring the world map or back tracking, but it can also be handy for keeping the party's level low or skipping to story segments without interruptions. These features give you more control of how you spend your time in-game and the whole experience is better for them.
The issues I’ve highlighted weren’t impactful enough to be real concerns, whilst the new features and graphical improvements really helped me delve into this classic again. Props go to Silicon Studio for an excellent port, and here’s hoping for a fully realized HD remake one day.

FFVII has long been my favourite game of all time ever since I played it back in the 90s. I also enjoyed VIII and X (but somehow missed ever playing IX), but I think I enjoyed this more than any of them. It's just a fantastic game, they really don't make them like this anymore
First the port is pretty good. The 3D models (especially those of the main characters) look a lot better than the originals and the spell effects it seems have also got a makeover and look very nice. The 2D backgrounds however are the original low-res textures which look fairly ugly to be frank (although they been smoothed and filtered), especially at first. But you do quickly get used to them. The menus and dialogs have gone HD, as have the character icons, the Tetra Master card game etc. The cutscenes have also got a makeover and look pretty good. I've encountered no technical problems.
Secondly, the game. It's just fantastic. Magical. This is what RPG gaming should be like. Compared to the previous 2 titles, IX has gone with a more medieval/steampunk vibe which I love.
What makes this game truly great are the characters which are the best bunch of any video game I've played. The writing is just superb. You really really care about each of them. Then you have music from Nobuo Uematsu, which is possibly my favourite of all the FF games. The story isn't quite at convoluted and complicated as VII and VIII and probably better for it. There is a lot of humour and light heartedness in the game, but it gradually develops into weighty themes about love, life and death, and the central guiding message is about the importance of friendship. We also have the most organic and "real" romance of any FF game, and the most wonderful ending.
With a good PC port and 10/10 game, this is a must buy if you haven't played it before.

Some games you play for the mechanical gameplay, others for the beautiful visuals. Rarely you find a game that keeps you playing solely on the merit of its story. LISA is one of these rare occasions. Overall, an unforgettable game experience that resides amongst my favourite titles of all time.

You play as Private Miller of the United States Marine Corp and Private Dimitri Russian-Name of the 62nd Rifle Division and later the 3rd Shock Army of the Soviet Union Red Army.  You get two perspectives on the war between the American Pacific Front where people yell loudly in a language I don't understand and try to stab you, and the Eastern Soviet Front where they scream in two languages I DO understand and actually kind of giggle at how evil everyone is.
World at War is a continuation of the shooting, and multiplayer, made popular with the first Modern Warfare game, only this time it has a World War 2 spin to it instead of a modern spin. Weapons still have this meatiness to them mostly thanks to the big punchy blood sprays you get when you hit someone, but also because of some of the animations your targets do when they get hit.
World at War also stands out from earlier games in the series, for at least the time, for being actually pretty violent. Limbs can get blown off, people get beheaded, burned bodies get all crispy and grilled beef patty looking, and screams of pain are a lot more frequent and common.
Single player took me around 5 hours to get through on veteran difficulty, including deaths. So your average, competent shooter fan could probably breeze through the campaign in 2 to 3 hours on the lower difficulties.
The tone whiplash from character to character is also so intense I flew out of the driver seat and smashed into a nearby dumpster filled with other confused, injured homeless men who steal cars.
The marines are always reluctant to be where they are for the most part. Most of them just kind of want to go home and stop having people yell “BANZAI!” At them before charging them with a live grenade or a gun they mistook for a pointy stick.  While the Russian campaign has you followed around by a man named Victor Reznov, someone so kill happy that he actually gets visibly upset when others don't want to kill people as much as he does.
I can't actually understand what the Japanese soldiers are saying, but if it's anything like the Germans then hoo-baby, that is some Saturday morning levels of villainy. Outside of the usual order barking and lines carried over directly from Call of Duty 2 and 3, you sometimes get a few moments where the Germans talk to one another that isn't canned dialogue. And it actually feels like they wanted to make a Wolfenstein game but were told it had to be Call of Duty instead.  I don't know how true to life it is, though, I wasn't there. I was in the States at the time experimenting with peyote and boxing for sandwiches.
There's also a few decisions you have to make during the story, but none of them really effect anything other than what path you'll take to get to the same place or if someone gets killed or gets killed but more painfully. Except for the end where you have to make a decision that's also kind of lack luster because I actually kind of forgot one of the characters the decision involved was actually important since I kind of mistook him for just another friendly NPC throughout the story.
The game play works with singleplayer, for the most part anyways. Sometimes they throw so many enemies at you that are so gunning for you over the dozens of other people on the battlefield that it can be pretty frustrating to move around. Chucking grenades into your hiding space while you try to regenerate health, forcing you to move and change positions, only to open you up to about half a dozen hitscan weapons that can, at the same time, throw your aim off because obviously it's going to be hard to aim when you're getting bullets put in your immortal death god body. For most of the game, its alright, but later parts of the game it's just needlessly trial and error.
Outside of the single player mode there's also a multiplayer mode made popular with the previous entry in the series. World at War builds on what Modern Warfare started with a few hit or misses. The dogs for instance can leave me alone and never come back, but from what I can tell, kill streaks are kind of frowned upon by a good portion of the community anyway. I can understand, the recon plane is fine and all, but the more aggressive ones kind of let people who are already crapping on others crap on them even harder and stinkier.
It's still fun, though, and World at War still has a pretty decently sized community playing, even more than the most recent entry in the series, and that one had space guns.
It's no Quake 3 or Enemy territory, but it's still a pretty decent arcade shooter, with enough game modes to keep you busy for at least a little bit. There's also a progression system that's mandatory for the COD series at this point where you unlock new weapons and perks as you level up, but there are actually servers set up with the experience boosted by a couple thousand points, so you can just grind out your progression for an hour or so if you just want to even the playing field with more long time players, at least in the equipment department.
If you're just looking to pick up a Call of Duty game to just kill some time, then this is probably the one you want to go with. It's cheaper and still has a pretty populated multiplayer scene, so you can at least get your 10 bucks worth. Other CODs do multiplayer and even singleplayer better, but you can't really go wrong with World in Kerfuffle.

Put simply: Papo & Yo is one of those games that gives you something to think about (if you're paying attention). Those just looking for another brain-bending puzzle game on the level of Portal will likely be dissapointed as the puzzles only seem to stump those who don't immediately grasp the full scope of what can be done with the gameplay mechanics (raises hand...). If a pretty puzzler with a unique aesthetic and healthy dose of introspection into how children deal with fear and familial violence is your bag, then buy and download now. (No that's not a spoiler. The live action trailer and the opening dedication when you start the game pretty much give it away.)
Without trying to sound hyperbolic, the game's message might be too on the nose for those players who have dealt with the issues being explored, but then again that might be the whole point here. That aside, I often found myself stopping to admire the simplistic yet beautiful visuals of what I assume was inspired by the infamous favelas of Brazil. More than once I stopped to take screenshots of the various pieces of street art (to call it graffiti would be to sell it short) on display, something I haven't done since my time with Spec Ops: The Line.
It's a short game and only sticks around long enough to make its point known (about 3 hours) which might turn some players off. If however you're someone who likes to repeatedly ask themselves, "What is the game trying to tell me here?" during a playthrough, I think you'll find a lot to love (and hate, but in the good, engaging kind of way.)

I'd like to put an asterisk on my recommendation. It is a good game, in my opinion worth buying and playing, and I enjoyed every moment of it.
However, here's the caveat: it's not a challenging game. It's very much Railroading: the game, with a few obstacles to get you more invested in it (still better than "Dear Esther"). To me, that's not a problem, because the game's atmosphere, music and visuals are excellently designed, and the brazilian voices (I'm assuming it's brazilian) are a delight to listen to. For some however, this might be a problem.
If you need a proper challenge to enjoy a game, this is definitely not for you. As mentioned, the puzzles are simple; just find the next switch to open the path to the next setpiece. A few puzzles require a bit of fiddling to solve, in particular a basketball court that took me a few reloads to get back on track, but it didn't make me use my head as a scratching post.
It's a short game; as you can see from my play counter, it was completed in less than 4 hours. It's short, but sweet, and I'd argue that's its selling point; it doesn't drag out the overarching theme about substance abuse ad infinitum, and while the ending didn't grab me, that's not a fault of the game. It's nice to see such work put into telling the message of substance abuse seen through the eyes of a young boy, as it is quite a serious problem in the world today, and the game is just beautiful, as I've already said. Buy it for the experience, not for the challenge.

A gorgeous and interesting 3D puzzle platformer with a subtle story which is told through the gameplay. Papo & Yo offers up a great looking, fun game with a depth of story substance which never once interrupts the great gameplay. The game treats the player with enough respect to draw their own conclusions and is never overt or crude in its approach. It's a hands-off story which compliments the gameplay, and it's wrapped up in a gorgeous world with good mechanics.
The best parts of Papo & Yo come from it's strong commitment to the story in the form of real elements rather than text or purely cutscenes. Everything is focused around that, and at times gameplay choices have been limited or altered to compliment the subject, and vice versa. There's one puzzle, for example, where your goal is to move the Monster to a new position while he's sleeping on a wooden centipede. After figuring out the mechanics of the puzzle and moving him into position, he catches a frog which results in your progress being reset and having to start again. In any other game this would be frustrating and forced, but here it's a subtle allegory of trying again and finding an alternative approach after you fail in the name of progress. Even things like the music of each puzzle serve to compliment the spirit of the story.
If you remove the story though, Papo & Yo is still a very good 3D puzzle platformer on its own, and just playing through it without thinking about the content matter is pleasant fun.
* The art style and set design is another compelling reason to play this title, the streets and buildings have a strong South African/Brazilian look and feel, and add to the fantasy
* Puzzle design occasionally feels wobbly, but for the most part is unique, interesting and wonderfully different to the approach most other games would take
There are no real gameplay problems to speak of in Papo & Yo, and everything is done pretty well. However, there are some minor annoyances and technical problems that will jar the experience for some, but overall wont really take away from the experience as a whole.
* Movement and controls are a little less responsive than I'd like, and it's common to fall off a ledge or have to repeat a step a few times to get something right
* Due to the unique design and style of some puzzles, it's sometimes unclear what the game wants of the player next, despite the useful help system
* For some, the story is too obvious and the flashbacks give too much away at the start of the game for the ending to have any impact
Priced at £10.99/12.99€/$14.99 at the time of review, Papo & Yo doesn't feel overpriced, but is very short, with just 4-6 hours play time. It routinely goes on sale for -75% or less, and waiting for a sale to get the most value out of this one is a good idea.
There's an achievement for playing through the game without using any of the hint boxes, and another for collecting all the hats in the game which only becomes available after completing the game once. These two achievements make playing through the game again some time in the future more compelling

Will say, it is a overall really solid game. Mixes a lot of the classic playstyles, with some newer touches like VA and plentyful powerups. (that granted, you will have 0 idea what most of them actually does) So yeah, it's a great mix of old and new. It also attemps to tell a more mature story, both for good and bad. As it has some characers and moves that feels more at home in a more "casual" story. Yet, it does said story rather well. So it's a give and take. It doesn't always manage to flip-flop between "srs bsns" and "roflmao" tones. I could probably have worded that better, but eh... I did love some of the running gags, but as said. It was hard to get a decent emotional shift in.
As for the gameplay, it's a healthy mix of "gotta go fast" and faffing about exploring. Certain characters pander more to certain styles. So there sould be something for everyone. (that are into platforming ofc) There are some bugs and glitches, but it's mostly clipping errors. I've yet to find anything that forced a restart or anything like that.
So it's very solid in it's structure. Something I would say is the weak parts of the game, is that it heavily relies exclusively on memorization. And I know some like that, but to me, that's just a crutch to pad out gameplay. Especially at some parts with incredibly cheap traps. Or bosses with bs, 3 hit moves, that can only be dodged by using your special attack, as it makes you momentarily invurnable. So it is impossible to kinda stroll in and clear several of the bosses on your first try. As you can't without having done them before, due to said prior attacks. You need to know them beforehand, else you just get instantly killed by the unavoidable attacks, that has to be negated with a timed invurnability. Might not be a problem to some, but I found it to be one of the frustrations in the game. Even if some of the bosses are literally just unfair, (and that can be a good thing) they are unfair in a bad way, so to speak. Both due to as said that you gotta memorize the moves, but some moves are just a tad bit too cheap (and often off screen).  So be prepared to have some cheap part of a level, or a boss rack up a number of kills, or K:O's on you.
Graphics are a nice retro mix. Though even there it has some contracitory tones. Like, one of the characters has to me, one of the most hilarious "hanging" animations in any pixel game to date. Which, to me at least, felt a little off in the more serious sections of the game. If there's something I think could have been a nice touch (and might be in FP2) is if the character you played got "roughed up" so to speak. Like, at low health, they looked a bit battered and bruised. As, again; with the tone. It just feels a bit odd aestetics wise when the character has 0 hp left, and stands around as if nothing is wrong. Would also have loved if you could on rare ocassions trigger a sort of "last stand" to use a cliché term. Like, instead of dying (either by slumping over, or exploding in a ball off fluff. Have to just say I love how they chose to do the two death animations in this game xP I've missed the cartoony aspects of this style of games) get a timer like the one where you are drowning. Maybe tint/dim the screen a bit, and possibly slow down the character some, and give a chance to grab a health item before the timer runs out, and the character faints. (or it could be a 100 % thing to happen for a specific character. Kinda like the character from Metal Slug that can take 2 shots before dying) I dunno, I think it'd really fit the whole "against all odds" the game is going with. Just feel it'd be neat with some "shiz just got real" indicator. Right now all that happens is that the health bar blinks a little.
Though, I know such thing would add a lot extra sprites. But yeah, would at least imo be a really worthwhile addition. I haven't finished the game with all character on all difficulties yet, but even with just one character, I pretty much got my money's worth. One thing I was a bit "eh..." towards is how the replayability is handled. In that it's mostly "multi-path", so if you make one wrong turn, or at times: one of the two turns, you cannot go back. So, again: it relies on you memorizing. Which as said: To me ruins some of the whole "adventure" feel. You can't get everything in one run, you can't beat bosses the first time around. You succeed only thanks to being a magical time traveler. While I could be sorta okay with having to re-run, or at least grab the stuff with other characters, (that's totally acceptable) I do greatly dislike how I can't charge in, hypotetical guns blazing to a boss, and outwit and beat them through skill. Rather having to do a tideious grind in order to figure out their pattern and moveset.
Still, I really like the game. It's solid, has good character and gameplay. It's what you expect, with some twists and turns.

Using the dodging in the game as well as the sprint, tactics come in to play in this action-packed combat that is Lichdom - Battlemage.
CONCEPT
I always liked the Elder Scrolls games - perhaps you've heard of them (wink) and always thought there wasn't enough magic built into the most popular game, Skyrim. This is litterally that, but the opposite. With more spells than you can imagine, I cannot wait to unlock the abilities to make black holes, controll the minds of my enemies and send a toxic shudder through their bodies. I've only played 100 minutes of this, and I can't wait to play more.
ENEMIES
Holy. Crap. This... this is some darn good AI here. When an enemy is wounded, it will retreat quickly, searching for a corner to hide around or a pillar to camp behind. If it cannot find anything, it will stand for a moment, panicked, and then attack again. The Minibosses are also excellent, with the occasional spells they cast they can demolish you pretty quick, and I'm sure the main bosses are even better. I haven't gotten the chance to meet one yet!
Some things to IMPROVE about the game:
MENU
I know this is very touchy and not a priority, but this Menu needs to be fixed. I like how it's at the side, it's just very... stiff? When I hover over something, it instantly has a backround. I'd prefer if it lights up with a small animation, maybe with a nice little sound effect? I know this is just a small thing, but it'd make it look more professional.
NPCs
I don't know if this is just because I can only play 100% smoothly on lower graphics, but at least when I play, NPC's mouths do not move. This irritates me - please add this feature a.s.a.p. Also, when someone is talking, I can turn my head to hear them quiter - I love that - but the logic doesnt make sense, because if I just walk away it stays the same (Loudness? How do I say this? :I). Maybe make it so the character locks into conversations.
That's it, really. So if you're considering buying this game, make sure you do, it's great, and has a bright future!

This game is the definition of easy to play, hard to master. You have a deck of 8 cards of which you draw 4 from in a match, and using those 4 cards you have 12 "pillz" and 12 life points to work with. You have to use those pills to multiply your cards power as attack, in order to beat the enemy cards attack. This will allow you to damage them and you win by taking away all their life points, or by using all cards and ending the match with the highest life points.
But it is much deeper than that, each card has an ability, these abilities have many different properties from reducing your opponent cards damage to reducing their power, or allowing you to poison them so they take damage round after round. Each card also has a bonus, as there are many different clans in the game, having 2 of the same clan activates the clan bonus for those cards, this can vary from stopping your opponents ability, to reducing their attack.
I could go on but here are a list of pros and cons of the game:
I love Urban Rivals, this game has been around since 2006 and I first started in 2007, it has been slow for some years but in the past 2 it has revitalised itself. This game is great if you are a busy person, play it on your phone at work or on a journey as the matches are quick and fun. Packs are often very fair in handing the most expensive and powerful cards out as they are not fixed and are just random, this is fair for a pack opening game nowadays.

The previous chapter ended with Heptitus stealing your first quarter key. Mel and her friends must find a way to take it back and after that, to find the rest of the keys around the world. Will they foil the Lord of Twilight's plan to take over the living world? Besides, now that Lydia managed to get a way into the team, will Mel and her reconcile their differences?
Aveyond 3 was fragmented in four chapters. This one is the direct sequel of Lord of Twilight and as usual, the story is well-written and full of humor: Galahad and Tej'Imal are still fighting each other as the married couple they are, Edward is still the naive best friend, Lydia is a real sneaky snob, though she's not against helping Mel, Stella is still suffering from amnesia and Mel is still an expert in sarcasm, now amplified with Lydia and her gowns. Also, the game allows you to choose between six characters as Ulf, an Orc, is joining you and is probably the only serious one.
The game mechanics are still the same, though now, you have a mage in Lydia, with offensive spells as Stella is mainly an healer. Allow me to copy-paste the mechanics from my previous review as nothing changed. You level your team up thanks to combat (and well, even if not used, the characters are also leveling up), unlock spells for the mage and the healer, change their weapons or clothes so that their characteristics can be improved. You have also an inventory with scrolls, food, potions, etc.. to use during a battle (or not) to heal or to help hurting opponents in front of you. Some of them are tough - sometimes, the best is to come back later with a better team.
Some quests needs to be done in order to advance in the story, while they're appearing as being a side-quest just for the money. Others are just bonus. But given the fact that you need money to buy stuff or to fast-travel, any quest is worthy to be done. Besides, when defeating enemies, you can loot them and find also money or items. You have also chests to open or bags to find.
Now that you have a pirate ship to travel, you can finally use the docks and explore the world. The enemies are stronger there. With the compass, you can come back to where your boat is docked. It can be a faster way to travel. I loved Venwood with the elves or should I say that it was my favorite city soundtrack in the game.
Aveyond comes also with three difficulties: Easy where you're stronger and where most of the enemies don't spawn again after a defeat (yeah, I'm playing in this difficulty), Normal where every is balanced and Hard where you'll die more frequently - though even in Easy, I've been wiped. Well, if a character dies, you can ressucitate them but if your team is wiped, it's game over and it's up to you to load the auto-save (when entering a new screen) or a save of yours.
Notice that I didn't begin the game with a team at level 0. Indeed, at the end of the first game, you can choose to save your game so that it appears in Gates of Night menu when you're starting a new quest. It means that I got all my money, all my equipment, all my inventory to begin with.
Aveyond dates from 2009 and from an earlier version of RPG Maker but the graphisms are still good. Besides, the landscapes are now really varied: volcano, beach, jungle, forest, fairy kingdom, desert,... The soundtrack is really good.
As I passed 8 hours in the first, I expected the same length for Gates of Night, though apparently, the time was multiplied by two. I know that I spent a lot of time trying to find people for the quests, without forgetting that I managed to get asleep for 20 minutes on my keyboard while playing. But well, Gates of Night is really long.
Aveyond 3-2: Gates of Night is an excellent sequel to Lord of Twilight and I don't regret the purchase, so, I can recommend it to anyone trying the RPG genre or that doesn't like to spend minutes on a skill sheet or on anything else.

If even a tad more of the story was included at launch or at least one interesting mission included at the beginning I may of swayed to the recommended side. Once more story is in then I may change my review to that.
I do like the concept of the game and the terrain looks great but that is where it currently stops for me until more is added. I beat the game in 26 minutes and this includes doing the story, exploring, and throwing some random boxes around for fun.
You play as the "dog" which you can move, boost, jump, and grab objects although it looks rather plain in my opinion. You start off with being told a bit of the backstory of what is going on, I then was instructed to proceed outside to the next objective. At this objective I was instructed to find 3 boxes and move them to the skylift. After I completed that task I was told to go to the mine, an unforunate accident occurs there and that is the end of the game...currently.
This game will be story driven which is why at the moment I cannot recommend it, there just wasn't enough of the interesting bits added in for the launch which I wish I could of seen. Anything other than moving boxes could of been a better objective to start off with before further story is added on later that way I could of felt a bit more invested in the story before waiting for the rest to be put in. The game itself runs quite well, no bugs or crashes from my playthrough at least. Option of VR or Play right off the bat in the menu which is great for those who want that.
I hope to see in the future a bit more added to the surface as it already looks quite good in my opinion but could do with a tad more added to it, and will await for the rest of the story. Papo and Yo originally invented for the PS3 is renowned for it's role as an empathy game. One of the few games on the market aimed specifically to evoke an emotional empathy response from it's player, this is largely because the developer Vander Caballero found here...
has decided to use the expression of game art to exercise his own personal demons.
While it was largely inspired by the game 'ICO' there is a more larger similarity to the game 'Among the Sleep' and 'Brothers' in the way that the developer has chose to use cute characters and backgrounds to handle some adult touchy subjects such as alcoholism and physical abuse.
The story revolves around a young Brazillian boy named Quico who cowers in his bedroom closet while his father storms past. He then escapes into a magical slum world he creates where he finds a girl Alejandra who at first sees Quico as a threat, but who eventually aids him in his adventure. He is also joined by a robot toy named 'Lulu' which always has his back and a monster who is usually somewhat love-able who sleeps a lot and you can have fun bouncing off his belly, but when he ever has French Cuisine he launches himself into a rampaging devil. All set out on a magical journey which ends both bitter and sweet.
The amazing slum background which would have Salvador Dali jumping up and down on a cat in excitement is sheer magical and enchanting to explore. While the puzzles aren't that sophisticated, some can be challenging on the basis that they are slightly vague and will have you scurrying either for a hint box placed in the game which you can don on and run around in or for a youtube walk through. In truth you've probably just missed something obvious like the fact that you can move the buttons as well as press them.
Your first run through will be greeted with a metaphor of what happened in the developers personal life, you will also be challenged to go through the entire game a second time, this time without the need of a hint box and the further realization that 25 collectible hats have been hidden in the game.
So what are the metaphors in the game? Unlike other games which often be coy about the matter and leave it open the gamer's digression. The developer here wants his story to be told. (Spoiler Alert) The developer (quico) grew up with an abusive father (monster) who was an alcoholic due to the fact that he had accidentally hit someone in his car and killed them. The developer's mother (lulu) always was there for Quico until one day when the monster seemed to have killed lulu (severe abuse) eventually she did get better though through the help of Alejandra (a mixture of the developers first love and his literal little brother) .They at first tried reasoning and hiding the frogs (alcohol) which was making the monster angry. But after one severe abusive bout which took the life of Alejandro Quico eventually realises that he cannot cure this monster and instead has to let this monster go from his life for good. As Quico grows up he drifts away from his dependance of Lulu and pushes the monster away from his life for good after what he witnesses with his attack on Alejandro.
The game is well made, because the puzzles aren't that difficult no severe feeling of accomplishment is ever made and so the moral of the story is some what less victorious in feeling. The monster in the game just tosses you about too and is not really that fearing enough to make you sympathise as much as you do in 'Among the Sleep'. The biggest enemy of the game though is it's price. With such a noble meaning and story to a game you would think that they would lower the price so that more could enjoy as the game is also hardly long enough to warrant a large sum. However it should be noted that making games can be a very expensive journey. When asked why he chose frogs to represent bottles of alcohol, the developer replied that it was largely to do with cost. They originally wanted chickens to represent bottles of alcohol in the game, but to put chickens in the game would have cost them $15,000. Since they already had frogs in the game they decided just to go with the frogs and scrap the chickens idea. I have many question marks with that last statement???
Anyway the game is seriously worthy of a glance especially if it goes on sale...

To be honest I'm surprised there are so many positive reviews for this game. It is an okay game, and I mean that in the nicest way possible. It is incredibly accessible and heavily story driven so anyone can get through it with relative ease and experience the story.
However, that is probably the root of my largest complaint. My main gripe comes with the fact that almost all the "puzzles" in this game are not very clever and feel more like a chore. I never once had an "aha!" moment because it was always incredibly obvious what one needed to do to proceed. This isn't necessarily a negative for all people, but for me it is. For the most part they are just repetitive tasks you must complete to advance to the next zone.
Most people rave about the story, and I thought this would be enough to redeem the game for me. Unfortunately, it wasn't. The ending came as no surprise as I thought they were very in your face from the beginning about the identity of the monster. I did however find the meaning of the frogs and their effect on the monster to be used in a way that was well done.
Indeed, it wasn't all bad. The game did a good job of easing you into the mechanics and slowly building upon them as the game progressed. I also liked how when the monster became enraged the whole environment shifted and the monster came at you at just the right speed, This was enough to build tension most times I was caught off-guard (not realizing there was a frog around).
Lastly I want to say I did enjoy the music and art direction within the game. And a few of the levels (especially towards the end of the game) did some very visually interesting things which made me wish that same creativity could have been used to increase the difficulty of some of the puzzles.
In conclusion, I do not recommend this game for the current price of $14.99. However, if you happen to find it dirt cheap (perhaps around or under $5) you might want to give it a go. It is certainly a little adventure, but not one that I would probably take again.

Imagine being thrown into an endless arena and repeatedly flinging spells at enemies so you can watch them die in entertaining ways and constantly coming up with more efficient and/or entertaining deadly combinations?
If this premise sounds like fun to you then Lichdom can provide endless hours of grinding enemies into the next generation of spells that would become much worse for the next enemy you'll meet because in Lichdom you're only as great as the spells you create.
Sure, the story can be interesting and the voice-casting is excellent but the main draw is being a Battle Mage and being able to take on multiple enemies who would kill you if you gave them the chance! The more you play, the more powerful you become and that's a great promise for any RPG to deliver on.
It's also refreshing to see a game that doesn't make melee combat be the focal point of damage while Casters must cower in the back row and fling a Fireball every once in a while! The game looks amazing and the ownership of every death you plan for each enemy feels great and keeps me coming back for more. The spell-crafting feels empowering and it's difficult not to feel smart the first time you use a new spell you just crafted into that new Sigil you've just unlocked.
I recommend this game if you can get it for the $20 price-tag it originally had but I whole-heartedly hope the story/plot and other aspects would prove the game worthy at the $40 price tag post-launch.

Freedom Planet is a sort of retro 2D platformer, heavily inspired by the SEGA classic, Sonic The Hedgehog. Overall, the game is very good to play. The story, although not the greatest, is okay and didn't bore me at all. The graphics are in the same vain as that of Sonic classics, even some of the abilities, particularly Lilac's abilities look like that of Sonic
The gameplay, although challenging and sometimes frustrating, very solid and very good. The music is very good and I loved every piece of music played in the background
The voice acting for me was the weakest part, although I do appreciate when a game does full voice acting, which Freedom Planet does, I feel that the lines weren't recorded in a professional studio as I can hear background hissing on some of the voice actors lines. The voice acting too ain't bad but ain't the greatest either and the volume in the voice acting varied, sometimes, the loud music would drown the actors speaking completely which kind of bothered me
But overall, Freedom Planet is a nice challenging game to play and I highly recommend it to anyone who loves playing game such as Sonic and wants a change. Plus, Freedom Planet 2 is coming out so YAY!

Extremely clever level design with diverging paths through each level, encouraging level replays to get the fastest time and pursue S-rank scores.
2D sonic levels are fast and feel very smooth in general, and include most of the classic physics, controls, and sounds. These levels are usually shorter than their 3D counterparts, but have a great flow.
3D levels are a bit more platforming-heavy, but still have some very fast parts, and Modern Sonic's homing dash and boost abilities are put to good use. These levels do not flow quite as well as the 2D levels, but are visually striking and still manage to feel good.
Challenge levels range from fun level variations to frustrating gimmicks, but are largely decent twists on the gameplay, and are mostly optional for the main story.
The soundtrack is wonderful, containing remixes of many level themes from throughout the series.
The story is pretty much a throw-away but frames the coming-together of classic and modern Sonic decently enough to not be distracting. Although the final level and boss battle fall a bit flat, the game is overall a joy to play.

After the more modern/sci-fi settings used in FF 6-8, Final Fantasy IX is a return to the series roots. It takes place in the world of Gaia, a world full of knights, mages, magic, and other traditional high fantasy. The story initially follows Zidane, who is a member of a band of thieves who is charged with kidnapping the princess Garnet of Alexandria kingdom. In a twist, Garnet is actually looking a discreet transport from Alexandria and consents to the kidnapping as it fits her own agenda. They are joined by Vivi, a young child black mage who is also accidentally kidnapped and knight captain Steiner who is Garnet's royal bodyguard and is loyal to his kingdom to a fault. The four are eventually joined by other party members and are swept up in adventure, conflict and conspiracy as tends to happen in Final Fantasy games. Also in continuing with trends in other Final Fantasy games, the plot does sort of take a dive off of the deep end at around disc 3 or so. Without getting too spoiler-y, the traditional fantasy setting does get strangely thrown out the window at some point, but the game is still worth playing if you appreciate good writing.
What sets this game apart from other Final Fantasy titles for me, aside from its setting, is its well written characters. Now those of you who have played other Final Fantasy games may be rolling your eyes at "well written characters", but I think it really applies to FFIX in a way that no other FF game before or since has achieved. The characters in FFIX aren't the flat, one-dimensional stereotypes of characters that are found in most JRPGs. There's also none of (or very little of) the angsty JRPG melodrama found in the rest of the series. The characters in FFIX are more subtle and nuanced which speaks volumes for not only the writers but the translation and localization process this game had to undergo. This game even has humor. Like legitimate, actual, intentional humor. And it works. Usually when humorous dialogue is written in a Final Fantasy game, it's facepalm material. It's funny, but for all the wrong reasons. FFIX gets it right in a way that really endears all of its characters to the player.
The battle system is... well... it's just fine. There's nothing really wrong with it. But there's also nothing really right with it either. There's nothing too broken like FFVIII, but also nothing that really sticks out and grabs your attention to make you want to keep playing just one more battle like FFVII. It's pretty straightforward and standard for a Final Fantasy game. It's pseudo turn based with the ATB introduced in previous games and your characters fit into pre-defined roles of black mage, white mage, summoner, knight, thief etc. Just about the only thing noteworthy is that all abilities you learn throughout the game are learned from using a specific weapon a certain number of times in battle. For instance, if you want to learn the "fire" spell, you have to equip Vivi with the "Fire Staff" or whatever it's called. This creates a sort of interesting dynamic where the weapons and armor you have equipped for your party may not always be the "best" speaking strictly statistically. There's also the new "limit break" system called trance, where your character becomes more powerful and gets access to new abilities, but this triggers pretty much just randomly and always seems to happen when you're in a random, easily winnable battle and never against a boss when you really need it. So yeah, the battle system is... just fine I guess.
What's way better than "just fine" and another notable reason to check out this game is another superb, phenomenal, varied and otherwise spectacular soundtrack composed by Uematsu. I think Uematsu has gone on record saying this was his favorite soundtrack he composed. It's not necessarily my favorite as a whole, but picking a favorite Uematsu soundtrack is like trying to pick a favorite burger off of the menu at Red Robin. I love them all. Standouts are the "Battle Theme", "Stirring in the Forest", "Crossing Those Hills", "Border Village Dali" and "Hunter's Chance" but the whole soundtrack is really a standout as tends to be the case with Nobou Uematsu.
Summary
It may not have the best battle system and the plot gets a little weird about halfway through, but FFIX is still worth checking out if you like a well written story with well defined characters. The writing and soundtrack are enough to carry you through when the battle system is being dull and the story is getting weird. This game really is pretty charming once you get invested in it and it's become one of my favorites in the Final Fantasy series and just in general
