Let me start off by saying that FFIX was my first Final Fantasy game and because of that it became my favorite so it's difficult for me to be unbiased in my review.  For the sake of this I will focus on this title's validity as a PC port.  PC gamers may see the framerate which is regulated to 15 fps in-game and 30 fps in FMVs as a negative for this title but being as this is a Playstation-era game with pre-rendered backgrounds the framerate doesn't hinder gameplay.  I was completely oblivious to the framerate throughout my entire playthrough and if it hadn't been for the FPS counter in Steam I would have never questioned it.  In-game character models are updated to show more detail and to be less jagged around the edges but still keep that familiar PSOne look.  The best way I can think to describe their look is to think N64 character models which to me always looked more solid than their PS counterparts.  The boosters are the biggest change to this version.  There are numerous boosters that affect gameplay drastically with a few being located in the "config" menu that cannot be turned off once they are turned on in a single playthrough.  The less game breaking and to me ultimately more useful boosters can be found by pausing the game and using the shoulder buttons (assuming you are playing with a controller).  These boosters can give you full MP and automatically put your characters into Trance, make you deal max damage (9,999), turn off random encounters, or speed up the gameplay.  These last two I recommend for anyone who wants to do a "pure/cheat-free" run but is hindered on time.  One flaw I did not notice back in my childhood that became painfully obvious while playing this port was that the game suffers from horribly slow battle time.  Here is where the game speed booster came in handy as I would use it for level and ability grinding but turn it off during boss encounters.  I can't recommend using this booster outside of battle because you character can quickly jump across the screen and it can be easy to lose track of them, anyone who has fiddled with emulators will be familiar with this.  The no random-encounter feature is a godsend for end-game when you are maxed out already or when you just desperately want to leave an area as the encounter-rate in the game is fairly high.  The story remains faithful to the original with the same translation as before and outside of boosters the gameplay is untweaked from the original.
The only cons I can think of would be that the pre-rendered backgrounds didn't receive the same enhanced treatment that the character models and uncompressed FMV sequences did.  I understand that some pre-rendered backgrounds move and that the original uncompressed files could have been lost but it would have been nice if the game had looked polished in its entirety rather than just partially.  Still this is a small nitpick that doesn't detract from my recommendation of this game.  The Continue feature also seemed to be unreliable as I would sometimes receive a Game Over if I wasn't too careful during grinding sessions and be forced to rely on an old Save instead of the Continue feature.  I quickly learned to frequently save though so this feature became a non-issue for me.  Due to its sporatic nature I wouldn't recommend using it and to instead stick to the tried and true Save/Load option.  In short:
Pros:
-Optional boosters can remove tedium for those looking to just enjoy the story or those with less time than others
-Enhanced character models breath new life into the visuals
-Uncompressed FMVs let us see how they were meant to be seen.
Cons:
-Some boosters cannot be turned off so if you save and decide later to revert you need to restart.  Thankfully these particular boosters are not mapped to shoulder buttons and are had to accidentally turn on.
-Pre-rendered backgrounds still look muddy and the muddiness is only accentuated by the clean visuals of the character models and FMV sequences.
-Continue feature is unreliable and generally sporatic in terms of where you pick back up.  If you are level grinding against difficult enemies (say Grand Dragons) and are afraid you may get a Game Over I recommend relying on the Save and Load features instead.
Neutral:
-Framerate lock may or may not disappoint some but doesn't take away from the visuals or gameplay in any way.  Personally, I couldn't even tell.

Now that the game has left early access, after 2 years I'm changing my review from a NO to a tentative maybe.
Castle Story has finally released 1.0 and come out of early access. The game is now finally in a playable state, there are still some small bugs, but I havent encountered anything gamebreaking.
The concept behind this game has always been a great one, but during early access it was just not playable. You can now actually play the game, and have a decent amount of fun doing so.
HOWEVER, this 1.0 patch still feels more like a proof of concept than a fully fleshed out game. The foundations are there for something amazing, but the game is still lacking depth. There are 3 game modes, a sandbox mode and 2 modes facing enemies, and when faced with enemies it becomes pretty hard to build anything more than some basic walls and fortifications. Sandbox is where you can really play around with creative ideas, but there is just no motivation to do so.
I really really hope the devs continue to work on this game, as it could be something so great. I would love to see things like non-military unit classes, the addition of water, maybe some kind of "town management mode" where there are no enemies but the challenges of feeding/maintaining your population.
As it stands I would recommend this game... but probably not for the current price. Buy it for the aesthetics, or if you just want a game to relax in front of. Otherwise, maybe keep waiting to see if the devs are still actively working on Castle Story, or if they have just rushed out a 1.0 version to finally put this project to bed.

This is going to be used as a textbook example of why you should never buy an early access game.  These guys sold a lot of copies of an exercise turned tech demo.  If I were in their boots, I'd be done.  Why make a game when you cut your losses and run... and by losses, I mean a whole lot of cash up front with absolutely zero accountability to finish the game.
Yes, early access means it's not done... and that's the problem with early access; It never has to be done to be sold. NEVER!
I wish I was back in school where I would make little "game" concepts.  A few exercised examples and you pass.  Never had to worry about making it a full functioning game... that would have taken the entire semester if not longer to finish. ...but if I polished it just enough to put on kickstarter... cha-ching!  A few days or months of work for a pay out equivalent to the entire gaming dev life-cycle.  From a purely financial point of view, the payout from work is done.
Even though this game hasn't been fully released yet, it feels done.  The gameplay is great, you can run it off a toaster. Overall great game!

FTL is possibly one of the best Rogue-like adventure games of all time. You can play this game 100 times over and you'll never get the exact same playthrough twice. The variety of ships, enemies, stories and characters culminate to create a vast experience enjoyable for most people. I say most because this game may take some people off-guard with its intense difficulty.
There isn't much of a story in FTL as it is just a "go here and destroy this" type quest. However, that is where the beauty lies as the journey is more enjoyable than the destination. You will be travelling through multiple different sectors meeting aliens, being attacked by pirates, getting caught in a Nebula storm and much more. You will create your own stories throughout your journey and you can take on a multitude of side-quests throughout each run.
The Gameplay in FTL is a lot of inventory and ship management mixed with smart decision making, and ship battles. There is a lot of depth to each of these so here is the summary of each:
Upgrading your ship with the finest weapons, robots, augments, systems and crew members is imperative if you want to make it past any sector. There are three main ways to get these: buying them, destroying enemy ships and hoping to get some or through quests. The currency for FTL is Scrap and scrap does not come easy. You'll be wanting to go through as many points in a sector as possible to earn enough scrap to upgrade anything. Weapons are important as you will start with very basic (but with some ships it's nothing) weapons for offensive purposes. What they do is simple: shoot enemies and kill them. Robots are specific as they can help repair your ship, defend it from intruders, shoot down missles, shoot the enemy ship etc. Augments are special upgrades that can range from useless to amazing like having all your weapons be charged up with every jump. Systems are dire as they guide you to buy more upgrades later on. As your ship's starting systems are limited, you must purchases upgrades to improve them as well as your reactor power. You cannot have 4 high power consuming weapons as your system won't allow it. Crew is also important as they can help your ship work better, as well as fighting of enemies, making repairs and adding a bonus on your primary systems. (I forgot to mention fuel but it's pretty self explanatory).

Planning your course through a sector can be the difference between making it through with a lot of profit and being left floating in space waiting for your annihilation. Choosing which sectors to go through can be life or death decisions;
Once in a sector, it's careful you plan which star points to go to as they will dictate if you're going to end up in a dead end or make it to the end beacon. Decision making through quests can be important as well as some decisions can make or break your run. There are many random encounter and quest endings that vary on your decisions. Foolish decisions can lead you to damaged systems, loss of scrap, loss of crew etc; whereas wise decisions can do the opposite for your benefit. Decision making moves further into Ship Battles as well.
Possibly the best feature of this game. It includes a lot of what was stated previously as everything you do (gathering resources, upgrading etc.) is to survive each Ship Battle you encounter. You will possibly face anywhere between 30-50 ships (or more) per run and you need to ensure your survivability. Each ship battle will start with you seeing what they have and making decisions on what to attack and at what time. There can be a lot said about weapon variations, but it's too much detail to go into. Ship Battles will get progressively harder with each sector as your enemies' ships will be more and more upgraded, but so will you. Each battle could be your last and it really puts you on edge, but it is also very exciting. Pausing, firing, targetting certain systems, using drones, de-powering and re-powering systems are all done in Ship Battles just to ensure you get through. Think of it like a boxing match: Your enemy throws a powerful left hook and you need to dodge so you can follow up with a powerful counter. You're always going through the motions with each fight but you must also adapt when something doesn't go right (and trust me, it won't). Ship Battles are extremely entertaining and are the meat of the game - anyone can enjoy them as they include a diversity of options and techniques that anyone can learn.
FTL: Faster Than Light is an action-packed game with in-depth management systems that will keep you addicted for many, many hours. Don't let its artstyle fool you, as it is a brutally difficult game (even on easy), but no two runs are the same and it will keep you occupied, playing, hoping to beat the boss for days to come. Definitely worth $10.

Lichdom: Battlemage brings to the table exactly what it promises: an unshackled mage.
You are limited and doomed only by your own inability to use the surroundings, kiting path, specialization of spell combinations and staying mobile.
You can have active 3 schools of magic and in this build that I tried, the choices are:
•	Ice - Perfect for control and for lining up the big guns
o	Increased duration of chill
o	Damage reduction while casting
o	Slowing/Freezing enemies
o	Increasing critical damage of subsequent spells
•	Fire – De-Buff and Destroy
o	Damage over time in an AOE area or as single point spell
o	Stagger your foes
o	BBQ what is frozen for nice explosion
•	Kinetic – Just started with it
o	Does low damage in itself but on a frozen target, it hits like a truck
•	Parasite – Just started with it
o	Gives a De-Buff of flash eating parasites to one or more foes
•	Control – Just started with it
o	Mind control of enemies, self-explanatory
•	Lightning – Just started with it
o	Forks out, electrocutes bunched up groups
You are given 3 spells per school and a barrier that you can customize:
•	Barrier
o	Protects you
o	When activated while being attacked, you can trigger a Nova of the currently active school of magic
•	Nova
o	When triggered (timing during getting hit) unleashes even ranged damage to the attacker (thorns effect)
o	Can freeze foes around you/burn them/maybe toss them away?
•	Target Spell
o	Single target spells with various effects and shapes
•	AOE
o	AOE can deal damage or de-buff everything that is caught in it.
The only loot in the game are spell components that you can mix up or split up again. There is a rarity in spells (white, green, blue …).
You can combine it as you want.
I love foes getting entangled in corners while being hammered.
The game style might feel a bit repetitive: dodge, freeze, hit, run – repeat but its fun.
The story line good and involving, I would love more content besides the N+ as I really liked it for the 50+h I played it.
I definitely suggest getting it, it’s well worthy the 15 Euro!

This is hands down my favorite indie title that I've played to date and the best "Sonic" title that I've played since Sonic 3 & Knuckles. It hits all the right nostalgic notes in its presentation from its beautiful backdrops and Treasure-esque enemy design , its colorful characters clearly inspired by the Sonic titles of long ago, its catchy soundtrack, three characters choose from and more on the way (which offers plenty in terms of level variety and unique playstyles), and all of that is wrapped up in a package that just results in a game that's just fun to experience.
A few things that seem a little off are the voice work (which ranges from good to rough) and the fact that some characters don't seem to have the same amount of shading that others do (though I'm sure this latter complaint could be fixed with a few patches). The story is compelling enough to me but if you find that it doesn't interest you or that the aformentioned voice acting is hard to swallow the good people at Galaxy Trail have provided a handy classic mode so you can skip all of that and get right to the gameplay.
All-in-all I couldn't recommend this game more. Give it a shot and experience an amalgum of pretty much everything that made the Genesis era of gaming great.

WOOOOOO do I love this game. This is easily some of the most fun I've had in a 2d platformer for a while, and while comparisons to the old Sonic games are unavoidable (I mean c'mon you even have the different colored shield bubbles and loops and crap), this game definitely stands on it's own feet and is a ton of fun.
The game is all about fast paced platforming and action, and it pulls it off miraculously. It rewards you for going super fast and constantly urges you to get back on track if you stumble, it feels really good to navigate through the game. The characters all control fantastically and run through the different areas in their own ways.
Only real complaint is that it's redonkulously short, and the story is kinda garbage. The dub really isn't that bad, especially for the primary antagonist, but the story as far as it's writing is concerned is WAY too ambitious for the game's length. If the game was 2-3x as long you could probably flesh out the narrative much more cohesively, but the constant whiplash in tone gets to be jar droppingly absurd, and all around just kinda left me with a feeling of, "Did they really need to go that route?" when playing through it. The VAs were great for their respective characters but the story would have undeniably benefited way more if it stuck to a light hearted adventure to take down some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that wants to steal a gem.
Get the game though. It's pretty fantastic if you like 2d platformers, especially if you were a fan of the old Sonic games before he got washed up.

Papa and Yo is not Subtle. It takes its abusive father metaphor and beats you over the head with it. I applaud what the creator is trying to do; even more so knowing its based on his childhood but, I think the game needs a better writer.
Plot:
The plot is about you letting go of your abusive and alcoholic father. Its not a bad place to start but thats all the game has plot wise. Very little character building or reasons to get attached to the characters. The only other npc is a girl that helps/hinders you who may be your sister but is unliklely due to the lighter skin color and almost no resemblance to you. *spoiler* She dies... or just gets abused.
I have to say, I hate ambiguity. Not that ambiguity itself is bad, but few people know how, and when, to use it. Papa and Yo uses it as a crutch because 'I guess' the writers could fill the gaps with something they thought was interesting? I dont think the ambiguity is needed as much as they used it.
Gameplay
The gameplay consists of puzzle platformers. They are very simple puzzles and it gives you hints if you get stuck. Pretty bog standard as far as these things go
Aesthetic
This is where I feel the game wins. Its damn beautiful with creative use of the environment to assist the puzzles. With the exception of a few technical pop ins, the game looked great.
Sound
The sound was... alright. It did the jobs but nothing really stood out. There were also moments, like at the temple when you make the monster angry, a short music piece plays over the normal music and it doesnt sound good.
Length
Its 2 hours. Im not sure if thats good or bad considering I wasn't really having fun, or an interesting experience. I feel like any more and I would have just stopped playing. At least I beat it because of its short length?
If you really like puzzle platformer and non subtle plot threads strewn with ambiguity, then this game is for you. If not; give it a pass.

FFIX is definitely one of the best Final Fantasy games made.
Story: 10/10. The characters, especially Garnet, are absolutely amazing. This game starts so small, and later grows into a rich story that becomes so much more than what it appears to be.
Graphics: 9/10. This Final Fantasy actually has pretty good graphics when compared to the others of that particular generation.
Combat System: 7/10. The combat system in FFIX is only slightly better than the worst combat system FFVIII. There is a lot of balancing issues among the characters. Some characters you only need to use either heal, life, or blind while nothing else gets used. You could possibly summon Eidolons which use a ton of MP while doing almost the same damage as one melee attack. Very wasteful.
Probably 80% of all the abilities in the game aren't even worth using. Sometimes I ask myself why they even bothered putting a particular ability in the game. Some abilities on physical attack characters do less damage than regular basic physical attacks. Keep in mind, I am not talking about the support abilities you put stones into which are very useful.
This game’s turn based system is also very biased towards enemies, especially bosses, causing grief. The steal command is absolutely horrid causing more grief. The developers also implemented many one-shot attacks which are unavoidable causing even more grief. Then add insult to injury, when the enemies/bosses get an extra turn, the biased turn system! In my opinion, the developers probably wanted to increase the difficultly of the game, but instead they caused griefing.
The developers defintely went in the *right* direction with this system in my personal opinion. The idea of white mages, black mages, heavy melee, light melee, and thieves is great. They just didn't quite hit the mark with the gameplay aspect. It honestly feels like the combat system just wasn't finished.
Item/Weapon System: 9/10. Great idea. Love the way they designed the weapons, armor, and synthesizing.
Card Game: 4/10. Not worth the time or effort.
Music: 7/10. Above average in my opinion; could have been a much wider variety.
The Bad Guys: 6/10. Not very intimidating or interesting.
All in all, this game is one of my favorites for sure because of the rich story. The combat system was the biggest let-down; however, don’t let this scare you from the game. I still love this game even with some of the problems it has.

I, like many, originally backed this game on Kickstarter. The very nature of kickstarter is like most other investments, where the backers are absorbing all the risk on a promise of some sort of return, be it financial or in this case, a game. Of the various things I've backed on Kickstarter, this is the only one I truly regret.
Why?
Anything that I say has already been said in other reviews. The progress in development has been incredibly, painfully slow. Games that were pitched/came out after Castle Story have rapidly over taken it in every way. Commonly cited examples are Space Engineers and Prison Architect.
Even if you could objectively state that development progress isn't slow, consumer psychology is a powerful thing. Why are goods sold for £0.99 instead of £1.00? We perceive it to be far cheaper, when the reality isn't such. If people believe development progress to be slow, then it's slow unless you definitively prove otherwise.
So if I agree with the other reviews, why am I coming out of the woodwork?
It's the antagonistic nature with which this studio engages with the player base. There will always be people who are unhappy, it's the very nature of exchanging money for goods/services. However, beneath all the anger and poorly chosen words are legitimate concerns and questions that go unanswered, or worse still, answered with equal levels of vitriol and abrasion. Think of the silent observers, like I used to be, quietly asking the same questions? Some of the exchanges between the community and the developers of this game are legitimately scary. Reading the castle story subreddit was an eye opener.
In conclusion, it wasn't a mistake to back this game originally. With the information I had and the strength of their pitch, I was happy to invest and I would do it again. However with all the information available to all of us today, my opinion is that investing would be a mistake. All I can hope is that it would stop them treating the people that invested in their ideas, which by extension means investing in them as people and their future, with such contempt.

Castle Story is an interest base building/rts hybrid that manages to do a bit of both to a satisfactory degree. Over the course of development I have had more than my fair share of enjoyment from this game. The game features multiplayer, sandbox, survival and conquest game modes, managing to cover pretty much all the bases you would look for in such a game. The map editor also allows the game to stay interesting past the typical honeymoon phase.
Castle Story is not a game for someone who wants a very complex, deep game, it is primarily a voxel sandbox that allows you to do some truly crazy stuff. It that is what you are looking for you can easily sink 25-35 hours into this game no problem. If you want some more handholding and gamemechanics, games like Stonehearth are probably a better shot.
The game has been in development for a long time, but having played it since before the 0.3 release I feel the game is in its most polished state currently, and does a good job in accomplishing what it sets out to do, if nothing more.
The game currently is for those who prefer a strategic basebuilder or tower defense game, and someone who can amuse oneself, if you are the kind of gamer who needs a more on rails experience this is not the game for you.
P.S. The devs are incredibly friendly from my personal experience, and are very active in the community, something that has helped keep this game alive.

The face of hope: Underground (yes, it's uncapitalized like that) is a horror-ish FPS that should not be purchased under any circumstances.
Simply put, there is no rhyme or reason to the level design, it feels like the developer had a bunch of assets kicking around that they decided to staple together and sell on Steam for a quick buck.
An underground subway train-station will lead into a mine, which then leads into a science lab, which then leads into a room with a big hedge-maze because why not?
Like, you even find holes and gaps in the level assets where they weren't lined up properly or blocked off (the very first room in the game has tunnel sections that lead out of bounds).
Again, clearly an asset flip made for steam cards, don't bother with it.
PROS:
- It has cards.
- Cost me $0.50
CONS:
- No music
- Poor sound-design.
- Ugly graphics and incohesive environments.
- Clearly an asset flip with little-to-no effort concealing that fact.
- Flash-light is horrible.
- Runs at a solid 10-20 frames per second.
- Models pop in and out at random, sometimes they won't properly render in at all.
- Game ends on a cheap "TO BE CONTINUED?" after only 30 minutes of gameplay.
SCORE: 1/10

A beautiful and heart-wrenching game entrenched in metaphor. This game left me shocked, silent and with a lot of thoughts to process. Our story opens with Quico, a young boy living in a Brazillin favela with his abusive alcoholic father. Retreating into his imagination, we follow his adventures through a surreal landscape as he interacts with his friend Monster as his means of coping with the real world. Beautifully written and and powerfully executed, more than once I felt on the brink of being physically ill at many of the implications and how they related to Quico's life.
In terms of gameplay, it's a fairly standard puzzle-platformer. As you travel through the favela you'll be pulling levers, hitting buttons, manipulating the landscape in surreal ways, and either coaxing Monster to aid you, or running from him. The puzzles are fairly simple and never frustrating, nor do they ever interfere with the game's atmosphere. In terms of music, the atmosphere is only boosted by a gorgeous soundtrack (which you can purchase along with the game). The game's only downfall is how short it is, as it can be completed in less than a day.

that asside, I think Final Fantasy IX is definitely a god game
the game looks nice in terms of graphics, or at least, as nice as it can be. the gameplay is simple but effective and the story is  really interesting, it has a nice build-up to the main plot and the characters are likeable. The game is also a throwback fest to older final fantasy titles, and its nice to be able to spot all those references
that being said, the game, or at least, the port, is not without its faults
although i did say the game looks great, it can be a bit of a clash between the high-res character models and the low-res pre-rendered background. some sound effects are way louder than others, and its a little bit anoying when you can't have the option of just turning the SF volume down, only have it on or off.
in terms of plot, yes it has good pacing for the main plot, but it has the tendency to give some backstory to other characters to only then never touch at them ever again. it only gives development to certain characters, giving something lackluster to others or simply none at all (I'm looking at you Quina. though they are a comic relief char so maybe its ok?)
for gameplay, there's not much i could say against it. Yes it has some game breakers but so does every other final fantasy game.
overall, although not perfect (far from it actually) its certainly a fun game and i definitely recomennd it to anyone thinking of playing it.

The very idea of a badass mage game was very interesting so I took on shot on this early access game and I am very glad I did. The controls and simple and intuitive and pretty quickly I was teleporting in and out of close range mixing it up with long range AOE attacks, well timed blocks that reflect whatever the current element you're weilding back on your attackers and the blink nova attack attached to your teleport. Like a lot of action oriented games I can see the game maybe becoming a little repetitive but since this is early access I have high hopes htat the devs will mix up the combat more as the game progresses. Although early in my playthrough so I only have 2 elements so far the idea of swapping elements on the fly to mix up attacks and strategies is a fun one. The crafting system is also fun as you try and discover the different ways the sigils combine to boost everything about your spells from the pure damage, to damage over time status effects and even the speed of the casting or charging of the spell. The story is interesting so far and hasn't detracted from the game at all like so many games have done in the past. All in all a good start and I wish the devs luck with the rest of the games creation. It is good to see another Early Access game that is working and fun to play. Get the fun down first and you can refine the experience as you go.

If I could describe the game with one word I would use elegant. The game is very well presented, from start to finish you can see that the developers put their hearts in the game and took care of every little detail.
While the game's story and action may be outshined by other games this one is presented in such a form that stands out. With all game markets going nuts to more futuristic plots , this game takes place in the 50s and recreates that  atmosphere perfectly.
While the main plot is a bit predictable, the game offers a few plot twists that may suprise the player. The games also walks on a thin line between childish and mature, you will jump from sections with extremly vulgar language, cheap humor and weird situations to very brutal and shocking moments. I have to add that the voice acting is top notch.
The game starts to show his age in terms of graphics, I remember the first time I played how amazed I was and now it looks  a little dated, especially Joe's face when up close. The graphics are still beautiful to look at although but today's standard they look a bit simplistic.
The game is pretty linear, even if it is an open world game it is not a sandbox, you just drive from one place to another and jump from chapter to chapter. There are no side quests which is quite dissapointing since you meet many people who would potentially give you missions they don't do anything in particular. The DLCs are focused more on little missions like those but they kinda lack atmosphere ( I would still buy Joe's Adventures since it fits in the story and playing as Joe is funny. It also has the best missions out of the 3 DLCs).
You probably won't have enough time to try all the guns, vehicles and you will  want more gameplay. The DLCs take care of those but like I said they are not worth in their entirety.
FINAL VERDICT: I can't really call the game a masterpiece but it's ambitious and tries to get to that status but dosen't quite get there. I have to give the game a strong 8.5/10 . You may want to wait for a price drop tho.

Freedom Planet is quite possibly the best Sonic the Hedgehog game ever made. There's a lot of baggage with that statement, but it's also the clearest, most succinct way to make you understand what this game is. Freedom Planet could have exploded straight off the Sega Genesis with its wise-cracking heroes and manic levels and funky platforming physics and infuriating bosses. While all of those elements might not be good things, it forms a package that's one of the best nostalgia trips and all-around solid platformers on Steam.
You play as Lilac the dragonlady or Carol the catlady as they try to stop an interplanetary warlord from totally boning their pleasant little planet. Both characters have dramatically different styles of play, down to being able to utilize different features of the levels. Lilac can double-jump and fly short distances, while Carol can pounce and climb walls. Though their abilities are lifted largely from the characters of the early Sonic games, the ways they are combined in Lilac and Carol give you an enormous amount of control over your characters and how they interact with the levels. In truth, I came away feeling like Freedom Planet controls better than any of the games it was inspired by.
Part of this success stems from the levels themselves and their open designs. Sonic games had a habit of splitting stages into fast stages where you run through loops and tunnels, and slow stages where you do careful, plodding platforming. The levels of Freedom Planet are far more open than that, and are designed around letting you progress however you like. The main paths have lots of straightaways and loops and such to tear through, as well as plenty of open air to launch into. But there are also side paths and platforms you can navigate to using your character's powers that hide secrets and collectibles. The open-ended designs do a lot to keep you playing, since if you tire of one style you can just switch to another.
The levels themselves are explosions of hues, seemingly pulled right from the 256-color excesses of the 90s. Each of the many areas also has plenty of gimmicks, from slot machines to levitation and everything in between. One clever level lets you board enemy airships and disarm them from within. The music and sound effects are more than up to the task, taking you back to your days camped out in front of the TV with familiar tunes and jingles. There are plenty of power-ups and doodads to pick up, but if I have one gripe with the gameplay, it's that a lot of the items are not clear in their use or explained in any way. Much like the games of old, you need to consult a manual to find out what all the shields and tokens do.
That's not my only gripe, either. The bosses in Freedom Planet are an eclectic and creative mix, but become very unforgiving in their patterns only a few levels in. They are absolutely fair, and learning their patterns well enough to beat them is very gratifying, but there is almost no margin for error with some of them. The game showers you with extra lives but I went through a huge portion of them just on the bosses in the last quarter of the game. And if it seems like I'm talking around the story... well, I'm very thankful there's a mode that loses all the voice-overs and cutscenes. The plot is nothing special but many of the cutscenes drag on and on, and the VO work is awkwardly amateur-hour. Some of the story beats are unusually melodramatic, including a seriously overblown torture scene which doesn't help matters in the least.
It's a shame the story falls so flat and is told so poorly, because everything else about the presentation is fantastic. The graphics, sound, and controls evoke all the best parts of the Genesis era and make Freedom Planet a joy to experience. There are plenty of collectibles to find, an extra character to unlock, time attack modes to tackle, all on top of gameplay that'll take a good three to four hours to get through. It's not quite the accomplishment that Shovel Knight is for NES games, but if you long for the halcyon days of Sonic, or just really solid, frenetic platformers in general, Freedom Planet is for you.

While you do get to Sonic it up here and there, the vast majority of the gameplay is tight platforming and high-stakes combat with a dash of wall running and springs. There's lots to explore and discover, but the stages are designed for time trials as well; imagine a more competent Sonic CD if you will. Heck, even the story stuff is suprisingly well done as far as Saturday Morning cartoon-esque plots go. That said, having to play as one main character to get key plot points for the other is kinda dumb, and the VA work gets pretty slapdash at points.
So yeah, it's good, buy it if you like well-made platformers I guess.

There's not too much I can say about this game without spoiling the plot and diminishing its emotional impact, but here's what I will say.
This game is relatively simple, as far as mechanics go. It's a basic puzzle/platformer; it isn't too difficult skill-wise, nor will you likely get stumped by any of the puzzle elements. Mechanically it's actually a very easy game - even taking my time and messing up a bit here and there, I still finished it in less than 4 hours. Despite that, it was one of the most difficult games for me to complete on an emotional level.
I really relate to the main character, Quico. What this game lacks in mechanical complexity it completely makes up for in emotional intensity and engagement. It will hit you right in the feels, over and over. It's not hard to tell that this was a very personal subject for the game's main creator, and I think he and the creative team tackled it very well. They have my utmost gratitude for making this game. Honestly, if anyone ever asks me about my relationship with my stepfather, rather than explain it to them with words I could just have them play this game. It definitely goes onto my favorites list, and although I can't say it's one I'll play again anytime soon, I'm very much grateful for the experience it brought me.

This review stems from the recent patches applied to Company of Heroes 2. Aside from the slant being completely to the Soviets since the game's debut, the designers have taken a drastic step over--doubling down on the power and "might" of the Soviet war machine, which was in reality a joke that would have never stopped Nazi Germany's steamrolling into Russia for the two years that it was on the offensive, were it not for the Western Allies. Before I get too far, I understand this is an arcady-game that isn't meant to be 100% historically accurate, but some things should at least TRY to represent the real war on the Eastern Front. The recent nerfing of the German tanks, particularly the King Tiger and Panther tanks, is ridiculous: Somehow, an SU-76 and SU-85 can out shoot the King Tiger's 88 despite the latter having the unquestionable power during the real war. If you want to make the game balanced, then don't dumb down the firepower or protection of the German tanks, just make them have bigger issues like mobility and repair speed, like they did in the real war! When it comes to the Western faction of the game, how is it that a quad .50 on the back of an M5 Halftrack able to down a Stuka in the blink of an eye but multiple 40mm Bofors can't do it to a Sturmovik that's flying around for over a minute!? Further, I know a T-34 can take more punishment than an M4 Sherman, but when you have five Shermans engaging one T-34 in close combat, you'd think the Shermans would win overwhelmingly, right? Wrong, due to the recent patches! I'm sure there is a lot more to list, but these were the most obvious and the most annoying for someone who prefers to take the American and German factions regularly. The one thing I will say that is somewhat realistic is that the German vehicles plaster the American ones unless the latter has overwhelming AT and air superiority, as they did in the real war. That's about all I have to say. Hopefully it gets fixed back to the way it was originally.

While my preferred entry in the "holy trinity" of the Final Fantasy series is VIII (to many's chagrin), FF IX has always been a solid entry and one I generally look forward to revisiting every few years. To begin: FF IX is a fantastic JRPG. A decent story, great characters, and simple combat. There's not a lot of depth here, but it's overall a pretty fun game.
The entire reason i'm writing this review, however, is to critique this particular port of the game. Overall, it's a decent enough port, but does have some issues.
I've yet to find the cause, but the framerate feels a bit laggy compared to the PS1 original. It doesn't hamper the experience too much, but it is noticable. Additionally, Xbox One controller users (and potentially other controllers) have a weird bug associated with them that causes the selections to freak out, and the only way to resolve it currently is to turn on your controller AFTER starting the game, which doesn't have a 100% chance of success. For XB1 controller users with the wireless adapter like me, that can be very frustrating, especially because FF VII and VIII worked perfectly fine with a controller even if they required something like XPadder to assign controls. Once you gor XPadder configred, you never once had to worry about controls again.
The graphics haven't been improved much, but natural AA and higher resolutions available to the PC offer much clearer models with more details visible. Backgrounds are not as clear as you would hope, but ah well.
Overall, it's a decent port of a great game. I personally feel that VII and VIII recieved better Steam versions, but they have the advantage of actually having existing PC versions. If only IX was as nice as Lightning Returns PC is, then that would truly be something to celebrate. There's nothing so wrong here to prevent a purchase, however.

If I could describe the game with one word I would use elegant. The game is very well presented, from start to finish you can see that the developers put their hearts in the game and took care of every little detail.
While the game's story and action may be outshined by other games this one is presented in such a form that stands out. With all game markets going nuts to more futuristic plots , this game takes place in the 50s and recreates that  atmosphere perfectly.
While the main plot is a bit predictable, the game offers a few plot twists that may suprise the player. The games also walks on a thin line between childish and mature, you will jump from sections with extremly vulgar language, cheap humor and weird situations to very brutal and shocking moments. I have to add that the voice acting is top notch.
The game starts to show his age in terms of graphics, I remember the first time I played how amazed I was and now it looks  a little dated, especially Joe's face when up close. The graphics are still beautiful to look at although but today's standard they look a bit simplistic.
The game is pretty linear, even if it is an open world game it is not a sandbox, you just drive from one place to another and jump from chapter to chapter. There are no side quests which is quite dissapointing since you meet many people who would potentially give you missions they don't do anything in particular. The DLCs are focused more on little missions like those but they kinda lack atmosphere ( I would still buy Joe's Adventures since it fits in the story and playing as Joe is funny. It also has the best missions out of the 3 DLCs).
You probably won't have enough time to try all the guns, vehicles and you will  want more gameplay. The DLCs take care of those but like I said they are not worth in their entirety.
FINAL VERDICT: I can't really call the game a masterpiece but it's ambitious and tries to get to that status but dosen't quite get there. I have to give the game a strong 8.5/10 . You may want to wait for a price drop tho.

I didn't anticipate that a CoD game could serve as a vivid reminder about the greatest cataclysm in human history. That being said many times the game removed whatever sense of "fun" I was having & replaced it with remorse, guilt, & self disgust at having to participate in the pitiless butchery of war. Sonic Generations brings the best of both worlds in terms of Sonic gameplay with excellent 2D platforming and solid 3D runner/plaformer gameplay. The game features stages, music and callbacks from previous entries in the franchise, making it a huge nostalgia trip for those who have stuck with the franchise since an early stage.
2D levels will have you traveling through level design akin to that of the Genesis era of Sonic games, with a bit of 2.5D segments to make it feel fresh. 3D levels will have you run through obstacle courses with short segments of 2D and 3D platforming sprinkled within them. The game is incredibly fun to play through, although it is very short. You will find yourselves completely beating the game in about 4-5 hours if you don't hang around side challenges. These side challenges do extend the length of the game and reward you with Artwork and Music Tracks from Sonic's history, however they will start feeling repetitive after a while. The story of the game is pretty much nonexistant, with only a few unremarkable cutscenes sprinkled around; you'll find yourself drawn to the gameplay more than the story. Boss battles are present, some are pretty creative, some are what you'd expect.
The main draw to this game for me is the modding community, you'll find many great mods available to try out and mess with this game, making me wish that other previous entries in the franchise were available on Steam just so we can mod them as well. Overall it's one of the best Sonic games in ages and I recommend that anyone new to the series starts here.

I'll admit that most Sonic games aren't that good, but the few times they're good they're really good. Sonic Generations is thankfully one of those. There's 2 gameplay styles: classic and modern Sonic. Classic Sonic plays almost exacly like the classic 2D games, which is a great thing. The major difference is that the spin dash is very powerful. It's a more limited style, but it's definitely Sonic. The modern Sonic plays like the day stages of Sonic Unleashed and Sonic Colors, with 3D boost-based stages mixed with some 2D sections. And this is how a 3D Sonic should be, giving a great sensation of speed. There's 9 stages each with 2 acts, act 1 for classic and act 2 for modern. The main stages are based on a selection of stages from past Sonic's, and they are greatly designed, even if i feel that the selection could be better. Each act has 5 separate challenges, however they're mixed. They feel a bit rushed and like a cheap way to add more game time. For example, 1 of these challenges is just a time trial of the main stage. But there's a few that i enjoyed. There's also 7 bosses in total, and they are generally good, except for the last boss. One thing that is missing here are the special stages, but perhaps it is better without them. You can also get and equip skills with various effects, including Super Sonic. The story is very basic but it gets the job done. And the soundtrack is amazing, with great remixes from the original songs. As a whole, the game feels a bit rushed and incomplete. It's like the developers first put their effort on the main stages (thankfully), and then rushed the challenges and maybe the bosses, scrapping special stages. There's also an online mode, but it's just the main stages with leaderboards. There's also an addictive 30 second trial for each stage. The PC version unfortunately isn't well optimized, but there's plenty of mods out there to increase your play time. I personally recommend at least the Unleashed Project mod, but you should try some more of them, especially stage mods. While the game could have more content, what's here is mostly pretty good. If you're a Sonic fan, this game is a must have. Even if you're not but are curious, Sonic Generations is one of the best ways to see what (the good) Sonic games are all about. But get it on sale.

Iron Snout, developed by SnoutUp & released on the PC on Jan 27 2016. It has an average user score of 8.2 on Metacritic
. A single snout against hordes of wolfs? Yup, as silly or absurd this may look/sound, this is actually a darn well polished product and one that requires precision, reflex, quick thinking or just plenty of luck and button mashing. Regardless, this is an original title which has been thoroughly thought of and executed perfectly - if compared to some other indie titles. The focus on it's gameplay & it's mechanics is what makes this title really darn good & a heck of fun gaming experience ..and of course, plenty of dead wolfs.*snort snork*
At first glance, some may find it offensive whether due to religion or culture reasons playing as a snout while some may discard this tittle as it look like a product designed solely for kids, a "childish" game, not meant for the serious/hardcore gamer. If you are able to look past all these reasons and give yourself a chance, give this product a chance. All it takes is just 1 minute of your time. Is 60 seconds too much to ask for?
What awaits you is a completely "taken by surprise" experience. It is a absurdly shockingly simple product that delivers a shockingly fun gaming experience.
Controls and visuals:
Controls are straightforward, visuals wise its very simple; at least its clean & bright. I have no complains on the visuals & I don't need a 3d engine for it. The game emphasis is on the gameplay not how good looking it is.
Gameplay:
Your goal and only goal is to survive the endless waves of wolfs.
That's it? Yes. So how is it possible for a product with such a simple game design rack up all these positive reviews? That's because it was executed perfectly with Fun as the sole focus. The fight for survival is interesting and unpredictable. The wolfs come in various weapons/stuffs. Wolfs with throwing axes, wolfs on a bouncing spear, wolf dangling on flying rockets, wolfs with basket? With the recent update there are police wolf with batons? shields? a wrecking ball style wolf? wolf with handbags, cross dress wolf? and the list goes on..That sounds crazy?! What is this? Yes, that's exactly what makes the whole product unique and interesting.
If you play plant vs zombie, the feeling is similar where you encounter zombies with scuba diving equipment, with a pole, with newspaper, riding a ice maker vehicle. etc.
The fights are NEVER DULL, it is intense and challenging enough for the masses; whether you are young/old/casuals/hardcore players. Anyone and everyone can have fun. All it takes is a 1 minute of your time.
My Personnel Experience:
When I first saw Iron snout on launch, I didn't know what to expect but as it was released as a Free 2 Play game and there were already hundreds of positive reviews, I decided to give it a shot. It was a shocking experience for me to see that with such a simple game design, people were having ton of fun due to the creative design on the enemies; the wolf's. The ability to steal their weapons and temporarily used it against the wolf/the ability to use the environment to help you against the wolf made the game even more interesting. I had lots of laugh when I saw what the wolfs were capable of. All of this is only possible when your game don't break/have weird bugs. The mechanics were simple but most importantly, it worked. Perfectly! so, kudos to Snoutup & its team for the effort and making this original game really fun.
I personally did not encounter any errors nor find any glaring issues. Do I see myself playing iron snout a year from now? No, not really. Maybe just 5 minutes from time to time. Here's why, despite the ton of fun it has to offer, I have already experienced everything so I definitely would want to try out other games. Unless Iron Snout comes out with new content/new game mode or a possible co-op function or host periodic events, it wont be able to retain its player base in the long run. I sincerely hope that snoutup is aware about this and have plans release new content/host events/introduce new game mode/features in the future.
I just realized hours ago before this writing that certain people may have issues playing a character that resembles a pig. From where I am from, you'd be surprise what drama certain religious quarters can stir up. I hope that the devs can consider to provide skins/alternative characters to be played as instead. I know it sounds really silly but if you want to reach out to wider audience, you'd have to consider things like this.

My Summary:
This is really hard. The amount of fun that iron snout has showered me is really generous. abundant. 200% More than any other indie product has ever offered. On top of that, there's no flaw as well. Objectively, this should earn a perfect score. lol. [After 30 minutes pondering] It pains me to say this..It's still tearing up my soul inside out as I try my best to remain objective@fair for a useless self-important self-rating-score. xD *rips hair* *drums roll* So, on the scale of 0 - 10, my personal rating for Iron snout is a 9/10. With a nomination vote! There I said!

So, i got Mafia 2 cheap on Steam, and finally played it trough. I played and loved M1 but compared to that, M2 is simply no competitor.
Pros:
+Grafics
+Music
+Atmosphere
+in generell good story
Cons:
- Real unrealistic damage model for the cars (also compared to M1), also you cant shoot while driving anymore (which for me was one of the most fun thing in M1).
- No free roam mode, no sidequest, no reasons to do anything beside the story.
- Many bugs, and not only small ones one could laugh about, but some real game braking ones.
Like one in which instead of the final cutscene of a mission you get a blackscreen and cant finish the mission thanks to that. Or when you even cant get to the end of an mission, because you cant enter a house, because you cant open the door to it anymore, because you robbed a bank or store (you need to earn a lot of money in this particular mission) and the only thing you can do about it is to play the whole chapter (not the last checkpoint, not the mission, THE WHOLE CHAPTER) without robbing any banks or stores... + some more s*it like flying through the air after loading the last checkpoint, etc.
seeing that this is a praised AAA title, and that there are so many big bugs after all this time that never got fixed, is really a gamebraker.
- So much useless stuff.
Let me explain. For example, the city is filled with stores, where you can buy food, clothes (like 5 different pieces at best in 4 different colours) or weapons from, or rob them for money. But there is absolutly no need for them. Food restores your health, but you heal yourself anyway up to 75% after a few seconds behind cover. I never needed to buy any gun in the whole game, because by just picking up the weapons of my dead enemies, i get so many guns, i didnt know what to do with them anyway.
The only reason why you would need money at all is probably to repair your cars, which you want to hold on to. Cause all the guns and clothes you bought, you will lose anyway in the game. (Three times you start off with nothing right from the scratch, so you also loose everthing except your stored cars 2 times). But again, by simply playing through the story you get enough money to never worry about anything, so there is no need to rob any store.
There are also phones and phone booths which you can interact with, but again with absolutly no function, cause it will just tell you, that you dont have the number of anyone anyway.
You can switch on all the damn water taps the game can offer, but again without any function.
You will meet two characters, which tell you to come by from time to time and they will get you a job.... but again there is no meaning behind that. Yes the 2 NPCs are standing around all the time and are even highlited for you as important persons on your map, but during the game i was  checking them 5 times, and never got any sidemission.
I can live with "stupid" stuff, if it at least good for a laugh and therefore offers some sort of function or usefullness.
Like when you interacted with a toilett in M1 and your character tooked a 3min♥♥♥♥♥♥which you couldnt interrupt... this was an easter egg to mock the player and funny to look at, but M2 is full of things that dont have any meaning or funtcion of whatsoever.
It seems that the developers wanted to copy GTA and included all this stores. But in GTA you can actually do something with them. Like playing bowling, or dart, or poker as minigames. Buying different houses and things for them.
Here they are just for show, and their "functions" seem to be only excuses why they exist in the first place.
There are no sidemissions, nothing to do except for the main quest, no reasons why you should explore the city.
Conclusion:
I would give it a neutral oppinion if Steam would allow it, seeing that i still enjoyed the story and atmosphere, but since i can only give a positve or negative review, and anoying bugs here cost me up to 2 hours of my life, and there is absolutly nothing to do beside the main story...
(which is usually drive from A to B (for a very long time) and shoot all the badguys in B, then drive (for a very long time) to C to get your friend back home - cause you are the only main character who seems to know how to drive (seriously, you will meet a dude for the first time and he will say "we take my car" and than he is just standing there and waiting until you get on the driver seat) - than drive to D (your home) to officially end the mission. If you die or get caught by the police, you must repeat the whole driving part, thanks to the ridiculous few automate safepoints.)
... i have to give it a thumbs down.
But if you can get it cheap and only are interested in the story anyway, (and have a high tolerance for annyoing bugs and scouring the community forums on how to over come them), do it.

12/10/14 UPDATE: There's a new patch! Nope, nothing in the way of actual content...they've rewritten three major aspects of the game (graphics, AI and new voxel engine). REALLY?! After over two years of development, they're still rewriting the basics. If this doesn't say "STAY AWAY" to you, then nothing will.
ORIGINAL REVIEW: This might be an awesome building/fight game in about eighteen years or so. I love building games, and as a result I get easily bamboozled by the promise of games like Castle Story -- take charge over a group of vaguely humanoid bipedal lumps named 'bricktons' and have them build castles and buildings and such, make weapons for them so that they can defend themselves against all manner of goblinry. There's gonna be mayhem and fighting and explosions with arrows and stuff flying everywhere. With catapults and everything.
Unfortunately, as it stands right now, it's little more than a tech demo -- the UI is flaky, making it difficult to mine and build anything. The Bricktons tend to stand around more often than actually do work due to incomplete AI. Despite excellent graphics and animation, the game itself has a unique lack of polish to it -- it's tough to even know what to do in a logistics sense, and the UI makes doing it a struggle even when you've figured it out.
What's worse is that Castle Story has been in development for an amazing length of time for it to be in such a state (just over two years at this point, and their kickstarter has been funded to the tune of $702k when they asked for just under $30k). As best as I can figure out, the development team had to rewrite vast sections of their game for some reason or another at some point last year (rumor has it to accommodate a Linux version, which is preposterous if it's true).
However, their development blog of late has been more concerned about their going to PAX East and moving to a new office than trivialities such as the state of their game (and reading between the lines, it would seem as though their time at PAX didn't go so well...which is hardly a surprise given the state of the game currently).
All-in-all, avoid Castle Story for now. Hopefully it's coming out in the next two years or so and I can change my recommendation. I play a LOT of early access games, and this one is frankly the second worst when it comes to time in development.

Final Fantasy IX is incredible. I am so happy to finally play through this game again here on Steam. I beat it twice before and  just did again for a third time.
The art design when looked at for cohession is pristene and gorgeous. The new HD models of the characters do an excellent job of looking good while not clashing too greatly with the lower-res backgrounds.
I experienced no major problems playing this game, though occasionally when booting up the game I did encounter some minor stutter, or very rarely a "not responding" situation, but they quickly right themselves. I never experienced a CTD, and in the world of computer games, thats actually quite the accomplishment.
I didn't really touch the in-game boosters added to this version, except for the max-level one when I got a tad lazy grinding everyone to lvl. 99. But I'm sure they serve their purpose.
Of course, the true reason anyone should play Final Fantasy IX is for its story, which is masterfully told and, in my opinion, is genius in design. It may indeed be the best Final Fantasy in the way it's told. All characters and moments that are part of the story tie back to its central themes. The threads of its plot are interwoven so skillfully and moments are very impactful.
The ATB battle system can feel slow at first, though you'll quickly get used to it. The game is designed around it, and the slower pace, even compared to games like FFVII & VIII, lends itself to the very strategic nature of the battles. Many bosses and even normal encounters require at least a good degree of planning and strategy to overcome, and it is quite a rewarding feeling when you succeed.
Overall, this is the Final Fantasy game that doesn't get the love or praise it deserves. It's better told than FFVII and better designed than VI. It has everything you loved from FFIV and is missing everything you hated from FFVIII. Amazing game, and after experiencing it a third time, I'd call it the best Final Fantasy.
Side Note: Tetra Master (the card game within the game), is awful, confusing, and hard, even when you take the time to learn it. You've been warned.

This is the fourth time I'm playing this game now, since the PS1 days. I still remember their game discs were made in black, and that added on to the special feeling I have for FF9 since then.
I will not compare to other Final Fantasy games because each has its own attraction and audience. For me, FF9 feels like a throwback to the classic FF system. Although the mechanisms may seem simple, along with its simplistic graphics, it allowed me to "fill in the gaps" in my mind with my imagination, and allowed me to immerse in its story and emotions.
This is my Final Fantasy, and this is how I tell and re-tell the story. This is the fourth time I'm re-telling the story, and I still have more interpretations each time. Final Fantasy is about telling a story like no other games can. Yes, graphics may be a boon, but if a Final Fantasy game can't tell a story 10x better than its graphics could, then it has failed as a Final Fantasy.
I believe Final Fantasy IX has done that. It shows how great games don't necessarily need to have life-like facial features and individually-moving strands of hair. In fact, I'd rather let the mind fill in those gaps for me, as that is actually more enjoyable and personal than having everything laid out for me.
This is my Final Fantasy, and this is how I tell and re-tell the story. Have you told your story?

I first played this game when it had just been published in Europe, at my friend's house, till late night. I was captivated by the music, the story, the characters... Everything kept me under spell, till finally I beat it. Best three days of my life. Now that my PS2 console is busted, I no longer can play this but thank gods for this release, I can finally relive the best moments of gaming!
What I like:
Characters. I love Zidane and his attitude. Even though laid back, he has wisdom in him that he shares with others. Dagger, well, she's your everyday naive princess, but during the course of the game she grows up to be the ruler that her kingdom needs. Steiner... oh... Steiner! The sass he and Zidane exchange... I love it! Vivi is like me - introvert, uncertain, hesitant with low self-esteem, but underneath all that he holds the power to destroy the world if he so chooses. Sadly I can't do magic... but Vivi is still probably my number one character. Quina... the must-have comic relief... but s/he is till better than Jar-Jar :P (please don't kill me). Freya... I love her "To be forgotten is worse than death" phrase. She's my must have member in the main party. (I soloed the last boss with her! THAT was a thrill.) Eiko is that perky little girl that everyone loves... or hates... I personally keep her as a second healer in party. Amarant... no opinion. He's awesome but I hardly ever keep him in my party. Main villain, however, is just... meh. Kefka is better, Sephiroth is better... but I think he was made for the fangirls to drool. Those hips man... those hips don't lie!
Music: Uematsu-sensei deserves much praise for the music he composed. I love Melodies of Life theme song a lot, and I find  myself singing it to the tune everytime.
Story: 10/10, nothing else to say. Play it! Experience it!
New graphics give more depth to the design, so yes, I like it.
What I don't like:
The chance for random battles have obviously been decreased. I love grinding. In the PS version I wouldn't need to take more than 5 steps before the next fight, now I need to walk around for a minute before I get into a fight. I hope this issue is fixed or at least checked upon. I need them levels and I don't want to waste time by running around looking for random fights when those fights should basically come to me.
The battle UI is wayt too big! It's distractingly huge and the spell quickly browsing (RB/LB) the spell list make the cursor go to the bottom and not stay on the spot... I'm used to the PS version where the cursor stays on the spot and when quickly browsing the spell list the spell is easier to choose. I don't use "Wait" mode in battle. So... yeah... But it's fine, this is only a minor thing and I'm sure someone will come up with a solution.
Overall:
Play this game! It's 10/10, and all those old school gamers should feel the nostalgia when FURUSATO plays on the menu screen.

Truly frustrating game that has a ton of issues. First off is the microtransactions (some of the most unfair I've seen). The developers "rewarded" early buyers of the base game with an overpriced British Forces DLC over a year after the game came out. The idea that an entire faction wasn't even included in the initial release tells you what the devs are after: money. At least the intel bulletins aren't P2W, but they are expensive as they are practically ineffective.
But the worst part is the imbalance. The devs love to talk about how they are always refining balances so no faction is overpowered. But the US forces have ALWAYS been dramatically underpowered, especially in the early game, when riflemen squads, although numerically superior and fairing well from cover, can be mowed down or at least pinned by machine guns (which the Germans get straight away and the US forces cannot) before you barely realize they're under attrack.  You could argue this is historically accurate in terms of machine gun technology, but a great example of how the devs don't even care about this is in the Sherman tank. It's true that the Sherman wasn't as effective as German tanks, but it was numerically superior. This is somewhat reflected in the fact that you really need two Shermans, working closely together, to take out a German tank. HOWEVER, the Sherman tanks cost nearly as much fuel as they superior German tanks, which in addition to making it much more difficult to churn out two to the Germans' one, is historically inaccurate as they Americans had comparatively more fuel than the Germans.
Before people jump on me and say the US forces just aren't your playing style-- they favor people who are good counterers-- I would say a well-balanced game would let you play with the Americans with your own, head-on style-- not a bizarre, micromanaging one. These are the forces who successfully invaded Normandy.

I never liked Sonic as a kid, and I still can't get into it today. Had the Sonic & Knuckles collection for Windows 98, and recently got it to work on my current machine. Still can't like it for some reason. I'm just totally unable to get into the groove of it and end up quitting out of frustration.
Freedom Planet on the other hand? I don't quite know what it is about this game, but I love it. LOVE it. The main character Lilac is an absolute joy to play and I never get tired of zooming through levels with her and wrecking enemies. The game does makes sure to sprinkle in secrets and collectables throughout levels so it's also fun to take it slow and explore a little. The game is frustrating at times but in a way that makes you come back for more instead of putting you off. The controls are super tight, the music is fantastic, bosses are absolutely SAVAGE, and the main villain Brevon is surprisingly dark despite basically being green Dr. Eggman. The first time you face him as the main character caused a bit of genuine fear in me (and without spoiling anything, you SHOULD be scared).
My main criticisms have to do with the story. Specifically, the relationship between the three main characters, Lilac, Carol, and Milla. I also have issues with Spade and Prince Dail. Again I don't want to spoil much, but it feels like Freedom Planet needed to flesh out the character's backstories a little more, and instead left a lot hanging. Milla just kind of gets dropped into the story with little explanation, and Carol can switch with Lilac at really any time and not change much story-wise. I found Spade incredibly annoying (mostly his personality) and the fact that we never see Prince Dail or get a clear-cut idea of what happens to him at the end despite him being a pretty major (forced) villian kind of broke my heart. There are some DLCs planned though and I really hope that they patch up some of these issues.
So here's a quick pros/cons list that includes some stuff I didn't mention.
Pros:
> Action-packed gameplay + tight controls + perfect movement physics
> INSANE bosses (comes with a certain level of forgiveness + chances to rack up lives)
> Collectables/Secrets + multiple playable characters = Replay Value
> Music that fits the mood of each level perfectly, and is just fun to listen to
> Crazy animated cutscenes
> Well-designed atmospheric levels + appealing colors and attention to detail
> Despite my earlier criticisms of the three main girls, they're all still very charming and fun in a lighthearted E-rated way
> A beautiful nod towards classic Sonic with clearly a lot of thought and love put into it
Cons:
> Voice acting is cringey at times (but can be disabled)
> Shaky story + characters (will hopefully be mitigated by future DLCs)
Buy this game already. It's good fun, and worth your time.

Freedom Planet came about as the result of a Sonic the Hedgehog fan game coming to the realisation that it could probably be sold for actual money if it dropped references to Sega's intellectual property and threw in some "original" characters instead.

And by "original," I mean original in the Sonic the Hedgehog original character sense.

After being mostly complete, it went on to raise some funds on Kickstarter, a relatively modest $2,000 with some stretch goals, including a comic series, and new playable characters – none of which over two years later are anywhere to be seen, but I assume they are still coming since the game still does receive updates, and recently got a Wii U release.

So with its odd beginnings in mind, how does this fare? Well, not only does it hold its own against the very best Sega has to offer, it's also one of the best platformers I've ever played. It feels like a true evolution of a Sonic game, rather than a derivative, and in that regard I would say that this is closer to what Sonic 4 should have been.

You have a choice of three playable characters, each with a different set of moves and each one with an exclusive level to play. Lilac, a purple dragon, can perform speed boosts, an aerial spin attack that can also be used as a double jump as well as an assortment of kicks and punches. Carol, a green cat, does a bunch of quick scratch attacks, and a rapid kick; she also breaks out her motorcycle if she finds a gas canister powerup. Milla is slower and more fragile, but can make shields which double as short-range laser beam things, as well as fly short distances by flapping her ears. I have no idea what animal she is supposed to be. Possibly some kind of splotchy rabbit?

The game is split up into 10 levels. Each level is actually quite massive and varied in design. Very few levels end looking the same as when you started. On the second stage for example, you start off among ruins in a forest, and by the end of the level you're in some sort of mine, dodging machinery, and exploring caves and hidden rooms.

I found that through normal play each level takes a good 8 to 10 minutes to complete due to the sheer size and the number of different pathways you can use. Certainly you would not be able to see everything that's on offer on a single play through, which is also fine because the game comes with a whole bunch of achievements to keep you busy if that's your thing.

The levels also contain a slew of collectibles and powerups, which are always a welcome way of adding replay value. Collecting hidden cards will unlock things in the gallery. Collect blue crystals to earn extra lives and red petals to replenish your health. There are also orbs that drop from bad guys and treasure chests. The only use I've found for them is during the bonus stage, since the more you've collected, the more times you're able to roll the dice for bonus powerups and extra lives. Of course, to get to the bonus stage, you need to collect something else hidden in the level as well – a yin-yang symbol specifically. Lastly, are shield powerups. They prevent you from taking damage a few times, but also have other effects such as the water shield which allows you to breathe underwater, and there's the lightning shield that attracts blue crystals toward you. Shields also make you immune to certain elemental damage.

The excellent controls make the task of finding all this loot an enjoyable experience. The level of precision you get from your movements, and the physics affecting your momentum, gives you the feeling that you're totally in control. I wouldn't say the physics are as polished as Sonic's; it does feel like the characters lack weight at times and there's some odd goings with going vertical slopes, but it's still certainly one of the better examples of how to work physics into platform games.

I found myself having a love/hate relationship with the bosses. On one hand, they are a lot of fun. I found myself looking forward to each boss fight because the one that preceded it felt like an epic battle, and emerging victorious was deeply satisfying. On the other hand, they are also rather difficult and bordering on unfair if you're a greenhorn. Some bosses can wipe your entire health meter out in a single blow unless you've worked out their attack patterns and know when and where to dodge.

The game has a story mode but thankfully it gives you the option to play in "Classic Mode," which skips over the majority of cut-scenes. I say "thankfully," because the story is pretty weak, and the voice acting is a mixed bag. It might however be worth watching on your first play through to see how all the levels and characters tie together. If you enjoyed the story modes from the Sonic Adventure games, then you'll probably enjoy these too. It's a matter of personal preference, really. I don't think the voice acting meshes well with the retro visuals and bizarre creatures.

On the subject of presentation, the graphics do genuinely look like something you'd see on an older game console, in a good way. Faithfully recreating the look of 16/32 bit era games, it can have a lot of sprites on-screen at the same time, and a lot of rotation and transformation effects, so it would probably have been right at home on a PlayStation or Sega Saturn, save for the fact that it's presented in wide-screen. It would need one of those CD-based consoles to house its amazing soundtrack, which is a delectable selection of tunes that not only fit their designated spots in the game perfectly, but hold up strongly as a standalone soundtrack as well. The rest of the sound design ties everything together, with sound effects for attacks having plenty of punch, and explosion noises giving additional satisfaction to busting through a bunch of robotic enemies.

Don't be put off by the dubious origins of development. Freedom Planet is solid fun from start to finish. It's a game that's suitable for everyone, and packs in a lot of quality content even at its humble $15 asking price.
