Just over an hour in and I can tell that there is a lot of love and care put into this. Freedom Planet is a light hearted and exciting platformer that has a lot of mechanics and values in similarity to Sonic and Megaman franchises but implements those characteristics arguably better then the series it finds its fundamentals in. Take control of one of the many cute animated characters in their mission to defeat an empire of mechanicals, robots and their masters who are causing destruction.
Each level seems to be designed with a lot of option in mind that gives a player the chance to go about completion in the path they wish to choose and respects the players intelligence and does not burden with tips and guides during the gameplay allowing the player to overcome obstacles on their own as they should.
One of the most powerful parts of this game is its soundtrack. The music fits every part of the level design and gives exciting emotional emphasis and belonging to each level always feeling in place. Each tune is enjoyable in or out of the game and could be enjoyable even while playing something else or doing other tasks. Freedom Planet does give off a somewhat eco-friendly message and is self aware of that but doesn't throw it in your face like some can and really nails every aspect a side-scroll platformer could hope to accomplish. Excellent addition to anyones library.

Very funny and short classical point-and-click adventure game from the people who have brought us 'The Curse of Monkey Island'.
Now, that was a masterpiece even if it was created without Ron Gilbert, but... most of the later works by Bill Tiller and Larry Ahern turned out to be, well, not so good. 'A Vampyre Story' and 'Ghost Pirates of Vooju Island', in spite of their similar humor and visual style, were not successful and, to tell the truth, rather boring.
Luckily, 'Duke Grabowsky' falls almost in the same league as 'Monkey Island'! Something just like earlier Telltale projects, before they fired Dave Grossman and switched to gameplayless visual novels.
.
* Pretty graphics. Yes, it is 3D, but very bright, colorful and appealing! Even some piratey atmosphere is there.
* Music is great as well, although some bits of it are borrowed from 'Ghost Pirates'.
* Humor. Now, that is a welcome and longed-for addition!
.
* Length and scope - it is strange, but the game that was in development since 2014 (and missed its planned release date by one year) is very short - 2-3 hours at most. The story is strange (albeit still fun) and definitely incomplete, while no actual news of a sequel have been heard yet...
* General simplicity - why, or why there are almost no inventory puzzles? In a classical point-and-click adventure game?? Made by masters of the genre??? We do get to pick some items, but only a few of them, no combination allowed, and most of those items are just 'ideas', not actual objects...
Anyway, the game is definitely recommended - especially at a serious discount that will last for a couple of days more! Go and grab it! So they would finally make us a sequel. Or better,  a dozen of sequels.

Can games help us process psychological traumas? Or help us understand them in others? This unconventional game tries exactly that.
In Papo & Yo you play a little boy named Quico that finds his way through a dreamlike Favela, following a mysterious girl. The environment offers creative puzzles that emphasizes whats possible in the fantasy of a kid. But this fantasy is not only that, it is also a metaphor. After befriending a monster that loves to eat frogs but starts raging everytime it does you realize that not all is well in Quicos fantasy world, and even less so in his real world.
Without hitting you in the face with it Papo & Yo not only tells you, but lets you experience how traumatising domestic violence can be for a child and how it tries to cope with it. It handles the subject very delicately and at the same time offers great and challenging gameplay.
The shortness of it is not a weak point as it gets the point across with good pacing. It also features good art and music - Another example of how interactive media can offer mature experiences without clichés or over the top violence.

Great RTS game, very well done. Not a huge RTS guy myself but this game has me highly addicted. Love the WW2 setting, and the maps are on point! Also there is a big community of mods and more content (maps, etc) through steam workshop.
This isn't a Starcraft RTS, the game is much more intimate. You pay attention to individual units more, and each has it's advantages/disadvantages. Some have certain upgrades that can be purchased. Many units work great with others, and the dance continues. So much detail in the game/map/units/abilites/etc etc. Also seems more beginner friendly to me, an end game match will consist of an army of approx 10-15 units. So it's easier to micro-manage everything that is happening on the battlefield, as you're not dealing with hordes of units. Makes you remember certain units, when they have fought on the front line in many battles, and are now level 3 veteracy and shoot more accurately.
Also there is no "mining" aspect to this game. Everything is capture points, the more you hold, the more resources you are given. Which is great becasue I do not like that part of most RTS games. I'm not interested in mining and having to micro manage mining operations in a war game. This game lets me strictly battle. Love it. 10/10

This game will always be superior to the new battlefront II. Because it reminds me of a time when games were complete, and didn't have grindy walls for heroes. They were all unlocked for you, not only that this game has a lot to offer you. It's always going to be better because with each installment that Pandemic was making the games were improving, the first battlefront was a successful test to see if it would be liked, while it did have a lot of crude systems and not a very complete story it was okay. But Battlefront II did almost everything better, galactic conquest was better, the story was better, the multiplayer was a lot more fun. Not to mention when the first Xbox's live shut down this was one of the most popular games for multiplayer on the charts for that platform at the time. The greatest part about these games is that they're purely fan service, and that's what makes them awesome to immerse yourself in. Battlefront III, unfortunately which was looking really cool was cancelled. It looked like from the alpha gameplay that it improved everything from battlefront 2. Electronic Arts was given the chance to improve 2 times and they can't even create the experiences that I had from this game. And I agree with Valve when they say that this game is "Star Wars Battlefront II CLASSIC. Because it is.
Galactic Conquest is probably my most favorite mode, where you fight over the galaxy and take over planets and try to get each planet and rule it all. And you earn credits everytime that you conquer a planet, and you can unlock units like a jump trooper. Or a droideka if you're playing on the CIS. One of my most favorite modes in this game. And of course with the classes that you unlock you're not just given them you have to work for them
The story is about you being a veteran 501st clone trooper who is under the rule of emperor palpatine and is during the time of Order 66, and at the end of the campaign you run with your platoon and slaughter every jedi in the Jedi Temple. It's a really cool sequence. What's even cooler is that this entire campaign is voiced by one person Temuera Morrison, his performance was really good. There was great memeable quotes like, "Watch those Wrist Rockets!". "Just like the simulator!" All of the cutscenes were produced by ingame assets they weren't especially made, which reminds me a lot of another game called System Shock 2 which is another game that I love.
Space combat is really, really, really good. You would think that this is some tacked on mode just because they said so. The controls are good, infact there is yet any game that I have found that has space combat this good. Oh! What! Destiny has space travel, oh its just travel by cutscene that's fantastic. It's incredibly worth it. Except sometimes it can be kind of disorienting.
Not only that there is a mode where you can pick any map that you want, called Instant Action. You can select the maps and put them into a playlist. Venture Moon Industries took to Kickstarter to drum up funds for a title conceptualized and headed by Bill Tiller, a LucasArts alumnus who worked on the art for adventure titles such as The Dig, Ghost Pirates of Voojo Island and The Curse of Monkey Island . For any point-and-click adventure fan whose roots reach back into the heyday of the nineties, nothing more needs to be known —- the project practically bankrolls itself. And sure enough, the game was funded and made.
The result is Duke Grabowski, Mighty Swashbuckler. It’s a fun and compact little point-and-click story that has flavors of the Monkey Island series in its visuals and humor, but lacks the same zany logic and madcap puzzle design. Genre fans will find this game a tasty morsel with a clever swashbuckler-sword edge.

The Curse of Monkey Island is my first official point and click adventure. It's also the game that encoruaged me to take my english learning seriously. As such, you probably guess that game means the world to me.
Hence, I didn't think twice before buying Duke Grabowski. As soon as I saw the name Bill Tiller, I was sold. I didn't mind some of the reviews claiming the game is too short. I just wanted a brand new Curse of Monkey Island-ish adventure...
I start the game... The art style immediately feels familiar and charming. The music has that COMI vibe that I cannot resist. So I get introduced to Duke and other characters, solve a couple of puzzles and save the game, as I have to quit.
A few hours later, I start the game again, try to load the saved part and... well, no can do! The game crashes (showing the not responding message) when I try to do so. As for the auto-save, it's from the very beginning of the story, so it's of no help (apparently, the game auto saves very rarely).
This is a real bummer, and while I WILL probably start the game anew sooner or later, and finish it in one session (considering what others say about its length), I cannot recommend it since one of its basic features is not working. I also read someone else posting the same issue in the discussions, so it's not just me.
A shame, really... it's got that COMI atmosphere and vibe, but... that, in this case, is not enough. :(
If the developers fix this, though, I'd be more than happy to give it a thumbs up!
EDIT: As planned, I finished the game in one sitting. I finished an adventure game in 100 minutes. That's right... dead simple puzzles (you never have more than 3 - YES, THREE - items in your inventory), terrible animations and not-so-funny conversations. I'm terribly disappointed, but this game doesn't deserve a thumbs up, as much as I want to be wrong.

When i First did review Lichdom:Battlemage, many of the current features had not been implemented. the Game was in a reletively early access state. Now having put a total of 12 hours into the game (from its prior state and across several of the implemented features) i can say roughly how far this game has gone.
Its further than i might have expected in such a shot amount of time.
of the problems, there are the occasional start up crashes and the textures in cutscenes sometimes glitch up (though not as extreme as in the earliest stages of development, when Roths cape seemed to be trying to bisect him) and a small cutscene where the player is flipped upside down is marred somewhat by some minor graphic collision bugs. generally not as bad as in some other titles.
The key improvements to the game have been in 2 key areas, notably in the story. With a choice of either a male or female 'dragon' (the other character serving as your 'gryphon'), the story is much more clear and fleshed out, with the cult of Malthus threatening the world and you receiving the power to stop them and get personal revenge against certain members of the cult. the story flows at a good pace and it is not totally destracting from the main crux of the game- the Combat.
Combat in Lichdom consists of flinging spells at enemies, blocking melee attacks with barrier spells, blinking to dodge projectiles and melee swings and keeping an eye on your health bars. Its simple to learn- and then you start crafting spells. The Amount of customisation put into crafting your spells is, like the combat simple to learn, but harder to master. With 3 distinctively different spell focuses (my name for it, not the actual one), the variation in spells you can craft becomes more impressive and more about the players personal taste. Destruction is about blasting enemies into fragments of bone, flesh and spell effects in a gloriously spectacular fashion. Contol is about applying status problems to enemies, Freezing them solid, setting them on fire, or making them a thrall to your will (until they realise they had been readily chopping up their allies, turn on you and are reduced to a red stain of bone) is all part of keeping the player in control of the flow of battle. Mastery applies debuffs that help you keep the battle at the players level, forcing enemies to flee etc. The Focuses all blend together, with destruction magic synergising with contol for brilliant overkills.
Spell types are also in a nice varied collection. Targeted (Left Mouse) deal quickfire single damage, Barriers (Right Mouse) help to sheild damage or even hit the enemy with a well timed nova block, and  an aoe(Rmb and LMB Held down at the same time and then released) brings death to the enemy at a long range. Enemies also are just as varied coordinated as ever, with melee troops lunging at you and sidstepping harmful attacks, and ranged troops throwing lots of projectiles at you forceing you to move in case of a volley of fire.
All in all, the game still stands for some polish but I Have no problem with having a blast playing Lichdom:Battlemage. Good Job people, Keep up the good work.

I totally get where the frustrated reviewers are coming from, but if those reviewers had had a little more knowledge going in, I think their experience would have been totally different.
People who say the game is boring haven't figured out the spell mechanics. Imagine suspending an enemy tumbling head over heels in mid air, infecting him with bugs and a giant flying hive larva, freezing him solid, and then using pure kinetic energy to split him into a million pieces, at which point the bugs and flying hive emerge to attack the other helpless baddies you've already anchored to the ground as if they weigh the same as a small star. I think that fits the definition of a mage who's a total bad @$$. And that's just using 3 sigils 5 different ways (stuff you can do by the 3rd map). There are 8 sigils and 24 ways they can be used. Think of the possibilities!
But to do crazy stuff like that (and oh so much more), you /have/ to figure out the spell mechanics.
I've had Lichdom for years, am not a master of it, but still love it to death. And I have no patience for boring games. So I'd like to respond to a few common objections.
Objection: I don't get how the spell system works. It's too complicated!
Answer: You're right. You don't get it, and you're not suppossed to at first. The game is less a story driven set of interaction and more a story-augmented laboritory. It's designed for you to experiment. We'll come back to this idea later.
Objection: My spells took out the first few enemies, now I'm hopelessly outgunned, even though I've gotten new sigils.
Answer 1: Do not -- I repeat, do not -- use the Smart Inventory system. The developer released it after the game was already out because there were compaints about the complicated spell system. Pretty ironic since the Smart Inventory will almost definitely get you killed.
Answer 2: The game expects you to create your magic /yourself./ You /need/ to start looking at spell damage amounts, critical multipliers, and mastery application/consumption. Lots of scary terms there? Read the journal, watch the ingame tutorials, and read on the Steam boards. I've even got a
. If you don't learn how to create your own spells, you're going to be outgunned pretty fast.
Objection: The levels are way too long.
Answer: Really? First, when was the last time you complained about a game being too long? Long is great! Second, and more importantly, the levels are designed to be long to give you time to experiment. Because time and experimentation are what you need. The long levels are a way to give you tons of time to experiment while also giving you a sense of progression.
Objection: Not enough variety in mobs/they're repetative.
Answer: You're right. There aren't that many different mob types. But that's not really the point of Lichdom. The magic of Lichdom isn't in stumbling on a huge sewer monster and defeating his unique rip-time-open-and-rain-down-plauge-infected-frogs-from-ancient-egypt attack. The magic is in crafting spells that can obliterate that monster. The actual obliteration process is just the final piece of that fun magic that starts with experimenting.
So why all the negative reviews? What's happening is that people buy the game with the line "the first game where the mage is a real bad @$$," then they get frustrated when they can't vaporize monsters right out of the box. Then, when they play more, they feel cheated because they got more spell parts and sigils, feel like they're having to spam fireballs, and things just keep getting harder. It seems like the mage isn't a bad @$$. He's monster bait!
What those players didn't see was that Lichdom makes you work -- yes work -- to become a bad @$$ mage. But the work/learning curve is reasonable /if/ you're willing to play by the game's rules, which means you have to experiment and use your brain as you craft your magic arsenal. Accept early on that you can't win by playing the way you play /any/ other FPS. Lichdom takes patience, finesse, and (I kid you not) math. But the reward of watching as you rain down hundreds of thousands of points in fire damage on what, to lazy players who didn't learn spellcrafting, would be a terrifying, unassailable opponent is so worth it.

Duke is getting my write-in vote for the first December Steam Awards -- I'm calling it "The 'Booted Up' award -- not only did you vote for or help crowd-source this game, you actually installed, played, and finished it!"
I must admit, I was reticent about playing as Duke for a good length longer than the intro, but even with all his initial awkwardness, the big lug does grow on you.  The game itself is also a little awkward at times, but makes up for it with excellent backdrop art and music, logically-solvable puzzles (perhaps too easy), mostly-good dialog, and a great effort at having a response for nearly all combinations of item-on-item attempts.  All in all, I'm happy to have backed it, which is not something I can say often!

Cute -- puzzles a little more straightforward than older adventure games, but that's not necessarily a bad thing (because I'd prefer they not be *too* obtuse). I think the Coconut Tree Lady says about everything I might want to say about the main quest, but as a short little adventure game it's worth the $8 or whatever. Occasional production polish issues with the text but nothing that bothers one too much.

If you're a big fan of Monkey Island or Ghost Pirates of Vooju Island, this is a fun little diversion.
I wouldn't pay full price for it since it feels like act 1 of a much larger game, and abruptly ends, but it's decent while it lasts, despite some questionable voice acting by kickstarter backers and constant plastering of backer names throughout the game.  The character animations are also a little janky.
Hopefully if they continue this series, they can tighten up the graphics on level 3.

It's hard to say whether Duke Grabowski is a bad game with good bits or a good game with a lot of flaws. I guess each player can determine that for themselves. I had fun, but couldn't help but lament a lot of the poor execution and missed opportunities that plague the game.
It's very light on the gameplay, with actual puzzles being very scarce and quite unchallenging. The humour also doesn't live up to the LucasArts classics – not by a long shot. There are some funny moments in there, but a lot of it is very cringy, face-palm stuff.
However, the game is rescued by the fantastically charismatic art of Bill Tiller and the highly complementary music. Also, the interactivity is pretty fun. It could just be my nostalgic fondness for pirate adventure games, but I love exploring this little world that's been created for the player here. And Venture Moon definitely went the extra mile to ensure that there was a diverse range of unique responses to player interactions, rather than repeating a generic line for numerous commands (e.g. "That won't work").
Overall, I quite like the tone and sense of fun this game brings. I just really hope they go a little bigger in future episodes, and ramp up the puzzle difficulty. I'd also suggest getting some new writers on board, because the funniness level just isn't up to par.

The best Sonic game since the 16-bit era (Megadrive / Genesis). If you are like me that loves the old 2D Sonic games but think the games that came after the Megadrive were either♥♥♥♥♥♥or average at best, then this is the game for you.

Freedom Planet - a game that was supposed to be yet another Sonic Fangame suddenly transformed into a standalone project. Was that a good idea? In my opinion - yes.
Let us begin with the plot. It's not THAT special. It's visibly influenced by the plots of many of the 90's platformers and games. There is an evil overlord that comes out of nowhere and you have to save the day. And what makes this plot ordinary is the origin itself. However I do enjoy how they performed the plot, how they put it all to work. AND IT WORKS ABSOLUTELY AMAZING! The cutscenes are well-made and they are a nice bit of a break after completing a challenging level.
This game's mechanics are visibly influenced by Sonic and Mega Man games, with a tiny addition of some new, fresh ideas. It's better to play the game itself than to listen to me rant about it. I can say it's good. The characters have different skills and sometimes a different storyline.
The graphics are really nice, as befits the 16-bit platformers. The Sonic-style reference is HUGE! The only difference being the fact that it got more anime-ish. But I rather like that! The animation is smooth and looks great overall.
Music in this game is outstanding. I'd say that this game has one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard! The songs suit the levels they play in and create an unforgettable atmosphere.
This is one not-so-awesome point of this game. The voices perfectly suit the characters they belong to. The only problem about them is that in some of the voice-clips the voice-actors didn't put the proper expression, or that expression was too strong/weak. But it honestly doesn't disturb that much. It's actually difficult to notice it when you play. It takes a bit to notice it, so that inconvenience isn't that problematic. My personal favourite voice is Lord Brevon's voice. Xander Barriga, you did an awesome job.

This is an awesome, well-designed game that takes an original twist on the style of the retro Sonic games and expands upon it. Even being an original game with novel world, I get a sense of nostaliga out of it... Or maybe I'm confusing my sense of nostaliga with my sense of experiencing quality craftmanship. \_(^_^;)_/

Lichdom isn't a game for the faint of heart. It's going to brutalize your spirit the same as Demon Souls or Dark Souls ever did.
That being said, the game has a linear, moderate difficulty, story path to start, but there are added side paths that add much more of a challenge to the game. That is, if you don't just follow the way your quest marker tells you to go.
The game supports a couple of different playstyles, up-close and personal with timed attack blocking or ranged and kiting. However, when you act like a sissy, you get sissy enemies. They get confused and can seemingly leash in some cases if you backpedal repeatedly. It is possible to use your spells to interact with some objects of the game world.
The spell system isn't difficult to understand, you are allowed 4 of the 8 planned schools of magic the devs have planned. It allows for some interesting mix up of combat casting. Spell crafting is interesting, based on the spell items found off enemies and world objects, configure and augment your spells to suit your playstyle. However, the spell animations aren't as awesome as most would like them.
The game world is beautiful, very detailed, no problems or glitches running on maximum settings, obviously that will differ player to player. Very smooth running game, one of the better polished Alpha builds I've ever played.

I guess the keys to a good Squeenix port are:
1)  Don't have a PC release already (VII, VIII)
2)  Don't be 2D/Sprite-based (V, VI)
3)  Don't be ports of a flawed DS release (III, IV)
4)  Put time and effort into it!
Seriously.  This port is their best port yet (which is saying a lot, yet not much at the same time).  And they have another one (of X's Remastered edition) coming out in a few days.
-The FPS is still 30, but that's forgivable on the basis that it's a PS1 game.  Definitely a lot less jarring than the 30-to-15 reduction that IV and III see during battle sequences.
-Unlike the other PS1/PC titles, they actually used the PS1 soundfont, so the music on the PS1 and the PC is identical, unlike VII and VIII which used a generic PC soundfont.  The music even loops right (unlike I's iOS/Android port, or V or VI's ports!
-The UI is a lot less intrusive than you'd expect, since this port kept the iOS/Android UI.  The battle menus in particular are large enough to be visible from several feet away even on a smaller computer, but still not big enough to really take up half the screen.  After a while, it actually, dare I say it, looks pretty good that way, since there's little empty space to be seen in these menus.
-The GRAPHICS!  The original game had the characters look incredibly pixelated (not that that was really Squaresoft's fault), but this game looks absolutely amazing (as though they rebuilt the textures from the ground up).  Prerendered environments still look a bit out of place, but the models are pristine.
And as far as the game itself goes, nothing has changed.  It's refreshing that they didn't add anything (boosters aside) but didn't subtract anything either, meaning there's no real sense reviewing the game itself here when you can look a really good one from 2000 up with no problem.
If you have never played Final Fantasy IX, or if you have and would like some amazing nostalgia, or if you're an RPG lover, or hell, if you're a human being with a soul, play this game.

Iron Snout, developed by SnoutUp & released on the PC on Jan 27 2016. It has an average user score of 8.2 on Metacritic
. A single snout against hordes of wolfs? Yup, as silly or absurd this may look/sound, this is actually a darn well polished product and one that requires precision, reflex, quick thinking or just plenty of luck and button mashing. Regardless, this is an original title which has been thoroughly thought of and executed perfectly - if compared to some other indie titles. The focus on it's gameplay & it's mechanics is what makes this title really darn good & a heck of fun gaming experience ..and of course, plenty of dead wolfs.*snort snork*
At first glance, some may find it offensive whether due to religion or culture reasons playing as a snout while some may discard this tittle as it look like a product designed solely for kids, a "childish" game, not meant for the serious/hardcore gamer. If you are able to look past all these reasons and give yourself a chance, give this product a chance. All it takes is just 1 minute of your time. Is 60 seconds too much to ask for?
What awaits you is a completely "taken by surprise" experience. It is a absurdly shockingly simple product that delivers a shockingly fun gaming experience.
Controls and visuals:
Controls are straightforward, visuals wise its very simple; at least its clean & bright. I have no complains on the visuals & I don't need a 3d engine for it. The game emphasis is on the gameplay not how good looking it is.
Gameplay:
Your goal and only goal is to survive the endless waves of wolfs.
That's it? Yes. So how is it possible for a product with such a simple game design rack up all these positive reviews? That's because it was executed perfectly with Fun as the sole focus. The fight for survival is interesting and unpredictable. The wolfs come in various weapons/stuffs. Wolfs with throwing axes, wolfs on a bouncing spear, wolf dangling on flying rockets, wolfs with basket? With the recent update there are police wolf with batons? shields? a wrecking ball style wolf? wolf with handbags, cross dress wolf? and the list goes on..That sounds crazy?! What is this? Yes, that's exactly what makes the whole product unique and interesting.
If you play plant vs zombie, the feeling is similar where you encounter zombies with scuba diving equipment, with a pole, with newspaper, riding a ice maker vehicle. etc.
The fights are NEVER DULL, it is intense and challenging enough for the masses; whether you are young/old/casuals/hardcore players. Anyone and everyone can have fun. All it takes is a 1 minute of your time.
My Personnel Experience:
When I first saw Iron snout on launch, I didn't know what to expect but as it was released as a Free 2 Play game and there were already hundreds of positive reviews, I decided to give it a shot. It was a shocking experience for me to see that with such a simple game design, people were having ton of fun due to the creative design on the enemies; the wolf's. The ability to steal their weapons and temporarily used it against the wolf/the ability to use the environment to help you against the wolf made the game even more interesting. I had lots of laugh when I saw what the wolfs were capable of. All of this is only possible when your game don't break/have weird bugs. The mechanics were simple but most importantly, it worked. Perfectly! so, kudos to Snoutup & its team for the effort and making this original game really fun.
I personally did not encounter any errors nor find any glaring issues. Do I see myself playing iron snout a year from now? No, not really. Maybe just 5 minutes from time to time. Here's why, despite the ton of fun it has to offer, I have already experienced everything so I definitely would want to try out other games. Unless Iron Snout comes out with new content/new game mode or a possible co-op function or host periodic events, it wont be able to retain its player base in the long run. I sincerely hope that snoutup is aware about this and have plans release new content/host events/introduce new game mode/features in the future.
I just realized hours ago before this writing that certain people may have issues playing a character that resembles a pig. From where I am from, you'd be surprise what drama certain religious quarters can stir up. I hope that the devs can consider to provide skins/alternative characters to be played as instead. I know it sounds really silly but if you want to reach out to wider audience, you'd have to consider things like this.
 
My Summary:
This is really hard. The amount of fun that iron snout has showered me is really generous. abundant. 200% More than any other indie product has ever offered. On top of that, there's no flaw as well. Objectively, this should earn a perfect score. lol. [After 30 minutes pondering] It pains me to say this..It's still tearing up my soul inside out as I try my best to remain objective@fair for a useless self-important self-rating-score. xD *rips hair* *drums roll*  So, on the scale of 0 - 10, my personal rating for Iron snout is a 9/10. With a nomination vote! There I said!

Across my nearly three-decade adventure gaming life I have come to find two factors to be of incredible importance:
1. The Puzzles
2. The Humour
Duke Grabowski disappointingly falters on both.
Point and click adventures have long been plagued by nonsensical puzzles. Much to its detriment Duke Gabrowski has gone in the complete opposite direction, making its puzzles simple enough to be trivial.
The aim of the game is to woo three ladies in the game's locale, Bodacious Bay, turning it into more of a pirate-themed dating simulator. This of course reduces variety in the puzzles, unlike The Secret of Monkey Island's Three Trials. The biggest problem posed by this, however is that the puzzles are entirely independent of one another ie. no elements from one puzzle are to be used in any other. Compare this to the four map pieces of LeChuck's Revenge, which were all beautifully intertwined.
The game is also too short to call back to any puzzles, as was done with the voodoo doll and hangover cure in LeChuck's Revenge and The Curse of Monkey Island respectively. I do realise that this is an episodic game (despite not being stated anywhere on its store page) but I have found that episodic games tend to rarely utilise call-back puzzles anyway.
The jokes jump between puns and political incorrectness, almost as though it was written by my dad.
The dialog "options" are extremely limited. I always like being able to chose how I personally would react in a situation (often flitting between overly pleasant and unbearably sarcastic, as anyone who know me would testify is true to real life). The dialog options here though only seem to cater to Sloth out of The Goonies.
In such a short game there are too many attempts to reference classic LucasArts adventures (I counted 4) which came across as disingenuous and trying to play on nostalgia. To reference South Park's Member Berries "ooh, 'member Monkey Island?".
The music is absolutely fantastic and evoked memories of The Curse of Monkey Island, which drew me in immediately. Unfortunately the rest of the game didn not manage to live up to this. I highly doubt that I will be purchasing any further games in the series.

Within the last few years, a few of the former Lucas Arts gang got together and worked on my new Favorite game - The Cave (which is full of brilliant dark humor and even had Chuck the Plant). So maybe my expectations were too high with this one? Clearly the game has adult themes ( wooing women and "burying the family jewels in a wenches treaure chest" and so forth), but if that was the case then why the simplistic game? It really wasn't that challenging and the game was super short. The locations were minimal and the puzzles were so easy a child could do them. So I am confused as to what demographic they were trying to target. The sadest part of all is that the Lucas Arts gang was known for its brilliant dark humor, but that fell completely flat here. Everyone and their grandma compares this to Sonic, and it does have its roots in it, but it plays more like a PSX-era Treasure game.  By which I mean, it gets brutally hard and has ridiculous but lovable voice acting.  It captures the aesthetic perfectly; if you want some late-90s-style platforming, get this game!

So... the controls are tight and responsive, the levels are very well designed, the gameplay is satisfying and just feels good, and the often criticized story is... okay, yes. The story is a mix of "Saturday Morning Cartoon" and "Fan Fiction." But you know what? Maybe that's okay. I am not going to defend it as a great work of video game storytelling, because it's obviously not. That said, however, it was written and acted by a group of excitably enthusiastic amateurs with an earnest sincerity that I couldn't help but find charming. It was ham-handed, dorky, melodramatic, and a little incoherent at times, but that's okay. It's okay to like something that started as a work of fan fiction. It doesn't make one a bad person.
For many, this game will fall outside their comfort zone. I hope someday they can give it another shot without their phobia of "furries" or "sonic fans" getting in the way of their enjoyment, because there is a really really good game in here. But, you know, that's okay. It's not for everyone.

A Fun Game
...But not for everyone
Freedom Planet evokes the feel of the 2D games that came about the 32 bit era, with advanced Sprite animations and high-quality sounds and music. It takes inspiration from Sonic and Megaman games in particular, but also channels the soul of games made by Treasure during the 16 bit era like Gunstar Heroes and Alien Soldier (all of which happen to be available here on Steam).
High-speed Platforming action is the game's primary shtick, some characters play faster than others. On normal difficulty the game is fairly hard, but you can tweak the difficulty before you start your game. Unfortunately the physics aren't as tight as they could be. Sometimes the characters feel really floaty, and more often than not you'll discover that some characters can walk up walls with hardly any effort at all. Most of the time you can ignore this, but it may get on some people's nerves.
This game also features a fully-voiced story mode, complete with cutscenes between stages. These, though fun to watch, may require more patience for some. The dialogue is silly and cheesy befitting that of a cartoon show, with just a bit of dark elements maybe bumping it up to the standards of a dubbed anime of old.
Thankfully you can skip these if you're not interested, or just play with the stages alone by selecting Classic Mode upon starting your file.
I personally love this game, having grown up on old games and anime, but I can understand why a lot of people won't like this game. If you're just not interested in cartoony stories then the cutscenes and characters just won't appeal, and even then if you weren't interested in retro platformers or the old Sonic entries on the Genesis, then this game may not be what all the hype suggests.

When somebody not on my list of trusted curators tells me that I have to see something, my initial reaction is disbelief. When the reason I have to see something is because it "answers" the question of "games as art" I additionally add a roll of my eyes. Part of this is because I'm a media snob, part of this is because "indie" games have been legitimately over-hyped in recent years, and part of this is because there is no question in my mind that games are art or at least they often can be.
Papo & Yo was 2012's answer to the games as art question and I initially passed on it assuming that it was only getting hype due to being a) about substance and child abuse, b) foreign, and c) "indie" and not its merit as a game. I was wrong. Papo & Yo delivers as a game, an artistic endeavor, and a metaphorical journey in every way possible. With interesting puzzles, excellent art direction, and pitch perfect score, Papo & Yo leads you through a brilliantly imaginative, and malleable landscape all the while building the aforementioned abuse metaphor through interaction between the player and "Monster".
Unlike games with a similar theme such as: Among the Sleep, Papo & Yo manages to explore metaphor as much through gameplay as through narrative. The central puzzle is always how to deal with Monster, docile one moment, but filled with rage upon consuming frogs, which he cannot resist. As the game progresses it becomes increasingly difficult to deal with the beast and the player and the character of Quico grow to understand that Monster cannot be sated and must be dealt with otherwise.
Beyond the narrative or metaphor the gameplay in Papo & Yo is solid and enjoyable. Whether to prove to yourself that games can be art or simply to enjoy an fun puzzle adventure, Papo & Yo is worth checking out.

Exquisitely beautiful and deeply nuanced, Papo & Yo asks of its audience that they enter into a relationship with a monster, one that they're almost sure to regret.
I heard of Papo & Yo by chance, from a friend. It's a small game -- with only about 3-4 hours of gameplay -- from the even smaller Minority development team, based in Montreal. With an August 2012 release date, it's also relatively old by game standard; I bought it back in June on a whim, torn between rave reviews by people I knew and a few spectacularly bad ones by games journalists (although, if IGN still counts as games journalism by the time anyone's reading this, I will be well and truly shocked). I didn't touch it at all until very recently.
But Papo & Yo lives up to cult hype. Although relatively simple -- possibly too simple for anyone who doesn't struggle with puzzles and platformers the way I do -- the game's breathtaking environments, incredible soundtrack, charming cast and biting narrative are more than enough to compensate even the most "hardcore" of gamers. If you feel mocked by the quotation marks I put around that word, please feel free to send me one (1) mug of your tears, and possibly a signed Polaroid of you crying next to today's paper so I know that your pain is real, and that my general disdain for the "gamer elite" has found its intended target.
Papo & Yo's lead protagonist -- Quico -- is a young boy buried in the depths of his own imagination, struggling to cope with the trauma of life with his alcoholic, abusive father. Based on the childhood experiences of creator Vander Caballero, Quico retreats from his father's abuse into a dreamlike version of (what is ostensibly) his own neighborhood. In Quico's mind, his Brazilian favela becomes a magical place where buildings can sprout wings and legs, and Quico himself can run across the rooftops and jump between them with ease, accompanied by his toy robot, Lula.
At first, Quico's dreamy paradise is a perfect escape; puzzles are quick and fun, and interacting with the world is a beautiful, uplifting experience. But it isn't long before the Monster that rules Quico's conscious life follows him into his subconscious one, and begins to color the once-tranquil world of Quico's imagination with violence and fear.
Truthfully, it's impossible to talk about this game without talking about the nature of abuse. The narrative is squarely pointed at it and as an abuse simulator, Papo & Yo is unnervingly effective. Having been in several emotionally abusive relationships myself, I saw my experiences mirrored onscreen. Monster is visually intimidating, but -- when calm -- actually takes on a strangely charming demeanor. He seems nice; a little gruff and bumbling but protective, scooping Quico out of danger when he gets in over his head, blinking up at you when you crawl on his belly, and even throwing a soccer ball back and forth with you. He's dumb and single-minded, but sweet, for the most part.
But when Monster's temper flares -- when he comes into contact with anything that alters his mood -- he becomes a terrifying hellion, and anything in his way falls victim to his rage. When Monster gets angry, almost nothing can dissuade him from hurting you... and he WANTS to get angry. He pursues the thing that drives him into that fury more doggedly than he pursues anything else. Soon you're not just trying to avoid letting Monster get angry, you're bracing yourself for the inevitable. 'When will he get mad next?' you start to wonder. You become more vigilant -- both of Monster's behavior and your own -- because it isn't a matter of
something will set Monster off again, but a matter of
.
At a certain point, Monster's temper isn't just something you fear; it's a fact of life. You have to be aware of him at all times, and you can never leave him to his own devices for too long. It becomes tedious managing him all the time. Monster hurts you when he's angry; he hurts people you like, and destroys things you care about. You can't get rid of him, but he's becoming something you can no longer bear to live with.
There's something to be said for the way Papo & Yo brings you through this cycle: from meeting the person to meeting their insurmountable problem; to taking that problem on as your own and being weighed down and exhausted by it; to beginning to fear and loathe the person for all the harm their problem is doing to you; to eventually wanting that person gone more than you feel obligated to them. I've lived that cycle several times, and being brought through it again by the game felt organic and real. For this exact reason, I can't bear to play through this game a second time; there's a few achievements that can only be earned on a second playthrough, and due to the realness of what I experienced, I don't anticipate ever going back for them.
The narrative is clearly where this game sings; gameplay is where it often sighs. There were a few key moments where I felt railroaded into interacting with Monster and his anger. I personally liked how incredibly forgiving the gameplay was -- to my knowledge there are
failure/death states -- but jokes aside, I
understand why some players have found it less than engaging in the past. Puzzles are relatively easy to solve and sometimes a little tedious as a result. Platforming in 3D is, as always, a little clunky, especially when jumping between platforms. Gameplay is very obviously second fiddle to the story Papo & Yo strives to tell, and although the mechanics in interactions with Monster feel very cohesive and in service of the narrative, most of the platforming segments do not.
But, despite being less narratively resonant than desired, overall I found the platforming segments pretty fun. Part of this is that the platforming enhances my understanding of Quico as a child -- it's generally playful and inventive, combining both common, visible objects and imaginary, fanciful ones, something which is relatively common among children Quico's age. The world becomes his playground, even in moments of great peril at the hands of Monster; there's an emphasis both in gameplay and in narrative that Quico isn't mentally, physically, or emotionally equipped to cope with or retalliate against his father's abuse. His only choice is to make up a story where he can survive it more easily. It also drives home what I think is a very important point: abuse follows abuse survivors everywhere they go. Abuse affects you so deeply, that Quico's incapable of even imagining a world without it.
Ultimately, I think the mechanical/narrative discordance in Papo & Yo is minimal. It might be more noticeable if the game was longer, but if you sit down and marathon it in a single day (which is completely doable), I doubt you'll think twice about it. Papo & Yo is a bold, powerful game, and has a lot of incredibly important things to say -- I recommend playing it immediately.

But for the repetitive and tedious puzzle sequences it dulled the gameplay because I already knew what would do what and how it would be done.
Don't get me wrong, the storyline IS there, but the fillers for what little storyline is present consists of moving gears and wishing your walkspeed was faster.
The visuals are great, as well as the decorations, I was constantly exploring the maps out of curiosity and hoping that I would run into an easteregg (I found one near the end of the game).
For full price, I do not recommend buying this game because it is quite short, and your money would be better invested in a game where you could spend many hours on. Plus, the storyline is present, but not very strong. If you are considering buying it during a sale (I got mine 75% off), then I say there is no harm  if you have done your research and know this is a game you will enjoy for its price.

I truly believe “Duke Grabowski: Mighty Swashbucker!” has the potential of becoming the best adventure game that Tiller, Mocsy and Grant have delivered so far, as long as they fix the -mainly technical- flaws this first part brought out.

As a gamer who started out playing the old Sierra adventure games, I found this a lot of fun. Likable characters, great art, and a well written story all ombine to make an enjoyable game. It was rather short by modern standards, I'll admit, but well within what I would expect from an adventure game. As a backer of the game's Kickstarter, I was not disappointed.

Before you read on, this game is both short and easy. So if you are the type that needs  to get the maximum bang for his or her buck then you are wrong here. If you want to be entertained and don't mind to spend the amount of money of a bucket of popcorn for 2 hours of entertainment, read on.
Duke Grabowski is a short but sweet adventure game that is highly entertaining but suffers from easy and far between puzzles (there are maybe 10 items that need to be used) and rather bad character animations. The atmosphere is spot on and reminds me of the better Monkey Island games, in particular the backgrounds are outright beautiful. Through the entire 2 hours that it took me to finish the game I had a smile on my face and even my wife - who hates videogames with a passion - could't resist to catch a few minutes.
For the price, I think it is worth it. Having kickstarted the game, I paid probably twice as much and I must say while it is not the best game I ever kickstarted, I am happy that this got made. If this is what Double Fine Adventure would have been if they hadn't gotten far too much money, then I would have prepared that version!

I backed the kickstarter project of Duke Grabowski.
It was advertised as:
"
The game is modest in size. We're keeping it small and achievable.
- 9-12 detailed backgrounds by Bill.
- 4-6 major new characters, depending on how this campaign goes.
-  Comic-book style, hand-drawn cutscenes.
- Succinct 2-4 hours of gameplay.
"
So I knew it will be a short game from the beginning.
It took me ~2.5 hours to reach the end.
Puzzles remain at beginner's level.
Usually there are only two inventory items - often another person represents an object to use in a specific situation.
Overall it only feels like an introduction to an adventure - maybe 1/5 of a story,
..but I would like to continue to play!
It looks nice, sounds good and Duke is a cool dude.
But right now it's not more than an appetizer.

A touching pirate adventure that made me chuckle on a good few occassions - a lot of love went into the dialogue ('Touch the grog kegs? Nah, they've been tapped already.'), and the art and animation is charming. The puzzles are logical, while still presenting some challenge - I was never frustrated, but I was rewarded.
Only minor gripes are a couple of small UI bugs - nothing that got in the way of the experience - and the fact that Duke has to turn on the spot before walking to where you click, which makes him feel a little unresponsive.
All in all, a very enjoyable adventure with a lot of nice moments. Worth your time and money if you enjoy adventure games and / or fun dialogue.

It has to be mentioned that you're buying an episodic game at an episodic price. The first episode will only take you a little less than two hours to complete.
THAT SAID, there's a lot of promising material here. The protagonist is unique, the inventory system is novel and opts for using IDEAS over tangible items, and the backgrounds are GORGEOUS!! Every new screen is a visual delight. I'm not as enthused about the 3d models but I'm sure (or I hope) they will improve with each episode.
The fact that there's no indication of how much future episodes will cost, or the whole 'season' price, concerns me a little bit. I assume you won't get the whole series for free, but I've seen a lot of episodic series on Steam go kaput after one episode. I hope there is some good faith showing of a roadmap at some point.

You won't find any overly taxing puzzles here, but it's got a solid presentation, with strong voice acting, music, design and characters.  Worth a look.

If anyone reading these reviews is wondering why the overall review score doesn't reflect the number of reviews, it's because most of the reviews here are from people who received game keys for this title, as it was a kickstarter project.  Reviews from people with keys aren't included in Steam's review scores.

If you've been longing to play a game close to Monkey Island, this is the game for you. The graphics looks sweet (and will remind you of Curse of Monkey Island), the puzzles aren't that hard (so you won't need a walkthrough!), the soundtrack is lovely and quite fitting (even if it's from another game by the own company, set in the same universe) and I can't wait for the next part. Actually, a lot of times I thought about Monkey Island. This is a must-buy, even if you miss the old LucasArts adventure games. I give this first part a 9/10. A welcoming game to our collection. I backed this product when they did a crowd-funding. Not disappointed and worth the money.

As with all games I backed on Kickstarter, I like to state upfront that I did back the game and for this one I actually was allowed by the team to do the voice work based for the character that suffers from looking a lot like me! It's okay, I'm an old engineering professor, I get ignored by students at least five days a week; don't feel bad adding yourself to the list!
With that out of the way, I really enjoyed this fun little game. Duke is a member of a pirate crew that has just found themselves without a captain. Duke wants the job and being the strongest, he can use muscle to get it but the crew has another idea; if big and loud Duke with all the social graces of a seasick crocodile (to borrow from Dr. Seuss) can woo three women like a pirate captain should, then he can be captain. So Duke sets off to woo three women if he can figure out what woo means.
Fortunately, Duke finds some ladies who need his help and thus we have a game! The ladies quickly realize he has been set up to fail, but they also see a would be captain who is really happy to be helpful especially if it involves tossing bad guys about! They are happy to tell the priate crew they have been wooed in exchange for the help that Duke is able to provide. This is innocent fun and much of the humor comes from Duke being so naive but having a good heart.
The game is billed at 2-4 hours and I think the two is closer to the truth. The puzzles are not terribly difficult and the results are more or less as expected. The artwork is bright and the music jaunty so the entire atmosphere of the game is laid back and relaxed. The main characters are fun and despite my appearance (saving the day I might add by fumigation) the secondary characters are a lot of fun and add to the fun. If you have ever played adventure games, you will have no difficulty in guiding Duke through his tasks, but you should have some fun along the way.

I am enjoying this game tremendously, it is well worth the $5 it was on sale for in the steam summer sale. The tag line is something like 'build the city of your dreams'. Unfortunately it is a little too simplistic to achive this, but it is quite challenging and enjoyable as is.
The name is quite self-explainatory...
You build your own world and then cover it in cities. In building a city, you layout property zoning and manage the provision of civil services to make sure all the little people ('sim(s)') have what they need to be happy and healthy.
It does have some dissapointment to offer...
The game casts education, labor and wealth in a very narrow-minded way. Just about all of the civil services you have to provide your people are education-related, and the only incentive to give them education is to make them more successfull and promote wealth. More wealthy community = more features and money to play with. In reality education is a life-long process. You spend your whole life learning as much as you can (ideally). Posing education as all about wealth is basically saying life is about wealth. If that is all your life is about, you are indeed a pitiful creature. I wish the design of education in the game would have been done differently. The simulation aspect of the game is very rigid. For example, if you don't want your people being brainwashed, you can kick the church and military out of town, but it won't affect anything but your city income. In reality, that would likely improve the education and crime rates of your community, but the game does not simulate with that level of depth. Your choices do not affect the gameplay, it will always happen the same way in every city. Do it right = more money, not = game over.
... but it is still fun, and even at times exciting.
You really have to put some thought into how your city should be made. There are many basic principles you will pick up on early in the game, but every time you think you have it all figured out, you will discover new problems and reasons to re-evaluate your strategy. Every city will probably be better than your last, and the progress is represented graphically in the types of buildings your people construct. Early in the game you will get mostly little boring buildings, but as your population grows accross your entire region (after you make a few decent cities), the buildings get bigger and cooler and house more people/jobs. One BIG PROBLEM with this game though is that it is very crashy. If you don't save ragularly, you will likely find yourself losing decades of development quite often.

As one of my favorite games of all time (in my top five for sure) and an integral part of my childhood, this classic JRPG has always held a very special place in my heart. But even when I put aside those rose-tinted nostalgia goggles, I can safely say that this one is a timeless gem and well worth playing if you haven't done so yet.
I've played through the entire game and completed all side objectives multiple times back in the PS1 glory days, when FFIX was in its original 4-disc form. When I found out that this perennial fav of mine was being brought to PC in a remastered state, I was overjoyed-- and also, like many other fans, a bit worried that the port would be of poor quality. I anxiously awaited its release, and when it finally came out I was extremely relieved to see that the game was nearly perfect. They even kept the quality of the lovely and memorable musical score intact.
The character models look better than ever in high-res, and for those less fond of that JRPG grind there are now optional cheats to breeze through the game (though I'd never touch 'em, personally. I'm an FFIX purist like that!)
Controls work fine with either a controller or keyboard/mouse, but I recommend using a controller as that is the way the game was meant to be played.
The only issue I've got (and it's a relatively minor one that not much could've been done about) is the blurry backgrounds, which in most PC resolutions are quite noticeably fuzzy. This is unfortunate, as these pre-rendered backgrounds feature some very stunning art and help to create the game's amazing atmosphere. But fortunately they can still be appreciated, even in this state. It's far from a deal-breaker, at least for me. It bugged me a lot at first, but I can deal with it now. It just takes some getting used to, and it also depends on the specific resolution you're using.
The story and its characters remain as timeless and charming as ever, and it's the same emotional thrillride for me that it's always been. I will never stop adoring this game, and I'm really pleased to have it back in my life.
It's also worth mentioning that if you enjoy finding a whole lotta secrets and all sorts of hidden goodies, this one will not disappoint. Persistence and exploration are rewarded.
TL;DR --> An above-average port of the best Final Fantasy game of them all. If you haven't played FFIX yet, you're missing out.

Issue Resolved: the patch on June 27 has resolved my issues with Final Fantasy IX. The mouse pointer no longer centers when using a movement key. Thank you, Square, for fixing this bug. I am changing my review as a result.
Original Review:
I had been looking very forward to playing Final Fantasy IX for the first time. The story had me quickly engaged, and I was looking forward to my new adventure. However, the technical issues and bugs with the controls have soured me on this game.
As a disabled gamer, it is important that a game functions well in windowed mode with an on-screen keyboard. Final Fantasy IX currently has a very severe bug that centers your mouse pointer on your screen whenever you hit a movement key (WASD or the arrow keys). A game should never move your mouse pointer when you are not using the mouse. You press any of the directional for your character and the mouse will move. This is very irritating when using an on-screen keyboard.
This bug will also affect controllers if you are plagued with the character continually moving in one direction even when not pressing a joystick. Thus you will be required to use keyboard shortcuts to quit the game.
I recommend staying away from this game until Square takes the time to fix these issues.

text:
Among any Final Fantasy fan, most of them all have different ideas of what the "best" game in the franchise is. I can't say that IX is definitively the best, but it's definitely up there as far as quality games in the series goes, and for a good reason.
The story is one of the best I've ever seen in a JRPG. All of the characters are lovable and hard to forget. My personal favorite is Vivi, the young Black Mage. Without spoiling too much, he goes through a lot of difficult things, mostly existential, and if you're anything like me it will probably make you cry.
The graphics are wonderful, even to this day, although the character models have been upgraded. There are complaints about how the backgrounds are blurry, and well, they are. But when you're focusing on playing the game you kind of don't notice after a while. The FMVs are beautiful looking for a game that came out on the PS1.
The battle system is great, still using the ATB system like the older games in the franchise. This means you can choose to be active to fight in real time, or you can wait, which lets you go through menus for items and magic. There's also Trance, which lets your character become stronger for a short period of time. Abilities are given based on what items you equip, each of them having different effects in battle.
To those wondering, this game isn't stretched to be fullscreen, because it will still show grey borders at the sides. I have it on 1366x768 and it still shows the borders. I personally don't care, but some people might be turned off by it.
Overall, this game is amazing, and if you consider yourself a JRPG fan you would be doing yourself a favor by playing it. I feel like the price is a little too high right now, though, even for such a great game. When it goes on sale, it's a definite purchase.

Papo & Yo is short, but powerful; powerful enough that I couldn't write a review immediately after playing it, because it was all still a little too intense.
I picked this game up as part of a Humble Bundle, knowing absolutely nothing about it, and installed it when I was in the mood for a bit of indie whimsy.  So it came as a bit of a shock when the opening animation sequence  made it clear that child abuse was going to be a prominent theme of the game -- I had been expecting cheery, light-hearted fluff, and this was looking instead like a terrible downer.  Within a few minutes, however, the setting and gameplay had drawn me in so much that I played all the way through in one sitting, even though I knew the game was writing me a ticket on the feels train.
The setting is an appealingly surrealist dreamscape rendition of a South American favela, blending fanciful magic with rusty corrugated iron sheets.  The frequent puzzles are inventive and fun, if not particularly challenging.  But the puzzles aren't the true star of this game; story is the shining star here.   Monster, your companion through most of the game, is a very thinly veiled portrayal of an abusive alcoholic father, and what the game does brilliantly is lead you into the mindset of a victim.  You'll love Monster, fear him, hate him, resent him and even pity him, often at the same time.  You'll find yourself doing ugly, violent things without even thinking about it, because you desperately need to avoid triggering Monster's rage.  You'll make excuses for Monster; you'll blame other things; you'll blame yourself.  You'll allow yourself to believe that you're in control -- that if you just play the game well enough, you can keep Monster content and placid indefinitely.  And, inevitably, it will all come crashing down on you.
The majority of "game as art" projects I've seen have been gross, pretentious failures that abandon concepts of gameplay in favour of marching the player on a directed tour through the creator's personal vision, and the interactivity of the experience is reduced to token actions in what is otherwise a sort of animated film or ebook.  Papo & Yo is a high-art game that gets it right; there's a real game here, and it's the gameplay makes it immersive.  Once you've been drawn in through the puzzle game elements, and you really care about the characters and what happens to them, the harsh, wrenching story elements become that much more powerful.
Having such mature themes, this game is admittedly not for everyone, but, as far as I'm concerned, it's a masterpiece.

You could describe this game as a 3d person puzzle platformer. But it has a strong art style and emotional theme which makes it really unique. The story elements and characters in the game are very memorable, and the game is very good at invoking an emotional response as it has a deep theme.
The art style is very clever. It looks like a city in a developing country, so it is an interesting game world to explore. But all the puzzles are environmental, you can move houses, collapse walls and generally change the world around you to progress. There is also a lot of platforming to move around and help solve the puzzles but it is not punishing.
The world gets more and more abstract as you progress and as you piece together the background story. After playing a number of AAA games back to back, this game was a breath of fresh air and I really enjoyed it.

Pros:
* Very deep and satisfying combat system.
* Great procedural generation keeps things fresh for... how long have I been playing this, almost 150 hours???
* Enormous variety of ships, weapons, systems and species. Each ship requires a different approach, and on every run you are required to make do with the tools you chance upon, making for a unique experience.
* Hard as nails
* Perma-death
* Terrific sound track
* The game with the most "Star Trek" vibe I have ever played, even though it isn't actually Star Trek (and has more of an emphasis on combat than ST would).
Cons:
* It's a very "gamey" game for better or worse. The flavor text might give the impression that FTL is a roleplaying experience; it isn't. This is min-maxing heaven through and through, but that said, it's darn good at what it does.
* The AI is kept intentionally stupid (otherwise it would completely crush the player) and at times doesn't play by the same rules as the player. For instance, you'll encounter enemy ships with loadouts that make no sense (nothing but beams that can't penetrate shields, with no other weapon to lower the shields), the AI fires each of its weapons as soon as they are charged without synching to actually penetrate the shields, the AI targets random rooms, including absurdity such as targeting empty rooms with ion weapons (ions are meant to disable systems), the AI isn't allowed to vent rooms to deal with boarders the way the player usually does, etc.
* Healing everyone and waiting for oxygen to refill after every battle can be a bit tedious.

Enjoyable little point 'n click that is the result of 2014 Kickstarter campaign.  Those familiar with the team's previous games (A Vampyre Story and Ghost Pirates of Vooju Island) will know what to expect: an adventure game in the LucasArts style with particularly gorgeous background art.  The game is short (about two hours, but likely up to twice that if you want to exhaust all the dialog) and is priced accordingly, and thanks to securing a publisher will be followed up with up to four more episodes.  This first episode, however, is completely self-contained, so have no fear of a cliffhanger.
The game is exactly what it's advertising itself as, so you should know if you're in its audience.  Recommended.

A point & click adventure games with swashbuckling pirates and funny dialogues.
Duke Grabowski is quite a lovable character despite his foolish and crude nature. The backgrounds are gorgeous and consistent, the world is appealing and believable. The story is quite simple and straightforward but it's quite enough to be enjoyable. To me, this game is also an improvement on Ghost Pirates of Vooju Island on several levels : the writing and narrative is done much better and isn't confusing this time, the gameplay is smoother, characters are more likable/memorable, better voice acting.
On the other hand, the game is a bit too easy : the puzzles would have benefited from more complexity and layers to them, the inventory is not used enough because there isn't much to pick up and try combinations with.
Considering this is a low budget game and the first episode in a serie, I'm happy with it and I'm quite confident the sequels will continue to improve on it. Anyway, Duke Grabowski is totally worth the fun and price. Looking forward to the subsequent episodes !

If Steam had a maybe option for a recommendation I would probably give it to Duke Grabowski, Mighty Swashbuckler. There really is nothing terribly wrong with the game but there is nothing great either.
The gameplay is pretty typical for a point and click adventure game and it works well for the most part.
The story has its' moments but in other areas it could have used some work. It might just be me but the game seems to think it is funnier than it actually is. I can see that the game is trying to be quirky/funny but I just didn't laugh that often.
The graphics are also kind of hit and miss. Some of the backgrounds and characters are really good while others could have used a little work.
The music and audio is pretty good. The voicework for the most part is quite good but there is the occasional character that could have been better. The music is pretty good even though it is a little repetitive.
The two biggest problems with the game are the length and difficutly. Duke Grabowski, Mighty Swashbuckler is a pretty short point and click adventure game. The game is only two to three hours long depending on how much you explore the world. If you rush through the game you probably could finish the game in less than two hours. The problem is that outside of replaying the story there is no reason to replay the game so you will likely only get around two to three hours out of the game.
The issue with the difficulty is that the game is so easy/straightforward that I can't see people being challenged by the game. The good news is that the game doesn't have any of those frustrating puzzles where you just have to try every option until you discover what you are supposed to do. The problem is that the puzzles are so straightforward that if you have explored the island you will know immediately what you have to do for every puzzle. If this doesn't matter to you it isn't much of a problem. If you are looking for a challenge though you aren't going to get it from Duke Grabowski, Mighty Swashbuckler.
Basically Duke Grabowski, Mighty Swashbuckler is a very average point and click adventure game. It doesn't really do anything wrong but doesn't do anything great either. If you don't love point and click adventure games, it won't be for you. If you love point and click adventure games, are intrigued by the premise and don't mind an easy game I think you can get enjoyment out of Duke Grabowski, Mighty Swashbuckler.

Mafia 2 is a great game with an excellent story, good combat system and amazing driving but it's not for everybody.  The story, whilst excellent is fairly short; I beat the game in about 10 hours at the hardest difficulty setting. If you don't enjoy cutscenes or slow moments, this game isn't for you. For example, the game has a section where you have to clean a toilet; you're forced to do this as an unskippable event which adds to the emersion but it's certainly not fun. The game also tries to be emmersive as there is a lack of fast travel which does get tiresome after some time, especially if you die in a crash and get sent back across the map.
The game tries to add in some realism as your car needs fueling after a while and if you crash too hard, you need to get out and repair it. You can only take about 3 bullets (on hard mode) so most of your time in combat will be spent waiting in cover for enemies to pop up at you. The combat is fun but it feels like whack-a-mole at times.
The checkpointing is what ruins the experience for me. One mission tasks you with going through a building to find one guy - the mission is about 20 minutes long and there are about 4 checkpoints with cheapshots everywhere and a cross map drive. This is probably my biggest gripe and lost this game a point /10.
Soundtrack fits the time period well, songs are not to everybody's taste but will appeal if you're in to older music or jazz and blues.

Let's get it out of the way.  This is a good port, with some dents that need to be ironed out but it's nothing major.  If you are looking for a HD Remaster or Remake, this is not for you.  Yes, all the FMV have been re-rendered in HD and are skippable.

This is my favorite final fantasy. It was when i played it on PlayStation and it still is now. This game is almost perfect.
In general by gameplay it's similar to Final fantasy VII and final fantasy VIII. The graphics and overall world design are very similar. This is the last open world Final fantasy game where you can travel freely around the world in a flying ship. After IX the series got worse. I‘m in no way saying that newer games are bad, i still enjoyed them but they lack so many things from older games and some of them shouldn‘t be called Final fantasy because the only thing they have in common with Final fantasy is moogles. But i must admit they have some improvements like no random encounters and faster battles.
The combat in this game is awesome. I think it‘s the best from all three (VII, VIII & IX). VIII was the worst because everyone could be a mage or a healer or whatever. In IX characters are who they are. Garnett is a white mage and Vivi is a black mage, same goes for every other character,  you can‘t change that. Only mages can cast magic for example. Also not everyone can use eidolons, they‘re something special now, not unlike VIII. The downside of combat is that it‘s a bit too slow. When fighting the same enemies again and again it‘s little annoying to waste your time on those long fights, but it‘s not a big deal, you get used to it.
This game has a game within a game. A card game. I really love it, i don‘t get why people are hating it so much? Is it because they don‘t know how to play? Of course it‘s not as good as Gwent in Witcher 3 but it‘s really fun.
What slightly annoys me is absolutely no information on side activities or a way to track collectibles. I know it‘s good when the game doesn‘t hold you hand and i really don‘t need the game telling me what to do and where to go, but i really hate when i‘m forced to replay the whole game if i miss something. So it would be nice to be able to track your progress, to have some checklist or something.
The graphics are really improved. Character models look sharp and CGI is amazing. Even today CGI looks gorgeous, you can see Steiner‘s eyeliner perfectly clear. The background images on the other hand are untouched and they‘re low quality and blurry. I read that SE lost the HD backgrouds and couldn‘t do anything about it. Don‘t know if that‘s true. Anyway it‘s playable and the game is still good to look at.
The game runs at 4:3 resolution with nice black borders on the sides. It doesn‘t bother me, i‘m just happy i can play this game on PC finally.
I see people complaining about this game how it is a bad port and everything is crap etc. Don‘t trust those people, they‘re wrong, everything is fine with the game. People just like to complain, some of them expected a complete rework of the game maybe. The port is really good, it‘s nothing like VII (didn‘t play VIII on PC yet). The controls are good, you can change button mapping in the config menu. The game runs at 30fps, world map is locked to 20fps and CGI is locked to 15fps. But i don‘t really care about fps in this game, it‘s not a fast paced game where 30fps is barely playable, so it doesn‘t have any influence to gameplay. And the game is really old, so it‘s understandable.
A big thank you to SE for in-game cheats. You enable/disable some of them any time you want and some are permanent when activated. I really like no encounter mode, it‘s handy when you‘re looking for something. You can speed up the game which makes the grinding faster and your party level up faster. Also you can turn on 9999 damage, which again makes repetitive fights faster. Just don‘t use these on bosses and important fights and don‘t ruin the game for yourself. The three permanent boosters are: max gil, max level and max abilities. These should be helpful when you‘re replaying the game if you missed something on your first playthrough.
The story is another thing this game shines in. Every character has their story, there‘s lots of dialogues in the game so prepare to read. But characters don‘t talk some boring nonsense, everything is interesting to read and time flies fast. The character stories can be funny or sad, you will laugh and want to cry while progressing through the game. The characters are really different in this game. I think none of the game in the series has such variety in races. The main character Zidane is a boy...with a tail. Another character is a Rat and Quina...well i don‘t know, she/he has no gender and loves frogs.
Also i like that your party now travels separately. Your party members are separated by the story and for some time you play with one half of the party and then you play with other characters in other location. That way most of the party members are leveled up and you get to use them all unlike in previous games where you have 10 characters and you‘re forced to play with only 3 or 4 of them.
The world, the world is beautiful with beautiful cities and villages, each having their own stories.
I recommend this game to everyone. Even if you don‘t like jRPG‘s. This is not a generic jRPG, this one is exceptional. If you like good stories, you‘re not against reading through dialogues and want deep and fun combat buy this game. Considering the price it should be a no brainer, the game offers a lots of content and you will spend hours playing it.
