Papo & Yo is a short (but very intense) puzzle adventure that turns around the struggle of a boy named Chico, as he explores an imaginary world (to eventually find a cure for the "monster", which clearly represents his father). This game develops a story about a theme that's obviously not the most feasible one, but it does so in a way that almost shock you (in a positive way).
The gameplay could be described as a first person puzzle but there's so much more to it, in terms of colours (this game has some of the best colour palettes i've seen in a videogame), sound and interaction with the environment, within most of the levels your role will be to literally shape the space around you in a way that will let you solve the puzzles and move ahead. In some ways this feels as a "metagame", in a sense that it challenges you to go after preconceptions, no matter whether they're related to space or to what the space stands for.
I would *strongly* encourage everyone to play this game. There isn't possibly not much of a age limit or any interest span that should stop you from playing.

Every now and then I find a game that is entirely mediocre in every way, and I have a hard time with my overall recommendation of it. Papo & Yo fits squarely into this category – it’s never bad, but it’s never more than simply okay either.

For positives, I can easily say that Papo & Yo is a very pleasing game, visually. You spend the majority of your game time in a favela in Brazil, solving Alice in Wonderland-esque puzzles with floating platforms and clever mechanics which change your landscape in interesting ways. It doesn’t take very long to progress through, and feels mostly tight with controls and camera movements.

However, there seems to be just a layer of polish in all aspects that prevents this game from being better than average. The animations are choppy, and some game mechanics, such as jumping puzzles, may not feel as accurate as other platforming games.

The story is my main dividing point. Although the narrative is essentially a very dark memoir, everything that you really need to know about the tale is shown to you up front. When the curtains are pulled back for a big reveal, you are basically shown what you’ve known since booting up the game – the monster is your father, and the poisonous frogs that put him into an uncontrollable rage are bottles of alcohol. It almost seemed odd that they decided to spend so much time at the end of the game devoted to showing you this, as that is the outset of the game.

To be fair, Papo & Yo has its heart in the right place, it just could have used a little more time to shine up what’s already there. However, this game is entirely skippable. Not recommended, unless you can find it as part of a package deal or it’s on a steep sale.

The game deals with the trauma of these memories tastefully in a very unique, visually appealing world. The trailer shows you honestly what the gameplay is like; third person puzzle solving. This game holds the template on what RTS games are supposed to be.
World war 2 theme: Cover, artillery and resources such as oil and human life were gambled by nations.
Now you can experience history without dying in the process. :)
Features:
Cover system, retreat option, vehicle direction (tanks have weaker rear armor)
Reactive fog of war with obscurers such as smoke.
Veterancy- you get rewarded for experienced units, they gain more abilities as they scale up into late game
Resources are areas of the map: you need to spread out and sometimes overextend to gain fuel
Victory point condition adds tension to the game
Less micro intensive - e.g dont need to press S multiple times to get produce a worker unit, dont need to build numerous base buildings so you can concentrate more on the action!
You can comeback from a losing position depending on luck, time and opponent skill!
December 2017 patch is amazing! Update is the best gift from Relic Entertainment with community support.
Multiplayer is the best experience and holds the most value for this purchase.

Oh Capcom....I truly don't understand what you were going for with this.
Let me preface this by saying that I'm completely open to change, and I know that the RE franchise is no stranger to drastic change over the years. With that being said though, I'd like to explain why I think THIS change doesn't suit the RE franchise, and thus why I gave this game a Negative Review.
The first thing you'll probably notice when you get into Resident Evil 7's Demo, is that it seems to be drastically different from the previous last few entries in the series. (Namely 4 5 and 6) I'm going to assume that Capcom had heard the criticism from fans about some of the rather ridiculous stuff that happened in those particular entires. The game had definitely gone from its survivor horror roots and become more of an action based game with silly quips about it. Leon's "No Thanks Bro!" from RE4 and Chris punching boulders in RE5 are pretty good examples of a drastic tone change over the course of the years.
However, at least in my opinion, this wasn't an entirely bad change. Resident Evil 4 5 and 6 were all incredibly fun games with tons of replayability. I was also in favor of the idea of Co-Op. I've put so many hours into Co-Op campaigns of RE5 with buddies of mine, I'm honestly a bit ashamed so admit how many hours we've dipped into 5 alone.
Another thing to say is that the Revelations games were phenomenal! These were released after 6, but were prequels following along with the story of Resident Evil. Letting us see and play as old characters and going back to the survivor horror roots of the previous games, while still maintaining the fun gameplay that 4 had originally introduced.
Capcom however seems to have incorrectly looked at their fanbase. They seemingly looked at the bad response of Revelations 2 due to their choice of releasing the game in episodes and not one full campaign, and not at the actual good response of the story, tone, and gameplay. I'm going to guess this lead them to think that they needed to look at what was popular in the Horror genre in gaming, and emulate that. So one of the Capcom executives hopped on youtube and typed in "Scary Horror Game" and stumbled upon a trailer for Outlast and said "That! Let's just make that!" and hence RE7 was born.
I'll be honest, the game really isn't that bad. It truly did give me a few scares, it runs relatively well on my slightly oudated hardware, and it's got a great atmosphere for a horror game! Quite honestly if this was a reboot of Resident Evil or a side game similar to how they handled the Revelations series, I'd be completely fine with it! However, this is not a sequel to the RE main series of games. This does not feel like Resident Evil in the slightest, and it's not even due to the camera change. Everything feels a tad too serious, the game plays oddly slow, and yes I'm not a fan of the first person perspective. We also have yet to see any mention of previous characters making a return, or how this ties into the events of 6 (and yes I expect some kind of connection to 6 since they're calling this Resident Evil 7) I'll wait and see how people review the game once it launches, but I personally am not a fan of this drastic change in the franchise. If you wanted to make it a true survival horror game then they should've improved upon the Revelations series, not make Resident Evil-Outlast Edition. You literally play as a damn camera guy! Come on Capcom. Anyway yes I realise this is just a demo, but these are my thoughts on it.

If you want to play the game in any resolution besides 4:3 do note that there will be grey sidebars to "fill in" the extra screen space. EDIT:
I'm still playing right now but I figured I should comment on some of the positive aspects now that I have a better grip on the gameplay and am not rushing a review before leaving for work. First, the impact of magic is badass. When you play, particularly when using fire spells, the first thing you will notice is that the impact of spells is unlike any other game out there. Embers shoot off of enemies, and there is even a nice touch where nearby foliage can be scorched. I adjusted my graphics preset to medium and am happy to report that there seems to be very little loss of visual fidelity while at the same time a noticeable increase in performance. I still wish there were more advanced options, and choosing a preset is definitely favorable to customizing your options, as it will often result in worse performance.
I maintain that the level design is very linear, however, there are branching paths. Upon starting a new game I was able to experience a rather engaging mini-boss fight that I did not see before. As for being able to run past enemies, it is not as severe of a problem as I initially thought. Enemy AI is fairly competent (ranged enemies keep their distance and even take cover from spells while melee enemies rush you as expected), however, the problem seems to be that enemies are tethered to certain areas. This is fixed in a few areas, like the boss arena, that require you to jump into an arena, however the problem still persists in many places. I would like to see enemies be able to follow you wherever you go and maybe even a new enemy type that can outrun the player.
Animations are very high quality. Incinerating skeletons and watching their burning forms recoil and slump to the ground is satisfying, and all the enemies move and attack in realistic ways.
I still think that the slow motion dodge (though extremely cool) is a bit too powerful, though I definitely see the merits of ranged combat now that I have to deal with the pesky archers. If anything, AOE attacks seem underpowered considering they take longer to charge up than any other attack and are used for close range, a situation where the dodge move would most likely be far more effective and easy. I'm sure there will be plenty of balancing, though.

****End Edit
From what I've played so far, I can say it is alright, especially for pre-alpha.
There are not a lot of spells that are available right now, but I'm sure they will be added later. First the things I don't like:
-Sluggish movement
-No jumping
-Lack of crosshairs and ambiguous UI
-Problems with dialogue being voiced (don't know if voices are integrated yet or this is my problem) and some artifacting problems
My biggest concern, however, is the level design. I was able to beat the entire game (thus far) by simply running past enemies and then later spamming the slow motion move that burns/ices a path. Very disappointing. Spellcasting right now simply isn't that fun. Most enemies rush you and certain spells are FAR more useful than others. The basic projectile spells pale in comparison to your slow-mo and AOE attacks, but take a similar amount of time to charge.
I can say that the game does look pretty good, particularly in the lighting department, though it is not perfectly optimized yet. Again, I will require some more playthroughs. As of right now I have run through the first mission and about half of the second one. The story is fairly nonsensical, unfortunately. It looks like effort is being put into it, though, so maybe more context will be established in the future. Right now it is DEFINITELY pre-alpha. As long as some of the balancing problems are fixed, the game is optimized a bit better (and we are given some advanced graphics options), then this will be a worthwhile release. Right now I'm coming away feeling lukewarm about the whole thing, but that isn't a bad thing at all considering the early state of the game.

It's a good, speedy platformer that borrows a lot from classic Sonic games. In a lot of ways, it even surpasses them. The controls are nice and crisp, the level designs are amazing, and the music is fittingly intense.
However, Galaxy Trail has also managed to surpass Sonic Team in the ongoing competetion to make the worst boss fights. The biggest problem with Freedom Planet is a ludricrous difficulty spike on every level just before the boss. It's the kind of difficulty spike that makes it hard to want to keep playing after each level. Yes, the level designs are amazing, but the bosses in this game soak up damage and repeat the same attacks over and over and over. Even the easy ones are a chore to get through. It doesn't have the same precision of a Megaman game, so it's an infuriating exercise in wondering how the developers thought you were supposed to avoid that. Changing the difficulty doesn't help, either.
The story is also one of this games weak points. You could play with it off, but I like keeping it on, just to give the developers an audience for the story they clearly want to tell, even if it's not that good of a story. When you can tell that a lot of heart went into the story, it doesn't really matter whether it's good or not.
Overall, I'd say this is a must-buy for Sonic fans, and strongly recomended for platformer fans. I know I just spent a lot of time listing off all of the bad things about this, but it's a good game.

Where to start? LISA is an RPG that takes place in the post-apocalyptic world of Olathe, a barren wasteland where the only survivors that remain are (mostly shirtless) men. What little civilization that remains is controlled by gangs, and porno mags and whiskey have become the main currency of the land. Enter Brad Armstrong, former karate instructor and current drug addict with
emotional baggage stemming from a life of abuse.  Brad's world is changed when he finds a baby girl, perhaps the last in the world. Knowing what would happen if she was discovered, Brad hides the girl and tries to create a better childhood for her than he ever had. The story kicks off when Brad returns one day from a drug-addled bender and finds the girl missing. He sets off into the insane world of Olathe, desperate to both find her and deal with his own addictions.
The game was made with RPG maker, so the mechanics of combat are rather simplistic: you control 4 characters in a party and engage in turn-based combat with any enemies you encounter. While this may seem like a downside, the saving grace of this system are the party members you can obtain. There are tons of lovable weirdos you can add to your party, ranging from luchadore wrestlers to a depressed delivery truck driver. Each character has their own set of skills, so there are countless ways to build your party and synergize their skills with one another. Nearly all the available party members have interesting personalities and most are hilarious (my personal favorite is the fish lawyer who throws restraining orders at your enemies), though sadly not much time is spent on the majority of them.
One of my favorite aspects about the game is how it turns moral choices into concrete gameplay mechanics. In many games, choices often amount to a "good" or "bad" choice to make, with little effect on the game besides an ending received. One main way LISA translates your moral choices to gameplay is through Brad's addiction to Joy, a drug that "makes you feel absolutely nothing". For the tortured residents of Olathe, feeling nothing it all is often preferrable to their lifetime of pain and loss. When taking Joy, Brad will be healed to his full health and will do massively increased damage, making the drug an extremely potent combat item. Brad also periodically goes through withdrawal symptoms as well, where his attacks do zero damage. The game goes to great lengths to show how Brad's Joy addiction has harmed his life, and then places the decision to take the drugs or not into the players' hands. Will you take Joy, even if it is the morally 'wrong' choice? This same idea comes up later into the game, where your decisions can significantly alter combat for the rest of the game
.

This game is, in a word, stunning.
Since I opened Papo & Yo, I've been admittedly obsessed. The way that the developers (Minority) managed to tie in mature and serious themes like alcoholism and domestic violence without using gratuitous violence or gore is commendable. In fact, Papo & Yo doesn't contain any gore at all! The story is truly captivating and you find yourself getting increasingly attached to the characters as time goes on, despite the minimal use of dialogue.
The gameplay itself is mainly a mix of casual puzzles and platforming. It's a simplistic way of bolstering the narrative, and was implemented amazingly. There are only a few achievements, but I had a lot of fun getting them all. A second playthrough of the game allows for collecting hats (which appear on dolls seen throughout the game).
I'm not one for writing serious reviews, but this game is deserving of nothing short of a proper review. Completing this game felt like a spiritual experience, and I'll be sure to do it again soon. Whatever the price is for this game right now, it's worth every penny.

For the most part, people who dislike the game criticise the genre moreso than the game itself. Fair enough, as I would very much appreciate a spiritual successor done with better focus on fairness. However, that might take away the soul of the game.
The game is balls hard and unforgiving, but that's for the better of it. The AI sometimes seems to be "stacked against you", but in truth it's all down to RNG: what weapons/systems they have, what part of your ship they are going to hit, how many shots are you going to miss. This will be frustrating and most certainly be better if designed differently (i.e. use pseudo-random number generator) -- apologies for possibly offending you, hardcore folks.
That said, FTL's biggest selling point is replayability. Sure it stinks that your best space vessel was sunk by an extremely lucky autodrone, but in the grander scheme of things, it's not that important as opposed to these points:
1. There are plenty of unlockable ships to keep things fresh. That's not really true at the start of the game, which is a big drawback.
2. There exists a list of events to expect from each sector that can be both beneficial and vice-versa. That knowledge can come  from combination of wiki or personal experience.
3. Planning/Strategizing: The Kestrel, your starting ship, is one of the most well-rounded  spacecraft in the game. Depending on the loot you get, you can develop a battle plan to counter one of the following problems:
a) countering enemy drones and volley of weapons + keeping HP above 0
b) breaking through multiple layers of shields + disarming the opponent
c) managing crewmembers and ship power, not letting a fire break out or oxygen to run out, dealing with intruders and boarding the enemy, etc...
d) keeping up with the sector: upgrading the ship in time so that you won't feel underpowered (pretty tricky especially in hard mode)

This game is very hard. And very unfair. If you can get past that, there is some decent fun to be had trying to get your ship across the quadrant. Just don't expect to reach the other side more than a handful of times.
You must also love micro-managing.

During the endgame char epilogues the last few words of their lines of text kept cutting off. And during the I Want To Be Your Canary performance, at the end of the credits, the auto advancing dialogue went way too fast.
The worst and most distracting element was that it looks like Kuja had female breasts. It's not there in the FMVS but his normal character model shows him as having a really bulky chest or it's boobs. I don't remmember seeing this in the original. Lots of invisible faces on character models and monsters when the camera is too close, faces as in poligonal sides being invisible. And some seams look broken like with Freya's tail- made it look cut in two a the end.

Cried so many times, goofy smiles. pure delighted smiles, laughter, embarassment, cheering them on. For the most part, people who dislike the game criticise the genre moreso than the game itself. Fair enough, as I would very much appreciate a spiritual successor done with better focus on fairness. However, that might take away the soul of the game.
The game is balls hard and unforgiving, but that's for the better of it. The AI sometimes seems to be "stacked against you", but in truth it's all down to RNG: what weapons/systems they have, what part of your ship they are going to hit, how many shots are you going to miss. This will be frustrating and most certainly be better if designed differently (i.e. use pseudo-random number generator) -- apologies for possibly offending you, hardcore folks.
That said, FTL's biggest selling point is replayability. Sure it stinks that your best space vessel was sunk by an extremely lucky autodrone, but in the grander scheme of things, it's not that important as opposed to these points:
1. There are plenty of unlockable ships to keep things fresh. That's not really true at the start of the game, which is a big drawback.
2. There exists a list of events to expect from each sector that can be both beneficial and vice-versa. That knowledge can come  from combination of wiki or personal experience.
3. Planning/Strategizing: The Kestrel, your starting ship, is one of the most well-rounded  spacecraft in the game. Depending on the loot you get, you can develop a battle plan to counter one of the following problems:
a) countering enemy drones and volley of weapons + keeping HP above 0
b) breaking through multiple layers of shields + disarming the opponent
c) managing crewmembers and ship power, not letting a fire break out or oxygen to run out, dealing with intruders and boarding the enemy, etc...
d) keeping up with the sector: upgrading the ship in time so that you won't feel underpowered (pretty tricky especially in hard mode)

This game is very hard. And very unfair. If you can get past that, there is some decent fun to be had trying to get your ship across the quadrant. Just don't expect to reach the other side more than a handful of times.
You must also love micro-managing.

FTL is a hectic balancing act full of tough decisions. You have to play with the hand you're dealt and roll with the punches, but the immediacy and versatility of the tactics mean that you have an incredibly broad range of options for tacking your opponents.
When you struggle to beat it on Easy, you'll discover that there's an incredible depth to draw on if you want to even attempt a Hard mode run.
The soundtrack is sublime.
You will play this and you will die without getting a chance to even think about what caused your death, and you will have fun.

This is without a doubt the best Sonic game in recent years. I have to say that if you are a Sonic fan, this is a must buy. I would say it's much better than Unleashed and a nice improvement over Colors. In this game, Sonic still has the boost feature from Unleashed and Colors as well as quick step, grind rail switching, and even some color powers from Colors. But the main feature of this Sonic game is that you have two Sonics now. The modern Sonic with all the tricks he's had from Adventure, Unleashed, etc. And the classic Sonic we've all known since the original trilogy. Story wise, it's ok. It's nothing too special. It does have a twist which I won't spoil, but this story pretty much only exists as an excuse to let us use classic Sonic in a newer game which is fine. Sonic's friends like Amy, Tails, Cream, Knuckles, etc are all there. But there only purpose is to be side characters. This is only about Sonic, but you can play as other characters with mods if you want. Moving on, this Sonic game is an anniversary type of game and it includes remastered versions of classic stages like the very first Green Hill, Sky Sanctuary, and others like Speed Highway. And you can fight past game bosses like Death Egg and Metal Sonic in HD and 3D for the first time! There's some others which I won't spoil, but just know that there aren't too many bosses. So you might end up disappoined if you were expecting a ton of bosses from the classic games or something. There's also missions for you to do after you beat the normal stages. But they're mostly optional so you can move on if you're not interested in all of them. I have to say that even if you have never played a Sonic game before that you should still give it a try. It's good, however, it isn't flawless. The game is pretty short and if you've played previous games like Unleashed and already know how to play, it's gonna take you a few hours at most to beat it. I beat it on my first playthrough. The upside though is that there's PLENTY of extra mods for you to play. The amount of hours I've put in are mainly due to mods like the Project Unleashed mod. Which is pretty much all of Sonic Unleashed's first day stages but with Generation's play style which is excellent. And there's even a mod for Sonic Colors' Tropical Resort stages which is also nice. Overall, I totally recommend it and I'd say that after beating the main game you should definitely add a lot of mods. But, if you don't plan on modding, just pick this game up on sale. 9/10

I was nervous after the FF8 port being the mess that it was that one of my favorites of the Final Fantasy series was going to be demolished by an official PC port. I'm happy to say that wasn't the case.
The addition of the game boosters allow for more variety in playstyles, and generally speaking the graphics upgrade looks fantastic in the cinematic scenes. However, some backgrounds were scaled with less grace and frankly look a mess. Scenes where scene and character models collide suffer the worst and can seem pretty jarring (the scene near the start where Vivi is introduced is one of these - if you encounter it and think it's unbearable, turn back).
The addition of the mouse controls are interesting, but finnicky. The default keyboard controls are also weird imo, so if they bother you, hit "v" asap and switch them up to something more logical. The game does manage to switch fairly seemlessly betwen the mouse controls and the keyboard, though, which is nice.
I'm pretty simple with my desires from ports - I want it to look good, sound great, and generally not interfere with my love of a classic game. Overall, I think this meets those criteria, and even adds in some bits which some may find good use for. I'm still early on, though, and will update if I encounter any inexcusable problems further down the line.

Many years ago I'd come home from school and immerse myself in FF9. It became an obsession.
And I must admit I got excited when it was released on Steam. This was the FF that I played most and enjoyed most so I immediately bought it.
It holds up incredibly well for what is now quite an old game. Good old fashioned turn-based combat and plenty to keep you occupied. If you're a fan of the final fantasy series you'll already be quite familiar with its appeal, and this classic drew me in all over again.
If you're not familiar, here is a basic rundown (no spoilers):
You control the main character, Zidane (or "Tailboy" as some of us may have called him...) along with the usual crowd of Mages and Warrior types. As you progress through the story you come across random battles and bosses, where you control a team of up to four in turn based combat mixing attacking, healing etc. There are skills unique to each character which makes it worth swapping the team around from your eventual pool of 8 characters. By equipping certain items you can learn more skills and both active and passive abilities to make your team ready for any challenge.
The story itself keeps you interested and makes you want to carry on long past the point you were planning to stop.
Any downsides? I suppose the random battles can seem lengthy in loading and finishing so sometimes you may end up looking at your phone inbetween but generally I've found it to be rewarding replaying one of my favourite games.
Always worth having a guide handy to see little things you may have missed, the Chocobo side quest can be very rewarding (though grindy) and playing the card game can be good fun too.
For the money this is well worth it, and I feel far outshines the newer FF games.
Edit: I thought I'd add - you will be humming certain tunes FOREVER

What can I say about my favorite game? Only positive things. Final Fantasy IX is definitely one of the best games and RPGs ever made. It's my favorite along with FFVII and VIII, there are other beloved FF games too like VI or X. But these three classics done by Squaresoft stand above the others. Playing FFIX always reminds me why it has a special place in my heart.
Originally released in 2000 for PS1 around the times when PS2 had released or just before. I remember receiving this back then <3 and I have replayed it countless times during the years, bought it for PS3 and Vita also lol. I fell in love with the story and characters instantly when first played this. I love the music so much too...Nobuo Uematsu is in my opinion the best composer for video game music, FFX was the last in the franchise he worked as main composer. His music just makes the games so alive. Even if FFIX don't have voice acting, the dialogue combined with such beautiful music alone makes you feel a lot just like with the previous games ;).
FFIX tells the unforgettable story of amazing and likeable thief Zidane Tribal, who gets entangled in a epic journey with the lovely princess Garnet Til Alexandros ^_^, best black mage ever Vivi Ornitier <3, a faithful and often dumb/funny knight Adelbert Steiner and many other great characters.
It's a journey to save the world, while forming a strong bond of friendship and finding answers, for example to their existence or memories. The character development is excellent. A beautiful story with a lot of funny, light hearted, touching moments and also with many mature and dark moments. The cutscenes are epic too.
Gameplay is really great and IX has the ability system, where you can customize your party defenses etc, depending on the situation. It has my favorite Chocobo minigame too, Hot&Cold where you hunt for treasures.
The port itself is very good, graphics are sharper, xbox controller works perfectly if use it, lots of achievements, combat hud is a bit bigger which is okey, includes some boosters that can help newcomers (like no encounters) and also music isn't messed up like in VII or VIII ports. One downside for some might be grey bars at the sides of screen, it didn't really bother me as I've wanted to play this so much on Steam. But still experiencing this game without them is the best feel and there is a simple ReShade mod in community guides, which I installed. That removes them so can enjoy fullscreen better.
I love how IX return to the more fantasy style with mages, knights etc and I feel like it has everything that a masterpiece requires. A game that I still enjoy playing after 16 years is something special. I always love returning to this game. The newer Final Fantasy games simply don't feel the same. They don't capture the magical story and give feelings that these good older games did, but maybe FFXV will return to the good ones. There are still some moments in IX story that make me shed tears <(T_T)>.
I recommend everyone to play this <(^_^)> and especially those who like more old-school games. If you don't like other FF games, well you might enjoy this. Those born after PS1 era or who just didn't experience it much and that possibly can't enjoy older graphics, I hope you give this a try. Because it's a truly wonderful piece of art amongst thousands of games. It's also one of the most memorable love stories ever.

Actual review (yes, cities skylines taken into comparison):
This is the supreme reigning king of city builders. While in time it will likely be beaten by Cities: Skylines, as of now this is still the best in terms of purely easy to use UI, fun things to do (the TL;DR is easily possible ingame), sheer number of mods, and customizability. I have thousands of hours in on the simcity series as a whole and only bought this on steam as another version (I still use disc/GoG versions more). The majority of the hours went into either 3000/unlimited or this version, both pre-and post-rush hour expansion (included in this one).
Keep in mind this is also the HARDEST of the simcity games, and even on easy it is very possible to screw yourself over several hours in with a chronicly failing city that slowly decays into destruction on its' own. It's also one of the most fun, however, as SimCity 3000 did away with the terraforming (mostly) of simcity 2000, and this was the first (of 2) in the series to introduce regional gameplay with multiple cities interacting on a massive map. Big difference between this and the latest simcity, however, is that in addition to preset regions, YOU create them. You can terraform them, modify their size, city layouts/sizes literally using microsoft paint, plop the cities, set up the city interactions, etc. The only thing missing is the multiplayer, but with the city sizes in this being arguably 16 times larger than simcity 2013, that more than makes up for it as you will sink dozens of hours into filling up a map and customizing it the way you want to with what is also the best UI in the series, doing a lot of the work for you and letting you optimize where and when needed.
So, why would I even recommend this over Cities: Skylines?
AS OF RIGHT NOW. As of the time of this review, Cities: Skylines is a fantastic city builder with a mass modding community and...that's it. There is no regional play, terraforming has to be modded in to be performed mid-game, the art style is VERY bland and probably has less than 100 buildings the game can call upon to place down in zones, the UI when placing roads and such has a lot of issues that make it much harder to use than it should be, there's a lot of missing features that have to be modded in, and the ability to truly customize the city is significantly lower than in this game. While I will continue to play cities skylines, I have the game heavily - and I mean HEAVILY - modded to even begin to replicate the magic of SimCity 4 and its' predecessors. I feel like the game was designed around being better than SimCity 2013 which in some aspects (art, soundtrack, pure...fun things to do, customizability) it isn't, but the major missing things in SimCity 2013 (city sizes, DRM, lack of map editing) were what drew people in. That, and the game expected it so it would have a large modding scene to fix what the developers didn't add. That's understandable, as the dev team is VERY small for Cities Skylines, but the thing is that SimCity 2013 lowered the bar of city builders to a point where Cities: Skylines was no longer just below it, but far above it.
Understand this: I WILL continue to play cities skylines. And I believe it is a great game. But it is going to take a monster that can do what Cities Skylines did to fix the SimCity 2013 formula, and also take the time to add in what SimCity does RIGHT, before there will be a city builder capable of dethroning this one. It has to look and play the part, and give the user the ability to have FUN above all with customizability, destruction, and other random things that occur (like piloting a military chopper guns blazing into your own house...like you can in this game).
If you do NOT own this game and are a fan of city builders, I highly encourage you to get it now. At a price of $20 for the base AND its expansion, the only downside is compatibility with modern OS systems, and it is still possible to make it work with a bit of stuff done. What you're ultimately getting is the definitive city builder, and what remains the king of city builders that many of us fondly remember from our childhoods and will continue to remember. This is a timeless game in ways others simply cannot and likely will not ever live up to.

Do you enjoy easy puzzles? Do you enjoy repeating the same tedious easy puzzles over and over again? Then you will love RE7!
The Resident Evil series was something I grew up with and I've been dying to see this series return to its glory days. But instead of looking back to see what made the series great and what can be improved and added; Capcom instead chooses to copy what other successful games do only not as well. Resident Evil 5 and 6 tried to immitate games like Call of Duty, Gears of War and Left 4 Dead because those games were achieving success. The end result was Chris Redfield gunning down hordes of African junkies in broad daylight and having fistfights with boulders while mashing QTEs. Capcom promised a return to the series roots with Resident Evil 7, but at this point with Capcom's record breaking number of times that it has screwed over its consumers it is plainly obvious at this point that their promises are worthless.
I'll get to the main flaws with the gameplay momentarily but first let me get my biggest gripes out of the way:
My first and biggest complaint about this game is why is it called "Resident Evil"? When I first saw this game at e3 I thought this was a new IP until I saw the title at the end. It got even worse when I first got to see the demo.The game is a complete ripoff of PT, cashing in on the fact that Silent Hills was cancelled clearly. It takes what PT did but does it not nearly half as well. While PT was supposed to serve as a fun little ARG to get people talking about Silent Hills, RE7 demo fails at even that. The dummy Finger perplexing solvers for weeks until Capcom gave the community the finger and told them the riddle was unsolvable until a future update, thanks Capcom.
Remember how I mentioned earlier how Capcom continues to base Resident Evil around the success of other franchises? This is no different. The game also rips off other successful first person survival horror titles such as Amnesia, Outlast and Alien Isolation. Simply being a horror game does not make RE7 a Resident Evil game. Imagine if they turned Metal Gear Solid into a first person shooter?
(I wouldn't put anything past Konami at this point...)
The gameplay itself is tedious. The first time through is not so bad, you move through the house trying to find various items to solve the puzzle. The game tries too hard to scare you with bumps and bangs in the house without any sense of ambience or dread. Eventually you will get your first bad ending. Then you have to do everything all over again, and again and again... Gets boring the second time but you have to keep doing these same chores over and over until you figure out how to get the good ending.
Eventually you get to the basement and you finally feel like something interesting is going to happen. You get locked in a room and are forced to fight a monster. What a disappointing combat sequence. Taking a single hit from the monster makes you infected which is an automatic fail which means you have to start the game all over again. But doing a perfect run on the monster without taking damage is a headache with such stiff controls. This isn't an epic boss fight like in past RE titles with an elaborate and fun strategy. Here you have to kick the monster over, break the door, grab a gun and shoot it in the leg 4 times in a row. But with such stiff aiming there's a good chance you'll take a hit and go back to the chores a couple of times before you finally get it right. One of the big arguments I hear from people who support the new title is that it will be a "much smoother" gameplay experience from the older RE games. But after you experience the stiff controls of this game you will be begging for tank controls.
After the success of REmake sales you'd think Capcom would get the idea now that people want the classic Resident Evil to come back. There's even rumours that RE2 remake is going to be over the shoulder. I honestly hope RE7 is a success  but from what I have played of the demo I won't be buying it any time soon.

After seeing the trailers and gameplay for Mafia III i decided to purchase Mafia II and see what all the fuss was about. Luckily, it was on sale for €5.99 instead of its original €29.99 . Needless to say that the price I purchased it for was a steal. The game features great 'car-feel', shoot-outs, interesting characters and story. Let me explain each one in detail.
'Car-Feel'
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Driving a car in this game was beautiful. It made me feel like I was actually in the 1940's and 50's. Cars are also a big part of the story as well. Since you can't take a taxi and the map is not too big, you get the great pleasure of driving everywhere, this may be in the finest of sports cars or the most beat-down piece of crap you can find, its your choice.
Shoot-Outs
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
As there was in real life, there are plenty of shoot-outs or gang wars which occur throughout the story in the game. Each shoot-out is unique because you are in a different area every time and if it is not in an area you are familiar with, you truly feel like you can die at any moment, and you can! Although it does use the classic 'Stand-behind-cover-and-all-health-regen' mechanic, one shot to the head will kill you! Shotguns one-shot you and Tommy guns♥♥♥♥♥♥you!
Interesting Characters
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Throughout the game you meet a very wide array of characters, bad guys and... good guys? It seems like every character in the game is a nice guy to the main protagonist, Vito, in the beginning but then they turn into real snakes :(
Everyone wants to climb higher in the mob and will do anything for it. Besides snakes, there is also Joe. Joe is the most loyal friend you will ever encounter... Even more than real life :) :) :/ :(
Story
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The story in Mafia II... is the best story I have ever seen in all my time of playing video games and I genuinely think it should be the sole reason someone should buy this game. There are plenty of memorable characters and moments. The story follows Vito Scaletta, an italian American man who comes home from war and gets himself involved with all the mobs in the city by doing work for them and trys to make a name for himself.

Maybe you're here because you're on the fence about purchasing, or maybe you're here even though you've already purchased the game, but are still here for some inexplicable reason. Regardless, I hope this review will inform you of where this game really shines, and where the trailer doesn't do it justice.
Freedom Planet offers classic hedgehog based platforming/running sequences, with a little more emphasis on combat, paired with tighter momentum control. Each level consists of platforming sections, punctuated with plenty of mini-boss rooms and regular enemies - especially on the last few levels,
. There are four characters in total, each playing in different combat styles. Lilac uses faster, more mobile attacks against enemys, while Carol has a slightly slower, higher damage output combat style, with added wall-jumping ability; both use recharging energy bars for their special attacks. The third character, Milla, has the slowest attacks and movement, but uses no energy bar in addition to being able to momentarily fly. Finally, there is Torque, who although being the least durable, utilizes a diverse set of gadgets to help him through each fight and is only available in select stages in classic mode.
Freedom Planet has one of the best OSTs I've heard in a while. Consisting of lively tunes in the main stages, complemented by intense, upbeat boss music and brought home by an epic rendition of previous tracks during the final confrontation. If you listen closely, you might even hear some familiar chord arrangements reminiscent to the classics Freedom Planet took inspiration from! The soundtrack really enhances the feel of each situation, and gives boss fights that extra kick.
Now, while the voice acting may not be top notch, it has plenty of character in the script and animation. The plot itself is the classic villain-dooms-entire-world-in-order-to-achieve-their-goals archtype. This doesn't bog down the story in any way though, as the villian in question has some very clever and sinister moments; his first spoken line is cocky and vile all at the same time. In addition, each character is unique and has a roll to play in the story's events.
One playthrough can take anywhere from a couple hours, to about 80 minutes (my current best). The achievements add some extra goals to strive for, and can be earned with relative ease once you figure out the layout of each stage. It took me roughly 48 hours of gameplay to get all the acheivements, which also includes in-game collectable cards; containing concept art, quotes, and music.
Though it is more forgiving than the platformers of old, Freedom Planet provides an ample challenge, plays well, and gives off that oldschool charm without rooting itself on the base of nostalgia.

For example, in the very first mission, you walk to Joe's house and hear a wife yelling at her husband as he tries to fix their car. Eventually he gets mad and leaves, at which point you can fix the car for the wife. It's not like a cut scene, and if you had stolen a car instead of walking there, you would have never even seen it. Like I said, this game is like a movie that you play. I don't know if there are choices you can make, like at one point there was a prison fight that I lost, and I don't know if that had any affect on the story. Definately buy the DLC if you buy the game, the cars in game are really slow and not much fun to drive, but if you get the Greasers pack you get a few hot rods that are a blast to drive. Overall, this game is an absolute masterpiece and I can't wait to play Mafia III.

There is a point when too much RNG is just too much, even in a roguelike. This game goes well beyond that point.
Edit:
I actually don't mind the hit/miss/dodge thing, even if those numbers could get really high resulting in some absurd situations. The problem I have is you can't build how you want unless you get lucky. The shops have limited and random loots, and events are double rng in that you have to trigger then get the right outcome. That is what I mean by "too much RNG even in a roguelike"
My other gripe is there is no real progress/upgrades to be made. In the roguelikes that I like you still die alot but so long as you didn't botch the hell out your run you earned gold or something to upgrade your runs in the future. None of that here, unless you count the ships that may or may not be upgrades depending on how you want to play, and again even if you get the ship you want you must contend with the RNGfest of gearing it like you want.
Obviously this is my opinion and plenty of people clearly enjoy "making the most" of whatever the game throws at them but its not my cup of tea and I don't recommend this game if you feel the same.

I've owned this game since at least 3 years ago. I have come back with each ground breaking update that appears in my feed. I reviewed this game with a lengthy rant primarily focused on the idiocy behind their AI system. Things like archers killing friendly units, builders losing all brain function (for many reasons), bottlenecking resource usage with tons of AI loops. I have to say some of it is definitely more polished, and I didn't see friendly fire.
Positive Changes:
- The UI is much closer to a polished game rather than a mobile app from the last rendition. It has functional graphics options, and looks unique to the game now. UI scrolling bars could be bigger than 2 pixels wide though.
- There is clearly more content, more units, and more depth for lengthier play.
- From what I could tell archers don't friendly fire anymore, thanks.
Problems:
The pathing AI still suffers from the same exact issues that I originally complained about in 2014. Granted, it's seemingly not as frequent, but there are some new bugs.
- I had a mining worker that couldn't find storage with 9 open storage all on "accept all", kept dropping rocks by the crystal.
- Infinite loop of bricktrons trying to get past each other around a stump (in the case that I saw).
- Randomly braindead bricktrons, still happens, although they don't stay braindead until you restart now. I just moved them away and reapplied their task and they go for it.
Fix the bugs with the pathing AI and I'll come back and rate this game recommended. I'd love to play this game's new content fully, but it's still a buggy mess, albeit finally a less buggy mess. I've started and graduated college in the time this game has had these ongoing issues. I genuinely give this game a fair chance each time I try it.

If you think Dark Souls is hard you should see the first boss of this game. These three little girls with their jump rope are almost impossible to defeat. They really made a steep learning curve for this game. It probably wasn't even playtested or if it was, it was done by machines with perfect algorithms too difficult for humans to reproduce.

I recommend this port mostly for those who haven't played it yet, this is because it still holds up as one of the best FF games SS/SE has ever made (and is my personal favorite). I haven't found anything about this port that severely detracts from the overall game experience.
That being said they could (and should) have done a better job with some things. If you have a PS1 version that still works on a machine I would recommend just playing that again.
PROS
- Being on PC for availability sake
- Music is still great
- Overall game flow is still good
- The new HD models are nice, and the re-rendered cutscenes more-or-less hold up at 1920x1080
- Cloud Save points at the start of every new screen (basically whenever the screen goes black and has to load) for people who like that type of thing or forget to save frequently.
- A few cheats to make the game easier (or harder) for people who may like that stuff
MIXED
- Adjusted Text - The new font used for the game is changed to be more clear with the HD format, however the style could have been better chosen
-Menu layouts could have been better, some functions are too deep in the menu flow when they should have been more accessible (like quit). Also it would have been nice to have the option to quit at any point in time through the in game pause menu.
CONS
- While the Pre rendered still have a gorgeous design, they didn't receive the HD treatment
- Some of the dialogue scenes will inexplicably pause for extended periods of time before finally catching up with themselves, so the game has some bugs that could still be ironed out.
- There's not really a huge incentive for people who already have the game in some form to rebuy it, even at the 20 dollar price -- it would be nice to have a place to view previous cutscenes, concept art and other such things.

With an amazing story surrounding it, beautiful pixelized landscapes, a beautiful soundtrack and awesome characters, Freedom Planet is worth the 15€/15$ Valve normally charge for it, here on Steam.
If you're familiar with the 2D Sonic games, I think you'll find yourself in a similar but better experience, in Freedom Planet (this coming from quite a big Sonic fan).
Personally, I also think this is a game where you'll hardly put up with any FPS drops. Since even my super slow laptop can handle this game at 60 FPS.
Now for my very first playthrough, it took me around 11 hours to complete Adventure mode, which focuses on both the levels and the game's narrative. It probably takes slightly less if one manages to complete the story with one of the characters without focusing on enemies, pickups, collectibles, one certain easter egg and without dying even once.
Honestly, I have no complaints about Freedom Planet. It's worth its price! And if you're a Sonic fan (particularly the 2D games), you're gonna love it and see just how AWESOME one similar game can be without the famous blue hedgehog in it.
As for the haters... call this game a cheap Sonic knock-off or whatever you want to call it. Trust me when I say it is NOT a Sonic knock-off. This is a indie game full of intense moments, a great story, excellent and well developed characters and good platforming without having too much of it.
Whoever sees my small review, thank you for taking your time reading it, plz respect my opinion and have fun with this masterpiece of an indie game.

After seeing the trailers and gameplay for Mafia III i decided to purchase Mafia II and see what all the fuss was about. Luckily, it was on sale for €5.99 instead of its original €29.99 . Needless to say that the price I purchased it for was a steal. The game features great 'car-feel', shoot-outs, interesting characters and story. Let me explain each one in detail.
'Car-Feel'
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Driving a car in this game was beautiful. It made me feel like I was actually in the 1940's and 50's. Cars are also a big part of the story as well. Since you can't take a taxi and the map is not too big, you get the great pleasure of driving everywhere, this may be in the finest of sports cars or the most beat-down piece of crap you can find, its your choice.
Shoot-Outs
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
As there was in real life, there are plenty of shoot-outs or gang wars which occur throughout the story in the game. Each shoot-out is unique because you are in a different area every time and if it is not in an area you are familiar with, you truly feel like you can die at any moment, and you can! Although it does use the classic 'Stand-behind-cover-and-all-health-regen' mechanic, one shot to the head will kill you! Shotguns one-shot you and Tommy guns♥♥♥♥♥♥you!
Interesting Characters
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Throughout the game you meet a very wide array of characters, bad guys and... good guys? It seems like every character in the game is a nice guy to the main protagonist, Vito, in the beginning but then they turn into real snakes :(
Everyone wants to climb higher in the mob and will do anything for it. Besides snakes, there is also Joe. Joe is the most loyal friend you will ever encounter... Even more than real life :) :) :/ :(
Story
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The story in Mafia II... is the best story I have ever seen in all my time of playing video games and I genuinely think it should be the sole reason someone should buy this game. There are plenty of memorable characters and moments. The story follows Vito Scaletta, an italian American man who comes home from war and gets himself involved with all the mobs in the city by doing work for them and trys to make a name for himself.

The Worms series has long been held dear by its fans for its endearingly comical, cartoony and unconventionally turn-taken nature of battle, and in my personal regard, offers a gaming experience that I highly value and recommend as an ideal respite from the typically hectic shoot 'em up fare. Whenever I want to relax, have fun and enjoy a good few laughs dispatching foes without the pressure of real time vigilance demanded by first person shooters, Worms is most definitely where it's at.
If you're new to Worms, Reloaded is perhaps the best iteration through which to get acquainted with this loveable series. It's visually crisp and vibrant whilst being effortless to run for the majority of systems, with gameplay that is unwaveringly slick and reponsive; a refined culmination of all the earlier iterations that adhere to the classic 2-D visual format.
There's one prevalent trait of Worms games that makes them somewhat notorious - it's ever so easy to make a blunder, whether it's by virtue of throwing a grenade only to have it fall in the vicinity of an ally or even bounce right back at you; underestimating the amount of jetpack fuel required to reach your desired destination and then dropping like an ill-fated little stone; fumbling an ambitious attempt to ninja rope across a body of water and plopping straight into it - the list of both witnessed and hypothetical follies goes on, and this is a notable part of what makes Worms so pricelessly tide-turning and amusing although unsuitable for those excessively proud individuals who could never so much as poke fun at themselves!

There is a point when too much RNG is just too much, even in a roguelike. This game goes well beyond that point.
Edit:
I actually don't mind the hit/miss/dodge thing, even if those numbers could get really high resulting in some absurd situations. The problem I have is you can't build how you want unless you get lucky. The shops have limited and random loots, and events are double rng in that you have to trigger then get the right outcome. That is what I mean by "too much RNG even in a roguelike"
My other gripe is there is no real progress/upgrades to be made. In the roguelikes that I like you still die alot but so long as you didn't botch the hell out your run you earned gold or something to upgrade your runs in the future. None of that here, unless you count the ships that may or may not be upgrades depending on how you want to play, and again even if you get the ship you want you must contend with the RNGfest of gearing it like you want.
Obviously this is my opinion and plenty of people clearly enjoy "making the most" of whatever the game throws at them but its not my cup of tea and I don't recommend this game if you feel the same.

FTL is everything you look for in a good roguelike. Short(ish) game length, randomized adventures, and brutal difficulty.
One of the main complaints against FTL is that the random generator has too much control over your performance. That both is and isn't true. Yes, some games will go better than others. Yes, you could play a one-crew ship and get boarded by four pirates right at the start. But those are rare occurances. Nearly every game is winnable if you know what you're doing.
...OK, at least half of all games are winnable if you're really, really good...
...and playing on easy...
AND I WOULDN'T HAVE IT ANY OTHER WAY! FTL is punishing. FTL is random. FTL is diverse. And that's everything you can ask of a roguelike.

FTL is a procedurally generated space exploration game that has you maintaining a ship while fighting other ships and trying to get to deliver a message or something to some group of people. It can get repetitive, but it's a fun game in short bursts that I find myself coming back to from time to time.
If this game looks cool to you, get it. If you don't like games that are dependent upon luck, don't.

I've owned this game since at least 3 years ago. I have come back with each ground breaking update that appears in my feed. Things like archers killing friendly units, builders losing all brain function (for many reasons), bottlenecking resource usage with tons of AI loops. I have to say some of it is definitely more polished, and I didn't see friendly fire.
Positive Changes:
- The UI is much closer to a polished game rather than a mobile app from the last rendition. It has functional graphics options, and looks unique to the game now. UI scrolling bars could be bigger than 2 pixels wide though.
- There is clearly more content, more units, and more depth for lengthier play.
- From what I could tell archers don't friendly fire anymore, thanks.
Problems:
The pathing AI still suffers from the same exact issues that I originally complained about in 2014. Granted, it's seemingly not as frequent, but there are some new bugs.
- I had a mining worker that couldn't find storage with 9 open storage all on "accept all", kept dropping rocks by the crystal.
- Infinite loop of bricktrons trying to get past each other around a stump (in the case that I saw).
- Randomly braindead bricktrons, still happens, although they don't stay braindead until you restart now. I just moved them away and reapplied their task and they go for it.
Fix the bugs with the pathing AI and I'll come back and rate this game recommended. I'd love to play this game's new content fully, but it's still a buggy mess, albeit finally a less buggy mess. I've started and graduated college in the time this game has had these ongoing issues. I genuinely give this game a fair chance each time I try it.

this is why i really want steam to implement a 5-star rating system instead of Yes/No. this game is really a mixed bag.
the core gameplay was superb. it was sonic as usual going though the stage as fast as possible. i really-really-REALLY enjoy all the primary stages. it was fun and satisfying. also, the map is so beautiful and massive.
and then theres the bonus stages/challenges where you have to complete at least one of those to get a stage key to proceed to the boss battle. it is really unpleasent. it isn't sonic. it's more like a standard platformer like mario. the bonus stages lack the main attractor of sonic games, Ridiculous speed. also it lacks some depth. it get boring quickly
also there's the rival/boss battle. where you have to defeat eggman, shadow, silver, perfect chaos, and metal sonic to get the chaos emerald. it's good, but in my opinion it's too repetitive and pretty confusing. seriously, you will get bored by rival battle because it's just to repetitive. but it isn't what i would say a dealbreaker, because if your looking to do some speedrun, it's still pretty enjoyable. (ps, the final boss is just awfully confusing and weird)
finally, the camera setting, the bug and lack of optimization is just awful. if you sometime run to fast, the camera would be stuck in its last setting. (example. when sonic is grinding, sometime the camera would orbit around him and it would stop if sonic stop grinding. sometime, it wouldn't stop orbiting.)
i also got a lot of framedrops. in Egg Dragoon, some of the object like the boost pad would disappear and when you get close enough, it would suddenly appear. and when i mean close enough, i mean like 2 meter away from sonic. it doesn't give you enough time to react to get to the boost pad, and the boost pad is somewhat essential to defeating eggman.
also, i still don't understand why sega always stuck with making the settings (input, graphic, etc) outside the game. so everytime i wanted to change a setting, i have to quit the game first, launch the config, make my change, then launch the game again. just unpleasant.
TL;DR
Core gameplay is excellent.
the Nostalgia is REAL
bonus round is awful
rival battle, and boss battle is good, but leave something to be desired
The lack of optimization, bug, and stupid camera is just awful.
overall - 6/10. and please, only buy this on a sale. it's not worth the full price

I don't like platformer.  I don't like jumping puzzles.  I especially don't like timing puzzles.  I'm not very good at any of those.  Because of that, I should not have liked this game.  But I did.  I liked this game a lot.
The gameplay was simple enough that I could play through it without getting seriously frustrated by my lack of skill; but still challenging enough not to be boring.   The puzzles that did not involve jumping and timing were very clever, but for the most part still logical and intuitive once you got into the flow of the game.  There were a few odd moments where the puzzles did not make a whole lot of sense, and I was force to rely on a walkthrough; but very few (unlike so many modern puzzle games, where randomness is used as a cheap and easy substitute for cleverness).  The mechanics of the game are very entertaining in themselves, particularly once Lulu is introduced.
The game design is beautiful; and the creators use of an uncommon setting was brilliant.  The third-world backdrop meshed very well with the fantastical elements; creating a seamless world with it's own unique and readily-identifiable logic.  The artwork is stunning, and the inclusion of works by actual environmental artists nothing short of amazing.  The similar use of third-world characters, rather than white Europeans or stereotypical fantasy creatures is similarly inspiring.  The music is beautiful, and in spots almost breathtaking, wonderfully blending traditional and orchestral sounds.  Atmospheric and fun at the same time.
I would be hard pressed to find any flaws in the game.  If I did, I would say that parts of the ending felt a little out of place.  Some of the scenes and actions didn't make quite as much sense as they could have, and the symbolism is a bit heavyhanded; but that's still a fairly minor quibble.   The game is a bit shorter than most of its type; but too much longer and it would have started to drag.  The pacing never leave it feeling too long or too short.
One warning is that the background story that emerges from the game is disturbing, becoming increasingly so the closer it gets to the end.  This is ultimately a story of addiction and child abuse; and is accordingly dark and sad.  Fortunately, the writers do not beat the player over the head with moralizing; and manage to balance the darkness with a keen sense of human resilience.
I cannot recommend this game enough.  I picked it up at a huge discount during one of Steam's big sales; but would can easily recommend getting it even at full price.
There's just better stuff to spend your money on...

The game tells a story of a troubled boy through a fantasy setting in a Brazilian favela. While the idea is great, the potential is not fulfilled since the way the story is presented fails to make you really identify and care for the boy. It has some fantastic moments but it feels like the creator lost some immersion in an effort to avoid making it depressing.
The puzzles are not hard and the resulting animations are great but all of them feel like a variation on the same puzzle. The platforming part is not hard either but the controls are definitely lacking. It is not accurate in movement and in depth causing you to miss simple jumps and redoing the part again.
The art style is really great. The scenes are beautiful and deliver wonderfully the favela feeling, especially the wall drawings. The characters are inventive and well animated and the subtle graphical effects really enhance the magical felling of the game.
I really liked the different direction this game is taking and I would very much like to see another title from this developer - hopefully with more attitude to the story and improvement to the technical side. Took me about 5 hours to complete the game.

An interesting Indie platformer/adventure game with only a few minor things that set it back. I have to say it does remind me a lot of what Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons does in terms of story, conveying most of it through the gameplay and what you see rather than dialog, but this game does have dialog occasionally so its a little more clear sometimes what is going on. Even then though this game isn't what it seems like at first, without ruining it you will find out what the real theme is about and the metaphor for the monster as you go through.
You play as a kid, Quinco who comes across at one point a big monster, who has an unhealthy appitite for poison arrow frogs and a very bad temper; he eventually becomes your companion on the story as well as your little robot protector Lula. You are following a strange girl who claims you are "cursed" and are on a journey to find out what is going on, and where you really are. Through out you need to platform and solve puzzles to progress through the areas of the game, many revolving around the monster himself. There are no real boss fights to speak of in the game.
The game has some pretty good looking visuals, nothing that is going to push your machine to its limits but its very nice and the world itself very interesting and somewhat surreal at times. The game also has some fantastic music in it to go along with the visuals and perfectly fits the tone of the game and what is going on.
The game controls fantastically with a controller and KB+M, however despite the game implying you to use a controller, I personally at least found it to play better and be more enjoyable with keyboard and mouse, so the port gets that right. In terms of perfromace there really isn't much to complain about, there are certain times where the frame rate will drop but quickly goes back.
The issues with the game unfortunatly come from the design itself: while it is part puzzle game, the puzzles themselves aren't very challenging and are very itterative and repetitve, on top of that the game is short, very very short. Four hours is the most you can expect out of it, that's on first playthrough, but given how linear it is on subsequent playthroughs and knowing what to do, you could get through it in under three potentially. There is little incentive to replay the game too, outside of 25 hats hidden around the game to find, of which unlocks upon beating the game the first time. Besides that there are no other kind of collectibles or distractions, the puzzles, gameplay and story are the only attraction here.
The story attempts to be emotional and moving, which it does pull off many times, but at the same time once you learn certain things it kind of falls apart and become predictable and that hold it has wears off, doesn't ruin the game though by any means.
Overall, its a short, very easy, but enjoyable adventure through an interesting world and is charming at the same time. Its definatly worth playing through at least once, maybe twice if you are interested in collecting all the hats and achivements, but I cannot say I would recommend it at full price, but consider that part at your own discretion. All that said I did enjoy this game and I do recommend checking it out. None of the minor issues I mentioned are enough I think to deter from this nice puzzle/platformer.

It says "Classic" in the title for a reason folks. 12 years ago, Pandemic Studios released one of the most exhilarating Star Wars experiences to date. There's nothing like booting up a round of Conquest, online or offline, and hearing the beautiful blend of blasterfire, battle chatter, and iconic musical pieces from the first 6 films. At its core, it can be validly argued that this game rips off Battlefield (the main mode being Conquest), but what makes it unique from Battlefield are the Jedi/Sith, capital ship combat in space, Galactic Conquest (a mode where you battle with the enemy across the galaxy for ultimate control), third-person mode, faction-specific classes, the immersion of the Star Wars universe, and above all, unbelievable modding support. Sure, the game IS 12 years old, but with graphics/model enhancement mods you can make it look so much better. Even though no mod will ever be able to come close to the immersive worlds that DICE and EA have built, this game blows both Battlefront (2015) and Battlefront II (2017) right out of the water in gameplay solely with its core gamemode, Conquest (one of my favorite gamemodes in any videogame). It's a lot more tactical, with every class not only playing a part in teamplay but in the world as well (Heavies can place mines, Engineers can repair, support classes can use Remote Droids for scouting). All vehicles spawn in the map by themselves, making them possible to be destroyed without an enemy inside them. Friendly fire is normally not an enormous nuisance and provides realism to the combat. And get this: it had Droidekas on launch. It had MagnaGuards on launch. It had numerous heroes and villans such as General Grievous and Obi-Wan Kenobi on launch. It had a complete, albeit unremarkable campaign on launch. And what some may consider to be a nail in the coffin: this game was released before TF2 introduced paid loot. That's right: ZERO MICROTRANSACTIONS. This gem is from a time when games were released in a complete state on launch, and if you're a Star Wars fan, this game is a must-buy for this and the other reasons listed above.

From the short time I've spent with Gloom, it seems to be somewhat ambitious. Some of its stylings may remind you of a blender mix of games like Bloodborne and Binding of Isaac but put through the lens of Limbo.
At its core it has some interesting stuff. To start with you got your attack, your roll, you have a gun that pulls from your bullet supply, and you also have a parry button that also pulls from your bullet supply but is very generous in its timing that grants you temporary invincibility. The parry mechanic definitely gives is a boost in terms of interest for me since it has a decent risk-reward mix. The game feels alright to play, it's a little floaty in parts. The hit sounds could use a little punch, but that might be due to the game's aesthetic and general mood.
The rogue-lite elements seem interesting enough, nothing to complicated. Lots of the random items make me think of Binding of Isaac in terms of how powerful some of them can be. The levels aren't terribly interesting, mostly hallways with a couple of shops dotted in there. It could definitely benefit from some hazards, light platforming (and to go with that, an aerial attack).
Although the way it is setup definitely feels like a gauntlet of rooms as opposed to a level to explore or something, to play devil's advocateon that point.
I find the visual style to be quite striking, and it makes the game's artist/s utilize unique silhouettes as opposed to some games relying on recolors. Attacks are always very visible, being a stark white, which is good for readability.
Overall, Gloom has a neat game at its core that could use a nice chunky update or two to make it a good one. I grabbed it for less than the crap I buy at a fast food joint, so I have no qualms when it comes to whether or not it's worth the money.

Faster-Than-Light is a space strategy game that epitomizes the feeling of "just one more turn..." With every jump you land in a randomly generated star system that, combined with a awesome soundtrack, makes you immediately want to replay after you finish. You have a limited amount of power that you must managed between several sub-systems, including weapons, shields and oxygen.
Your goal is to destroy the super-weapon in the other side of the galaxy. Upgrade your ship, buy new or more powerful weapons or even hire crew members to become as efficient as possible.
Simply because you were able to dock with a space station with no trouble before, doesn't mean that you'll be able to do it again. Sometimes you'll get fuel, sometimes you'll get a experimental weapon...others you'll get infected with a deadly virus that kills your crew, or attacked by crazed cannibals. Remember that every situation is random and different.

I've seen worse, but I'm glad I didn't pay for it (got it during free giveaway). At the very least, I can't recommend it at full price.
It feels like an arcade game. That part is mostly personal preference, I guess.
Tanks don't have crew modelled, and, while some modules can be damaged, it's mostly a matter of draining hitpoints. And it typically takes about half a dozen penetrations to kill a tank (less for heavy vs light tanks, but even then two hits). Infantry usually survives any but the biggest explosions. While this does help balance shells and grenades some, I'd rather they'd choose other ways to balance it.
AI is very poor, both of the units and AI-players.
Your infantry does not jump for cover if a grenade lands near them. They just keep doing whatever they were doing - and, if it's a satchel, they'll all die. Makes "mousing-skills" far too important. AT-guns, and MGs have limited arcs of fire, and need to rotate to change that arc. They do not do that automatically, which can really ruin your day if a tank is just outside of the fireing arc of your AT-gun, and proceeds to kill everything, simply because the gun didn't turn.
The AI-players don't seem to try to win. I was playing 2 vs 2 with 3 standard-difficulty AIs, and disabled one enemy's base, captured 90% of the territory - at that point, my ally simply stopped helping. The post-battle stats showed that it had maxed resources (flat line at the very top), but stopped producing units. Battle dragged out far longer than it should have because of that. I can see behaviour like that making sense on easy difficulty, but you should be able to lose on "normal".
There's some cases of lazy programming. Structures that can be built, but not repaired (e.g. sandbags, barbed wire), and units able to build stuff, but not repair it.
Some minor annoyances, like calling an anti-tank version of the Ju 87 a Stuka (Stuka means dive-bomber, and that anti-tank Ju 87 has only 3.7cm cannons as weapons, and is no stuka).
And then there's pay2play. You get only the russians and the germans with the base game - and only the eastern armies of germany. And even of those you don't get all the content. There are "commanders" you choose before the battle, and they have special abilities. These abilities range from a type of unit you can call, to passive abilities, to fire-support from planes and arti, to recon. As one example, it means that the base game doesn't include the "Tiger" tank for germany. Another example is that you cannot block tank movement - unless using AT-mines, but that won't stop allied tanks from destroying your sandbags.
Really, if it was full content with the base game, or at least the full content for the two armies provided, I probably wouldn't give it a thumbs-down. But I feel that hurts your options too much.
