Pros:
Track deformation is very cool, using the ruts really makes a difference.
Gameplay is very responsive.
Sounds are very good, the bikes sound great (Compared to other games)
Cons:
Track deformation does not work off the main tracks, and does not work on some jumps. (Ironically the part where the most deformation would occur).
The bike models need some work. The 125 two strokes have 250 expansion pipes on them, and the front sprockets on the ktm bikes are completely screwed up. They look like miniature sized rear sprockets.
The wheels on the bikes have a very poor spinning animation. They spin very slowly regardless of what speed you are going and makes it look like the bike is floating over the ground.
No roost. Not very satisfying.
The clutch does not work right. If you are in gear, rev the engine, and drop the clutch, the bike sputters and bogs down and just barely moves. This happens on all bikes, all the time, regardless of the terrain or anything else. However if you rev it in neutral and drop it into first without the clutch, that seems to work okay. I don't know how they thought this was okay. The clutch doesn't even really seem to serve a useful function.
The angle at which your rider turns the bars around tight corners is extremely sharp, and makes it look like the front wheel is skidding. If you turned the bars that sharp irl you would eat it.
The two stroke bikes have lower stats than the four stroke equivalents. This is completely unrealistic and probably my least favorite part about the game.
I will admit that in real life, a different brand of exhaust may have better performance than another. But in a game, it should not be like this. I would really like to put a FMF pipe on my  250 2t, but in order to get full performance you have to put a Scalvini on it. I don't really understand why they made it this way.
You cannot remap the r1 (or right bumper) button. It is forced as the button to activate "rewind", a feature which lets you pause and rewind the race if you crash or screw up. I immediately turned this off as soon as I saw it, only to find that even when its off it still does not let you use r1 for anything else, it just sits there a useless button, even though I would very much like it to be my rear brake...
The AI opponents are not very challenging. You can easily win pretty much every race on realistic difficulty and pro physics no problem.
Crashes are not realistic. You can land directly on someones head and they wont be phased, they'll just keep on riding. You can do a complete front flip after you case a jump, and somehow stay on the bike. In fact, most of the time you do stay on the bike.
Crowds on the side of the track and in the stands are the same generic models over and over. I thought we were past that kind of stuff? I mean Come on this is a current gen $50 PC title.
There are no free ride options. I refuse to acknowledge the compound because it is ONE level and you can ONLY freeride on it. You cannot do any actual races on it. You should have the option to freeride on any and every track/level in the game. Period.
There are very few tracks. For $50 it should come with a lot more. I understand DLC and am fine with it but you shouldnt run out of different stuff to race on in one day.
Despite all the negatives I am still having fun playing this game. I don't know how.

I followed the development of this game closely since its beginning. And it developed quite well in this time.
What is BlobCat?
BlobCat is mostly a puzzle game that sets you into the role of rescuing (dice)mice from the (blob)cats by laying out a path for the mice to reach their safe holes. As both animals are not very clever (they just run where their nose points) the player has to help by placing arrows or manipulating parts of the level to lead the mice to their safety. But beware the cats must not reach any of the safe holes first. Depending on how many arrows the player placed, they get a star rating showing how well their solution is.
What makes BlobCat special?
It's a passion project of a studio of two developers achieving high quality gameplay combined with nice graphics and a fine-tuned soundtrack. The rules are easy to learn and cleverly used to build up a enjoyable difficulty/learning curve. Every world adds something to the game to either help or obstruct the player. It even has an online and couch competetive mode (playable with mouse/keyboard/controller) where you will have to lead as many mice into your own mousehole while obstructing your competitors.
I definitely recommend buying this game as you will get several of these "just one more level" moments out of it and additionaly supporting a small new indie developer.

I'd challenge anyone who doesn't believe that video games can be art to play this game and still support that opinion.

I loved "Brothers: a tale of two sons" and Steam thought I'd also like "Papo y Yo" but I didn't.
***
They're similiar in that both games have beautiful (and I can't emphasise this enough) scenery, great music and an emotionally charged story that eventually ends in drama. They're also pretty liniar and the puzzles don't require a brain surgeon to solve them. So why didn't I like Papo y Yo as much? Probably because it kept giving me hints where I didn't really need them, prolonged gameplay by making me run all over the place way too many times, gave away the story with its achievement list and kept moving the camera angle right when it was vital for the character to go where I wanted it to. Also, I felt like it was trying too hard to be a tearjerker but it didn't really find a way to get me connected enough to the characters so that I'd empathise with them.
I feel like it'd be a shame to not recommend this game, but 11 € seems pretty steep to me; if childhood trauma based games with good music and pretty art are your thing, by all means get it, but wait for the sale.
EDIT: My second playthrough was better as I avoided all hint and training boxes and I spent considerably less time running away from Monster - knowing your surroundings does come with a tactical advantage.

Sonic Generations for PC is an OK port of an awesome game. It's very clear that it was designed for consoles (Omochao gives instructions like "use the left stick" even when you're using a keyboard), and there are a few bugs in the PC version.
For whatever reason, Sonic occasionally decides to somersault to the right over and over again, and sometimes runs forward infinitely without my input. While these bugs make it almost impossible to complete the game, they're thankfully quite rare. After purchasing a new 360-compatible controller, they went away entirely.
The game performs pretty well (~20 FPS on my old, cheap system, and a solid 60 FPS on my GTX 970), but I was annoyed by the fact that it doesn't support 5:4 monitors. I'm stuck with huge black bars on my 1280x1024 screen.
There are also quite a few third-party mods and level packs available for the game. The Unleashed Project, for example, is a total conversion of the game with the daytime (normal Sonic) levels from Sonic Unleashed.
If you can get this game on sale or as part of a bundle, I'd definitely recommend getting it.

I love love LOVE this game. I did not expect to get such a wild ride from Freedom Planet. The art design is fascinating, from the varied and unique level style/design, to the enemy design. A few odd and peculiar enemies here and there that may tilt your head, lift an eyebrow, but that doesn't matter because they are so damn cool with their unique design!
Let's talk about the music. Uhhuhhuuuh the music. It's like butter to my ears and it keeps me coming back just to listen to it. Truly a special soundtrack accompanied to this game by the folks at GalaxyTrail. Each track is very well written, comparable to music for classic 90s sidescrollers. Each levels theme is fitting and it simply makes half of the game; without it there's no way to fully enjoy Freedom Planet.
I have no major personal discrepancies with the game other than the screen crunch, which have me guessing my location, where enemies are off-screen, projectiles, or where to precision platform. It's just like the classics in that regard and I never cared for that aspect. However, warming up after my first playthrough gave me a lot better grasp on the concepts in the game. And even my first playthrough death count was enough to make me shudder.
There is definitely a difficulty in here that I'd highly recommend getting used to before judging completely. I didn't think I was going to fully get through the game at first because of my biased opinion with the difficulty. But it was very rewarding defeating a boss and going on to the next level, hearing that next level tune. Buttery. Even now after consecutive playthroughs, there's still a difficulty, but it's not a cheesy type difficulty. You can clear areas and bosses fairly once you've warmed up to them like previously stated and still have it feel rewarding. Would totes recommend this indie platformer.

Does have some ways to combine items to make things a bit more interesting, but the puzzles are not particularly difficult. For a kid, or someone who hasnt played adventure games before, this will be about the right level of difficulty.

Once you aclimate with the artstyle and pacing it's an alright game for fans of the show.

There's also some fighting which spices up the game but feels like a tac on.
Now to the puzzles. They are refreshingly moderate. Don't get me wrong. I like me a hard puzzle. But it's nice that there is one or another game where I didn't have to go look up a guide because I'm stuck for more than 15 minutes. This plays really fluently with the dificulty always staying at the same level and solutions to the puzzle are quite comprehensive. It also doesn't bombard you with a lot of hints.
Marcei DLC is definetly worth it. It extends the game for quite a bit and bring a quite suprising ammount of new locations.
Definetly recomended for fans of the show or people who would enjoy a more layed back, relaxed adventure/puzzle game.

Sim City 4 is still the Gold Standard city building simulation game, 12 years and counting.  This game still is at the top of the throne because of all the customization and modification you're able to make in this game.  With several websites solely dedicated to hosting SC4 mods, you are left with endless possibilities in how you want to design your region and cities.  The only misfortune this game suffers from is that is doesn't have the modern luxuries of new games(enhanced graphics, better hardware support, better core features to name a few), but the modification to this game helps alleviate most of this issues.
While my time on Sim City 4 is limited through Steam, I have certainly put in over 1500+ hours of game play throughout the years, and it remains one of my favorite games of all time(a game that I certainly keep coming back to over time).  If you're into city building games, this is a must for anyones gaming library.  Even after 12 years, every city building game that comes out has the same questions, which is, "Can this topple SC4 for best city build sim?".  Each game has failed to dethrone this champion(Cities:Skylines might be the best bet).  With all that said, if you haven't played this game, I highly urge you to make this an addition to your library, you will not be disappointed!

They say this (tied with SimCity 2000) is the best SimCity game ever made. And one can see why. SimCity 4 is filled with features and freedom that modern day renditions tend to lack. And despite being 10 years old, this is still THE game to play if you're looking for a SimCity experience.
And whilst yes, much of SimCity 4 has become outdated compared to recent City Builders; and it's somewhat behind in terms of the interface and streamlining of modern games; there are few games out today that offer the same feeling. The only game I can think of that comes close to this in terms of offering a balanced and enjoyable city building experience is Cities: Skylines, and that hasn't even been released yet.
So my verdict: A classic with gameplay that is still relevent. And whilst it's only mere days until the promising game Skylines comes out, meaning that anyone looking to play a game whilst waiting would already have taken their pick, SimCity 4 is one of those games with features that just don't get made the same anymore.

A more personal, subjective critique after having played a lot of the highway level (a game mode where you dodge cars on a 2D surface, that move from top to bottom), would be some of the following.
You earn coins by completing levels, and picking up coins that spawn randomly. When you fail a level, you lose a "life". You have to buy lifes for coins or you can't continue to play. How is this a good idea?
The cars seem to spawn completely pseudo-random. The extra coins spawn anywhere on the field, including the very top, where it's not worth risking to get hit by a car, and lose progress towards the 30 - 60 seconds timer. And if you don't pick it up, it will stay there forever instead of despawning, so a new one can spawn someplace else.
New game modes are locked behind a hefty amount of coins, that you already spend on more lifes, and maybe some of the power ups. Possibly locking the only game mode that some individuals might be interested in, in this mediocre game, which seems counter-intuitive.
The only "sound" in the game are (probably) stock music assets that mostly don't go well together with the gameplay. It's a lazily thrown together playlist. A better approach would've been to handpick music, that match the level/timer length, and go well with the kind of gameplay.

I haven't really written a review before but this game really pushes me towards writing one. The game itself evokes images of Lovecraftian proportions with its melancholic blacks and whites and oppressive overtone. The story to the world is provided piecemeal with each item you collect and record onto your Necronomicon and it truly helps add onto the mysteries of the Common Dream. The combat is methodical and tests your patience, albeit it is also clunky at first to get the hang of how the flow of combat is supposed to fit together. The soundtrack is gorgeous and the background set pieces are beautiful, which saddens me considering how little of the game is there. The game is particularly short when you've gotten the hang of the combat and the patterns of the enemies and bosses (or power through with a Gatling gun saved exclusively for all of the boss fights) but it really was an enjoyable experience. My recommendation is this: I bought the game at full price because I want to support the developers into either extending this game or making a new one with a similar aesthetic, but your miles may vary if you're not exactly devout to the whole 2D Bloodborne monochrome aesthetic. If you're interested, by all means, buy it now or buy it later, but I'd buy it all the same.

Missing Translation is actually made up of two games: one is extremely casual and the other is equally as ambitious. The casual surface game is made up of three puzzle types that are repeated twenty-five times each, increasing in difficulty until the set is finished. The puzzles are of the zen brainteaser variety and the soundtrack is pleasantly simple. This is where you'll get more than half of the achievements too. It would be fine if this was all Missing Translation had to offer - unoriginal and uninspired - but fine.
The remaining two achievements hint at the ambitious hidden game within Missing Translation and are just as easy as the rest of them. The first achievement requires you learn how to use the speech tool which wasn't used in any of those seventy-five puzzles or to finish the game. The second asks that you use that speech tool along with a small bit of language that was given to you in order to solve a pretty standard puzzle. Once you've asked yourself what would happen if you used this new ability on those creatures you've seen around, you've started to uncover what this game seems to have been made for.
I can't guess if this game is going to excite, calm, bore, intrigue, or just frustrate you. I'm not even sure how I feel about it. But it's free and it didn't even take me two full hours to get all of its achievements. So really, what do you have to lose by finding out for yourself?

Pros:

(+9)

I honestly struggle to come up with many bad things to say about this game, but I do have some nitpicks.
-Not a very long soundtrack, and it does get grating after a long time. (-2)
-Gameplay gets repetitive after a while. Different ships force you into playstyles you may not enjoy or do well with to spice it up. It works for a lot of people, but not so much for me. (-3)
-Modding support is unofficial, and managing mod setups across systems is a hassle. (-3)
-Doesn't play nice with the following: 4:3 screens, low-resolution screens, high-resolution screens, controllers.
4:3 screens, your options are to stretch the game super tall (terrible) and have massive borders on the top and bottom (meh).
low-res screens, the game doesn't work at all. It runs at 720x1280 and cannot be changed, so anything below 720x1280 won't work at all.
High-resolution screens, the game still runs at 720x1280 no matter what. Hope you don't mind blurring.
Controllers are nada. Keyboard and mouse are it. Fine by me, but this could irk some. (-15)
-Not THAT many different random events, and you start to see a LOT of repeats after 5-6 runs. (-6)
Verdict:
As long as your system falls within the relatively wide band of compatible systems, you'll be fine. Super high-end rigs with 4k monitors as well as systems with low-res screens will struggle on this game. The developers have made it clear this isn't something they'll be fixing.
Compatibility issues aside, wonderful game with a wonderful sound track. Highly recommend.

Let's talk a minute about the executive producer of this game Jun Takeuchi. Jun worked on RE1, RE2 and RE5.
"Following the release of Resident Evil 6, producer Masachika Kawata noted, Capcom had a lot of internal discussion regarding the direction of the next installment. Capcom staffers recognized that the scale of the last game, which had bioterrorism attacks happening across the world, had grown out of hand and as a result what made the series special had been lost. To regain that, Kawata's boss, Jun Takeuchi, who is the executive producer of the game, requested that the series be "stripped down to its core": horror. The developers figured scaling back the game to one location and using a first-person perspective to immerse the players in the environments, would be the best way to achieve that."
I highly recommend this demo. As a 32 year old gamer I can tell you, my gamer gut says this final game is going to be one hell of a scary ride.

I have mixed feelings about Papo & Yo.
On the other hand I want to love the game for it's unique feel, but on the other I feel it is lacking on many fronts.
At it's best Papo & Yo offers beautiful artwork and sceneries, entertainment and a fun challenge. At it's worst, it is very repetitive, frustrating and even boring. It also hosts a selection of glitches, that aren't that big of a deal, but do leave an unpolished impression.
The story had me intrigued at first, but lost me after a while because of it's slow progress. Also, it's really not well carried out tbh. I did however finish the game for I wanted to get to the predictable end. Seeing the credits scroll down on the screen didn't offer the satisfaction I thought it would, other than finally getting the game off my to-do list. It was a bit like finishing a mediocre book.
Still, I won't advice to steer clear of the game. If you have the patience and are willing to forgive some annoyances (many that are due to budget) Papo & Yo delivers a different kind of gameplay experience that other game makers should learn from and improve on. It is good to see that more and more people like Vander Caballero (the creative director, who the story is based on) take the effort to get off their high horses at big game studios to go and discover their own path.

I'll say 8/10. If you are interested in this sort of game, you should play it. It is good, but it is not a great 9 or 10 game.
It is a puzzle game, figuring out how to get from here to there, moving platforms, jumping, etc. The puzzles were varied and unique, and I was sometimes challenged, but never frustrated.
The plot is that you are a boy, running through a magical version of Brazil (maybe, I wasn't sure). You spend most of the game in a poorer section of the city, but you can pull levers to make buildings move. You have a beloved robot companion, a monster that follows you around, and a mysterious girl.
But all of this is a dream, because in the real world your father is an abusive alcoholic. Monster, is of course, your father. Normally, Monster is Ok. You can use him to jump to higher ledges, or activate switches. He walks arounds, and sleeps a lot. But when Monster eats a frog he becomes a flaming demon of pain.
This game did a great job of controlling my emotions. In the beginning, Monster isn't so bad. Maybe even helpful. But as the game progressed, I found myself hating Monster. Really hating him. And hating frogs. I would smash every frog I saw, and I have never wanted to murder (no defeat, not slay -- murder) a monster more.
If you want to experience the thrill of Brazilian favelas in the timespan between the 2014 world cup and the 2016 summer olympics, Papo and Yo is your game.

Presentation: A
This game’s graphics are very pleasing on the eye, and do an excellent job expressing each level’s atmosphere. The amount of detail put in the graphics is incredible, it’s a lot like Sonic CD. The game also runs at 60fps, and hardly ever drops. However, Freedom Planet has this thing where the character’s sprite itself will tilt if they are on a slope, rather than having a different animation, like Sonic does. Most of the time it’s fine, but if there’s a very tight slope into a pit, and the character is on that slope, it kind of looks odd.
Music: B+
Freedom Planet has a very memorable soundtrack, all the sounds do a great job at expressing the type of situation you’re in. However, at first I didn’t really find them too memorable (maybe because of the sounds being much louder), it took me my second playthrough to really enjoy them. Definitely a soundtrack worth buying, but it really didn’t catch my ear the first time through.
Story: B-
Contrary to a lot of people’s opinions, I enjoyed Freedom Planet’s story quite a bit. I liked the voice acting a lot, and it has good character development. However, the first time you play the game (especially as Lilac), you’re going to be a bit confused.
I LOVE how the story transitions into each level logically. This is usually a given for most platformer games, but Freedom Planet does this very well (unless you’re playing Classic mode, even then it ties the levels together sometimes). The game explains the crisis beforehand, and then making a level about the crisis in most of the later levels. This helps set up the already amazing atmosphere the presentation provides.
Level Design: A
The level design is what impresses me most about this game. It’s very well thoughtout, especially for a Sonic-type game, where a lot of the time it will cheap you out. All the levels are a BLAST to play through, because it can either be very speed orientated, or you might wanna explore the levels; they are pretty expansive. The classic Sonic games do this pretty well, but I feel like this game just does them even better. The fact that enemies won’t hurt you if they aren’t attacking compliments the lack of cheap enemy placement. The best part of it is that it’s still get’s pretty dang difficult near the end; but it’s a good difficulty.
Of course, this all applies to MOST of the game. Sometimes the game will throw a sucker punch, but the high amounts of health your character has makes the situation a whole lot less worse.
Another thing the game sort of has troubles with is making the bosses fit with the levels difficulty. In most of the early levels, I would hardly die in the actual level, but it would usually take me a bunch of tries to fight the boss. It’s usually a tradition to make the boss harder than the level, so that it’s more of an actual ending, but I feel like they went a bit overboard.
Gameplay: A
Another impressive part of the game, this game is EXTREMELY fun. The fast-paced gameplay is fun enough, but finding alternate pathways using the unique course elements found in the levels just makes it all the sweeter. The fact that it runs on 60fps makes the experience feel very clean from start to finish. The gameplay is extremely solid, being almost entirely bug-free. The most bugs I found was with Milla, and those bugs generally involve the Phantom Block move (for example, you can see Milla holding nothing if you go into the water while holding a cube, works best at Jade Creek). Despite those small bugs, I didn’t run into any game-breaking glitches, so that’s good. One thing that this game nails is the combat system. I’m VERY impressed by it. Unlike a lot of Sonic games, the combat is very fast-paced, it requires you to be on your toes. Beating up the enemies and bosses with the vast variety of moves your character has makes you feel really awesome.
Length: A-
On your first run on normal mode, it will probably take about four hours to beat. However, with the other three (soon to be five) characters, it adds up to a hefty twelve hours of gameplay. Because of the characters, the game also has great replay value. All the characters are unique, and barely share any differences with each other. Carol’s gameplay is all about close-combat, having a powerful aerial attack IF you pounce beforehand, a flurry of kicks that makes her invincible while she’s using it, and can easily retreat from a boss with the previously mentioned pounce. Lilac’s more about precition. She has this Dragon Boost attack that can be angled either up, or down, so sometimes you have to angle it in the correct angle, while being at the best position. You can mix up the opponent with Lilac’s extra options for melee attacks, depending if the player is holding upward, forward, or downward. It’s a lot like Super Smash Bros. Milla is more of a defensive character. Although she has a devastating attack with the block combined with the shield, it takes a while for the block to charge, and the beam is easy to whiff if you’re trying to speed run the level. The main use of her shield is to reflect projectiles that enemies shoot. She also has a projectile herself, unlike the other two characters. Milla has a flutter jump that covers a lot of vertical distance, but she also has much less health than the other two, making the already difficult boss fights even more difficult. Some of the characters even go to different stages that compliment their play-style, adding to the variety of each playthrough. Once Torque and Spade are added, the amount of content in this game will grow significantly.
Total: A
Freedom Planet is an amazing experience. Although there are some flaws in the story and some gameplay elements, the game plays much like a Sonic game, but it does have a lot of things that give it’s identity. People who say “oh, that game is just a classic Sonic rip-off” haven’t actually taken the time to experience the full game. This hidden gem is definitely worth it’s cost, so if you like platformers, do yourself a favor and buy this game.

A lone federation ship must pass through a gauntlet of hostile alien space systems in the brutally difficult roguelike sci-fi adventure FTL. Just like its namesake, you must navigate each system by making faster-than-light jumps between locations and discovering new worlds and challenges all while fleeing a rapidly advancing rebel fleet while carrying the secret of how to defeat its most fearsome weapon: the rebel flagship.
Gameplay in FTL is simple and straightforward. You can move crew from room to room in your ship, leaving them at stations like pilot, engine, and shields to boost the efficiency of those systems. Attacks are all performed by clicking weapons and then clicking on the enemy ship on the right side of the screen. Power management is also a big part of the game with reactor energy being scarce at times and requiring you to juggle allocation to specific systems when needed. Occasionally enemies will also teleport into your ship (something you can also do) and you will have to move crew around to fight or flee.
This game is both really forgiving and also really unforgiving as far as roguelikes go. For example, if the rebel fleet does actually catch up to you, you have a chance to escape and it’s not an immediate game over. Having specific species of crew or ship systems will often give you blue dialogue options which are guaranteed to be successful. On the other hand, the RNG can be downright brutal and some runs will be doomed to failure if you cannot accrue the necessary weapons and systems to face the final boss. Certain ship configurations, such as the stealth ship, are especially vulnerable to bad RNG and will require many a restart before you finally get the right mix.
Despite its crazy high difficulty, FTL is really fun and you’ll likely find yourself spending hours and hours trying to win without even realizing it until you check your clock and notice you’ve spent half a day flying around in space.

Pros
+ Satisfying, slick combat
+ Combat is telegraphed but not too easy
+ Stat progression within a run is not too hard or too easy
+ A good run or two rewards you by letting you start a few future runs with a few random items, meaning some incentive to play well instead of just fishing for a good starting item room
+ Bosses are also learnable and not just mad HP sponges
+ Dat graphical style. This is not just pixels because that's trendy, or minimal because that's easy. The artwork is well-crafted, clear, and gorgeous.
Variable
* Little to no persistent unlocks - less roguelite grinding
* Level structure is linear progression through rooms of randomly chosen enemies from the level's pool. No "Bad map layouts"
* No traps, just enemies.
Cons
- Limited number of enemies. While this means there's less "Oh god how do I fight X enemy type", there are still few enemy types. Get good at fighting them, instead of just getting OP.
- Stat progression within a run can be RNG dependent

This game is great but it's controls aren't tight enough. As it stands taking actions quickly in succession feel delayed and clunky. For example, it's difficult to time the controls to properly attack after jumping. There needs to be attack cancelling and visa versa, things that make games like Tower Fall Ascension such a great 2D brawler, that actions are responsive and feel "right". Also hitboxes are wonky IMO.
In short, some of the games extreme difficulty is derived not from lack of skill, but from less than ideal implementation/mechanics.
Problems that need to be fixed for this to get a +1:
* Clunky controls
* Jump or attack cancelling
* Fire hitbox is huge, meaning you get burned without really being in the fire
* Enemy hitboxes are huge, making jumping over them sometimes too difficult if not timed perfectly
Otherwise the game is fun, the enemies are interesting and surmountable, the items are not insanely overpowered or underpowered, and the blending of popular rogue-like themes is a success! Needs to be tightened up though before it's anything more than a frustrating missed opportunity.

Castle story is a fantastic Alpha release game, still under progress but great for those who want to build their own castles while balancing resources and construction skills.
The thing to remember is this is an early release game with plenty more in the pipe line to build on!

Show of hands…how many of you used to build castles as a kid using Legos or the equivalent? Okay, how many of you used to pretend that your little Lego men would have to defend said castle from G.I. Joe, The Ghostbusters, or whatever action figures you happened to have out at the time?  If you did in fact raise your hand, then you may enjoy “Castle Story”.  In a nutshell, it’s a voxel-based strategy game that tasks you with building a castle for your army of bricktrons.

At present, the game features two modes: survival and sandbox.  While there is multiplayer, reports indicate that it is extremely buggy and unreliable.  The world editor, a selection on the main menu, is grayed out altogether.  Still, it’s exciting to see that these are planned features as I’m sure there are a lot of folks out there who’d love the chance to team up against the onslaught.  Speaking of which, survival mode doesn’t hold back any punches.  It’ll throw you onto a map with nothing but a few bricktrons, complete with a ticking clock that’ll spawn waves of enemies when it expires.  It’s a scramble from the very beginning to collect resources (stone, wood, and crystals) in order to construct some type of structure.  Sandbox is a bit more tame, doing away with bad guys altogether and allowing you time to practice moving around the interface.

The game is still very early Alpha, meaning that it is far from done…at present, there’s not even a tutorial in which to get your feet wet.  Still, there’s enough going on to at least get a feel of what you’ll be doing, if you decide to buy into the Alpha via Steam’s Early Access.  I’ll be honest…there is a bit of a learning curve.  With the tutorial being out of the picture (as of 1/15/14), I found myself scratching my head often. If you’re someone who isn’t easily frustrated and are used to the bugs and gameplay changes that come with Alphas and Betas however, you may find the experience to be a positive one.  As for me, I’m enjoying what I’m seeing thus far and see a lot of potential here.  Once the bugs are shored up and the tutorial in place, this could end up being an extremely fun and addicting game.  Time, of course, will tell.

A lone federation ship must pass through a gauntlet of hostile alien space systems in the brutally difficult roguelike sci-fi adventure FTL. Just like its namesake, you must navigate each system by making faster-than-light jumps between locations and discovering new worlds and challenges all while fleeing a rapidly advancing rebel fleet while carrying the secret of how to defeat its most fearsome weapon: the rebel flagship.
Gameplay in FTL is simple and straightforward. You can move crew from room to room in your ship, leaving them at stations like pilot, engine, and shields to boost the efficiency of those systems. Attacks are all performed by clicking weapons and then clicking on the enemy ship on the right side of the screen. Power management is also a big part of the game with reactor energy being scarce at times and requiring you to juggle allocation to specific systems when needed. Occasionally enemies will also teleport into your ship (something you can also do) and you will have to move crew around to fight or flee.
This game is both really forgiving and also really unforgiving as far as roguelikes go. For example, if the rebel fleet does actually catch up to you, you have a chance to escape and it’s not an immediate game over. Having specific species of crew or ship systems will often give you blue dialogue options which are guaranteed to be successful. On the other hand, the RNG can be downright brutal and some runs will be doomed to failure if you cannot accrue the necessary weapons and systems to face the final boss. Certain ship configurations, such as the stealth ship, are especially vulnerable to bad RNG and will require many a restart before you finally get the right mix.
Despite its crazy high difficulty, FTL is really fun and you’ll likely find yourself spending hours and hours trying to win without even realizing it until you check your clock and notice you’ve spent half a day flying around in space.

I did not want to like Freedom Planet. The trailer couldn't focus on a single part of gameplay for very long, and it just had the main characters parroting lines that vaguely explain the plot but have little context cohesion. Then again, what's there to explain as far as context goes? BIG EVIL GREEN GUY is destroying PLANET CHINA. You must destroy
the space invaders before they destroy you!
Without spoiling anything important, I'll just say that I enjoyed every bit of the story. Yes, parts of it were campy and it had a few plot-holes that probably aren't going to be filled for a while, and some of the jokes feel a bit forced when short-rich-kid is onscreen, but that can all be forgiven. Most of it's clean, and it's a light-hearted adventure where you get to be Hero-Pants (not her real name), a badass dragon-girl with hair-tentacles that can do the shoryuken! She's joined by a kung-fu catgirl on a motorcycle (her best friend), a not-evil space invader (who has a grudge against the main villain), and some orphan girl (plot significance unknown for the time being but she does some cool things in the background) on a quest to prevent the theft of a sacred artifact that provides power to the three neighboring countries involved in the story.
No, they never mentioned "The Three Kingdoms" in "Planet China." The writers are more subtle than I am.
In fact, the writing is really good. The villain is competent, correctly identifies the main threats to his plans, and doesn't sit on his rear-end waiting for Hero Pants to come destroy everything. He actively sets effective traps, ambushes, and even gets down to business personally when his subordinates start having trouble with certain player-controlled obstacles. He even gets a torture scene despite this being an E-rated game, complete with interrogation. The writers didn't pull any punches here: a competent villain is a villain players take seriously.
Hero-Pants herself, by comparison, is a pretty flat character. She's the hero, she kicks butt, she keeps a cool head in risky situations, and is the first to jump head-first into any situation where a hero is needed. In short, she's what she needs to be as a character, but she's also a cool big sister to the orphan girl she adopts. Hero-Pants also distinguishes herself by existing in a story where nobody ever criticizes or mocks her for being female, and the game itself never forces her into an awkward, forced romance sub-plot. She may not have much that makes her "special," but she's a great protagonist and the writers are awesome for their work on her.
Even in gameplay, the three playable characters have different movesets and playstyles. Hero-Pants is the overall "best at everything" character, Carol is strong but requires a little more skill to use in melee and has to climb walls like Rockman X instead of just floating or dash-attacking upward, and Milla has less health but makes up for it with ranged attacks and a shield.
The levels are fairly typical for the style of game: you have a jungle level, a sewer level, aquatic ruins, a spaceship, an ancient temple, a couple of snow levels, and the rest of the usual goodies. That said, there are only two levels with "pitfall deaths" and it's completely logical to have them in those levels because you're either on dogfighting airships or on a spaceship where the airlocks have been opened. There are a couple of moments where the design could use a little polish, but overall it shouldn't be too difficult to get through the levels.
The bosses can be a different story, though. After a few levels they start to reach Rockman / Gunstar Heroes difficulty, which is *extremely welcome* in a platforming game. Part of me hates to admit it, but I actually had to turn the difficulty down to 'Easy' in order to beat the final two levels, and I *still* had a lot of trouble against the final boss in his "I don't need my giant mech, I'll just take care of you in melee" form. Again, loving that the game doesn't hold the players' hand or pull its punches in the boss fights. It just makes the victory that much more satisfying, just like how classic gaming was.
I think my favorite moment in the game is the boss fight where the four primary heroes team up to battle a giant battlemech while racing through the streets. There's another team-up boss fight in the game, but this one comes out of nowhere and it's
Just try not to get too caught up in why the citizens of Planet China use medieval weaponry and armor while having access to telephones, television, cyborgs and "databases" detailing the lives of the planet's inhabitans.

I really recommand this game. It is like a fusion of Sonic3&K and Dust an Elysian Tail (another very good indie game).
The game is beautiful and makes the best out of the 32 bits pixel art. The voices are properly dubbed, which adds a nice touch to the experience. This is especially true considering that the story mode has a whole plot that is fully animated and that doesn't skip important parts. The team really worked a lot on this project and the finish touch is there.
About the gameplay, it's a good old sonic-like game with lot of mechanics. In fact, the feeling is so similar to sonic that I was at the beginning frustrated to no be able to run as fast as in a sonic game. And the loss of speed right after a jumper is also somewhat annoying. But it's a small matter compared to all the moves you can do. And since you have 3 playable characters, you can replay the game 3 times with a different style of gameplay (but it's not *that* different).
The musics are quite good too. Not epic but definitely adequate to the sonic 2d era and pleasant to hear. Too bad I couldn't change the volume of the sounds.
About longevity, you'll have a whole day to play for your first run (progression is saved and you can continue from last savepoint). For such kind of game where you run at full speed through the levels, that's really a lot. And the best is that's not repetitive. There are really a lot of various contents. And concerning the difficulty, I find it well balanced and progressing nicely with the player. Bosses are maybe a bit too challenging, especially the last ones, but the infinite continues makes sure that you'll eventually beat the game. Once you finished the game with lilac, you can replay it with two other characters and with new powers, which is appreciable. A timer and a classic mode (no story) is also there for those who want to speedrun the game, which is nice too.
If you miss the old sonic games from genesis megadrive, or if you liked Dust, you really should play this game. It regularly in sales, but I feel it is worth the whole price too. Definitely recommanded.

First off let me mention I came into this game after debating on buying it but the trailer won me over. I thought it would be nothing more than a fan-made Sonic clone, but it's much more than that. I can't, and shouldn't, call this game a Sonic clone. To be honest, it revolutionizes the 2D Sonic-esque style of games.
GAMEPLAY:
While the gameplay is heavily inspired by Sonic games, the game makes dramtic improvements to Sonic Team/SEGA's 2D level design. No longer is the game "Hold Right to Win" and is more opportunity based. You have less branching paths as 2D sonic games, but the various oppotunities to do option A over option B becomes evident after the second level.
CONTROLS:
This is hands down the tighest game I've played all year. The controls are extremely responsive, whether you play on a controller or a keyboard. There's so many movement options in this game, and it just feels great to play.
VISUALS:
The 16-bit visuals are great here, and I'm extremely impressed by all the animation the artists pushed into the game. There's a couple of interlacing issues/tearing, but it's nothing to big.
SOUND:
I could go on forever about how great this game's soundtrack is. It rivals a lot of studio titles today. Moreso than the soundtrack though, I love the sound effects. The sound effects here make the game for me. Hitting enemies feels GOOD. Really, really good infact!
FINAL THOUGHTS:
This game is easily my indie game of the year. I love the level design, how the team improved upon  their inspiration (2D Sonic Platformers), and just how good it feels to play the game. This game has a lot of key aspects covered, and you'll love it if you pick it up. I won't say this game isn't without flaws, though. Hitbox detection is one of the game's worst offenders, both for enemies and the main characters. There's a few enemies that are poorly designed as well, and blend in to backdrops and levels. Voice acting is a nice bonus, but a lot of the dialog between characters have conflicting volume levels and displacement. Listening to the dialog is a nice bonus, but it's unessecary.
All in all, if you love any kind of 16-bit Genesis-style game, any kind of 2D platformer, any Sonic game in existance, or just love indie games - pick this game up. I'll blow your expectations out of the water.

This is a combat focused game with minor rogue lite elements.  The combat itself is tough but fair, and it actually becomes quite easy when you know the enemy patterns and have a good build.  This provides the player with a nice feeling of earned mastery - which is great because this game really is just about the combat.  There is no real exploration beyond just moving straight ahead in the dungeon, and upon every victory or defeat the player will begin in the exact same position upon restarting (with the exception of accruing tokens which can be spent to generate random items).
For what the game attempts to be, I think it succeeds admirably.  My only complaint is that the game is short:  I collected all items and beat the true boss of the game in about 6 hours.  For experienced players, each run will take only about 13 minutes or less.
Still, it's an enjoyable experience, and I plan to keep playing until I get the last few achievements.

Gloom is a challenging and atmospheric game that is packed with more lore than you might give it credit for at first glance. This game kind of a cross between Bloodborne and Binding of Isaac. DISCLAIMER: I've made all the music in Gloom, so I may be a little biased. I will try to write an objective review of the game regardless - take it as you will.
I've taken part in beta testing Gloom and I've put roughly 20+ hours in it (in addition to hours played in steam). I've played the game with both, controller and keyboard and controller is absolutely the way to go.
When it comes to game mechanics, it is mainly about stamina management and learning the attack patterns. The amount of different items and weapons is quite big which makes every single run different. I've also noticed that at the start I favoured certain items over everything else and I almost never used guns. However the more I played the more I started to value guns and other items I didn't use before so I would say that they all are pretty balanced. But still, there are some weapons which seems to be worse than others.
The game is very difficult at the start and it took me hours to get in to it. So if you still find yourself struggling through the first level after hours of gameplay, you're not bad, it's just... difficult. I haven't played this kind of games ever before, so it could be one of the reasons too though. After you start to learn the game, it gets easier and the first level starts to feel pretty much like a runover. For me this happened after I stopped being greedy and when I began paying more attention to the stamina bar...
The monsters and bosses are quite well made in my opinion. All of them are unique and have different attack patterns. The satisfaction after killing a certain boss after dying to it like 10 times is guaranteed. Some of the monsters do have similar attacks though but I don't know if it's good or a bad thing. It makes it easier to react to attacks, but at the same time it takes away the "unique monster" feeling. The projectiles or the attack animations are different though, so it doesn't bother me.
I like the gloomy artstyle but I would've loved some little color details mixed with that. The blood-particles could be red or there could be some kind of bright colored effects, like colored particles going around the weapon when it's upgraded. Also I would've liked if the weapons looked just like they look in the Necronomicon. There could be more different sound effects too.
About the lore.. well, I can't say much. I'm not one of those type of gamers that are interested in the game lore in any way. However there is a lore which is told by the item descriptions and other dreamers at the hub. If you are that kind of a gamer who likes to find out why everything happened and generally like to solve mysteries and all that kind of stuff, there sure are a lot of lore for you to go through. I know that the dev put a lot of effort into the story, so I hope that someone enjoys it.
To sum up the pros and cons of the game:
+ Big variety of items and weapons
+ Enough randomness and different in-game scenarios to keep the game interesting
+ Very simple and comfortable combat mechanics to use (parry, roll, jump, weapons and guns)
+ Good game structure to make it viable for speedruns
+ Token-system to give player some advantage at the start
- Weapons could be more detailed and there could be some LITTLE color details
- There could be more visual effects and sound effects
In conclusion, if you are looking for a challenge and have the nerve to keep trying despite of failing, this is a game for you. If you don't like games where saving is not an option, this isn't a game for you.

An indie game that promises a crisp and punishing rogue-like(-like) playstyle and delivers in spades!
Gloom is hard done right! The enemies, happy to group up and give you hell, have telegraphs and modest movesets, which has let me (in the 3-4 hours I've been playing) feel real progression: I now know how far the doggies jump, which enemies don't get stunlocked by my hits, when a parry will fit better than a dodge... etc
I think my favourite part about this game is how rich and diverse each life can be. Every weapon (and their upgrades) not only scales differently and has different stamina costs, but has different ranges, attack patterns, and swing delays.
Add to the weapon pool all of the items you can come across, and you can really have back to back runs that feel nothing alike!
Rogue-likes live and die based on their replayability, and I can see Gloom staying fresh and fun for a long time to come.

Due to circumstances of a misunderstanding on my part that led to a very vitriolic video I have agreed to re-review the game. I will be leaving the original review below, but here is my current opinion of the game:
As far as Rogue-Lites goes Gloom does a fantastic job of being tough but fair with it's difficulty and it's controls (with rebindable keys) being very intuitive and easy to pick up.
However, the controls themselves are a bit sluggish and I am not a fan of the graphical aesthetic at all. Throw in permadeath, a game mechanic that I do not enjoy whatsoever, and I found this game to be frustrating and not very enjoyable.... and yet from an objective standpoint I can still agree that Gloom IS a good game.
For what it is attempting to accomplish it does so very well and for fans of the genre, this will be a very enjoyable game. Unfortunately I will not be one of those that will enjoy it.
********************
Original Review:
Gloom drew me in by a fairly well done trailer. Unfortunately the realities of the game did not live up to expectation. The core mechanics are solid, but the lack of mouse support for even the options menu made the game a chore to deal with even in that regard. Also the keymapping, while reasonably standard for this genre of title, lacked rebindable keys and the controller support was laughable. Forcing you to use the D-Pad instead of the better positioned and more familiar thumbstick. Also, this game had no persistent levelling that I was able to determine during my First Impressions Review.
The controls are clunky and I value my time more than to play a perma-death game with no persistence. While fans of that style of game might possibly enjoy this, I felt I could not in good conscience give it my recommendation.

Pros:
- Clocked the main campaign at 9 hours (5 Episodes) and the DLC chapter at 1 hour and 45 minutes. Totaling 10 hours and 45 minutes.
- Had fun interacting with the characters of the show.
- Overall liked the visuals of the game (But it has its issues).
- Lots of puzzles (If you're into that sort of thing).
- Stellar voice acting by the main cast.
- Funny and witty dialogue for the most part.
- Chance to explore a bunch of different locations from the show and interact with its inhabitants.
- An abundance of in jokes, references and easter eggs that fans of the show will appreciate.
- Cool to see a fanmade character appear (Sunny).
- Lots of interactables.
Cons:
- Game can get really slow at times to the point of it getting boring (Especially Chapter 3).
- Some characters aren't voiced by their original voice actors.
- Visuals sometimes look like someone tried to mix multiple different artstyles (Cartoony, photorealism) but it doesn't mesh well.
- LSP is incredibly annoying in this and is far more antagonistic than she is on the show.
- You'll end up visiting certain locations multiple times which gets stale at times. The Marceline DLC fixes this issue though.
- Some jokes and dialogue is very hit or miss.
- No replayability.
- Combat isn't very good and just ruins the pacing.
- Sometimes character dialogue is skipped at the last second.
- Dialogue should have been made skippable as checkpoints can be sparse at times.
Overall:
- This is something only fans of the show can enjoy, so if you're not a fan do not even think about getting it.
- I enjoyed the game. It was fun playing as and interacting with characters from the show. It was also cool to visit locations and get the chance to walk around and explore the areas. The amount of hours I got out of the game is worth the price. But if you want to play it safe, get it if it ever goes on sale.

About time I reviewed this game. I mean, I'm doing it for the Steam Awards badge, yet I've felt that *itch* of reviewing this game since I finished it two years ago. I'm going to keep it short while trying to describe what this game does best.
**THIS REVIEW IS SPOILER HEAVY**
This game perfectly captures the sheer randomness of life and the psychological problems that that randomness carries with it. It also depicts two very common (arguably the only ones) ways of facing problems and coping with new, unexpected situations be it by taking it all way too seriously (in a fatalistic/pessimistic way) or by taking it as lightly as necessary to laugh at the situation you're presented with (even though it sometimes greatly affects other characters), and how solving these problems will most of the time affect others around you, sometimes making you lose them, turning them against yourself or reinforcing your relationship with them. In this sense (and god forgive me for saying this even though I'm not a religious man) the game deals with relationships WAY better than some other hundreds-of-hours AAA RPG's. It's not just your "This guy now hates you" or "Frank will remember that" way of dealing with relationships; It's way deeper in that even commodities like sleeping or going to a specific place can make you lose any of your partners FOREVER.
Now, about Brad as a character and pretty much centerpiece of the "main" saga (though most people will argue that Lisa is the main character) without counting any fan-games around it: It's a character that is written as a human being. It's one of the most organic characters I've had the pleasure to play as since I started playing videogames. He deals with the scars Lisa's troubled life and his childhood have left on him in the most realistic way. You have a character that not only wants to make up for his father's mistakes (that ultimately led to Lisa's traumatic death), you also have an egocentric character that only cares about his own past and wants to control Buddy's life in the process. Yet the only things he wants (and was completely denied of in his childhood) are love, to belong somewhere and have a family (even if it was presented to him in the weirdest of ways). He tries to achieve this by being overprotective with Buddy, while Buddy herself tells him she never asked for that. And there it is again, randomness. The randomness of being born to a context you never wished for and being taken care of by people you never wanted to meet or didn't want to damage in any way. That's the topic that LISA takes on quite bravely and excels at it.
Nothing to say about the combat system, just that it's quite easy (I haven't tried playing without using joy though) and quite traditional too, kind of like Earthbound's, with the exception of certain moves which require key combos.
You seriously have to play this game. You're missing out.

This is the pinnacle of gaming. I am not kidding. When people say gaming, words associated are 'fun' and a form of entertainment. Most people (keep in mind if you are on this site then you probably taking gaming fairly seriously in terms of everyone else.) think gaming is a time-waster or a 'turn-your-mind-off' source of entertainment, like a Michael Bay movie.
This game will change your mind, I promise.
Now I see games up there with books and movies, sure you can turn your mind off for mindless fun OR you can pursue a moving, emotional and intense story, on par with any movie or book you've read. It's amazing, it's painful, it's tear inducing, it's LISA.
This game isn't for everyone. Firstly, you will want to play (ITS FREE DONT WORRY) Lisa: The First, you can find it on RPG
. Secondly, if you are sensitive, especially around themes of abuse (any form just to be safe) don't play this game. It will only hurt. And thirdly, is my own bias. The developer was inspired to create LISA based off his ex-girlfriend. As someone who can relate and emphaise with many themes in this game, either personally, or through people I care deeply for, this game does, quite literally, affect me in many aspects.
The price of LISA is normally 7 UK dollars (pounds) and the 'special edition' which comes with the DLC, soundtrack and art for an extra 6 quid, is worth it, the dlc is an extra 3/4 hours, over 80+ songs (most of which are amazing) and amusing (whilst not um.. 'beautiful') artwork, but it is up to you.
With the pretention is out the way, let me introduce you to this idea of integration of story and gameplay. Say something happens to a character in cut-scene, apart from a few lines of dialogue, what changes? Usually nothing. Now imagine if the gameplay of the game changed accordingly. Losing an arm? Lose an input for attacks, lose people important to your 'meta' party through rng, you can't roll back, your forced to continue, linking back into the story! The game designer is a  genius, especially when the player has to make choices, effecting both the story and gameplay.
Gameplay is fairly standard turn based combat, but simplified down (I despise turn based combat, only Pokemon and XCom 2 made it kinda fun) but at least you have input, you can create a combo to create strong attacks say: 'ADAS' for a fire attack or similar, making the game feel more interactive, and it does it's job.
LISA is scary, and horrifiying and beautiful and has really changed the way I think. I cannot thank the developers and everyone who influenced this game in any way. Thank you.

More disclosure from me. I may be the world's worst platform puzzle gamer. I am absolutely terrible at these things. So going into "Papo y Yo" I was a little hesitant but the great reviews and the relatively short gameplay time had me thinking "why not". "Papo y Yo" is the story of a boy named Quico dealing with an abusive alcoholic father. While hiding in the closet he sees a chalk mark on the wall and ends up falling into a dream like world and for the next 3-4 hours you'll be traversing this world in order to find someone or something to help you cure the Monster (AKA your father's demons). I really enjoyed this game. The game world was incredibly cool and the soundtrack was excellent. The gameplay is standard puzzle platforming but other than a couple frustrating moments this wasn't difficult at all, even for a rank amateur like me.  Some might take issue with the game length but I found it perfect. The pacing was excellent and there wasn't a lot of time wasted. The game wasn't perfect. I did come across a bug or two that would screw up a couple of jumps here and there and the gameplay variety was a little lacking (pulls this, push that etc.). Some may also find the game a bit pretentious (the monster = Quico's dad, frogs = alcohol) but it didn't bug me at all and I found "Papo y Yo" to definitely be a journey worth taking. 8=10 from me.

This was one of the extremely few games I have ever played where I felt the story matched the gameplay. The puzzles, while rather easy, were still fun to execute, but that was forgotten as the graphics, music, and actual gameplay were absolutely beautiful. I adored this game.

The gaming industry is at its best when a developer manages to turn a personal story into an enjoyable game.
Papo&Yo is a wonderful experience: the gameplay is fun and gimmicky, turning the landscape and urban architecture into puzzles, thanks to all sorts of imaginary devices, the kind a child (or a talented graffiti artist :) ) might draw on walls. Many times I just surprised and delighted by what my next click did, never bored and always looking forward to the next area to solve.
The game looks and sounds just right enough to draw you into the world and the story it wants to tell. Just stand still in the sun, look around at the colorful houses of the South American slums and listen to the silence. And the crickets :) Just beautiful.
Everything feels organic, in its right place and I don't want to tell you anything more specific, for fear it will spoil your own experience. I'm just sorry I didn't pick this up sooner, it's been sitting in my Library for months.
Do yourself a favour and put a smile on your face with this gem.
An unusual story, but still quite an enjoyable game.

It's just really mediocre overall and not worth its full price, although I'd recommend it on a sale if you're a diehard Sonic fan.

Overall, Sonic Generations is an amazing game. If you ask me, it's the perfect way to celebrate Sonic the Hedgehog's 20th anniversary. Why? Not only do you get to play as Modern Sonic, but also Classic Sonic (he introduced me to videogames, believe it or not). So, needless to say, it can appeal to you whether you're a fan of the 2D, Genesis classics, or even the modern, 3D games. Every level has been taken from previous games in the series, all of which were voted to be in the game by the fans. One cool feature within the game is the ability to choose what music plays in the background of a level. You can unlock music through collecting red rings (returning from my favorite Sonic game, Sonic Colors) and completing challenges (a lot of which are a major pain in the neck to complete, let alone get an S-rank on). Oh, and if you were to ask me, I think people complain about the final boss fight WAY too much. It's not perfect, but it's not terrible, either (especially once you learn its attack-patterns and can collect rings efficiently). In conclusion, Sonic Generations doesn't quite have everything I expect to see from a Sonic game, but it is a masterpiece and it should be in every Sonic fan's collection.

Goodbye and Goodbye Baby are a good example of this.
Goodbye Baby having that motivational feeling.
Goobye being more sad and depressive.
or...
Bradley and Bradley Baby...
Also, how... The Sireen's Call, Father's call, Big boy's call, The Band's call,etc. Are the same track but use different instruments and try to send different emotions.

These reflect how the characters evolve through the game. Changing the way how they see or... feel things. How they change, and express what they feel. You have to sacrifice stuff for them, your items, your arms...
The characters that are unique and have their motivations and things they like or enjoy...

An know has to protect Buddy, the only thing on this world that makes him feel happy.
or
Rando, the antagonist, kinda, a man that want to restore this world, he wants Buddy to help him, but his army just doesn't
follow his commands, because he never speaks.
He is a broken man that hides behind a mask and a large black cape.
I  just think uhhh..., everything, about this game is amazing, and feel like... everyone should at least give it an opportunity.
LISA: the painful RPG, is just an amazing experience, where you get to see the destiny of the world not having any women and slowly decaying, there's no reason to live anymore and these men are just fooling around, but then Buddy appears and changes everything... You can understand the characters feelings because you have to be with them, and sacrifice stuff for them... It is painful sometimes... but the Joy makes it all better.
I think LISA is one of the best games ever created, because it has a lot of personality and emotional moments, while also supporting some comical funny moments in there.
I can't stop drawing Rando when im bored or just want to waste time, i can't stop thinking about this gem, and i'm completely fine with it.
quickie, LISA: the joyful, tho... it's... less than what LISA: the painful is.
Still recommended but... the painful is sooooo much better, the joyful just gives a bad end to the story, for the price of knowing more about Dusty and Buddy.

The Best Video Game I Ever Played.
I remember the day when it came out, this was one of the most exciting things I ever waited for, after playing the demo for about 30 something hours (!) just the demo! I was ready to play the final product, and hell I should have taken the time to really enjoy it cause I finished the game after 10 hours, like 2 days after the game was launched (I know the game is kinda short but it wasnt that..), although I did enjoyed it very much I wasn't 100% understanding what a masterpiece game I was playing! I just wanted to see what's going to happen next! and I should have taken a moment and just "living" the game and not just playing it.
anyway, enough about my silly and not interesting history with this game.
So how do I rate this?
1) The Best story in a video game I ever witness. I can say hundred of things about the story (that it packed with alot of easter eggs, characters that you gonna love, twists and even just a little interesting moments that will remind you scenes from classic movies like "The Godfather" and "Goodfellas" and of course the godly "The Sopranos".
2) Amazing atmosphere of the 40s/50s (and I wish there were more games like this that capture the "innocent" 40s from the posters about the war or just a nice commercials you can see on the side of the street, the language with the slang of that period of time, till the music of the era itself.
3) If we are talking about the music already I want to clarify something: there is more than 100 songs on the radio (combining all the radio stations from all the eras), and god... so many wonderful songs I got to know thanks to this game ("mafia 3" you better have the same amount of songs like in here!), and u shouldn't forget about the score that is just amazingly beautiful, You must buy the Deluxe version just to hear the soundtrack.
4) Voice acting is one of the greatest you can ever ask, the characters come alive with those great dubbers and it feels like you watching some high class classic movie.
5) Realistic and fun driving system. well.. we can say "bye-bye" to that in the third game :(
6) Unbelievable beautiful graphics that stands even today, the interior design in closed places are very well done and it just looks like a set from a movie, not just one table and a dude standing there and talking with you, and it doesn't have any FPS problems or all that stuff that happens nowadays, you dont really need a strong pc to run it well, it was a perfect game launch at the time, that's how you make a game people!
7) The Weather - its just amazing how every season has a different impact on the environment and the story itself, especially the winter, goddd how much I loved it, wish it was longer in the game though.
8) Shooting and cover system are very simply and yet extremely fun, I should also add the car and the clothes selections are great, nothing says more "mafia and the 40s" like a beautiful classic elegant suit.
9) Not too big and not too small city map that packed with fair enough interesting places to go to. I come to know every street and corner in this game, I don't even use the mini map (not very important information to this review but what the hell :P ).
10) Perfect ending for a perfect game (now I know there some people who didn't like the ending because they didn't understood it (that is just stupid) or because they wanted more of a "clear ending" although it was pretty clear but they just didn't get it... so ignore them and enjoy the freaking game!
Final Score: 10 out of 10

A charming platformer for all ages and walks of life. This game takes everything you know about typical indie games and turns them on their head. The game's story is a great and compelling one, not too pretentious or sad, but not too stupid or thin either. The graphics are well-animated 32-bit pixel art instead of crude "8-bit" sprites, and they even have some voice acting to go with it! The game runs perfectly, with no bad bugs in sight. All three characters play distinctly with their own abilities. The music is not the typical synthesized garboil you tend to hear, but rather, well-orchestrated, well-composed, incredibly catchy pieces. The only drawback is the very difficult boss fights. Some may be put off by the physics not being exactly like its inspiriation, the late Sonic the Hedgehog.

I must admit that I'm blown away, considering I was one of the naysayers that said this was a shameless Sonic clone. But nah, this ended up being one of the best platforming games I've ever played.
When it comes to platforming games, do we prefer quanity or quality? Look at it this way: most Genesis-era Sonic titles run through around 20+ medium-sized stages with a hint of exploration. Freedom Planet, on the other hand, goes for quality, presenting only eight-or-so stages throughout the main Adventure Mode.
When I speak of it in that way, it doesn't seem very enticing, but alas, how wrong you'd feel once you begin the game...
The main courses are ENORMOUS, using multiple checkpoints and screens. The paths are incredibly diverse and feature routes that cater to each of the three different characters' abilities. The first stage alone took me around thirty minutes on my first run.
When you play Sonic, your main focus is speed. You want to blast your way through to the end goal in the fastest time possible. When you play Freedom Planet, however, the level design suddenly sparks your curiosity and you suddenly realize that there is so much more than you're traversing. You take the time to explore, find secrets and collectables, farm lives, ect, all while maintaining your top speed. Whether you play it for exploration or for speed, the story mode will clock in at around five hours.
As we mention the story mode, let me put aside the claims stating that the story is "uninspired" or "cheesy." Now, you still have the choice to play the game without indulging in the story, but if you don't bring it upon yourself at least once to experience the Adventure Mode, you're by far not getting the full experience.
The story is, while mainly simple, shines with some of the cutest and charming characters that come to life with some surprisingly stunning voice acting. It actually kept me interested, and while the cutscenes tend to get tiresome (moreso in the first half), it still managed to clutch my full attention and I ended up binging two-thirds of the story mode by pulling an all-nighter during my first playthrough. (And truth be told, that's something I rarely do.)
The lore is simple, yet rich. The characters are memorable (for the most part...*cough* Spade *cough*). The conflict is familiar but stays within trope realm instead of full-blown cliche territory.
The soundtrack compliments the game's speedy and open atmosphere perfectly, with some of the best themes (Prince Dial's boss theme being my favorite in the whole game) I've heard from an indie game. It actually convinced me enough to buy the entire official soundtrack. Oops.
In short:
Pros
-Lengthy, exciting, diverse stages
-Story hits all your sweet spots
-You'll love the main characters. Trust me.
-Soundtrack
Cons
-Tiresome cutscenes in the first half
-Incredible difficulty spike towards the last act
Freedom Planet isn't a shameless DeviantArt-OC-Do-Not-Steal-Sonic clone. It's simply a love letter to not only the early Sonic era, but a lot of the fast-paced 16-bit games that many consider the magnum opus of video gaming's timeline.

is a city building and management simulator. Elected Mayor over a city-to-be or existing city, manage city development by laying roads, plotting land and zoning, constructing public service buildings and maintaining financial balance as you thrive to build a megalopolis.
: You are giving a lot of flexibility, from zoning density to street type. As your city grow, additional selection of power plants become available, and additional needs are requested such as water treatment facilities, trains and subways, ports and airports, as well as a variety of educational establishments, health and emergency services. You have a good list of additional tax options, each with their own downside and benefits. Keep a balance between how much financing you can afford, and how much you need, to give to each of your public services (as a whole or per individual buildings). More special buildings and landmarks become available as your population rises. You can even connect your different cities togetter with your streets, highways and railroads, if they are located on neighboring tiles on the map.
: You are limited to determining individual land plots and zoning type, with little control on what will actually be built. You may have small shops and fast food being build on high-density commercial areas you were planning to have towering office buildings on, or maybe cheap low-cost apartment blocks will appear on residential zones you wanted luxury condos in. City interconnection requires you to actually build the neighboring city, its streets not necessarily being aligned with each other's connections. Tax revenue is hard to come by, and you'll often catch yourself speeding up time and wait years to get enough money to continue building without resorting to high-interest loans. Public service coverage is radius-based, which forces you to finance overlapping territory, or leave out coverage in-between your schools, police stations and hospitals.
: ★★★☆☆ - It's up to you
The amount of micro-management you have, plotting individual land plots, and the amount of effort it needs to reach actual high-density buildings, makes
more of a town simulator than a large urban sky-scrapper city simulator. Still, it remains a good example of the genre and the best game in its franchise.

I got this game a long time ago with an Humble Bundle, and finally got around to play it.
I'm really really glad that I did. I loved this game, its astounding ambientation, its nice puzzle nature.
Let's try to be objective and methodic:
-Story: 7/10
The story isn't that great, but it's a break from classic puzzles, it's entertaining enough, and the end packs a punch.
-Longevity/Replay value: 4/10
This is the worst part: it takes 3/4 hours to finish it, and once you finish it for the first time, there is really nothing compelling
you to play it again.
-Difficulty: 6/10
Pretty much all the puzzles are very straightforward and easy to solve, with the hint box it's even easier. Both on the mental side and the skill required to put it in practice. Failing has no real consequences, as you never really "die" and the worst case scenario is losing a few seconds to respawn, but in the game everything stays as it was, so you don't even have to restart the level. This can be a pro (no frustration) or a con (shorter longevity).
-Aesthetic: 10/10
This is the strongest point of the game. The ambientation, some kind of favelas, and the effect that solving the puzzle has on it is simply amazing. It has something mystical mixed with some kind of visual poetry. I greatly enjoyed it. Also kudos to the creators for the cure put into every little detail. Just lovely.
-Concept: 9/10
Puzzles that change the conformation of the ambient surrounding you are not really so new, but not that common either.
Plus, the implementation is brilliant.
-Controls: 7/10
Pretty straightforward. Usual wasd + mouse, third person. The cam is usually fine, in some rare occasion can move awkwardly. But those occasions are very rare, and failing has no big consequences (see "Difficulty")
-OST: 8/10
The soundtrack is not, strictly speaking, memorable. But it always fit the game, is easy to the ears, nice, and really helps feeling part of the game.
AVG: 7.3

I also have to hand it to the composer, Brian D’Oliveira, for creating a light, flamenco soundtrack that ties in well with lightness of Quico’s steps and scenery. This praise all being said, the game isn’t without its flaws. Like many platformers, the game has an element of exploration which the designers failed to… explore. There’s plenty of nooks, crannies and hidey holes, but nothing in them. I even managed to find trapped teddy bears in many of them, but they seemed to be nothing more than coincidently-placed scenery. I felt that this beautiful and unique world was just a bit too empty, nothing to encourage me to play again and no reward for getting to these hard to reach places, not quite what I expect from a platformer
