Papo & Yo is a lot of things. It's a 3D puzzle game. It's interactive magical realism. It's a meditation on abuse and alcoholism. It's pieced together with a real familiarity with and affection for the assembled look of Brazilian favelas. And it has a autobiographical tone that's nearly impossible to find elsewhere in games.
The gameplay is decent. The setting and music are strong. But the real star of the show is Monster. The game couldn't exist without him. For a creature that says nothing and spends half the game sleeping, he's fascinatingly complex. You'll switch between trying to protect him and trying to escape from him at a moment's notice. You're trying to break his addiction, but sometimes you'll use that addiction to force him to do what you want. You'll find yourself clinging to the brief moments he shows some affection, even if it's nothing more than a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥toss of football. You want to like Monster, though you'll repeatedly ask yourself if you should even bother. It's a juggling act, but you'll find yourself practicing quite a bit of cognitive dissonance as you go from puzzle to puzzle.
The game isn't subtle in its metaphors, nor should it be. Think of it as a children's story about abuse. It's like Where the Wild Things Are, except instead of wild creatures as stand-ins for the anarchy of childhood, Monster stands for a child's perspective of the physical power, aloofness, and cruelty of adulthood.

This is coming from someone who has not played any sort of Call of Duty game before, and has not bowed down to the droves of people that hate Call of Duty just for being Call of Duty. So this is an honest opinion from someone who has no prior history, good or bad, with the game.
With that said, what can I say about this game? It's not absolutely terrible, but I can't recommend it to anyone that is not a Call of Duty fan already. I can call the game mediocre at best without pause to think. Let me just list out some of the pros and cons I have with this game:
PROS:
- WWII Setting. Still one of my favorite war-time settings of history in video games despite it having saturated the market many years ago and still left its mark in the gaming industry (In how modern FPS games have nearly abandoned the era. Battlefield has WWI and CoD is returning to WWII but overall the 1940s era of gaming is still down out of the count.
- Guns: I am always a fan of the armament that WWII supplied to both the Axis and the Allies so no complaints there.
- Pacific Theater. So many WWII shooters focus mainly on the European Theater and rarely the African Theater alongside the Pacific Theater, so to see half of the campaign take place in the Pacific is quite a treat.
- Zombie mode. It is NOT my type of thing but I know a LOT of people enjoy this game mode, and it spun off into its own big thing from here so if you enjoy zombie wave survival minigames then you would enjoy this mode. But if you are here for the solo campaign and multiplayer, well...
Unfortunately for me the bad outweighs the good, because after finishing the game I have quite a lot to say about it.
CONS:
- Cost & Length. This game has a base price of $20 and rarely (If ever) goes on sale for more the 50% off. They are asking $20 for a game whose solo campaign can be completed in 6 hours on Normal to Hard difficulty, a multiplayer that is practically dead for all I care, and a zombie wave survival minigame. I know that people can find enjoyment in the zombie mode and that servers do crop up occasionally, but overall for what it's worth to me this is not a $10 game.
At most I'd say it's a $5 due to the length of the solo campaign and how much time the zombie mode captivated me, resulting in just about 6.1 hours in total with no wishes to return to the game. That's about $1.6 spent per hour for people just interested in a solo campaign mode without zombies. This game is not worth about $2 per hour to play for me. Why?
- Campaign. Let me put it short and sweet: Take my sentence of "short and sweet" and then remove the "sweet" part. What gets left? "short and...?" Exactly. All the missions are extremely small and very short, and after spending less than 30 minutes on some levels they are already done! I would have liked it if they made less missions overall but lengthened the levels tremendously, because hopping between missions and being totally disjointed from each other vs. sticking to one mission and feeling the fatigue of war encapsulate is an entirely different experience altogether. The campaigns themselves weren't even that well thought out even, and felt really really monotonous after getting through the first four levels, which made the later levels an absolute slough to trudge through because of...
- Cheap deaths/Cheap difficulty. This all comes down to four things: Enemy respawns, small health, grenades, and color. Respawning enemies are always ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, especially when you have to take an objective. I want to play it safe and straight, so I would OF COURSE clear out an area before moving up. Oh...but what's this? Enemies will continuously spawn out of inaccessible doorways and won't stop until you move forward? Then let me KILL THEN AND MOVE FORWARD!
And the health! Wow if your health small. Doesn't matter if you can regenerate health if it only takes like 5 bullets to kill you because most people don't have the reflexes of a fox and pretty much everything is done trial by error. There are a lot of single player campaigns where you have to learn from a failure because you didn't know something ahead of time, but there is a difference between learning ahead of time and dying in the next minute because you just don't have enough health.
AND THE GRENADES. WOW. They tell you to throw the grenade when you see the grenade symbol, but you end up throwing your own grenade instead and dying. Let me tell you grenades are the cheaptest weapon in the game and have been the cause of countless deaths. There is a fine line drawn between being realistic (Which the grenades aren't even but whatever) and being a fun game; games should always strive to be fun firstoff and foremost. And dying every minute is not fun.
And lastly this isn't entirely Call of Duty's fault as every game was doing it, but making everything have this dull grey monotone color for everything, from the trees to the ruble, from the enemies to the gunfire, not only makes the game boring to look at, but it also makes everything very difficult to see. So what if you can't see enemies, right? That's how it's supposed to work, with their camo making them blend in with the surroundings? So what if gun barrel fire looks the same as a building, the sky, or even a BUSH? If that's the excuse to use then that is a terrible excuse. THEY ARE 5 FEET IN FRONT OF YOU AND YOU CAN'T SEE THEM. THAT IS TERRIBLE. Not being able to see anything leads to a lot of death in the game. Cheap death.
Is it a bad game? No. Is it a good game? No. It's simply mediocre. The first two hours of playing were fun and I wanted to see more. But as the game progressed further, I just became angrier and angrier. And when it finally ended, I didn't feel satisfied at all. I felt robbed. $10 for a short, difficult, and monotonous game that didn't grab my attention past the initial single player levels. Multiplayer is dead and unless you like playing zombies on your own then that portion is dead too. Paying $10 for a game with only 1/3rd of its content left to use. That disappoints me so because I really wanted to give this game an earnest chance and look beyond the franchise's preconcieved hatred of just being another Call of Duty game.
Take my advice, use your $10 to $20 elsewhere. If you want recommendations, here's what I suggest you get for the same price:
- Sniper Elite (Any of them). Rock solid single player campaign with very satisfying deaths and a decent length to it. Not forgetting to mention the later games have some excellent art direction.
- Medal of Honor: Airborne. Already $10 as a base price (TAKE THE HINT CALL OF DUTY. A 10+ YEAR GAME SHOULDN'T COST $20. ESPECIALLY WHEN 1/3RD OF THE GAME IS USABLE) it earns that full $10 price sticker. It only has 5 or 6 levels but they are REALLY thick and pack a punch and by the end of it you feel like you really did accomplish something. Compared to CoD: WaW's endings where I was just tanking everything and sloughing through to complete the game.
- Wolfenstein: The New Order. This game is fun to play. It's much more fast paced than CoD: WaW with a nice campaign and guns that pack a punch. Great for its price I'd say.
- Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad with Rising Storm. This game has a bit of a steeper learning curve as it plays more like a simulator than a traditional FPS game (Traditional by Call of Duty standards) but once you get over the hump of trying to learn the basics of the game, you will find a VERY much alive dedicated multiplayer and an absolutely rock solid single player campaign that portrays the struggle of the Russian front better than WaW did.
- Company of Heroes. RTS WWII. Need I say more?
- Day of Defeat: Source. This game's graphics haven't aged, but it is still a very fun game that not only has a lively multiplayer scene but can pretty much run on today's potato computers. So if you got a WWII multiplayer fix with a terrible laptop, Day of Defeat can service you just fine.

This game is an obvious homage to the classic Sonic the Hedgehog Genesis games and it shows with its speed, level design and music which are all probably the best things about the game. However unlike some cases with the classic Sonic games the level design in Freedom Planet is catered for speed at all times, not once does it feel like the game punished me for going fast with a cheap enemy placement. The bosses themselves are big scaled, creative and challenging at times even though they can have those 'obvious weak spots' you see in some Mario and Zelda bosses. They're still fun to play and that's what matters to me.
The game's flaws CAN be very noticable, and by that I mean it's constantly being presented in your face because there is non-stop voice acting and to be honest the voice acting is pretty mediorce, it's passable at best and at points feels like you're watching some cringey furry fan-fiction at worst, it's so distracting BUT the game does offer a "Classic" mode where if you don't care about the majority of voices and its pretty lame story then so be it, you can just jump level to level when you're done instead of having a large cut-scene in-between in the normal mode.
I think FP is a pretty solid game, it definitely has a lot of effort and heart put into it and it shows by how fun it is. I'd reccommend the Classic mode but if you're honestly curious about the voices and story then go ahead it's not the worst I've ever seen (still better than Mega Man X4). I reccommend this game.

I remember when I first played Resident Evil for the PS1 when I was a child; we had rented it from Ritz.
Until this point I was lost in a glossy and sparkly world of ♥♥♥♥♥ fantasy games like Spyro and Crash Bandicoot.
I vividly remember the first encounter with the 'concrete face' zombie. Those haunting, empty eyes slowly turning after decapitating your fellow S.T.A.R.S member. Then the real horror began. No direct visibility and awkward controls with limited turn speed. Desperately I tried to escape, with this monster always just out of sight, but it's horrific groans and decaying flesh lurching ever closer, always seconds from me.
Eventually I was cornered at the other end of the corridoor, the camera pointed directly down with nothing to see but Jill. Closer and closer he groaned and lurched, until he was upon me. Naturally I never read the manual and had no concept of 'press R1 and X to shoot'. Helpless, it slowly chewed into me, bite after slow bite in sprays of blood until I died.
I slammed the power button and ran away screaming, traumatised by those dead, hollow eyes of the 'concrete-face zombie'.
After 15 minuites of playing this demo those old feelings started to come back. The same intense horror and the helplesness...
This is an amazing Resi' comeback with all the guts and glory of what launched this series as the 'Father of survival horror'. I had been dissapointed with the departure from this series' roots towards a more action-focused game. But now it's back, and just how I always imagined it should be.
It's♥♥♥♥♥♥your-pants-scary all in first person, limited FOV with incredible graphics optimised to great lengths to ensure you will scream like the complete little ♥♥♥♥♥ that you really are.
There are no 'Press X to punch boulder' sequences or 'third person run and gun' that many of you baby Resi' fans grew up on. No, this is the real face of survival horror, this is the real face of a Resident Evil title.
I can't wait to run away screaming again.

Ahh, LISA. This game will wreck your heart, repair it, then wreck it again like it did to me. This game takes place in a degenerated, apocalyptic setting. All the women have died out and the only currency is porn magazines. However, there is a single girl left and you just happen to be the adopted father of her and happen to lose her. You will be faced with many hard decisions. While it took me 8 hours to beat, I enjoyed every second of those eight hours. There are the occasional funny moments and then moments that will literally destroy your heart and ninjas will suddenly start chopping onions. There is a unique, large cast of characters with their own unique abilities. The story is great and unique in its own way, like the amazing soundtrack. If you like games that are similar to Earthbound, then this is for you. Anyways, just go ahead and buy it if you read my warning and like Earthbound or just like RPGs. Have fun.

Original review:
I am a Kickstarter backer so I have been following the development of the game for about 1,5 years.
This ride started great, these guys had an awasome concept, gameplay movies to show and so I backed their project. They were supposed to deliver the beta in October 2012; now we are in Early Access and still in early prototype. But the real problem is the lack of information about the development process; dev. dairies are void of any solid info; they are just about bugfixes and trivial stuff; t-shirts, save/load game functions, technical mumbo jumbo.. We don't know where this game is going; no real direction or roadmap presented by devs. There is talk of a roadmap though; for many, many months if I remember correctly. I suspect they have not known what to do with their game since the beginning. I just can't explain the lack of any solid info about the game/roadmap/direction in any other way.
Since the first prototype of the game, over a year ago, devs have added a really, really broken survival mode to the game, a multiplayer mode which doesn't work, a few bugfixes here and there; nothing else.
Game has a lot of potential, a great concept but the execution is just plain bad; UI is horrible, there are no real updates, no content added in over a year since first release.
I do not recommend the game at this point. At this rate devs working on the game; come back in a year or two and maybe, maybe you might be looking at a good game. Otherwise just stay away for now.
About the game itself:
It's sandbox building game. You have minions doing various tasks like mining, cutting down trees and providing you with building materials on the map you choose; well you have just one map at the moment so no choosing. You issue orders to your minions to gather materials and then you go ahead and lay down blueprints for your minions and they build them.
In Survival mode; you have baddies on top of normal sandbox mode. But they have no AI so they just rush at you. Get an archer or two at a high place and you win. Baddies won't be able to climb more than 2 blocks high and it takes too much time to destroy the blocks; your archers will kill everyone while baddies are hacking away at the blocks.
Problems;
UI is horrible. unimaginative and clunky.
Camera controls are plain bad.
There are still problems with laying down blueprints for constructions. Pathfinding is broken, AI is broken; blueprints for big buildings are very problematic; your minions just can't build them due to pathfinding errors.
Especially big blueprints will give you a headache; you will have to zoom in, out, rotate the camera this way and that just to be able to lay down a blueprint. Misclick? Tough luck; some blueprints blocks just don't wanna be removed so you will end up dropping that building and start another blueprint.
Many times you will have to start a map over and over again to get minions to spawn at all; you will just start with no minions.
There is a catapult in the game with which you can hurl barrels filled with stones or explosive stones to baddies. Very clunky to use; you will end up not using it at all. You don't want to use explosive barrels too; you will just destroy your buildings with it.
No content added as of now. You just build aimlessly in the map. There aren't enough building blocks.
There aren't enough info about the game mechanics; how do you build that bridge for example? You will have to find some YouTube video by a fellow player to show you that.
Why can't you just put that block over there? Because you can't. And no one tells you why not.

A short review after around 3hrs of playing.
Let me start with the good things: Definitely a step in the right direction!
(+) Track deformation works a lot better than what I expected, has a substantial impact on gameplay and you really "feel" the track unlike in MXGP2 were you were just kind of floating above a solid track with dirt textures.
Also gives you a very satisfying feeling if you manage to hit a rut perfectly and exit the corner with a lot more speed!
(+) The handling is significant improvement as well, a bit more complex and difficult, now you need a few hrs and not only 20min to master it perfectly.
(+) The game-engine-swap was a good move, weather, tracks, etc... everything looks more realistic. (In theory)
(+) Engine-sounds, at least on most bikes, are ALOT better even with some very satisfying exhaust pops from time to time :)
(+) Whip/Scrubs are a bit better and kind of "free(e)r” but still much to do until MX vs ATV or Mx Simulator level. VERY MUCH!
BUT why do I still give this a no, at least for now even though pretty much every aspect got improved in the right direction?
(-) The career mode, oh my fkn god. I have never been so lost in such a simple game in my whole life yet. The mix between having absolutely no information about where you are standing and the awesome bug that randomly skips races for you or counts races that you won as "skipped" results in a feeling of "where the♥♥♥♥♥am I and what the♥♥♥♥♥do I still need to do"?

WHY do I have to do like 10 races in a row to get access to the career menu again were you have at least a few infos about where you are standing and the overall season. My thoughts throughout the whole career mode have been this:
When is this race series finished? Where am I placed? When can I change my sponsors? When do I get access to mxgp? Why the freakin hell on earth do I not get a single info about anything and yet I am being pushed thru race after race like a maniac. I have NEVER been so CLUELESS in my whole life in a game that in theory is so simple.
(-) The game is still to easy and not a bit challenging. Took me 30mins on the test track to master the handling and win every single race easily in pro mode on the highest difficulty "realistic".
(-) There is still not any feeling of "momentum". There is to little difference if you case a jump or master a line perfectly. In MX vs ATV or MX Sim, finding the perfect line and hitting every jump perfectly is the key factor of being fast and this results in an epic feeling of "flow". Which is not the case in this game.
(-) Even though in theory the graphics have improved, it still feels very rushed, unfinished/unpolished and overall more like early access graphics. Everything is a bit unsharp, specially rider & bike.
(-) The Whips/Scrubs are still garbage compared to other already listed MX games.
(-) The physics between riders/bikes are still weird and a bit frustrating. Normally, if you’d hit someone’s back wheel with your front wheel you'd be really fked. But in this game you can pit manoeuvre other riders? What the ...? The complete opposite of what happens in real life.
(-) A lot more.
This could have a been a really decent game and I might be if they fix the broken career mode. But again, for now really disappointing that a potentially great game has been rushed again, released unfinished and half broken.
And excuse my English, I am grumpy German still learning the master language.

Dream Pinball 3D Review - Raymond KT
Dream Pinball 3D fails at reproducing realistic physics, rendering it pretty much useless. Even if the player was given a sense of the weight of the ball and the flippers reacted like they should, you'd still have some pretty generic tables.
The table collection in Dream Pinball consists of a bunch of clichés and one ambiguous fantasy game. You've got your medieval table, your monster table, your dinosaur table… They're well thought out with the usual secrets, combos, and special modes, but they aren't inspired. The one machine that isn't easily described is Amber Moon, which appears to be a mishmash of sword and sorcery themes. A sexy witch/vampire lady adorns the table's artwork, but the standout sound effect is a bird call that doesn't sound mysterious or supernatural at all. Weird. Overall, the sound in Dream Pinball is pretty well done. Each table has its own soundtrack, appropriate sound effects, and a voice over giving you commentary.
The first thing any pinball wizard will notice about this effort is the flippers are terrible. They aren't governed by physics at all. There are simply two flipper modes: up and down. Flipping them doesn't result in any movement; they are transported from a resting position to an upright position. This denies the player the ability to finesse their shots with varying degrees of strength.
Also disappointing are the ball physics. The orbs don't feel like they have any weight to them. Each table has a "ballchange" feature that switches the material of your ball from steel to things like marble or walnut. The manual claims this will alter the weight and handling of your orbs, but in practice they don't feel any different. Sometimes it doesn't even feel like the ball is making contact with the flippers.

Papa & Yo is a tale of a boy and his Big peach-coloured-monster that in a less than subtle way is a metaphor for an alcoholic parental figure. The monster likes bright orange coconuts and can be manipulated to go and stand at places that makes bright white magic happen.
What's appealing about this experience is how this dream world is portrayed, and less so in how it functions.
The box city is vivid and playfully represented; cardboard boxes being picked up will make houses fly and move about to be placed in strategic places for our avatar to step on in order to progress.
Some houses will grow legs and move like cockroaches, others grow wings and fly.
I find these houses and what they mean to the main character more appealing than what the game tries to make me feel for the monster.
The monster is nothing but a tool for the main character to use in order to trigger bright white magic so that you can progress. I don't feel for the monster, and also with all this creative freedom that the kid has, why doesn't he make his way through without the monster? It means nothing to me as a player, there is no love.
The monster might just have been a ball and a chain locked to the kids foot.
And then when the frogs enter the picture, making the monster go inte a fiery rage when he consumes them, the monster's tediousness just increases making me like it less.
And liking it less would be fine if there just were some moment before that that established some kind of positive connection, but that never happens.
It would serve whatever narrative the game is trying to convey better if the monster was simply always there, following and being present without forcing me as a player to make it go places all the time.
But instead the game is tediously forcing the player to go through puzzles that after repetition loses what the game is trying to say about the relationship this kid has with the monster, the world, the girl, the robot and cardboard houses.
The movement felt when moving the character about is fluent and loose but comes to a chunky halt when the game demands you to yet again turn arbitrary levers in order to progress.
Or to make the monster do more stuff for you. Again.
I did enjoy what I played for the most part, with a little more thought put into what the puzzles could mean set to the context of what this boy is going through, it could've succeeded in saying something.
'Papa & Yo' has heart and genuinely cares, but needs more thought on how to make the theme of the game correlate with the player's choices.

Great game, definitely well supported. You can tell that the developers really care for the franchise, and want to make meaningful content. CoH 1 will always have a place in my heart that this will probably never replace, but I would be remiss if I said that CoH2 hasn't improved on the original. Little quality of life things like the ability to reverse a vehicle (keep your strong armor facing front!), reinforce en masse, vault small obstacles, etc. are great additions- whenever I go back and play the original, I definitely miss those improvements.
Some things are less meaningful than the original, which I think was done to improve balance and make the game more competitive. Off map artillery is less powerful than in the original game, and I definitely miss the V1 strikes, but in general it's a good step forward. Also, they made the platform highly modular, so steam workshop support for maps, mods, and more are a great addition to an already great game.
Some people might object to the DLC, but honestly I think it's great value for the money, with the exception of Ardennes Assault. (A phenomenal singleplayer campaign, but it was a little too expensive, and it isn't long or large-scale enough to be really replayable.)
In general, though, CoH2 is a great game. Destructible maps, great sound, interesting units. Would highly recommend.

Just simply not fun. Games pretty dated aesthetically and  the gameplay is awkward. This stems from largely cartoon-like shooting mechanics and  stiffness when maneuvering units. The largest sin this game commits is viewing squads as static objects. You have no ability to give personalized orders to individual squad members what so ever. To up the cartoon-like nature, even on the highest difficulty squads are also bullet sponges to everything except MGs and explosives.
Want to have your MG aim for a specific target while rifleman engage another? Not possible. Want to break the squad into two smaller fireteams to flank? Negative; you'll need two squads for that. Want to merge two smaller squads into a single unit? Not unless it's that units special ability.
Basically this game plays more like a traditional RTS than a squad based tactics game. If this game didn't have so much DLC and aesthetic customization, I'd assume it was a mobile port. This game is for the type of people who rant in YouTube comments about minute errors in WWII media. Comments like "Acksually, [x] unit would have been [here] during [x] battle. Generations strikes a clean balance between the nostalgia of the old Sonic games and the style of the newer ones, while keeping things prioritized: the story is in the background, cheesy but not convoluted; the sense of speed is always there and there are few "roaming" levels (almost none, actually) and the visuals are clean and colorful, never "gritty." It's a good homage to the classic games, and the best of the 3D games without any of the gimmicky junk (no gun-toting Shadow, no sword-wielding Sonic, no million different characters), and even in the levels from the newer games, it is kept to a minimum.
A Generations 2 is the ONLY thing Sonic Team should be working on.

Basically, except the "remastered" core 2D gameplay and a few good music tracks, everything here is between "mildly irritating" and "batshit awful". 3D-Sonic levels suffer from little to none playtesting, and so are flooded with both technical and design missteps. This situation tops at bosses -- they annoy and bore at the same time, and are completely screwed up with bugs. By the way, "annoying and boring" is also true about cutscenes -- I can't call them a story, it's just that -- and every single character, both Sonics included (yep, the "old" Sonic does alright with being unbearable and mute at once).
That said, gameplay is not brilliant at all. Levels for 2D-Sonic are mostly okay, although they suffer from several strange design decisions. Favorite case -- signs for death pits placed in such manner they rather mock your fatal error than give valuable info. Ironically, 2D-sections for 3D-Sonic (oh yeah, his levels aren't 100% 3D, with constant frustrating shifts of perspective) might play somewhat better because of "modern" Sonic's moves serving as last chance of escaping stupid death. If you won't step into another glitch, of course.
But all could be forgiven (or tolerated) if the assets are great. Well, first of all, there are not much of them: only nine locations, each from a different series' entry, and each divided between two Sonics -- 18 levels, plus horrible bosses (and a miriad of challenge missions that reuse main levels). Decent amount, but certainly not a great nostalgic trip to all the places of glory. I don't give a damn about modern Sonic games, so I don't particularly hate them -- but only one location per each of the first three games? Come on already. That just doubles the bad taste from poor QA.
All in all, too much of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t for a few good moments. If this is the "best Sonic game since Sonic & Knuckles" as some internet folks say, all the others must've been flat out horrible.
It's pretty fun, for those who like Sonic. If you don't care for the blue hedgehog speedster now, don't expect this game to change your mind. Easily worth the 7$, kinda pushing 30$.

MXGP (1) was meh. MXGP 2 was a step in the right direction. MXGP 3 was a HUGE LEAP in the right direction. I've been playing motocross games all my life as well as racing motocross IRL all my life. This is by far the best (arcade) motocross game I have ever played. The realism and fun factor are the best I've ever seen in a game like this. In my opinion they mixed simulation and arcade perfectly. Not to mention it looks absolutley beautiful! The rider body movements flow and seem real. The AI choose multiple line choices and give you a run for you money at times. You can actually hook into the ruts that the riders make themselves on the track! (not just the premade little berms). You have more control over the whips and scrubs (When, how much and how long). It is simply the most immersive motocross game thus far. I give it a 9/10 because they obviously still need to work an a few small things like bike sounds and the physics could use some touching up. But over all I am so excited this game is what it is and it makes me even more excited to see what milestone has in store for their next game.
Oh btw the way the 125's are an absolute blast and great perk of this game :)

It seems to me that there are three kinds of reviews for this game; people that think it's so-so, people that think it's pretty good, and people that think it's one of the greatest artistic works of human history. This review is the third kind.
In all seriousness, this game is simply incredible if you're into this sort of genre. DEFINITELY buy this game if you're interested in story driven games. Of all the games I've played over the years, this one is a close three on my Top Ten Mega Powerhouse List of Video Games, the two higher ones being just as well-made as this one and ranked as such more as a matter of personal preference. But I digress. The story is phenomenal, with complex themes and imagery that were carefully crafted by basically one person with a really good idea in his head. I've had to play through it more than once just to figure it all out, and I still learn more as I play it.
The whole thing is also wonderfully written. It's incredibly dark from the get-go, but doesn't take itself too seriously and isn't afraid to have fun with the world. So, it never gets boring and effectively sits on a gradient between lighthearted goofiness and genuinely disturbing.
It's made up of pretty standard, generic RPG mechanics that aren't that surprising, but it's still nonetheless fun to play. I'd say the RPG mechanics are props on which the story rests, and they're pretty solid props at that.
Of course, it's not perfect. But, the only problems I see in this game are a bit nitpicky and come from some fairly minor mechanics in the game that I would personally change if I could. They're small and certainly don't impact the story at all.
Technically, this game is called LISA: The Painful. It's the second installment in the series, with LISA: The First being the first and the DLC LISA: The Joyful being the third. If you're curious, LISA: The First can be downloaded for free on the internet and it's about two hours. It's a totally different kind of game from the other two (in that it's not a turn-based RPG), but it's nonetheless canon and conveys roughly what kind of story you're getting yourself into.
In sum, if you're looking for excitement, action, and entertainment, you might have come to the wrong place. But if you're looking for a really compelling narrative conveyed in a video game format, then you should look no further. I'd say it's arguably the most creative, moving, and thought-provoking story I've ever experienced in a video game, and it certainly trumps many well-known TV shows, movies, and books. I finished this game over a year ago and I still think about it sometimes. Assuming you can stomach how utterly dark and strange this game is, I can guarantee it'll be well worth your money if you're looking for a game with careful, passionate plot, world, and character development.

The story is very carefully revealed and if you don't get spoiled through reading guides or wikis, you'll be stabbed in the stomach with feelings. These aren't 'girly visual novel' feelings, these are 'I have never cried at a movie and I'm not scared of horror games; there's just something in my eye, please hold me' feelings. For some people, the topic may actually hit very close to home.
On a gameplay note, the gameplay itself is actually fairly simple though it can be periodically frustrating if you don't know what to do. It's a short-ish game, taking about 4 and a half hours to complete if you get stuck only on a couple of puzzles. Definitely worth it, especially if you get it on sale. I've had the game for over a year and I don't regret purchasing it.

I had read IGN's review of the fantastic Papo & Yo prior to playing, and I have to say; how wrong is Mitch Dyer? It's seems like he didn't have the patience for the simple puzzles and complained too much about the too few bugs, which were minscule.
And then I read Kotaku's review, and it was spot on: This game is a must play. It's imaginative, graphically impressive, the narrative is strong, the gameplay is simple enough. There's not too much wrong with the game. In fact, the only thing wrong with it might be some PC optimization, but lowering the settings a bit fixes that.
It was clear what the story was going to be about from the opening message and intro scene from the creative director and writer, a story about a boy with an abusive, alcoholic father. It's heartfelt and means well, but wasn't as inspired or hidden like how the masterpiece, Braid, shocks you at the end.
The game acts as a puzzler/adventure with platforming mechanics, jumping and stuff. It's done well, but a bit on the easier side. The puzzles were....simple, I guess is the best way of putting it. But it came with enjoyment, which Mitch Dyer didn't find it to be. The soundtrack and audio design is well done, I mean really well done. I was in awe of the composition and layering of instruments. Animation was fantastic, as expected; animators in Montreal do tend to put extra effort in their work. The graphics are visually impressive, great texturing, modeling, lighting, the favelas of Brazil are a great sight and I wish I could have seen more. But when the game starts to get more fantastical, the favelas become less important. The magical houses were sweet though. Also, fantastic lighting and shadowing.
I don't know what else to say, the game is great. Check it out.

***EDIT 03-15-2016***
"Just forget about this game for the next two or three years", I said... two years ago.
Castle Story is now far more functionnal. Your bricktrons have made tremendous progress in their pathfinding - they now DO manage to go where you ask them. They might still be a bit... slow to accomplish what you order them to do, but eventually, they will succeed - if what you asked them is possible, of course, and you might need a few try & retry to understand their particular logic. But still, as a sandbox game, it manages to realize a good part of what it was supposed to realize - wich is good.
"So why is your review still negative?", might you ask. Well, the answer is quite simple: right now, the game still isn't fun.
First of all, the bricktrons are slow, and building anything takes a HUGE amount of time. The IA isn't exactly helping about that, and it is a shame that the devs still haven't thought about the first button you would think of in this game - a button to fast forward, that is.
Second, there are little options in the matter of building. A few stone bricks, a few woodlogs (very complicated to use, by the way), you should be building very little variations of the same model of towers and walls pretty quickly. After two or three hours, the game is already awfully repetitive.
That's were the "invasion" mode might get fun: testing the resistance of your citadel by repelling infinite waves of ennemies. Well, problem is: too few ennemies variations, too few units, and most of all, the IA is a mess and cannot hope to compete with any RTS' AI. Your archers might actually be more dangerous for you own troops, and the knights never do anything right; and of course, you have no real control about the attitude they should use. So, for now, the strategy is rather plain: build a tall tower, put all your achers on top of it, rince, repeat. And pray that the ennemies don't get at the base of the tower, for your bricktrons are too dumb to lean and shoot downward. I picked this game up during the winter sales for ten dollars on a whim, not expecting much from it. While, encountering several annoying bugs. I've still found the game fun and worth my money. So far, the game currently has two modes available. Sandbox, and Survival. It also has a map editor, but it is currently disabled while the game is being reworked.
- Sandbox Mode
Sandbox is well, sandbox. There is currently only one map ingame for sandbox, but there are others open for download on the official forums.
You can do what you would expect in sandbox, you can dig, build and destroy. Unlike in survival, resources are limited. There are no mines, instead you will have to dig out into hills or into the ground for your rocks and crystals. Which takes much longer. The default map provides sufficient building space for you to build whatever you want, although you may need to level a hill or two. The way you set up your buildings in sandbox is not as important as it is in survival. Overall, I find sandbox to be rather fun when simply want to build, or test out how to construct things for survival mode.
I've encountered less bugs in sandbox than I have in survival mode. The biggest one I've ran into while in sandbox, is when destroying some tiles. [With the catapult or explosive barrels.] They will leave chunks on the ground which cannot be removed unless you dig further into the map and drop them off into the void below the islands.
- Survival mode
Survival mode is exactly as it sounds. You will need to build and hold out for as long as you possibly can before being overwhelmed. There is only one map currently for survival mode, but it comes with a normal and hard setting.
Resources are easier to get in survival mode. There are four mines around the map, and you can assign workers to pull out stone nearly instantly from the mines. Along with the stone, you'll get your orange crystal for explosives and your lighting, and your blue crystal for getting more workers, warriors and archers. Wood, however is still limited.
Unlike in sandbox mode. You cannot properly shape the terrain, on hills and slopes you can dig one block down for proper placement of your buildings. And another thing that is unlike sandbox, the way you build your castle is important. Stacking blocks ontop of each other, and not layering them properly can have serious consequences. Like having entire walls collapse, which will kill anyone ontop of them and not to mention the breach. Although repairs and building can be rather annoying, as sometimes your workers will take a few clicks to get them to actually want to go over and begin the work.
For each wave that goes by, more monsters will spawn and time will start to go down between the waves. While this adds in the challenge, the pathfinding in the game is incredibly poor. So unless you funnel them into a man made tunnel. They'll rush over to you and then suddenly spread out and go to attack everything in the area. While not a bad thing in it's own right. It is incredibly annoying with the combined fact that your warriors won't want to chase them some times. Which ends up in your enemies chasing your workers across the map, or running them in circles around a mountain. Along with the poor path finding enemies will locate any spot they can get into instantly and dart over there to climb over the walls. [Which is why I recommend you never build near any hills, or onto hills currently.]
Personally, I think sandbox is currently the better of the two modes.

When you wash off all the nostalgia and the want for a good Sonic game, all that's left is a mess of ugly animations, terrible controls, abysmall level design and to top it off - a terrible console to PC port.
The game is confusing in a way that is simply not straight-forward, which is the worst thing you can do to a Sonic game. No! Scratch that - the worse thing is putting speed stoppers all across the levels for no reason: bumpers, pits and spikes. The grand canyon of a gap between the two playstyles is astounding with always one of the versions - retro and modern, ending up with a level that can be best described as unfinished. The entire game feels more like a fan mod than a real published title. Hell - most Sonic mods have more polish than this game.
Don't get me wrong - the gift of getting to revisit these classic locations with cool new designs is something I treasure, but watching Sonic fight with unnatural animations and stupid physics brake the entire experience. Add absolutely stupid controls for a game of this type, constant software issues - crashing, bugging and a few "what the heck do I do now?!" moments and you have yourself a terrible, terrible experience.
Just a addition - same goes for the PS3 version, which simply refuses to work on my console for no reason.
I simply can't enjoy this game. From the awful level design to the confusing layout of the entire game, Sonic Generations comes with no recomendation to anyone. Least of all to true Sonic fans.
To them I can say only one thing - get a 3DS and buy the 3D versions of the old games. Thats as close as you will get to "new" good Sonic material.

After 7 hours I can honestly say that this is an 8/10 game.
Lets start with the improvements over MXGP2
1. New graphics engine, the game is by the far the best looking MX game ever created.
2. New whip and scrub system, in this game they put lots of emphasis on the new scrub mechanic. The new scrub
mechanic requires you to pull the two joysticks in the opposite direction over jumps. This new system gives the player more freedom and overall makes the bike feel much more nimble. The whips/scrubs are on par with MX vs ATV Reflex.
3. Terrain deformation, The trailers don't do the game much justice, the terrain deformation might look like it doesn't do anything. Trust me, it does, After a few laps on the track ruts and some minor braking and acceleration bumps begin to form, feels much more realistic than the previous games.
4. Weather, weather is a completely new mechanic. It adds dynamic weather to the tracks you are riding. The weather is just rain, and dry weather. The rain obviously causes mud, this mud makes the track much more slippery and the roughness also develops much faster. The dry weather causes dust clouds all over, nothing too overboard though. There are also tracks that are clear weather but have just been rained on. This type of track conditions creates a extremely slick track!!
5. New sounds, the new sounds in this game are incredible. In the high rpm range it sounds a little funky but still the best sounds in any motocross game I have ever played.
6. 2 Strokes, the 2 strokes are cool. Don't expect to be winning championships on them lol
These new features are enough for me to suggest you to buy this game. Even if you have the previous MXGP games I would suggest purchasing this.

Lisa: the Painful is ultimately an experience, and a good one at that; one which seamlessly intertwines its gameplay and narrative to create a compelling experience in both its main character--a victim of abuse named Brad--and the people of its post-apocalyptic landscape. While the narrative, world, and music are all certainly high points of the game, it could use work in its gameplay and level design.
Most notably, it pushes the boundaries of how we as players are able to use video games as a medium for discussion, particularly when it comes to more painful themes that many of us playing have likely never experienced ourselves while avoiding being outright overbearing or preachy. This is all on top of being downright hilarious at times along with a fun combat mechanic, some decent pacing (rare for a turn based RPG), and numerous lovable characters each typically paired with a wonderful opening scene and movesets which perfectly capture their own identities.
Level design and combat complexity are unfortunately bland for most the game. The setting pieces feature mostly plateaus with little variation as well as forcing the player to backtrack with some regularity to reach certain treasures. It's nothing unusual for many fans familiar with exploration games, but LISA is generally good at letting you explore while moving forward making this aspect somewhat jarring and simply time consuming. Combat makes excellent use of its status effects which often go ignored in many turn based RPGs, but that is about how complicated it gets.  I (who is not particularly good at video games) never needed more than a couple of tries at an enemy despite making every decision to make the game more difficult for mysely relying on primarily 2 tactics depending on whether if I was fighting a mob or a single powerful boss.
LISA has become one of my favorite RPGs due to its highly thoughtful assemblage and I can't wait to see what else may come from either Dingaling or fans of the game itself.

Is Company of Heroes 2 perfect? Far from it; But it holds its own place in the annals of RTS greatness.
The original Company of Heroes set the formula and the Company of Heroes 2 in my opinion improves upon it. Many features like vaulting, improved fog of war, and numerous other small tweaks have a tremendous impact on the feel and gameplay that separate it from the original.
Some of the new additions have largely gone by the wayside, the cold weather elements are mostly removed from the matchmaking, and many maps are simply bad, especially in the 4v4 playlist.
Pathfinding is downright atrocious. When units owned by different players contact each other they often refuse to move or a unit you didn’t tell to move will run out from behind cover. Tanks turn randomly, exposing the rear to the enemy and infantry sometimes get stuck on random objects (mostly when ungarrisoning buildings or building barbs/tank traps). Most of the pathfinding issues come from grouping too many units together but some maps just are too crowded and produce the issues more than others.
The single player campaign is not worth the time unless you separately purchase Ardennes Assault. The soviet campaign has few levels that I think provide enjoyment or have any redeeming value except the Tiger Hunt Mission and is quite insulting to the Russian people and the struggles they endured.
I bought the game when it first launched and it has come a long way from then, reached the top 200 in all factions and ranked 25 when US forces first released. The multiplayer community is just as active now as it was when it launched.
Even with all the negatives mentioned, nothing quite provides the same experience. I once watched a shovel fly off the side of an exploding tank, bounce into a window and then bounce out the other side. Men of War is the only other game that matches this level of visceral detail and it’s much harder to play, coordinate effective attacks, and even run sometimes.
If you enjoy WWII and RTS games, are looking for something with a good UI that just works (most of the time), and isnt too casual or too hardcore; then chances are Company of Heroes 2 will quickly become one of your favorite games.

Hide and Shriek is a competitive multiplayer game where both players are invisible.
Two players are pit against each other in a creepy school, with the aim of scaring the living hell out of their opponent.
To win the game, you either have to earn the highest score at the end of the 10 minute round by collecting orbs and setting traps, where as the second option is to scare your opponent 3 times in a row.
The catch is you are both invisible. There are multiple ways to reveal your opponent, and once you know where they are, you can activate your "shriek" which will trigger a floating head jumpscare on the enemy's screen, and get you points.
If you shriek and your opponent isn't close enough, you will be revealed for them to see for a short time.
The most common way to reveal your opponent is by catching them in a trap. You can collect different runes throughout the level, which all have unique powers. Sometimes you can set traps, and sometimes they will give you powers to remove any curses you might have. Runes can even be combined to give unique traits. Some can be very interesting, like sending your enemy to an alternate dimension to waste their time, or allowing you to dash through walls.
Some runes can be shot ahead of you, some can be traps set on the floor, some are on interact-able doors or closets etc. So there's a lot to play around with.
The main way to get points is to collect orbs and put them on your altar. You can even pick up enemy orbs in order to set up traps. I like to put theirs behind transparent cupboards, and then trap them. The whole game is about outsmarting your opponent.
As you level up and get achievements, you will unlock customizables for your character, which is quite fun.
Most stuff is balanced quite well. Although I have a problem with 2 powers. One of them being a wisp that follows your enemy and teleports them to another dimension. Even if you see the wisp, it seems for no matter how long you run away from it, it will catch up to you eventually. I don't know if there's a long timer on it or if it just chases you indefinitely, but that just causes it to be more efficient to just run into it as soon as you see it to avoid wasting time.
The other one, is a power that reveals all runes close to you, and your opponent. It kind of defeats the entire point of the game if you can just see your enemy constantly through walls, there's no investigation anymore. It's not even that hard to get that power, and it seems a lot of people have realised it and are using it the majority of the time, which is why I prefer to just play with a friend and avoid using that power.
Overall, I really am loving the game so far. The aesthetic and music is great, the idea is fun and unique, and it's just great to hear your friend scream when you trap them!

3. Larger multiplayer. Okay, this point is going to be more debatable than the last 2 points I mentioned, but I personally believe extending the game from a mere 1v1 experience to a 2v2 or even more could go a LONG way to making the game more enjoyable. 4. This point is ofcourse a given; better optimization. I find myself lagging from time to time and it can be quite frusterating.
Anyway, great game!

=== LONG REVIEW === WORTH READING ===
So you are looking down here trying to find out if this is worth your money. Well let me start of with saying its a great game with lots of potential and if you are willing to put up with a few bugs then this game can truly be amazing. The main bugs that I've come accross is the wheeles while riding spin very slowly no matter what your speed is (very noticable on half coloured rims. Another bug is that the no. on your jersey looks very glitchy when riding and can be very hard to read sometimes. Also small things like not properly pulling the clutch or a small texture gap between the right wrist.
But all around the for a game that has now been out for 2 days I think its acceptable for it not to be 100% perfect.
AI (very easy - hard) is practically the same.
Things I love about the game is that customization is detailed and gives you a variety of options. Bikes with different manufactures have different engine noises which sounds nice not some poor quality audio. The graphics are nice although trees look like crap but the bikes and terrain are very nice. Menu's are easy to navigate through and you can easily change bikes and edit your rider at most pre race menus. Track lines change depending on how many riders go in a specific line and this is very usefull on later laps. Other objects that are movable stay in the possition they are left in and can end up on the track. ( AI likes to crash into them :D) The controls are acctually very easy to handle and scrubbing is very controllable and after practice can be very easy to preform. Turning can get sharp and can be abit stiff if you don't more your weight.
BUT ALL AROUND LIKE I SAID AT THE START IF YOU ARE WILLING TO PUT UP WITH THE FEW BUGS AND GLITCHES HERE AND THERE THIS GAME IS TRUELLY AMAZING. I PREDICT THAT IN THE FUTURE THE CONTENT WILL BE MUCH BIGGER AND ALL THE CURRENT BUGS WILL BE FIXED.  ITS HONESTLY NOT A BAD EXPERIENCE RIGHT NOW AND I DEFINITELY ENJOY THE GAME AT ITS CURRENT STAGE.
PS I wouldn't bother looking at reviews with under 2 hours as you don't really  get a chance to experience the full game.

Okay, I played it for the first time tonight and just spent the past two hours playing it. I'll try to as unbiased as possible since I didn't have that high of expectations nor did I like the first two MXGP games. That being said, this game is super fun! I didn't like MXGP, MXGP2 I got a refund after the first couple of hours but this one is definitely a step in the right direction. I don't plan on getting a refund and so long as there are some players online, I'll play this game a lot.
Pros:
-Visually, the game is phenomenal. The best MX game we've seen yet. It works my CPU/GPU fans a bit but runs fine at 60 FPS. It really helps the immersion factor. Free roam camera and replays are cool!
-Ground deformation and ground physics are on point for an arcade MX game. I prefer it heaps over Reflex. You can actually ride and form ruts, wet ground insists on throttle control and tacky/dry dirt will keep your front wheel off the ground if you're too lean happy. Can't just hold it wide open 100% around the track, you have to brake to make a lot of turns.
-Riding options. I love that there are options for auto/manual transmission, front/rear brakes.
-Collisions/AI. AI is super fun to race against and the game has a nice collision front to keep things fun but not completely one sided.
-Customization. Some cool options for bike mods.
Cons:
-Air physics.  This is a massive flaw/con and my real only gripe. The canned whip controls isn't the only issue I have. Besides having a "one size fits all" whip animation, the fact you have to push the joysticks in opposite directions make no sense to me. But the biggest issue is the game controlling your bike in air for you and almost guiding you through the air to follow the track path. The game definitely has a path for you in air and it regretfully likes to float you along it. While you still can overjump/case things to a degree it assists/carries the bike waay to much which is really infuriating when you're trying to flow around the track using your own lines.
-Rider movement. It'd be nice if the rider moved more independently from the bike when you leaned the rider stick rather than the entire bike/rider rotate or pivot as one.
-First person camera. This may be a personal preference but it'd be nice if there was some options for this camera angle. As it sits, everything seems to move around way too much and makes it hard to use. It's very fun but it's like a bobble head attached to a boat on rough seas. I solely use First Person cam in other MX games so I'm used to it but this one could just use some refining in my opinion.
-Rider Name/Number. I'd really like if they chose a font for the bike and jersey that didn't look like complete♥♥♥♥♥ It's an ugly, small, skinny font with no "race" styling at all. The amount of customizing you can do to your bike to make it yours is awesome, yet the bike will always look like a craigslist special because of the worst possible number plates. Not being able to chose whatever number you want is a little frustrating and not being able to put your last name on your jersey is just completely stupid. Why limit the rear of your jersey to a nickname that is under 6 letters? Many last names are over 6 letters. Simple fix really, but yet it still hasn't been implemented.
-Bike sounds. They're okay but there's certainly room for improvement.
Overall:
Solid game for my MX game collection and my first MXGP game that I'll happily keep and play! As far as fun and play-ability go, I will rank this the same as Reflex. Visually heaps better, fun AI and ground physics. The only thing holding this game back from being the best Arcade MX game ever is the frustrating air physics.

Having logged plenty of time in MXGP and MXGP 2, I was very excited for MXGP 3. I have to say so far it very good. The added weather is very nice, air movement is improved, sounds are better and the ruts actually seem to make a difference.
Is there room for improvement? Of course (the gear is a big let down, but I get licensing can be difficult) It's probably the best motocross game I've played. I'll update after I have more time to play.
Edit: I've had time to play and it is a great game. I enjoy the way the ruts develop throughout and the riders seem to take different lines. However, sometimes they are oblivious and run right into you. Unlike MXGP 2, this doesn't automatically knock you down and you can push back. I wish the ruts from Moto 1 would stay and continue to develop through Moto 2 instead of starting with a fresh track every moto.
The addition of weather is a nice touch and their is a difference between a dry track and a wet one, notably your rear tire spins very easily on a wet track. Is it the best? No, but it's something.
I only have two big complaints, one that is not the fault of the developer. The tracks do get boring quickly, but this is to be expected since I've played 1 and 2 so much and it is a licensed game. If Youthstream doesn't add tracks, there will not be any new tracks in MXGP 3 (aside from compound, Charlotte, etc). The second is I wish you could go back after choosing a new team/sponsor/custom team. I went to select a new sponsor since I wanted to race my two-stroke in career mode and completely blew my MX1 season because it was an MX2 sponsor with six races left and only a big enough points lead for three missed races. There is no way to go back so I'm stuck looking at a missed championship. So be extremely careful when looking at the team so you don't blow your championship too.
Overall, nice addition of weather, ruts, better handling, increased in air movement and fun racing. Hopefully one day we get to see this developer do a series with the US Nationals.

Papo & Yo is a truly excellent 3d puzzle platformer has great gameplay, great visuals, and a great story.
The main gameplay sees you solving a series of puzzles using what's given to you by the environment. Each puzzle introduces some kind of mechanic and the 3D platforming gameplay gives you an interface to interact with that mechanic. Discovering what that mechanic does then figuring out how to manipulate it to progress is key and the game does an excellent job of letting you explore the mechanics without punishing you for trying something that doesn't work.  If you mess up, the game gives you a way to come back from what you've done and in the few cases where you can fail (such as falling off a cliff), you get put back in quickly so you can try again. This is a great way to encourage players to explore their options and try anything they can think of and is an example of how to do puzzles well. None of the puzzles are repeats, so each puzzle gives you something new to chew on without any filler. All of the challenges are really well designed and fun, while there were one or two puzzles that got a bit tedious, I wouldn't say any of them were unenjoyable. I did encounter one glitch where my character got stuck and couldn't move, but other than that everything was pretty solid.
The graphics of this game are excellent both artistically and technically. Unreal Engine 3 is being used in full force to create a game that looks nothing short of gorgeous. The game uses lighting and bump mapping to great effect, but this would be mean nothing without the creative visuals that the developers put on display. The game more or less take place inside the protagonist's imagination (that's not a spoiler by the way), so they get really creative with the environments. The color pallete is vibrant and absolutely beautiful to look at. The animation of the monster is also fantastic, although the player character's run cycle felt a little bit stiff.
Unlike most indie games that run on Unreal Engine 3, this game is actually extremely well optimized, and my GT 440 (which is somewhat old and outdated by now) usually got around 40 FPS on max settings.
Even though the gameplay and graphics are fantastic, the story just might be the best thing about Papo & Yo. I won't go into too much detail because that would spoil it, but the storytelling does a great job of telling a deep, emotional story in a mostly nonverbal way. What you see in the imaginary world of the character's imagination is allegorical to his life (and the life of the creator of the game), which makes the game feel the developer is opening up a very personal part of his life to you. It's emotional and beautiful there are some soulcrushing twists along the way.
Overall, Papo & Yo is a must-play for anyone interested in puzzle games or great stories.
A very heartfelt, metaphorical story with wonderfully creative level design and a childlike imagination to its puzzle mechanics. Highly recommended.

As for the game itself I recommend it for what it is, but I am not impressed at all as a Resident Evil game.
It's basically just like the other general good horror games to come out, but that isn't what I like at all and I will probably not pick this game up.
It's one of those, walking sims with scripted everything and general hiding about type horror games; that are almost always met with "omg best game ever" even if they are generally boring and unappealing to me.
Still people like those types of games, so I recommend it to those people.
Now I don't mean I expected guns blazing meat grinder like the past few RE games either, but I thought they would focus on horror and still stay true to Resident Evil itself; however it doesn't seem to be the case. There is ammo I picked up for a gun I never saw in the demo- so MAYBE there is some action, actual problem solving, and things more familiar with RE games- but we don't see any of that here.
The demo alone has a surprising amount of depth that might be too well hidden for some without some searching for a little help. However there are a few different endings in this demo for people to experiment and dig around for. That's pretty cool honestly.
This bit is personal thoughts on this type of game and can be ignored entirely if you are not interested:
As for scripted instances, they don't spook me. I don't get scared if I look behind me and there is literally no one in the entire hallway, but I touch a door and- oh some guy is grabbing me from behind. If they are not there, then they are not there, make up your mind. I don't see how that spooks people, for me it breaks any immersion and does the exact opposite.
If I don't feel my actions lead to increased or decreased danger, or that my behavior might bring about said conflicts- then there is no sense of dread or actual horror, you may as well just watch a horror movie. That also isn't as replayable for me.
I also liked the actual sense of action or dread original RE games would have, when things are closing in and you are out of ammo, or something like Nemesis just seems immune to your guns as it corners you, the gruesome fatality scenes and awesome atmosphere/enviroment of RE4.
The spirit of the best RE games like that seems to have been left behind, in favor of the generic traditional horror game tropes.

Hide and Shriek is a multiplayer online horror game, in which you face one opponent in the attempts to scare the pants off of them. From the creators of The Secret World and The Park, Funcom has presented another game from the world they have created where every myth and legend has come to life and people fight to keep those secrets hidden. The Secret World has been something I followed from the very early days when it was just a website with a hieroglyphic countdown and followed (Occasionally helping) with the Alternate Reality Games that helped unveil the clues to the world. It is by far my favourite MMO out there and anything set in the world always peaks my interest, so when I got the chance to play as a student from Innsmouth Academy, I was completely ready for it.
When I first looked at Hide and Shriek, I was more interested in the lore than anything else, it is set in The Secret World an MMORPG where every myth and legend has come to life, one of the most prominent aspects is the relations to H.P.Lovecraft and his stories. This is evident in Kingsmouth and the use of Innsmouth Academy (As well as the great Cthulian like creatures that you come across) and in Hide and Shriek you play as a student from said school or as a rival student from Little Springs High. When I first opened the game I was met with beautiful graphics and subtle magical like music, which definitely set the atmosphere for the paranormal. Due to my eagerness and traditional gamer style, I didn’t look at the instructions on how to play and just hoped into a game, with a friend I was currently in an online call with, eager to dish out some scares.
As my opponent knows, I love jump scares and I love to scare people in real life with this tactic, often just standing around doors and jumping out, to watch them get a fright. I’d be giggling for at least five minutes after and this was a great way to be able to do this at long distance. However, I was unprepared and my opponent had taken the time to read the instructions. Once in the game I was astounded by the level of detail, the number of objects that were in the room, I wanted to just wander about and look around, but I had a feeling my opponent wouldn’t give me the chance to do this. It was a shame, because as far as I know you can’t just load a custom game and wander around the map for a bit and due to the urgency of the timer, it made it quite difficult to fully appreciate the level of detail going into the map.

Hide and Shriek
1v1 First-person Horror
Funcom
Funcom
is a 1v1 first-person horror multiplayer game developed and published by Funcom.
The graphics are decent enough: each of the school classrooms has different props and cabinets to explore. Unfortunately, there really is nothing memorable about the map. Hopefully there will be different environments in future updates.
The game is a 1 versus 1 multiplayer first-person set inside a school. Both players are invisible, and they have two goals: either find hidden orbs around the school to gain points, or find and scare the other player 3 times in a row. Around the school you can open lockers and doors, and the easiest way to see your invisible opponent is when he peaks up the orb, which is going to float near him.
An extra twist to the game is that both players are wizards, and inside the school there are runes that are randomly generated each round. Each rune has a different perk, and you can fuse two of them to get a better spell. The spells range from locking doors, hiding jumpscares that reveal your position, knowing where runes and orbs are hidden, and even teleporting your opponent to a parallel realm where he loses points until he escapes.
The gameplay is truly original, enjoyable, and well balanced. It takes a little bit to getting used to the mechanics, but after a while you become a master shrieker. I especially like that when you are scared, you receive a jumpscare that can be customized by adding horns, eyeballs and frames to the skull.
The game is very challenging, especially when you first play it. You will understand how the rune system works by playing around with the spells, and you will get a lot of jumpscares. Lucklily, it isn't particularly frustrating. The only annoying feature was the teleportation to the other realm, which happened to me four times during a match, bringing me to the edge of rage-quitting.
The sound is very important in the game, since you can hear the sound of doors opening and closing, and the soundtrack is pretty good at setting the creepy but amusing tone that the developers achieved.
There are plenty of runes to find and fuse, pages of story to unlock and different masks to customize your jumpscare.
Overall, this is an highly enjoyable multiplayer game that delivers in fun and scares. Highly recommended!

Where do I start with this game?
It's amazing. That's where I start.
Sonic Generations is Sonic's 20th anniversary celebration, incorporating ideas, gimmicks, and, most importantly, levels from earlier games in the series. But, we'll get back to that later. For now, let's talk about the story.
This game's story is probably the worst thing about the game. It's not that the story is bad, but just the lack of story is disappointing. The Sonic series has had a lot of, um... "low" moments, and I which that Generations's writers would have poked some fun at the series, as a game like this would have been the perfect opportunity to do so. Plus, the story is just generally very simple and one-sided, especially for a modern Sonic game.
The story goes as follows: One day, Classic Sonic was running through Green Hill Zone when suddenly, a giant purple demon thing comes out of nowhere and starts to attack. Meanwhile, in the present, Sonic and co. are celebrating Sonic's birthday (even though they never say how old he is, 16 or 20), when the same monster appears, kidnapps all of Sonic's friends and FREAKING BACKHANDS Sonic to knock him out. When he wakes up, he finds himself in a white limbo. Sonic decides to go explore his surroundings and discovers a colourless Green Hill (which he doesn't recognize for some reason) and ends up unfreezing Tails who was frozen in the white limbo. Later, he unites with Classic Sonic to take down the creature (which we later learn is the "Time Eater"), restore colour to all the game's locations, save the rest of Sonic's friends, and find all 7 Chaos Emeralds. And really, that's about it. Sure, there are some minor sub-plots, such as Eggman being captured as well, but mostly, that's about it. There is a small plot twist at the end though, but I don't want to spoil it for you. Also that scene has one of my favourite lines in the game; "Dr. Robotnik!" "No body calls me that anymore." Damn.
But, the game more than makes up for it in the gameplay. In this game, there are two versions of Sonic, Classic Sonic from the Genesis, who looks and feels like the original (yet pudgy) Sonic from the Genesis era, and Modern Sonic, ripped straight out of Sonic Colours and Unleashed. Each level in the game is a level from a different Sonic game. You must play both the Classic and Modern acts in the stage to restore it. The classic acts feature Classic Sonic spin-dashing his way through a 2-D stage, while Modern's uses the newer "Boost-To-Win" formula. Every three stages, you must fight a boss, so you can move on to the next era. There are 3 eras in all: the Classic era (Sonic 1, 2 and 3), the Dreamcast era (Adventure 1, 2 and Heroes), and Modern (Sonic 06 [gross], Unleashed and Colours). There are also 3 rival fights: Metal Sonic, Shadow, and Silver, and 3 boss fights: Death Egg Robot, Perfect Chaos and Egg Dragoon (not counting the final boss). Without getting into the specifics, each of the 9 levels, rival fights, and boss fights, brings something new to the table, and are all a blast to play.
But, without a doubt, the best thing about this game is the modding community. Ever wanted to play as Mario or Pikachu in a Sonic game? Maybe play Sonic 06 with enhanced gameplay and graphics? Sonic GMI's got you covered. It's a blast to play around with fan creations like these. Thanks to the modding community, there are endless possibilities (see what I did there?)
This game is amazing, the music is top-notch as usual, it's well worth the hefty $32 CAD price, and it reminds us why we've stuck with Sonic through and through in the first place.
9.5/10
Even though the story may not be all there, the gameplay more than makes up for it, and the mods that people in the Sonic community create make the game the gift that keeps on giving.
...Or the hedgehog that keeps on... running? You know what I mean.
Just remember: Gotta go fast.

While Sonic games have been pretty mediocre for many years after Heroes being the last good Sonic game with such abysmal games such as Sonic 06, Secret Rings, Shadow the Hedgehog, etc. Suddenly, Generations (Colors as well) has been a godsend from Sega that there's a glimmer of hope that Sonic will actually return to being good (Until Boom came out and ended up being a combo breaker on the good game streak, but the tie in show is pretty good).
PROS:
*Tight controls by Sonic standards as most 3D Sonic games had very sloppy controls
*Beautiful graphics
*Improved hit detection with targeting
*Way past cool remixes of classic Sonic songs
*Accidental bumping into walls is less common than previous games
*2D levels are pretty fun to play, being fun as the original Genesis games
*VERY FAST
CONS:
*Wonky camera during certain parts of modern Sonic levels
*Kind of buggy (Sonic getting stuck behind objects then falling to his death, game freezing, FPS drops) but nothing major
*No classic Amy and Knuckles
*Jaleel White not reprising his role of classic Sonic, making him a mute character while classic Tails and Robotnik (would've been awesome if he sounds like Long John Baldry) have voices
This is the best Sonic game that came out since Heroes and Colors. Highly recommend playing.

Let me start off by saying that I did not aquire this game for free. I paid for it and am glad that I did. There are issues with it though, so let me start with those. When attempting to launch this game it generally won't unless you click Compatibilty Mode. That does the trick for me, but others have complained that it didn't do any good when they tried it, so fair warning. I'm using Windows 7.  There are several resolution settings, although there are a few that I've never run across before.
The second issue has to do with registration of the game. The form asks for alot of personal information, but once filled out it works for me, but a few have complained that once filled in the program refuses to run until all blocks are 'filled in'. I didn't have this issue.  I've noticed that the game has a tendency to crash if I inadvertently hit the Space Bar when the action gets frantic. Normally the Space Bar is used for the Plunger. If I can avoid that mistake all is well, although it has happened a few times, usually when I have an enormous score built up.
There are six tables, each with a different theme, and various difficulty settings. Novice. Normal. Hard. Expert. I wish the tables were brighter, but that may just be my personal prefrence. The tables are good, but aren't up to the standards set by Zen studios with it's Pinball FX2 game. Plus Zen offers 57 tables with more features and are about to release more. Pinball FX2 sells it's tables as DLCs with one free table. Dream Pinball 3D has no DLC stuff to buy. Many complained (not me) when a bug in the game forced Zen to reset the Leaderboards (not the Local scores though), but Dream Pinball 3D doesn't even have a Leaderboard. Just local scores. You can upload your scores with Dream Pinball 3D, but I have no idea where they go when you do so. This function fails to work alot of the time anyway.
This game is alot of fun though, especially if you like old-school pinball. The game itself is about 8 years old so it's starting to show it's age. The ball physics are good and there are actual goals to achieve, unlike Fantastic Pinball Thrills which has neither. The controls take getting use to. The Left Flippers are controlled by the Left Shift key, and the Right Flippers are controlled by the Enter key. Gameplay is solid.
The High Score screen has scores already entered as default scores to aim for. If you don't at least reach the lowest high score then the game will momentarily display your score beneath the high scores. As you achieve higher and higher high scores the target scores go up. So it becomes more and more difficult to reach the minimum, assuming of course that you never improve.  Learning the goals of each table and how to achieve them is key.  Some tables, like Amber Moon for example, have more than one way to increase the multiplier.
I like it. Currently 38 friends of mine own this game and 4 want it. I believe I have logged more play time than any of them. This may have to do with the difficulty some have had getting this game to work. Use Compatibility Mode. If you still have issues then try different resolution settings. The game was developed by A.S.K. Homework Game Development, who also developed Zaccaria Pinball for Android devices. This game has also been released for the DS and wii.
