This is right up there with Psychonauts for best game ever. It's a puzzle/platformer with emphasis on the platforming elements.
The puzzles are usually quite easy to figure out on your own, but sometimes quite difficult to enact. For instance, there's a level where you have to catch three frogs and destroy them before Monster catches you, and if you fail you start over from the beginning. It's the closest to dying you come in this game, but it's still quite frustrating.
I expected the story to be heart-rendingly moving, and I was still caught off-guard by it. It's that powerful.
One of my favorite things about this game is the setting. It looks like a favela if you look at it out of the corner of your eye, but if you explore and pay attention, you sink deep into the art and mood. It's one of the most fantastic and magical places that I've ever been in a game world. And just to emphasize this, you must revisit each level (except two of them) twice or sometimes three times, each time to do something different, and requiring a different perspective, which truly gives the city a sense of extent and volume. It's also so amazing the way nature and more magical eliminates insinuate themselves into the city, as if the city itself is invading something far older.
The mechanics of this game are also unique in a very well-thought-out way. For instance, most of the puzzles require you to rearrange the world itself, moving, stacking, and tipping the little shacks, and at one point, tipping the whole village on its side. This is the first game I've seen where you get the ability to make "long jumps" from another character (a rocket-propelled robot action figure named Lula) which can be detached from your character at will. Which means the game can take away your ability to jump far at any time, just to make the gameplay more interesting.
While I will say that this world drew me in so far, I didn't want to leave, and so felt a bit of withdrawal when the story ended after four hours, I can't help but note that the story arc is so smooth and coherent, it could not have been longer than it was. It ended exactly where and when it had to end. Given how little gaming time I have these days, it's probably best that it didn't take longer than it did.
Pros:
- Heart-rending story lovingly told
- Beautiful sets and models
- Clever game mechanics
- Just the right amount of frustration
Cons:
- The feeling of sadness slowly sinking into your soul the moment you beat the game and realize you must go back to real life now
Out of five, I'd give this game at least a seven.

In my personal opinion, LISA is the single best video-game ever created. That sounds like an incredibly hyperbolic fanboy thing to say because it really is, but it holds itself a comfy spot snuggled up in the molten core of my stone-cold heart. This game is not objectively perfect, it's quite unpolished actually. The game uses regular RPG Maker textboxes and menus, its UI looks simplistic, and its controls menu is so confusing that you might as well not even try to use it. But despite its imperfections, this game manages to seamlessly blend different atmospheres and genres to create a truly unique world full of laughs, screams, and heartbreaks.
We'll start with gameplay because that's what makes a game a game. The gameplay is great on specific fronts, but is otherwise exactly what you would expect from an RPG Maker game. So you recruit some party members, they level up and gain new moves, you level up and gain new moves, and you battle tougher enemies as the game progresses. Seems standard, right? Well here we enter some territory where LoveBrad (AKA Dingaling, AKA dingalingboy, AKA W2D, AKA Hidden Austin, AKA Austin Jorgensen) decided to leave his unique brainprint in the sand. You can recruit more party members than you can equip, some special moves are combos that let you do the unique attack while also getting some extra hits in, and there are like a billion status effects. I love this, it makes battles much more interesting and it's so much fun to find out which party members work with which. This is so much more engaging, and you'll need those party members because they can die. And I mean DIE, for real. You never get them back. You'll need to go out into the corners of this interesting world to find new party members you can recruit and level up. And while we're on the topic of leveling up...
Nearly all encounters in the game are unique. Every person you fight has their own name, and sometimes we get a look at their backstory or the game uses them for a gag. Just becasue they're bad guys doesn't mean that they don't get their own charm pumped into their disgusting sweaty bodies. But because they're all unique encounters, that means you can't grind. You have to really go out into the world and find new places, explore new territories, talk to people, and fight baddies with that previously mentioned charm. Can you believe it? A game in which you level up and get rewarded for going out and doing the sh*t that's actually fun? Not having to fight the same enemies over and over again? As my buddy NitroRad said with his wise mouth and sexy brain:
"You waste less time, but you have more fun."
And we still haven't even mentioned the overworld semi-platforming that adds a lot to the games exploration. In case you couldn't tell from the screenshots, this game is set in a 2-D world. You go up and down, rather than north and south as you would in any other RPG Maker game. This seperates the game from other RPG Maker games through it's look, and added vertical elements. This games f*cking world is god-damned filled with motherf*cking sh*t to f*cking do you f*cking *sshole.
So a good game finds a way to tell a story that compliments its gameplay, at least in my opinion. LISA does this better than any other game I know, it's story and gameplay are hand-in-hand. The game isn't too hard, but it can be challenging. There are moments in fact where the gameplay is downright unfair, and so are the story choices. The choices don't change the story all that much, but I consider that a good thing. You don't just see the consequences, you PLAY the consequences. You will have to make choices that change how the game plays, whether it be crippling yourself or surrendering during a mugging. This fits the tone of the game well and is perfect for the bleak, depressing, uneasy mood of constant tension this game has worked so hard to make you really feel.
This game isn't all bleak though. Although it's crushingly harsh the whole way through, this game slips in tons of black humor. The humor never interrupts the flow, and it always just feels natural. You'll be laughing at somebody who got kicked in the balls one second, then you'll be creeped out by the mysterious Joy Boys who wear masks with wide smiles the next, and before you know it the game will have spat you back out leaving only sadness and despair. The story so quickly and so subtly slides itself into different tones, and taking a break inbetween the bleak to laugh at some fart and butt jokes is always welcome in my book.
This game may have the atmosphere and excellent story down, but how about the small details? Let me tell you, if you think and read between the lines this game will reward you to no end. This game is just amazement after amazement with it's attention to the small details. These details aren't just cute easter-eggs either, although there are plenty of those, these little bits and bobs enhance the story. I'm going to provide an example, but this example contains some spoilers. If you really are on the fence about this game and believe that my insight might help you buy it then read on, but if you already are sold then just stop reading and f*cking buy it already:
Basically all you need to know about that section if you didn't read it is this: This game uses subtle details to tell a story in a way that is unique to video-games as a medium. It makes you feel rewarded for really thinking about the actions you make that you wouldn't second-guess otherwise in a way that isn't patronizing or too on the nose.
This is where I'm going to allow myself to just gush about certain aspects in a way that isn't very professional, not to imply I've been professional ever.
The Music: F*cking amazing, absolutely integrel to the experience of the game. The whole soundtrack was made in the trial for Fruity Loops by one guy. How amazing is that? You know what else this one guy did? F*cking everything in this game. The whole game was made by one guy.
The Art: Also incredible. It's not Cuphead or anything but the art fits the games goofy world perfectly, and the sprites manage to invoke the creeps or sadness which is all this game really needed.
The Humor: Low-brow and hilarious. This game never stops subverting expectations and being just generally funny. If you don't like violence or low-brow humor then this likely won't appeal to you, but I love it.
Tl;dr - Couldn't cry with my d*ck to this game so I had to use my eyes instead but now I can't stop/10

After finishing this, I can say that this is one of the most heart-breaking, tragic, and beautiful games I've played.
It made me laugh out loud, cry the least manly of tears, reflect on my past choices, and fear whatever enemy came next.
A lot of games give you an illusion of choice, and you choose the one that benefits you more, or whatever gets you the best ending. In this game, the desicions all effect the gameplay, and the story, one way or another. By the time you've made them all, you'll feel the weight of them all in your combat, overworld venturing, and in the cutscenes.
The gameplay is engaging, and all around fun. With constant fear of perma-death for party members, and the lack of healing items and money available, you're likely to finish most battles by the skin of your teeth. The sidequests can range from humorous simple tasks, to the most heart-wrenching optional content you'll ever experience.
The story usually is what hooks people though. It's a constant string of tragedies, with the next one never being too far away. The choices make you feel torn, even depressed sometimes. Because whatever you choose, it's likely to make your experience even more difficult than it was before.
All in all, this is the first game I've ever played that I can give a 10/10 with no second thoughts.
LISA may be painful, though it's the best pain you'll ever feel.

I hold out hope Milestone will step up and get the physics and pure power feeling of a motocross bike right, but this year it hasnt happened.

Clearly I'm going to be the unpopular opinion among a Very Positive game; at the end of this review I will paraphrase the entirety into a TL;DR, so feel free to skip unless you're
looking for a reason not to play a free game.
Missing Translation is a story (and I use that term loosely) about a fellow who ends up being in an alternate universe where others speak in a different language made out of straight lines. I'm sure there's a deep meaning to the game where if you really delve deep and sit down to analyse it, there's more beyond what's introduced, but to the average player, you just know yourself as a dude who is in this alternate universe trying to find thingamabobs to fix your diamond uhhh, thing.
The object of the game is to find three square components to a machine. Each object requires you to do 25 puzzles a piece. I'll identify my gripes with these puzzles separately:
Component 1 - Block sliding puzzle: The difficulty curve for these puzzles are like a roller coaster around the mid teens - you go from incredibly simple, to just painfully difficult, and back to simple. It's clear that the developer didn't sit down and curve these properly, because you will be hit hard, and then confused why that puzzle hit you so hard on the next few after. After about 18, the levels start getting repetitive, the challenge starts going away, and it just becomes a grind to finish.
Component 2 - "Light" slider: This one isn't too bad, it can get difficult, but like component 1, it suffers from becoming a dull grind after the first 15.
Component 3 - D-pad rotator: This puzzle was the worst. It's simple, but painstakingly long because the developer failed to create a counterclockwise rotation function. Just because you have to fully rotate these pieces, I estimated over 10 unnecessary minutes was tacked onto the whole set of 25 puzzles JUST because of the lack of counterclockwise rotation. If there were only 5 puzzles, fine, I wouldn't be salty, but you have to do 25 of the goddamn things, and it gets old and annoying. They rotate slowly, and you have to wait until they fully rotate to rotate them again, it's just a preventable headache.
After you receive all 3 components, you bring them to your starting point where you open a rift, and to everyone's surprise... ENDING SPOILER:
Missing Translation is a puzzler with a poor story and an even more unsatisfying ending. Nearly 40 of the 75 puzzles frustrated me - not because they were too difficult, but because they were dull, repetitive, or in the case of the D-Pad puzzles, just a broken system and a waste of time. I spent almost an hour hoping for a lot more, and was disappointed. I'm not giving this game a free pass because it was free. There are plenty of great, free immersive games that last about as long as this one and deliver a much better experience, the most recent one I played was
.

This is my first Steam review, and felt I needed to leave one for this game.
When this game first game out it was in a pretty incomplete state. For those who don't know the history, the CoH IP was owned by THQ. THQ went defunct about halfway through the development of this game and was picked up by SEGA.
The game got released and was quite largely panned (and rightly so) by fans of the first game.
However, since then SEGA have been nothing but amazing.
Supporty has been helpful, updates have been constant and new factions and DLC have been added (Ardenne Forest is a must buy, better than the base Campaign IMO)
Even with everyone screaming at them with how poor the game is they kept at it, and the game is all the better for it.
Is it better than CoH1? No, but is much prettier to look at, and improves some functionality.
The only negative? The microtransactions are horrific. You can earn "supply" and other skins/slight weapons perks playing games but it takes forever to get anwhere.
I've only just now got enough supply to buy a new commander, and I've played over 400 hours. This is the one aspect that has to be improved Sega. Otherwise this game is a gem.
The game is pretty cheap to buy now, absolutely worth giving a go. Even with all its flaws it is a fantastic experience

Cons: Short story.
Pros:
Graphics hold up six years later.
Engaging story, free of usual over-the-top antics of open world games.
Excellent voice acting.
Best open world atmosphere I\'ve ever enjoyed.
Perfect vehicle handling.
If you haven\'t played this game, you should. If you\'re expecting GTA, forgetabouit. This is a movie set in an open world, where you can choose to take the long way home if you want. I\'ve spent hundereds of hours on the Xbox 360 and plan to spend many more on PC, now that it\'s been added back onto Steam. The game really is a captivating experience that captures both the spirit of the 1940s, the 1950s, and the Mafia, rolling all three into a compelling story highlighted by well-written set-pieces and punctuated by some of the best voice acting put in a game. Graphically the game still shines, with PHYSX effects still stunning today. While the map is small compared to GTA V, it never feels small or cramped. Instead, each neighborhood has a specific feeling that includes arcitecture, pedestrian population and even the condition of the automobiles. Speaking of automobiles: no game has ever made driving so much fun in an open world. With normal steering/handling settings, the game has a very competent handling model that is both fun and approachable. With simulation settings and a controller for throttle/brake control, this becomes a driving simulation that rivals any other game. Cars have weight and handle like the beautiful barges they are. Graceful styling and recognizeable shapes make any fan of Automobiles from the 30s-50s feel right at home behind the wheel of a sport Smith Thunderbolt or an older Walter Coupe. Even with the Joe\'s Adventure and Jimmy DLC\'s, the game continues to amaze with some really nice set piece shootouts, surrounded by several extra hours worth of fun arcade-style open world missions which feel much closer to the form of GTA but without the sometimes over-the-top action sequences (you won\'t be landing a motorcycle on a train). Mafia II is my favorite game of all time because it takes me to a different time and place and let\'s me enjoy the life of Vito Scaletta. Buy it or somebody might break your legs.

The epidemy of 'Modern' Sonic.  If you want to know how modern sonic games should play, the act 2 stages are it.  A polished mix of speed and platforming with many different paths to reach the goal (and few glitches).  Each stage offers its own "gimics" and trials, with enemies reminiscent of games past; each stage will take many tries to get good, and you will still make mistakes.  Unlockables including music and powerups, which are fun and useful.
However, the nastalga of classic sonic is appreciated, but he seems clunky, slower to accelerate, and difficult to control (especially in the air) as compared to ports of genesis era games for the same system. The beginning act 1 stages are obviously homage to earlier games, but the later stages lack the speed (or opportunity for speed) that the origional games offered in general.
Kinda wish you could unlock different characters (with unique gameplay) though, you know, after you finish the game as sonic.
Final word? Worth the money and time.

First things first: I haven't had all the technical problems many of the negative reviews for this game have had. In fact, the game started up immediately, and other than some grumbling over the lack of resolution options I was in like Flynn. That said....
This isn't the worst pinball game I've ever played. It surpasses the likes of many video pinball tables in fact, such as Pinball on the Atari 2600, or the Colecovision, or the pinball games made with those black-only LCD screens.
On PC though? There are better, cheaper options, and when your biggest product tie-in is with Two Worlds, a series that A) the developers own the rights to and B) is known for being of questionable quality on its own, you know you have some problems right out of the gates.
Let's start with the basics, shall we? Other than the resolution issue visual presentation of the tables is okay. The menus are sparse at best, but they are easy to navigate and clear and concise in the function of all the options available. Tables have particle effects at times, and some mip mapping of textures on certain surfaces to keep things dynamic and interesting, though if you play with table glass enabled the reflections on said glass do get in the way of a lot of the table's detail. I still recommend keeping the glass on, however, because it also helps to cover up some of the bigger flaws the tables have in their artistic design, mostly centered around sub-par artwork in general. Several of the tables -- like Monsters and the aquatic-themed table -- bear more of a resemblance to discount store product packaging than they do to pinball tables, with a combination of poorly drawn characters and questionable photoshop work providing the bulk of their visual design.
That said, the visuals have little to do with the way the tables themselves play, which is, again, okay. Ball physics are ho-hum, with a feel closer to the old 3D Ultra Pinball games than the likes of Pinball Arcade or Pinball FX, but are perfectly playable and easily predictable, even familiar to those who grew up with older PC and console video pinball titles more than real-world tables. Likewise, the table designs are acceptable. There is little in the way of creative features or multiple playable levels to the tables, meaning tables often feel cramped and small. Many of the tables feature extra flippers placed in almost arbitrary locations, doing little to supplement the table's flow or play at all, with Spinning Rotors featuring a set of tiered flippers in the middle of the table that are, at best, completely useless, and at worst get in the way of the ball's path through obstacles. When the tables work, though, they work relatively well, with a fair amount of ramps and habitrails to keep them visually interesting. Goals on the tables seem sparse if not nonexistent, but for tables to just waste a few minutes with they could be worse. If there is one glaring gameplay shortcoming it's the lack of controller support, since I very much prefer to use a joypad when playing pinball games, but the controls the game uses by default are remappable on the keyboard and by default are quite similar to those featured in many other PC pinball titles.
By far the game's biggest disappointment is in the audio department. While table sounds are okay, if a bit teensy in their clickiness and identical from table to table, the music featured on the tables ranges from forgettable to completely absent. Announcers have the same basic lines for the most part, with generic phrases often used when just a little more flavor could have gone a long way to improve the presentation of each table's theme. As a result the overall audio experience taken from each table is basically devoid of any kind of character and severely hurts the feel of the game.
In the end, though, is Dream Pinball 3D worth the price?
The answer is a resounding "no." At least, not full price. I picked the game up at a severe discount (67 cents I believe) and feel in no way cheated or disappointed in the product I received for that price. If the game were even only marginally cheaper -- 4.99, say -- I would feel that I could provide a recommendation just because the tables are, in fact, playable and it's obvious there was some effort put in to make the game worthwhile. At the game's default price of 6.99, however, you're better off just saving up another couple of bucks and investing in a starter set of tables from the likes of Pinball FX 2, or picking up one of the Pinball Arcade sets when they go on sale (as they frequently do.) At best, Dream Pinball 3D is a second or even third-tier pinball title, worth picking up at discount and for variety, but with little other reason to recommend it.

The colors and magic of the world of children, tainted by the darkness and harsh reality of the adults. I will not dwell on what happens in the game, as some might consider that to be spoiler territory.
On the gameplay side, this is a puzzle game where reality bends and changes at will, leading to a sense of magic and surreality that is extremely pleasing.
For thoses who don't like to think too much about puzzles, there are always hints to guide you, if you ever need them. They are optional, so you're never forced to read a hint if you don't want to. On the whole the puzzles are a bit like Portal : you stop for a while trying to figure it out, and then you have an ha-ha moment and manage to move forward. So not complicated, but give you just enough pause to make it satisfying to solve it.
I really enjoyed the game, but got slightly frustrated toward the end. The game almost overstays its welcome. The goalpost keeps moving forward, you often think "this is it, i'm gonna see the ending", but there is actually one more puzzle to solve, and then another one, etc...Still on the whole the game is short enough for its own sake, and it's really worth to go through all of it to see the well crafted ending, and understand exactly what the game was all about.

just finished Austin Jorgenson's LISA and can say that, without a doubt, it is among the strongest indie RPGs I have ever played. I was hooked on the world of LISA with the slight taste given by the prequel, LISA: The First, which had me eagerly awaiting this title. The developer cites Mother as a key influence and that shows, but even more than the abstract game OFF, LISA has taken the wacky humor and surreal style of Mother into a dark and very adult place. Dingaling is able to take simple, old school pixels and work them into truly disturbing imagery. Lately, we have been inundated with post-apocalyptic settings that are xeroxed and re-sampled at will: zombies, plague, fallout and bad weather. All of those settings, done to death, are fairly grim, but none of them can even touch the misery suggested by LISA. Here we have a world where women are extinct and the surviving men, seeing no future for humanity, have transformed the society into a sort of prison yard where hopelessness is drowned in drugs and alcohol, and memories seem uniformly sad. The main protagonist, Brad, is driven by a past filled with abuse and grief, and literally sets himself against the will of the entire world. The player will be forced to make tough decisions in this game and to eventually think about and judge the outcome. Even as we laugh at sight gags and endless pro wrestling references, one cannot ignore the uneasy slithering quality of LISA. My greatest hope is that the game does well and Dingaling games develops more titles where the heart of the game is a great story, not the ability to snipe someone in multiplayer. Bravo!

While the title on Steam just refers to this as "LISA", its full name is "LISA: The Painful", and this game can certainly live up to that name at times.
This game really feels like a side-scrolling version of Earthbound in an odd, post-apocalyptic setting, packaged into a not-so-kid-friendly game.
Before I actually start talking about what this game is like, let me just warn you: this game may likely destroy your emotions.
The story is hard to discuss without being spoiled, but this game has a very serious feel to it in certain moments. However, there are many exceptions. I've never seen a game pull off such a perfect blend of seriousness and comedy. One second, you'll be laughing/chuckling over something which just happened, and the next second, the game will suddenly switch into "serious mode"; the transition just feels so natural.
As for the gameplay, this is best described as a side-scrolling RPG game. If you liked Earthbound, you will most likely like this game as well. It even has music from Earthbound in it. Speaking of which, the game's soundtrack is also pretty great and always fits with the setting. There are moments you will absolutely hate the game, though.
Before you decide to turn down the game from that statement, hear me out. I know that makes the game sound terrible, but it purposely makes you hate it by forcing you to make decisions you don't want to make. Once again, I don't want to spoil anything, but personally, one of the decisions I made actually made me stop playing long enough for me to lose interest in the game, then eventually pick it back up again and complete it while having no regrets (other than the decisions I made). In other words, without spoiling anything, you will more than likely regret any decisions you make. There isn't really much of a "wrong" decision to make, but some are more beneficial than others.
This game certainly isn't for the weak-hearted or the innocent, but it's an amazing masterpiece with pretty neat (and sometimes grotesque) pixel graphics with a great story.
There's also a DLC expansion to this game called LISA: The Joyful, which is basically a sequel. However, despite the name, it's much less joyful than the original game. It's still a good DLC (which describes the story even further), but it doesn't have as many comedic feels to it as the original and is 100% serious at nearly all times.

I used to only play AAA games, wondering why anyone would want to play a game like LISA in the 21st century. But a friend convinced me to try it, and it become one of my favourite games. While some big productions will fade away from my memory with time, I'll never forget LISA. 10/10

Alrighty, so for my 2 cents of this demo.
You watch a prologue before you start. You see yourself tied up and some guy is trying to cut off your ropes. Shortly after,  the screen fades out, then you find yourself on the floor in a dimly-lit living room of a strange house that you barely recognize. Your mission is to get out of the house and you find yourself walking around, solving the house's mysteries as well as getting used to the controls and mechanics of the game.
For the last few years, we've received a lot of indie horror games that are first person. The most noticable of these games that are being compared to this one are P.T. and Outlast. In fact, if you take the time to go around on many gaming forums, you will hear lots of people complaining that it's an Outlast clone, or that this game ripped off its ideas from P.T.
What many people dont realize is that Masachika Kawata, the producer of Resident Evil 7, stated in an interview that the idea of Resident Evil going first person was realized before P.T was created. Here is the original interview for anyone interested.
Also, on a semi-unrelated note, the gameplay of P.T was not the final product, so to be honest we really don't know what P.T actually is. As for the game being an Outlast clone, I will also respectfully disagree on that end. As I will be going into gameplay mechanics below, you will see many differences between Outlast and this game.
Going into the gameplay mechanics, you walk around a house with very dark and claustrophoic corridors, giving similarities that return to the original Resident evil. Puzzles also make a return as well, although they didn't exactly seem to be present in the demo. The team did state though that puzzles will be returning in other interviews, so it's safe to expect them in the full version. There is also a bit of combat present, as later on you'll be able to obtain an axe and a handgun.
I really do like how the handgun feels. It's hard to describe but if if I really had to say something, I would say the aim is like Resident evil 4's, but in first person. And the way how they blend it all together feels very realistic and fresh. If I did have a complaint with the handgun however, I would say that the handgun noise could feel a bit more empowering. When I shot it off, it didn't exactly give me as much of a satisfying feeling as the older titles. I would also say that maybe the handgun could use a small buff as well, but it probably doesn't matter too much as weapon upgrades are confirmed to be present in the final game.
The controls of this game feel superb. I would say the movement of this game feels like Resis 1 to 3 but drastically improved. You also have the 180 spin from REmake, which I can see being used to run away from enemies effectively. There's also a button which brings up your inventory, which is very reminiscient of the older Resident Evils. You can examine, combine, and use your inventory just like how you remember from the old days.
On top of that, even though it's not in the full demo, the gameplay footage on the internet show us many other elements from the past Resident evil series, such as cranks, additional puzzles and the usage of herbs. These mechanics are just a few of the examples that will drive this game closer towards the older style than its last two predecessors. We can expect to see more enemies and weapons in the game's future release.
Change is a word that many of us long-time gamers fear, and that's understandable. It can either make or break an IP. We have had many franchises ruined by change, which has given us lasting disappointments (looking at you DmC). However, if changes are done correctly, it can also breathe new life into a series. That, and developers need to take risks in this industry if they want to remain on top of their game.  For many years, we've received lots of TPS Resident Evil games as well as other games of similar style. It's even turned into its own genre. This style of resident evil has been present since 2005, and the series started to wear itself down after the disappointing Resident Evil 6. I realize that some may not agree with me on this, and that's fine, but the changes that have been made in this game have started to make me actually excited to play another Resident Evil game again, and that's a feeling I haven't had in a very long time.

Well, my first ever steam review.  I HAD to review this.  A of hardcore gamer for over 30 years, this is the only one that warrents my time writing and promoting.  This game is beutiful.  It is really clever, artistic, imaginative, visually stunning, charming, wierd, warm, cold, gripping, mesmerising,  refreshing, and has a deep emotional story line like no other game before it  (or probably ever will ).  And on top of  this the gameplay is excellent,  the puzzles are clever, amusing and addictive.   A lot of care and thought has gone into this game.  Its a true escapist adventure.   Its on a par with A Tale of Two Brothers, another meticulously crafted, emotional and beautiful adventure puzzler game.  I found both games evoked similar emotions when playing.   I'd rate TOTB as the greatest game I've ever played (from from all genres).  Its hard to explain why other than the powerful emotions it evoked.  This game nearly steals that title for the same reasons but not quite.   I would definately rate this as the most original game I've ever played. Worth every penny. Truly Stunning.  Basically you just have to play it!   Limbo and Machinarium, great as they are, have been bumped down the list.
